notes: Every defect has a stable id. Ids never change once published; a defect that is removed is marked retired rather than deleted.
detect.sql returns exactly one row and one column. detect.expect is the value it returns on a correctly built fixture.
A tool is scored by comparing the defect ids it reports against the ids listed here. detect.sql exists so the fixture can verify itself, not to define what a tool must run.
invisible_to lists the places a defect does NOT show up. A tool that reads only those sources cannot find it.
clean lists objects that are correct on purpose. A defect reported against anything listed there is a false positive, and counts against a tool's score.

clean.description: Objects that are deliberately correct. Nothing in this list is a defect, and a tool that reports one against these objects has produced a false positive. Scoring a tool on misses alone rewards reporting everything; this list is here so false positives can be counted too.

schemas.name: conformance
schemas.why: Exists only so the fixture exercises every native PostgreSQL 18 data type and every kind of constraint. It is not part of the Cross River Trading Co. story and contains no defects. 16 tables, 66 constraints, all correct.

verify.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'conformance' AND c.relkind = 'r'

kinds.description: The vocabulary a claim is matched on. class groups this document into five sections for reading; kind is the contract a scoring tool works against, and is finer. A claim matches a defect when the kind is the same and the objects overlap, so the kind is what stops an unrelated claim about the right table from scoring as a hit.

values.undeclared-relationship: A reference between tables that the data honours and the schema does not declare.
values.undeclared-key: A uniqueness that holds across every row and is declared nowhere.
values.wrong-key-scope: A declared key over the wrong columns, or unique at the wrong granularity.
values.unenforced-constraint: A rule the design relies on that the database does not apply, whether the constraint is absent, NOT VALID, or NOT ENFORCED.
values.wrong-column-type: A column whose type cannot represent, or silently alters, what it stores.
values.meaningful-null: A null used to carry a value rather than to mark one absent.
values.undocumented-convention: A rule the data follows that nothing in the schema records.
values.contradictory-data: Two places that should hold the same answer and hold different ones.
values.broken-reference: Rows, or code, pointing at something that does not exist.
values.duplicate-entity: One real thing stored as more than one row.
values.incomplete-data: A column or table filled in for only part of the rows it covers.
values.circular-reference: A cycle in references that the code following them does not expect.
values.unused-object: A table, column, index, view or routine that nothing reads, writes or maintains.
values.index-problem: An index missing, duplicated, redundant, or of the wrong type for the query.
values.maintenance-setting: A statistics or autovacuum setting that leaves the table or the planner wrong.
values.write-amplification: A design that makes every write cost far more than the change it records.
values.growth-limit: An object that grows without bound, or a bound that is about to be reached.
values.fragile-definition: A definition that has silently stopped matching what it was built over or alongside.
values.procedure-correctness: A routine that returns or writes the wrong answer.
values.procedure-performance: A routine whose cost is far above what the same result needs.
values.procedure-security: A routine that lets a caller reach data or code they should not.
values.no-primary-key: A table with no primary key and no unique index standing in for one.
values.collation-mismatch: Columns compared across a collation boundary, so an index built in one collation cannot answer the comparison.
values.referential-action: A foreign key whose ON DELETE or ON UPDATE action does something other than what the schema around it implies, including an action that can only ever raise an error.
values.row-security-gap: Row level security turned on without a policy that grants anything, or a policy that grants everything.
values.sequence-desync: A sequence whose current value disagrees with the column it feeds, so future inserts collide with rows that already exist.
values.trigger-order: Two or more triggers on the same table and event whose result depends on the order they fire in, which nothing in their definitions states.
values.over-broad-grant: A privilege given to more roles than the change intended, including every role that does not exist yet.
values.write-through-gap: A view or interface that accepts a write and produces a row it cannot then read back.
values.disabled-trigger: A trigger that is present in every catalogue and does not fire.
values.silent-data-loss: A write that discards part of what it was given, without an error or a warning.
values.backfill-artifact: Historical rows carrying a value produced by the migration that added the column rather than by the event they describe.
values.join-semantics: A join or set operation whose written shape does not produce the result set it reads as producing.
values.timezone-arithmetic: Date or time arithmetic that is correct only while the offset does not change.
values.trigger-scope: A trigger declared at the wrong level, so it fires a different number of times from the number of rows it was written to describe.
values.boundary-error: A range whose end is off by one unit of the type it is written in, so rows at the edge fall outside the set that was meant to include them.
values.incomplete-grant: A privilege set that names the objects a role was thought to need and omits one the same operation requires, so the role is refused work it appears to have been granted.
values.aggregate-semantics: An aggregate that counts or sums a different set of rows from the one the query reading it is written to describe, including an aggregate over no rows at all.
values.arithmetic-truncation: Arithmetic that discards a remainder or a fraction because of the types involved, giving a result that is systematically low or exactly zero.

defects.title: SKU is unique across every store instead of within a store
defects.why: The 2012 store had one shop, so a global unique SKU was correct. The 2014 multi-store migration dropped the constraint rather than replacing it with (store_id, sku), so today nothing prevents two stores reusing a SKU and nothing enforces that one store uses it once.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'storefront.products'::regclass AND contype = 'u'

defects.title: Unique index on raw email permits case-duplicate accounts
defects.why: UNIQUE on the raw column means 'a@x' and 'A@x' are two customers. The application lowercases on login, so one person can hold two accounts and see a different order history depending on how they typed their address.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT lower(email) FROM storefront.customers GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1) x

defects.title: Index on page_views.viewed_at that no query uses
defects.why: Created for a report that was replaced in 2016. It is maintained on every insert into storefront.page_views, which takes a row for every page a customer opens, and has never served a scan.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_indexes WHERE schemaname = 'storefront' AND indexname = 'ix_page_views_viewed_at'

defects.title: Gift message capped at varchar(255) with no validation
defects.why: The form accepts more than 255 characters and the insert raises an error the application catches and discards, so long messages are dropped rather than printed short. Nothing tells the customer.

detect.sql: SELECT character_maximum_length FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='storefront' AND table_name='orders' AND column_name='gift_message'

defects.title: Marketing opt-in is free text with four spellings for two states
defects.why: A varchar holding 'Y', 'N', 'yes' and null. No constraint, no default. Whether a customer may be emailed depends on which code path reads the column, and consent is a legal question.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT coalesce(marketing_optin, '<null>')) FROM storefront.customers

defects.title: store_id defaults to the literal 1
defects.why: Any insert that forgets the store silently books the sale to the original shop. The revenue lands in the wrong store's numbers and nothing errors.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='storefront' AND table_name='orders' AND column_name='store_id' AND column_default LIKE '%1%'

defects.title: A null store_id is a meaningful value, not a missing one
defects.why: Rows predating 2014 were left null and the convention became 'null means the original shop'. Every aggregate that groups by store either drops those rows or needs a coalesce nobody documented.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.orders WHERE store_id IS NULL

defects.title: timetz used for a review timestamp
defects.why: timetz carries a UTC offset and no date, so it cannot know about daylight saving and cannot be compared meaningfully against anything. Added by someone who read "with time zone" and took it for the careful choice. The columns beside it that genuinely hold opening hours are plain time, which is correct, so the one wrong type sits unremarked among two right ones.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='storefront' AND table_name='store_hours' AND data_type='time with time zone'

defects.title: GIN index on a tsvector column nothing populates
defects.why: The column and its GIN index were added, the trigger that would maintain them never was. The column is null on every row, so full-text search returns nothing and the index costs storage for no result.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.products WHERE search_vector IS NOT NULL

defects.title: shipments.order_id has no foreign key
defects.why: The fulfilment schema was built by a different team on a deadline and cross-schema foreign keys were left out to keep the loads fast. Orders have since been deleted and their shipments remain.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid='fulfilment.shipments'::regclass AND contype='f' AND conkey = ARRAY[(SELECT attnum FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid='fulfilment.shipments'::regclass AND attname='order_id')]

defects.title: Orphaned shipments pointing at deleted orders
defects.why: A 2019 retention job deleted cancelled orders. With no foreign key, nothing stopped it and nothing cleaned up after it. 212 of the 10,622 rows in fulfilment.shipments point at an order that does not exist.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.shipments s LEFT JOIN storefront.orders o USING (order_id) WHERE o.order_id IS NULL

defects.title: No index on shipments.order_id
defects.why: Every order detail page looks up shipments by order. With no foreign key there was no automatic index either, so each lookup scans the whole table.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid=i.indrelid AND a.attnum = i.indkey[0] WHERE i.indrelid='fulfilment.shipments'::regclass AND a.attname='order_id'

defects.title: Circular foreign keys between orders and returns
defects.why: A return points at its order, and an order points back at the return that caused it. Neither table can be loaded before the other, so any restore that respects foreign keys deadlocks on ordering and any delete needs both sides nulled first.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE contype='f' AND ((conrelid='storefront.orders'::regclass AND confrelid='fulfilment.returns'::regclass) OR (conrelid='fulfilment.returns'::regclass AND confrelid='storefront.orders'::regclass))

defects.title: macaddr and macaddr8 used for the same kind of address
defects.why: Two columns on one table hold hardware addresses in different widths, so comparing them requires a cast that is not always reversible. Whichever the newer device reports, one of the two columns is wrong for it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT data_type) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='fulfilment' AND data_type IN ('macaddr','macaddr8')

defects.title: (supplier_id, supplier_sku) is unique in the data and not in the schema
defects.why: The pair has held unique across every row since 2018 and the import job relies on it. Nothing declares it, so the planner cannot use it and the first duplicate will be accepted silently.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT supplier_id, supplier_sku FROM supply.supplier_products GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING count(*) > 1) x

defects.title: supply.receipts has never held a row
defects.why: Goods receipting was specified, tabled and never built. Received quantities are written onto the purchase order line instead, so this table is dead and the column that replaced it carries no history.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.receipts

defects.title: Payment amounts stored as double precision
defects.why: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly. Summing this column and summing the integer minor units the rest of the database uses give different answers, and the difference grows with row count.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='payments' AND table_name='transactions' AND column_name='amount' AND data_type='double precision'

defects.title: Ledger debits and credits do not sum to zero
defects.why: Refunds were never posted to the ledger. Nothing in the schema states that the two sides should match, so the imbalance has been growing since 2018 and no check has ever failed.

detect.sql: SELECT (sum(debit_cents) = sum(credit_cents))::text FROM payments.ledger_entries

defects.title: Index redundant with the leading columns of another
defects.why: An index on (coupon_id) alongside one on (coupon_id, redeemed_at). The composite serves every query the single-column one does. Both are written on every insert.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_indexes WHERE schemaname='marketing' AND tablename='coupon_redemptions'

defects.title: marketing.sms_campaigns is written by nothing and read by nothing
defects.why: The SMS channel was switched off in 2021. The rows were kept in case anyone asked, nobody has, and the table still appears in every schema diagram and every backup.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.sms_campaigns

defects.title: Entity-attribute-value table with untyped values
defects.why: Every attribute of every product as a text row, with a value_kind column naming the type it should have been. Nothing enforces value_kind, so 'number' rows hold text that will not cast and only a query finds them.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.product_attributes

defects.title: No index on products.brand_id
defects.why: The brand landing page filters on it. PostgreSQL does not index the referencing side of a foreign key automatically, so every brand page scans the catalogue.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid=i.indrelid AND a.attnum=i.indkey[0] WHERE i.indrelid='storefront.products'::regclass AND a.attname='brand_id'

defects.title: B-tree index on a jsonb column queried with containment
defects.why: The query uses @>, which only a GIN index can serve. A B-tree on jsonb can only answer whole-value equality, so the index is maintained on every write and never used.

detect.sql: SELECT am.amname FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=i.indexrelid JOIN pg_am am ON am.oid=c.relam JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid=i.indrelid AND a.attnum=i.indkey[0] WHERE i.indrelid='storefront.products'::regclass AND a.attname='spec'

defects.title: Subscription columns left on customers after the schema was dropped
defects.why: DROP SCHEMA subscriptions CASCADE removed the tables it owned and could not touch columns on a table it did not own. Three columns remain, populated for customers who subscribed before 2021, referring to a product that no longer exists.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='storefront' AND table_name='customers' AND column_name IN ('subscription_tier','subscription_started_on','box_preference')

defects.title: Overlapping promotion windows with no exclusion constraint
defects.why: The column is a daterange, which makes an EXCLUDE constraint one line, and there is none. Promotions overlap, so which discount a customer gets depends on the order the rows come back in.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.promotions a JOIN marketing.promotions b ON a.promotion_id < b.promotion_id AND a.active_during && b.active_during

defects.title: Composite primary key indexed in the wrong order for the query
defects.why: The primary key is (promotion_id, product_id) and the hot query filters on product_id alone, which a B-tree cannot serve from its second column.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid=i.indrelid AND a.attnum=i.indkey[0] WHERE i.indrelid='marketing.promotion_products'::regclass AND a.attname='product_id'

defects.title: Range boundary convention is inconsistent and undocumented
defects.why: One table uses a half-open tstzrange and the other a daterange whose upper bound readers treat as inclusive. Nothing records which is which, so a report that joins them is off by a day at every boundary.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT data_type) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE (table_schema='storefront' AND table_name='price_history' AND column_name='in_force') OR (table_schema='marketing' AND table_name='promotions' AND column_name='active_during')

defects.title: Polymorphic subject reference that no foreign key can cover
defects.why: A type column and an id column pointing at one of five tables. No foreign key can express that, so nothing validates the id. The CHECK still permits 'subscription', whose tables were dropped in 2021.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.tickets WHERE subject_type='subscription'

defects.title: Tickets merged into each other, forming a cycle
defects.why: The self-referencing foreign key permits a loop. Three pairs of tickets point at each other, so following the chain to the surviving ticket never terminates. support.fn_surviving_ticket exhausts the stack on any of the six.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.tickets a JOIN support.tickets b ON a.merged_into_ticket_id = b.ticket_id AND b.merged_into_ticket_id = a.ticket_id

defects.title: Audit log with no retention policy
defects.why: Nothing deletes from it, it is not partitioned, and no query reads it. It is the largest object in the database by row count and its only effect is to slow every write to the tables it audits.

detect.sql: SELECT (count(*) > 20000)::text FROM ops.event_log

defects.title: Audit trigger doubles every write to orders and tickets
defects.why: Each insert or update writes a second row carrying the whole old and new row as JSON. On the busiest table in the database that is a permanent doubling of write volume for a log nobody reads.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE NOT tgisinternal AND tgfoid = 'ops.fn_audit_row'::regproc

defects.title: Audit log entity_id is null on every row
defects.why: Both arms of the CASE in the trigger return null, so the column that would make the log searchable is empty. ix_event_log_entity indexes a column that is always null in its second position, and the log cannot answer the question it was built for.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.event_log WHERE entity_id IS NOT NULL

defects.title: Random v4 UUID primary keys on the largest acquired tables
defects.why: Every insert lands at a random point in the B-tree, so the index never stays warm and page splits are spread across the whole structure. The rest of the database uses sequential integers.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='legacy' AND column_name='id' AND data_type='uuid'

defects.title: Acquired tables store local time with no offset
defects.why: Silverback wrote wall-clock time. Cross River code reads it as UTC. Rows written during British Summer Time are an hour out and nothing marks which ones, so the error is unfixable without knowing each row's original locale.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='legacy' AND data_type='timestamp without time zone'

defects.title: The money type used for order totals
defects.why: money renders and parses according to lc_monetary, so the same stored value reads differently on two servers and a restore into a differently configured instance changes what the numbers mean.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='legacy' AND data_type='money'

defects.title: Acquired order lines reference a catalogue that was never imported
defects.why: A varchar holding Silverback product codes. No table in this database defines them, so every acquired order line names a product nobody can look up.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT product_code) FROM legacy.order_lines

defects.title: Strongly correlated columns with no extended statistics
defects.why: A postcode implies a city. The planner assumes the two are independent and multiplies their selectivities, so a query filtering on both underestimates its row count badly and picks a nested loop where it should hash.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_statistic_ext WHERE stxrelid = 'legacy.addresses'::regclass

defects.title: Customer bridge covers 97% of acquired customers
defects.why: 36 of 1200 acquired customers have no Cross River counterpart. Any report that joins through this table drops them without saying so, and the gap has not moved since 2022.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.customer_map WHERE customer_id IS NULL

defects.title: Bridge column points at storefront.customers with no foreign key
defects.why: At import time some targets did not exist and the load had to succeed, so the constraint was left off and never added. Nothing now prevents the column naming a customer who has been deleted.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid='legacy.customer_map'::regclass AND contype='f' AND confrelid='storefront.customers'::regclass

defects.title: One person can exist as two customers in two schemas
defects.why: Nothing keeps the two tables in step. An address change on one side never reaches the other, and they have been diverging since the acquisition.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.customer_map WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL

defects.title: Old and new order total columns disagree
defects.why: The dual-write trigger fires only on total_cents and status, so a job that writes total_minor alone is not covered. The contract phase that would have dropped the old column never ran, so both survive and disagree.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.orders WHERE total_minor IS NOT NULL AND total_minor <> total_cents::bigint

defects.title: View defined with SELECT * that froze its column list
defects.why: PostgreSQL expands the star at creation time. Columns added to the table afterwards never appear in the view, so the view and the table it claims to mirror have quietly different shapes.

detect.sql: SELECT (count(*) FILTER (WHERE table_name='orders') > count(*) FILTER (WHERE table_name='v_orders_compat'))::text FROM information_schema.columns WHERE (table_schema='storefront' AND table_name='orders') OR (table_schema='analytics' AND table_name='v_orders_compat')

defects.title: A view over a view over a view
defects.why: Each layer was a reasonable convenience. Together they mean a filter written against the top view cannot be pushed to the base table, so a query for one store reads every order.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_depend d JOIN pg_rewrite r ON r.oid=d.objid JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=r.ev_class JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname='analytics' AND c.relkind='v' AND d.refobjid IN (SELECT oid FROM pg_class WHERE relkind='v' AND relnamespace='analytics'::regnamespace) AND d.classid='pg_rewrite'::regclass AND d.refobjid <> c.oid

defects.title: A view no application has queried since 2023
defects.why: Built for a migration report that ran twice. It survives every schema review because a view looks harmless, and it pins the definition of two columns that would otherwise be droppable.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_views WHERE schemaname='analytics' AND viewname='v_legacy_revenue'

defects.title: CHECK constraint left NOT VALID over existing rows
defects.why: Added NOT VALID to avoid a full-table lock, with VALIDATE CONSTRAINT scheduled for the next window. The window was cancelled. New rows are checked, existing rows were never examined, and psql shows the constraint as if it held.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname='orders_total_minor_non_negative' AND NOT convalidated

defects.title: Foreign key left NOT VALID, duplicating an existing one
defects.why: A second foreign key on store_id, added NOT VALID by someone who did not check for the one added in 2014. Both are enforced on every insert; one of them was never validated and neither is needed twice.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid='storefront.orders'::regclass AND contype='f' AND confrelid='storefront.stores'::regclass

defects.title: Composite foreign key using the default MATCH SIMPLE
defects.why: MATCH SIMPLE is the default and means the constraint is satisfied whenever any column of the key is null. A row naming a promotion and no product passes the check and references nothing. MATCH FULL is what was meant.

detect.sql: SELECT confmatchtype::text FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid='marketing.applied_promotions'::regclass AND contype='f' AND array_length(conkey,1) = 2

defects.title: Rollup table and its source table give different answers
defects.why: The nightly job filters on placed_at since the last run, so backdated orders are never picked up. Whole days are missing from the rollup and present in orders. The rollup is what the board sees.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT placed_at::date d, coalesce(store_id,1) s FROM storefront.orders WHERE status IN ('paid','shipped')) o LEFT JOIN analytics.daily_sales_rollup r ON r.rollup_day=o.d AND r.store_id=o.s WHERE r.rollup_day IS NULL

defects.title: Segmentation table that has never held a row
defects.why: The model reached a notebook and never reached production. Three dashboards LEFT JOIN to it, so every customer shows as unsegmented and nobody has noticed the model is not running.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.customer_segments

defects.title: Autoanalyze effectively disabled on storefront.page_views
defects.why: The scale factor was raised to 10.0 to stop ANALYZE competing with the analytics window, which means the table must grow by a thousand percent before autoanalyze considers it. The planner's idea of this table is years out of date.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE oid='storefront.page_views'::regclass AND reloptions::text LIKE '%autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor=10%'

defects.title: Autovacuum switched off on the largest table
defects.why: Turned off during a 2024 incident and never turned back on. Dead tuples accumulate with nothing to reclaim them, and the transaction id horizon on this table advances toward wraparound unattended.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE oid='ops.event_log'::regclass AND reloptions::text LIKE '%autovacuum_enabled=false%'

defects.title: fillfactor 100 on a table updated on every sale
defects.why: With no free space in the page, an update cannot be a heap-only tuple and must write a new entry and touch every index on the table. Lowering it to 80 would keep most of those updates in place.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE oid='storefront.inventory'::regclass AND reloptions::text LIKE '%fillfactor=100%'

defects.title: Materialised view created WITH NO DATA and never refreshed
defects.why: Querying an unpopulated materialised view raises an error rather than returning nothing, so every dashboard panel built on it fails. The refresh was left to a scheduler that was never configured.

detect.sql: SELECT (NOT relispopulated)::text FROM pg_class WHERE oid='analytics.mv_daily_sales'::regclass

defects.title: Configuration table where 31 of 40 settings are blank
defects.why: The rows were created from a template listing every setting the application might one day read. Null and empty both mean 'use the compiled-in default', so nothing breaks and nothing shows which blanks are deliberate.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.app_config WHERE config_value IS NULL OR config_value = ''

defects.title: The same index created twice under two names
defects.why: Two indexes on (job_name, started_at DESC) with different names. Both are maintained on every insert and only one can ever be chosen.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index a WHERE a.indrelid = 'ops.job_runs'::regclass AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_index b WHERE b.indrelid = a.indrelid AND b.indexrelid <> a.indexrelid AND b.indkey::text = a.indkey::text AND b.indoption::text = a.indoption::text AND b.indclass::text = a.indclass::text AND b.indcollation::text = a.indcollation::text AND coalesce(pg_get_expr(b.indpred, b.indrelid), '') = coalesce(pg_get_expr(a.indpred, a.indrelid), '') AND coalesce(pg_get_expr(b.indexprs, b.indrelid), '') = coalesce(pg_get_expr(a.indexprs, a.indrelid), ''))

defects.title: Integer sequence close to its ceiling
defects.why: A plain integer sequence sitting at 2,147,000,000 against a ceiling of 2,147,483,647. When it wraps, the failure is an insert error on a hot path with no warning beforehand.

detect.sql: SELECT (last_value > 2100000000)::text FROM ops.import_batch_seq

defects.title: Hand-made year tables with different column lists
defects.why: Each was created from the shape of orders on the day it was made. orders_2023 predates the Meridian columns and orders_2024 has them, so a UNION ALL across the two fails and any tool assuming year tables share a shape is wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT (count(*) FILTER (WHERE table_name='orders_2024') - count(*) FILTER (WHERE table_name='orders_2023')) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='archive' AND table_name IN ('orders_2023','orders_2024')

defects.title: Partitioned table whose partitions stop before today
defects.why: Partitions were hand-created four quarters ahead and the last one ends on 2026-07-01. There is no DEFAULT partition, so an insert dated after that fails outright and the archive job has been failing since July.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_inherits i WHERE i.inhparent = 'archive.page_views_archive'::regclass AND (xpath('/row/n/text()', query_to_xml(format('SELECT count(*) AS n FROM (SELECT now() AS viewed_at) x WHERE %s', pg_get_partition_constraintdef(i.inhrelid)), false, true, '')))[1]::text::int > 0

defects.title: Temporal integrity applied to one price table and not the other
defects.why: The 2026 table uses PRIMARY KEY ... WITHOUT OVERLAPS and cannot hold two prices for one moment. The 2019 table holds the same kind of data with no such guarantee. Two price histories, two different sets of rules.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conperiod AND conrelid = 'supply.contract_prices'::regclass) - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conperiod AND conrelid = 'storefront.price_history'::regclass)

defects.title: Generated column is VIRTUAL because the keyword was omitted
defects.why: Before PostgreSQL 18, GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) with no STORED was a syntax error. In 18 it is valid and means VIRTUAL: the value is computed on read, occupies no storage, and cannot be indexed. Code written for 17 and deployed on 18 gets a different column than it asked for, and the failure is a missing index rather than an error.

detect.sql: SELECT attgenerated FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid='storefront.order_items'::regclass AND attname='line_total_cents'

defects.title: CHECK constraint declared NOT ENFORCED
defects.why: NOT ENFORCED is new in PostgreSQL 18. The constraint exists, is listed by every catalogue view, is shown by psql, and checks nothing at all. This is different from NOT VALID, which still checks new rows. 242 of the 12,145 rows in payments.ledger_entries have both debit_cents and credit_cents above zero, so the rule the constraint states is false of the table it sits on. A reader who sees the constraint reasonably concludes the rule holds.

detect.sql: SELECT (NOT conenforced)::text FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname='ledger_entries_single_sided'

defects.title: Second NOT ENFORCED CHECK, over rows that already violate it
defects.why: Written to record the rule that a refund cannot exceed the transaction it refunds. A CHECK cannot read another table, so the expression settled for a flat ceiling of one million pounds while the constraint kept the name of the rule it was meant to express. The name and the expression describe different rules and neither is applied, because the constraint is NOT ENFORCED. 17 of the 242 rows in payments.refunds are above the ceiling: a 2019 batch that applied the pounds-to-pence conversion twice. They were already there when the constraint was added and adding it did not fail.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.refunds WHERE amount_cents > 100000000

defects.title: NOT NULL constraint that is NOT VALID over 9,460 real nulls
defects.why:
PostgreSQL 18 stores NOT NULL in pg_constraint, which makes it nameable and lets it be added NOT VALID. psql and information_schema both report the column as NOT NULL. It holds 9,460 nulls. The backfill that was meant to clear them filtered on placed_at >= 2023-01-01 and reached only 172 rows.

The second-order effect is worse than the first: an invalid NOT NULL is still enforced against every new row version, so no UPDATE of any of those 9,460 orders can succeed until someone sets a currency. They are readable, deletable, and frozen.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.orders WHERE currency_code IS NULL

defects.title: Backfill date filter reached 172 of 9,632 candidate rows
defects.why: The backfill was written against the assumption that only orders since the start of 2023 could be missing a currency. The column was added in February 2023 and the default was set afterwards, so everything before that date is null too. The filter caught the six-week gap and nothing else.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.orders WHERE currency_code='GBP' AND placed_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-01-01' AND placed_at < TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-02-13'

defects.title: Cursor loop where one aggregate would do
defects.why: Walks every order for a customer in plpgsql and adds the totals up. One SUM does it in one pass. Worst on exactly the customers anyone looks up, because they are the ones with the most orders. Also declares a variable it never reads.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%FOR v_row IN%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid='storefront.fn_customer_lifetime_value'::regproc

defects.title: Integer division discards pence before applying the points rate
defects.why: Points are one per pound. total_cents / 100 is integer division, so the pence are thrown away before the rate is applied and an order of 999 pence earns nine points rather than ten. 6,383 of the 13,880 orders in storefront.orders earn one point fewer than rounding would give, a loss of 6,383 points in total. It is invisible per order and systematic across every customer.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.orders o WHERE o.total_cents IS NOT NULL AND storefront.fn_apply_loyalty_points(o.order_id) <> round(o.total_cents / 100.0)::integer

defects.title: Dynamic SQL built by concatenating the caller's string
defects.why: The search term is concatenated straight into the statement text, so a caller who sends an apostrophe changes the statement. Reachable from the search box. format() with %L, or USING, fixes it. The leading wildcard is a second problem: the query cannot use a B-tree index and scans the catalogue every time.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.fn_find_products('no such product'' OR name LIKE ''')

defects.title: EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN RETURN NULL
defects.why: Catches every error, including deadlock and out of memory, and returns null. The caller cannot distinguish a failed write from a row that was not there, and nothing is logged. When the nightly job stops updating stock, this is why, and there is no evidence anywhere.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%WHEN OTHERS THEN%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid='storefront.fn_adjust_inventory'::regproc

defects.title: SECURITY DEFINER function with no search_path set
defects.why: Runs with the owner's privileges and resolves unqualified names using the caller's search_path. A caller who creates their own event_log earlier in the path chooses what this function deletes, as the owner. One line fixes it: SET search_path = pg_catalog, ops.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosecdef AND proconfig IS NULL)::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid='ops.fn_purge_old_events'::regproc

defects.title: IMMUTABLE function that reads a table
defects.why: IMMUTABLE promises the same answer for the same argument forever. This reads a table that changes daily. The planner may evaluate it once and cache the result, and any expression index built on it holds values that were true at insert time. Reindexing silently changes query results.

detect.sql: SELECT provolatile::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid='catalog.fn_current_price'::regproc

defects.title: PARALLEL SAFE function that inserts a row
defects.why: A parallel worker cannot write. When the planner takes the marking at its word and parallelises the query, the statement fails at run time. It passes every test on a small table and fails once the table is large enough to interest the planner.

detect.sql: SELECT proparallel::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid='ops.fn_record_access'::regproc

defects.title: SELECT INTO without STRICT over a query with several answers
defects.why: Without STRICT, no rows leaves the variable null and several rows silently keeps whichever came first. There are 120 case-duplicate email addresses in this database, so the query genuinely has more than one answer for some inputs and which one it returns can change when the plan changes.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT lower(email) AS e FROM storefront.customers GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1) d WHERE storefront.fn_customer_by_email(d.e) IS NOT NULL

defects.title: One query per order line to fetch the product name
defects.why: A join does the whole thing once. Each inner query is cheap on its own, and the procedure issues one for every line on the order, so the cost grows with the size of the order rather than staying flat.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%SELECT name INTO v_name%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid='storefront.fn_order_summary'::regproc

defects.title: count(*) evaluated once per candidate row
defects.why: Counts page views to answer a yes or no question. Called across the catalogue it runs one count per product over storefront.page_views, 25,000 rows whose statistics were left stale in 2024. EXISTS with a LIMIT answers it without counting anything.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%count(*) INTO v_views%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid='storefront.fn_is_popular'::regproc

defects.title: Recursive function with no cycle guard over cyclic data
defects.why: Follows merged_into_ticket_id until it finds an unmerged ticket. Three pairs of tickets in this database are merged into each other, so for those six inputs it recurses until the stack depth limit is hit, which takes seconds and leaves nothing behind explaining why. A visited set, a depth counter, or a recursive CTE with CYCLE all fix it.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%fn_surviving_ticket(v_next)%' AND prosrc NOT LIKE '%depth%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid='support.fn_surviving_ticket'::regproc

defects.title: COMMIT inside a per-row loop
defects.why: Commits once per customer, so there is no transaction around the work as a whole. A failure halfway leaves half the segments written with no record of where it stopped, and rerunning is not safe. Each commit is also a separate WAL flush.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%COMMIT;%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid='analytics.pr_rebuild_segments()'::regprocedure

defects.title: Trigger function that rewrites the whole table
defects.why: Updates every row of storefront.inventory on every inventory change. inventory is also pinned at fillfactor 100, so none of those rewrites can be a heap-only tuple update. The function is deliberately not attached to a table, because a fixture that takes minutes to load teaches nobody anything. The defect is the code, and it is in pg_proc.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgfoid='storefront.fn_touch_all_inventory'::regproc

defects.title: Function whose only effect is to grow a log nothing reads
defects.why: Every call writes a row into ops.event_log, which has no retention policy and autovacuum switched off. The row is written, the table grows, and the information is never recovered.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%ops.event_log%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid='ops.fn_note_job_progress'::regproc

defects.title: RETURNS SETOF record with no column definition
defects.why: Every caller must supply a column definition list and must know the shape by reading the body. Nothing checks that they agree, so a change to the body breaks callers at run time rather than at deploy time.

detect.sql: SELECT prorettype::regtype::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid='analytics.fn_report_rows'::regproc

defects.title: Two overloads that disagree about the answer
defects.why: One takes integer and truncates, one takes numeric and does not. Which one runs depends on how the caller's driver bound the parameter, and the two return different discounts for the same inputs.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_proc WHERE proname='fn_discounted_price' AND pronamespace='marketing'::regnamespace

defects.title: Function referencing a schema dropped in 2021
defects.why: plpgsql resolves names the first time a statement runs, not when the function is created. This compiles cleanly, deploys cleanly, passes a smoke test that never calls it, and raises 'relation subscriptions.box_shipments does not exist' the first time anyone does. Nothing in pg_proc, information_schema or pg_dump reports it. Only calling it finds it.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%subscriptions.box_shipments%' AND to_regclass('subscriptions.box_shipments') IS NULL)::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'storefront.fn_customer_box_history'::regproc

defects.title: Validation placed after the RETURN that ends the function
defects.why: The check below the RETURN never runs. It was added in response to an incident, reviewed, approved and merged, and has never executed. The incident it was written to prevent has happened twice since.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.transactions t WHERE t.amount IS NOT NULL AND payments.fn_refund_allowed(t.transaction_id, (t.amount * 1000)::integer + 1)

defects.title: Staging table with no primary key
defects.why: No primary key and no unique index of any kind. It was built to be truncated between runs, so a key looked like overhead. It is not truncated between runs: a reload that partly fails and is retried leaves both attempts in the table, and nothing can tell the second copy from the first or delete one without deleting both.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'ops.import_staging'::regclass AND contype = 'p'

defects.title: Review table with no primary key
defects.why: The temporal foreign key on this table took all the attention and nobody noticed it has no primary key. Two reviewers covering the same supplier, product and window produce two identical rows that no constraint refuses and no statement can tell apart.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'supply.contract_price_reviews'::regclass AND contype = 'p'

defects.title: Acquired email column carries a different collation from the one it is joined to
defects.why: Silverback ran under the C locale and the import kept the column's collation so their own ordering did not change underneath them. Every Cross River text column uses the database default. Nothing errors, and the comparison between the two resolves to C, which is not the collation customers_email_key was built in. Looking up one customer across the bridge reads all 3,120 rows of storefront.customers; the same lookup written against a literal uses the index. The bridge is the only query in the system that makes this join.

detect.sql: SELECT co.collname FROM pg_attribute a JOIN pg_collation co ON co.oid = a.attcollation WHERE a.attrelid = 'legacy.customers'::regclass AND a.attname = 'email_address'

defects.title: Unique constraint that exempts the 36 rows it was added to police
defects.why: The bridge is meant to be one to one, so a unique constraint was added to say so. In PostgreSQL every null is distinct from every other null, so it permits any number of unmatched rows. 36 of the 1,200 bridge rows are unmatched and sit under a constraint that does not apply to them. The case it does catch, two bridge rows claiming the same Cross River customer, is the case that was never going to happen.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.customer_map WHERE customer_id IS NULL

defects.title: Refunds deleted silently with the transaction they belong to
defects.why:
Two foreign keys carry ON DELETE CASCADE and they chain. Deleting one payments.transactions row removes every payments.refunds row against it, with no error and no record that anything went. All 242 refund rows sit under that cascade, and the refund row is the only place in the database that says money went back to a customer. The cascade was added so a 2018 test teardown could delete a test order in one statement.

The hop above it, storefront.orders to payments.transactions, is written the same way and does not fire today: storefront.order_items references the order with no action, so the order delete is refused before the cascade is reached. The chain is armed rather than live. It goes live the day anyone makes order_items cascade too, which is the obvious fix when that error appears, and neither table definition mentions the other.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE contype = 'f' AND confdeltype = 'c' AND conrelid IN ('payments.transactions'::regclass, 'payments.refunds'::regclass)

defects.title: ON DELETE SET NULL onto a NOT NULL column, which can only ever fail
defects.why: fulfilment.shipment_items.order_item_id is NOT NULL and its foreign key says ON DELETE SET NULL. PostgreSQL accepts the pair and there is no combination of data that makes it work: deleting a referenced storefront.order_items row attempts the null, the NOT NULL rejects it, and the delete fails. The action was added to stop shipment lines blocking an order edit, and it blocks the edit exactly as before, under a not-null message that names a column the person deleting has never heard of.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint c JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = c.conrelid AND a.attnum = c.conkey[1] WHERE c.contype = 'f' AND c.confdeltype = 'n' AND a.attnotnull AND c.conrelid = 'fulfilment.shipment_items'::regclass

defects.title: Row security on with no policy, so the table reads as empty to everyone but its owner
defects.why: Row security is enabled on support.ticket_messages and no policy was ever written. A table in that state grants nothing, so every row is filtered out and no error is raised. The application has not noticed in six years because it connects as the table's owner and the owner is exempt unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set, which it is not. Any other role reads zero rows from a table holding 1,800 of them, and zero rows is indistinguishable from an empty table.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c WHERE c.oid = 'support.ticket_messages'::regclass AND c.relrowsecurity AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_policy p WHERE p.polrelid = c.oid)

defects.title: Ticket sequence set from a row count, 150 below the highest id in the table
defects.why: An archive trial emptied support.tickets and restored it, then set the sequence from a count of the rows it had loaded rather than from the highest ticket_id. The count excluded closed tickets, which the first pass had not restored. The sequence sits at 450 against a maximum ticket_id of 600. Nothing is wrong with any row in the table and nothing will report a problem until the next ticket is opened, at which point the insert fails on the primary key, and it fails again for each of the 150 ids the sequence has to walk back over.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT max(ticket_id) FROM support.tickets) - pg_sequence_last_value('support.tickets_ticket_id_seq')::integer

defects.title: A view hands every row of the row-security table to roles that cannot read it
defects.why:
support.ticket_messages has row security enabled. support.v_ticket_message_log selects from it and was created without WITH (security_invoker = true), which is still the default, so the view runs as its owner. The owner of the view is the owner of the table, and a table owner is exempt from row security unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set, which it is not.

Measured on a role granted SELECT on both: reading the table returns 0 rows, reading the view returns all 1,800. The view is a complete bypass of the control on the table, and it sits twenty lines below it in the same migration. Neither object's definition mentions the other, and nothing in psql's description of either shows the interaction.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c WHERE c.oid = 'support.v_ticket_message_log'::regclass AND (c.reloptions IS NULL OR NOT ('security_invoker=true' = ANY (c.reloptions)))

defects.title: Partial index the view it was built for can never use
defects.why:
ix_tickets_queue is partial on status = 'open'. support.v_ticket_queue, the only query written against it, filters status IN ('open','pending'). The planner uses a partial index only when it can prove the query's filter implies the predicate, and an IN list over two values does not imply equality with one of them, so the index is never used by the query it exists for.

Measured: the queue view plans as a sequential scan of all 600 tickets and a sort. The same query with the filter narrowed to status = 'open' plans as an index scan on ix_tickets_queue. The index is listed, it is maintained on every write to the table, and it is 150 pending tickets away from being the one the query wanted. A tool reading index definitions alone sees a reasonable index; the mismatch only exists in the pair.

detect.sql: SELECT (xpath('/row/n/text()', query_to_xml(format('SELECT count(*) AS n FROM support.v_ticket_queue WHERE NOT (%s)', pg_get_expr(i.indpred, i.indrelid)), false, true, '')))[1]::text FROM pg_index i WHERE i.indexrelid = 'support.ix_tickets_queue'::regclass

defects.title: Instants stored as integer Unix epoch seconds beside a real timestamp column
defects.why:
Silverback's API returned every time as epoch seconds and the import kept the column as it came, adding placed_at beside it. Both columns carry the same instant in 4,000 rows, in two shapes, and Silverback's own reports still read the integer one.

An integer epoch column has an end date: it overflows in January 2038 and gives no warning before it. It carries no time zone, so the reading depends on whoever writes the query, and here the correct one is UTC while the timestamp column next to it has no offset at all. Date arithmetic, BETWEEN on dates and any index a date range query could use all require a cast first. Nothing in the catalogue distinguishes this column from any other integer.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'legacy.orders'::regclass AND attname = 'placed_at_epoch' AND atttypid = 'integer'::regtype

defects.title: 25 promotions applied twice to the same order line by a re-run batch
defects.why:
A March 2026 batch timed out part way through and was run again from the top, applying every discount it had already written a second time. 25 (order_item_id, promotion_id) pairs now have two rows each, 50 of the table's 76 rows.

Nothing stopped it. The column pair that would carry a unique constraint is the composite foreign key that was added NOT VALID and never validated, and no unique index was ever put beside it. The duplicated rows are identical apart from the generated key, so no report reading this table can tell which of a pair is the real one, and summing discount_cents over an order double counts every line in the overlap.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT order_item_id, promotion_id FROM marketing.applied_promotions GROUP BY 1, 2 HAVING count(*) > 1) d

defects.title: Three foreign keys still listed on a table where none of them runs
defects.why:
A 2024 reload turned the triggers off to make the load finish, failed part way through, and never turned them back on. ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER ALL disables the internal triggers that enforce foreign keys, not only the ones somebody wrote: all 6 of them here, covering all 3 foreign keys on the table.

Every one of those constraints is still listed. psql prints them, information_schema returns them, pg_dump writes them out, and nothing anywhere records that they stopped running. 120 rows were loaded through the hole that reference a coupon, an order and a customer that do not exist. Re-enabling the triggers would not find them either: PostgreSQL does not re-check existing rows when a trigger comes back.

This is the case where reading the constraint list is exactly the wrong thing to do, because the constraint list is what looks correct.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'marketing.coupon_redemptions'::regclass AND tgisinternal AND tgenabled = 'D'

defects.title: Foreign key deferred to commit, so every transaction reads through a broken reference
defects.why:
The posting job writes the ledger pair before the transaction row, because the transaction's status depends on what posted. The foreign key refused that order, so it was made DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED rather than the job being reordered.

The reference is now checked once, at commit, instead of after each statement. For the whole length of any transaction that touches this table the rows point at a transaction that does not exist, and anything reading in that window is correct to see a broken reference: a trigger, a procedure, or simply the next statement of the same transaction. Nothing in psql's output for the table distinguishes it from an ordinary foreign key.

Deferrable is not wrong by itself, which is the point of this entry. conformance.fk_actions carries a deferred foreign key used exactly as intended and is listed under clean. A tool that reports every deferrable constraint scores a hit here and a false positive there.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE contype = 'f' AND condeferred AND conrelid = 'payments.ledger_entries'::regclass

defects.title: Column default that its own check constraint rejects
defects.why:
ops.job_runs.attempt is DEFAULT 0 and CHECK (attempt BETWEEN 1 AND 5). The two disagree about whether a first run is attempt zero or attempt one, and they are three lines apart in the same CREATE TABLE. PostgreSQL does not compare a default against a check, so the table was created without complaint.

Any insert that names the column works. Any insert that leaves it out takes the default and is rejected, and the error names the check constraint rather than the default, so it reads as bad input from the caller rather than as a contradiction in the schema. The scheduler that writes all 1,000 rows in this table names the column, so the table is full of rows that hide the problem. It is reachable only by the person typing an insert at a prompt, which is to say by someone already trying to fix something else.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint c JOIN pg_attrdef d ON d.adrelid = c.conrelid AND d.adnum = c.conkey[1] JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = c.conrelid AND a.attnum = c.conkey[1] WHERE c.conrelid = 'ops.job_runs'::regclass AND c.contype = 'c' AND cardinality(c.conkey) = 1 AND NOT (xpath('/row/ok/text()', query_to_xml(format('SELECT coalesce((%s), true) AS ok FROM (SELECT %s AS %I) x', pg_get_expr(c.conbin, c.conrelid), pg_get_expr(d.adbin, d.adrelid), a.attname), false, true, '')))[1]::text::boolean

defects.title: Statistics target of 1 on the join column of the largest table
defects.why:
Lowered to 1 during a week spent on slow plans, on the reasoning that a smaller sample would make ANALYZE finish faster on the largest table in the database. It was meant to go back to 100 and did not.

At a target of 1, ANALYZE keeps one most common value and one histogram bucket for a column holding thousands of distinct products. Every selectivity estimate on that column is then a guess drawn from almost nothing, and the planner chooses join orders and scan types from those guesses. The failure is quiet in every direction: ANALYZE runs and reports success, pg_stats has a row for the column, and the plans are simply worse than they should be with no error to attach that to.

The setting lives on the column, not in a configuration file, so it does not appear in any review of postgresql.conf and it survives every restore.

detect.sql: SELECT attstattarget FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'storefront.order_items'::regclass AND attname = 'product_id'

defects.title: Two BEFORE INSERT triggers whose result depends on their names
defects.why:
PostgreSQL fires row triggers on the same table and event in alphabetical order of trigger name. trg_a_derive_visibility sets is_internal from agent_id, trg_b_default_agent fills agent_id in when it is missing, and the first sorts before the second, so visibility is decided from a value that has not been filled in yet.

Measured: 600 of the 1,800 messages carry an agent and are marked external, which is the one combination the rule was written to rule out. Each function is correct read on its own, and the dependency between them appears in neither CREATE TRIGGER statement. Renaming either trigger fixes the data and changes no logic, which is also why a review of the two functions finds nothing.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.ticket_messages WHERE agent_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT is_internal

defects.title: bigint foreign key against an integer key, so the width that matters is the one left alone
defects.why:
The child column is bigint and the key it references is a 4 byte integer. The review that widened it went table by table through column definitions, and the parent's key is a serial declared elsewhere in the file, so it was never reached.

The extra range on the child is unusable: it can only ever hold values the parent has issued, and the parent cannot issue anything past 2147483647. The join between the two casts on every row. And the column that will actually run out is the one the review was looking for and walked past. PostgreSQL permits the mismatch without comment, so nothing reports it, and both columns look deliberate in isolation.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint c JOIN pg_attribute ca ON ca.attrelid = c.conrelid AND ca.attnum = c.conkey[1] JOIN pg_attribute pa ON pa.attrelid = c.confrelid AND pa.attnum = c.confkey[1] WHERE c.contype = 'f' AND ca.atttypid <> pa.atttypid AND c.conrelid = 'supply.purchase_order_lines'::regclass

defects.title: JSON kept in a text column, 12 rows of which are not JSON
defects.why:
The campaign tool posts its targeting rules as a JSON string and the column is text, because text takes a string. jsonb had been in PostgreSQL for four years by then and would have rejected the malformed ones on the way in.

12 of the 60 rows are not valid JSON: an older version of the tool sent the keys unquoted. Nothing rejected them and nothing has noticed since, because nothing reads the column in a way that would parse it.

The cost is paid the first time someone does. A cast to jsonb fails on the whole query rather than on the row, so a report that reads targeting works until it touches one of the 12 and then fails entirely, with an error about a token rather than about a campaign. There is no index that can reach inside the column and no constraint that could be added now without first cleaning the 12.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.campaigns WHERE targeting IS NOT NULL AND targeting IS NOT JSON

defects.title: Enum value added at the front, so the last status an order reaches sorts first
defects.why:
'refund_pending' was added with ADD VALUE ... BEFORE 'pending', because appending it would have put it after 'on_hold' and the list reads better with it at the front. An enum's sort order is its declaration order, so the value now sorts before every status an order must pass through to reach it.

Measured order: refund_pending < pending < paid < shipped < cancelled < refunded < on_hold. Any ORDER BY status_v2 puts the last thing that happens to an order first. Any range test inverts with it: status_v2 > 'shipped' excludes it and status_v2 < 'pending' is true for it alone.

Every label is spelled correctly, the column is the right type, and the check constraint this replaced could not have had the problem at all. The only thing wrong is the order of the values, and that order is not in the column definition, the table definition, or anything pg_dump writes about either. conformance.parcel_size is an enum declared in a sensible order and is listed under clean, so reporting every enum is a false positive there.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_enum WHERE enumtypid = 'storefront.order_status'::regtype AND enumsortorder < (SELECT enumsortorder FROM pg_enum WHERE enumtypid = 'storefront.order_status'::regtype AND enumlabel = 'refund_pending')

defects.title: char(12) collapses two supplier account codes into one, unrecoverably
defects.why:
Declared char(12) rather than varchar(12), because the finance system's account codes are at most twelve characters. char is blank padded and every comparison on it ignores trailing spaces, which is the SQL standard and is not what anyone expects.

The finance system reissued a retired code by putting a space after it, so 'ACC001' and 'ACC001 ' are two accounts on two different suppliers there. Here they are one value. Measured: looking up 'ACC001' returns 2 suppliers, and adding a unique constraint to the column fails on the pair.

No query recovers the difference. Casting to text or varchar strips trailing blanks too, so both read back as six characters. The column type did not hide the distinction, it discarded it on the way in, and the only place it still exists is the system the data came from.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.suppliers WHERE account_code = 'ACC001'

defects.title: The only record of which discount was applied is in an unlogged table
defects.why:
Set UNLOGGED during a sale week to cut the write cost, which is mostly WAL. It worked: the writes got faster, which is what was asked for.

An unlogged table is not crash safe. PostgreSQL truncates it during recovery, every row, with no way to get them back. It is also not replicated, so it is empty on every standby and missing from any backup taken from one.

This table is the only record of which discount was applied to which order line, and finance reconciles against it. None of that is visible from the table definition, which still lists its columns, its keys and its indexes exactly as before. The property lives on the table's storage, not in its schema, and a single character in pg_class is the whole of the evidence.

detect.sql: SELECT relpersistence::text FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'marketing.applied_promotions'::regclass

defects.title: SELECT on the payment tables granted to PUBLIC
defects.why:
The analysts asked for read access for a revenue report. Granting to PUBLIC was one statement; granting to a role meant creating the role, granting it, and finding out who belonged in it.

PUBLIC is not everyone who has been given an account. It is every role that exists now and every role created afterwards, which includes the ones created later for a service, a migration tool or a contractor. None of those will appear in a review of who can read payments, because the grant is not attached to any of them.

Measured: has_table_privilege('public', 'payments.transactions', 'SELECT') is true, and 2 tables in the payments schema carry a PUBLIC grant. Revoking it now breaks whatever has quietly come to rely on it in the two years since, and there is no record of what that is.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT table_name) FROM information_schema.role_table_grants WHERE grantee = 'PUBLIC' AND table_schema = 'payments'

defects.title: The constraint requiring supervisor approval passes every unapproved line
defects.why:
Nothing goes back on the shelf for more than a supervisor approved. return_lines_within_approval is that rule, written as CHECK (quantity <= approved_quantity).

approved_quantity is nullable, and correctly so: the line is created when the parcel is opened and approval happens afterwards. A CHECK passes a row whose expression is null, not only one that is true, and quantity <= null is null. Every line still waiting for approval therefore satisfies the constraint that exists to require it.

Measured: 86 return lines have no approval and were restocked anyway. The constraint bites only on approved lines, which are the ones a supervisor already looked at. Inserting an unapproved line for 9 units is accepted; the same line with an approval of 1 is refused, so the constraint looks alive to anyone who tests it that way.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.return_lines WHERE approved_quantity IS NULL AND restocked

defects.title: Two tables draw their primary keys from one sequence owned by only one of them
defects.why:
Written by copying the CREATE TABLE for fulfilment.carriers and editing it. The serial had already been expanded into an explicit DEFAULT nextval(), and the copy kept it, so this table's key draws from the sequence belonging to carriers.

Neither table has duplicate keys, which is the only thing anyone checks. The ids interleave instead: carriers hold 1 to 3 and the four service levels are 4, 5, 6 and 7. Inserting a carrier moves this table's next id, and the gaps in each read as deleted rows that never existed, so any count or report that works from an id range is wrong.

The sequence is owned by fulfilment.carriers.carrier_id. Dropping that column or that table drops the sequence with it and leaves this table's default pointing at nothing. The catalogue records that ownership on carriers and records nothing here.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_depend d JOIN pg_attrdef a ON a.oid = d.objid WHERE d.refobjid = 'fulfilment.carriers_carrier_id_seq'::regclass AND d.classid = 'pg_attrdef'::regclass

defects.title: The queue view is writable and a write through it makes the row disappear
defects.why:
The view has a WHERE clause and selects from one table without grouping it, so PostgreSQL makes it automatically updatable. Nobody asked for that; it is what happens when a view is simple enough. The queue screen was granted this view and nothing else, so its close button writes through it.

WITH CHECK OPTION is the clause that stops a write through a view from producing a row the view can no longer see. It is not the default and it is not here. Measured: an UPDATE through the view setting status to 'closed' succeeds, and the row is then invisible from the view, so the screen's own re-read finds nothing and reports the ticket as missing rather than closed. An INSERT of a resolved ticket lands in support.tickets and cannot be read back through the only object the screen has.

Nothing errors in either case, and the view definition gives no sign that it is writable at all.

detect.sql: SELECT (v.is_updatable = 'YES' AND c.reloptions IS NULL)::text FROM information_schema.views v JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = 'support.v_ticket_queue'::regclass WHERE v.table_schema = 'support' AND v.table_name = 'v_ticket_queue'

defects.title: The audit trigger on tickets is present, owned and inert
defects.why:
The 2026 ticket backfill rewrote every open ticket. With the audit trigger live that is one ops.event_log row per ticket carrying the whole old and new row as JSON, and the backfill would not have finished inside its window. Disabling the trigger for the run was the right call. Re-enabling it afterwards was step nine of a nine-step runbook.

The trigger still exists and does not fire. psql's \d lists it. pg_dump writes it out. information_schema.triggers reports it, because that view has no column for whether a trigger fires. pg_trigger.tgenabled holds 'D' instead of 'O', and that single character is the whole of the evidence.

Support believes every change to a ticket is logged. Nothing has been logged since the backfill, and the gap has no marker at either end.

detect.sql: SELECT tgenabled::text FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'support.tickets'::regclass AND tgname = 'trg_tickets_audit'

defects.title: A CHECK on token expiry that the passage of time turns false
defects.why:
Added so a token could never be stored already expired, which had happened twice. CHECK (expires_at > now()).

PostgreSQL accepts a non-immutable function in a CHECK and gives no warning. The constraint is therefore not a property of the row but of the row and the clock, and it stops being satisfied by rows that satisfied it when they were written. Measured: inserting a token that expired yesterday is refused, which is exactly what every row in this table becomes once it expires.

A CHECK is only evaluated on write, and a restore is a write. pg_restore loads the table with COPY, COPY runs the check, and every token that has expired since the dump was taken is rejected, which aborts the load of that table. The backup verifies on the day it is taken and fails on the day it is needed, and the error names the constraint rather than the clock.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint c WHERE c.conrelid = 'ops.api_tokens'::regclass AND c.contype = 'c' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM regexp_matches(c.conbin::text, ':funcid (\d+)', 'g') m JOIN pg_proc p ON p.oid = m[1]::oid WHERE p.provolatile <> 'i')

defects.title: The twenty most recently finished jobs are twenty jobs that never finished
defects.why:
"The twenty most recently finished jobs", for the ops dashboard. ORDER BY finished_at DESC is the obvious way to write that.

In PostgreSQL, DESC implies NULLS FIRST. It is documented and it is the opposite of what almost everyone assumes, because ascending order puts nulls last and nothing suggests the default flips. finished_at is null while a job is running and null forever for a job whose worker died, because the scheduler writes the row before it forks and only updates it when the worker reports back.

24 such rows have accumulated since 2025. They sort ahead of every finished run, so all 20 rows the view returns have a null finished_at and not one of them is a run the view was written to show. The dashboard renders twenty blank timestamps, which reads as a rendering fault rather than a query doing what it says. ORDER BY finished_at DESC NULLS LAST is the whole fix.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.v_recent_job_runs WHERE finished_at IS NULL

defects.title: Featured products held in an integer array, so nothing can reference them
defects.why:
The three products a campaign features. A join table was the obvious shape and it was rejected as heavy for three ids, which it is.

An array cannot carry a foreign key. PostgreSQL has no syntax for "every element of this array references that table", so nothing stops an id here from naming a product that was deleted or one that never existed. Measured: 10 of the 60 campaigns name a product that is not in storefront.products, left behind by the 2019 catalogue tidy-up. Deleting a product succeeds and leaves every campaign that features it pointing at nothing.

It also cannot be joined without unnesting, so the report that lists campaigns by featured product scans every campaign and expands every array. A GIN index answers "which campaigns contain product 7", which is the opposite of the question the report asks.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.campaigns c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM unnest(c.featured_product_ids) pid WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM storefront.products p WHERE p.product_id = pid))

defects.title: jsonb keeps the last of a duplicated key and the packed weight is gone
defects.why:
Some suppliers send the same key twice: their sheets list a packed weight and a unit weight and both are labelled weight_kg. JSON does not forbid that, so nothing rejects the document.

jsonb keeps the last value for a duplicated key and discards the rest, with no error, no warning and no log line. Measured on product 20: the source reads weight_kg 20.5 and then weight_kg 2.1, and spec holds 2.1. The catalogue shows the unit weight where the shipping calculator needs the packed one.

100 products are affected. The lost value is recoverable only because spec_source happens to still hold the original text, which was kept for debugging rather than for this. json rather than jsonb would have preserved both, and so would text.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.products WHERE spec_source LIKE '%"weight_kg"%"weight_kg"%'

defects.title: Eleven years of order lines all created at the same instant
defects.why:
order_items had no row-level timestamp and the Meridian model needs one, so the column was added with a default and NOT NULL in a single statement. It ran, it was quick enough, and every row came out non-null.

A volatile default makes ADD COLUMN rewrite the table, and the rewrite evaluates now() once for the whole statement. Measured: 16,001 order lines carry one identical created_at, the instant the migration ran, and the column holds only 2 distinct values across the whole table.

Rows written afterwards get their real time, so the column is correct going forward and wrong for everything behind it, with nothing marking the boundary. The value is plausible, which is why it survives review. Any report that cohorts order lines by created_at puts the entire pre-2023 business into a single day.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT created_at) FROM storefront.order_items

defects.title: 285 products are neither discontinued nor not discontinued
defects.why:
Discontinuation moved out of the buyers' spreadsheet. The column is nullable because the import could only classify the products it found in the spreadsheet, and the rest were left for someone to decide later. Nobody decided.

A null boolean is not false, it is unknown, and three-valued logic makes that bite in a way a null anything else does not. WHERE is_discontinued does not return those rows and WHERE NOT is_discontinued does not return them either. The two branches the application believes are exhaustive drop the same rows.

Measured: 2,000 products, 285 of them null, and the two branches together return 1,715. A product with a null here is absent from the live catalogue and absent from the discontinued list. The only way to notice is to add the two counts and compare them against the table, which nobody does, because the whole point of a boolean is that there are two cases.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.products WHERE is_discontinued IS NULL

defects.title: An unconstrained numeric cost that no two readers round the same way
defects.why:
The cost in the supplier's own currency, declared numeric with no precision and no scale, because nobody knew what scale the suppliers would send and unconstrained numeric takes whatever arrives.

It does take whatever arrives. Suppliers quoting a per-thousand rate send six decimal places and those are stored exactly. Measured: 594 of the 1,800 purchase order lines hold a value that is not equal to itself rounded to two places.

Every screen rounds to two on the way out, so a line reads 5.12 and a sum of a hundred such lines does not equal a hundred times 5.12. Finance chase the difference every month. numeric(12,4) would have made the rounding happen once, on write, where it could be seen. The type as written is not wrong about anything; it declines to decide, and pushes the decision onto every reader.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.purchase_order_lines WHERE unit_cost <> round(unit_cost, 2)

defects.title: The trigger that uppercases coupon codes runs AFTER INSERT and is discarded
defects.why:
Coupon codes are typed in by the marketing team and looked up by an application that uppercases whatever the customer entered. The fix was a trigger that uppercases the code on the way in, and the function itself is correct.

The trigger is AFTER INSERT. By then the row has been written and NEW is a copy: the assignment is legal, it runs, and PostgreSQL discards the result. Only a BEFORE trigger's NEW becomes the stored row. There is no error, no warning and no return value to ignore, so the trigger passes any test that inserts a row and reads it back through the same uppercasing application code.

Measured: 30 of the 300 coupons are stored lower case. Each one can never be redeemed, because the lookup uppercases first. The coupon exists, the campaign reports it as live, and the customer is told it is not valid.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.coupons WHERE code <> upper(code)

defects.title: A WHERE clause turns the outer join back into an inner one
defects.why:
Orders per customer, for the retention dashboard. Every customer is supposed to appear, including the ones who have never ordered, because a count of zero is the number the dashboard exists to show.

The LEFT JOIN is right. The WHERE clause below it is what breaks it: a customer with no orders gets a row of nulls from the join, and a null status fails o.status <> 'cancelled', so the row is filtered out again. The predicate belongs in the ON clause, where it would filter the joined side without discarding the customer.

Measured: 3,120 customers, 2,430 rows in the view. 690 customers have no order that is not cancelled and none of them appear. The dashboard shows no customers with zero orders and reads as though everyone who signs up buys something.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_customer_order_counts

defects.title: UNION drops 727 touchpoints that were two separate things the customer did
defects.why:
One row for every time a customer did something. Written with UNION because UNION is the word for putting two result sets together.

UNION removes duplicate rows across the whole result and does not stop at the boundary between the arms. A customer who placed two orders on the same day produces the same pair twice from the order arm alone, and a coupon is redeemed at the moment an order is placed, so the redemption arm repeats pairs the order arm has already produced. Every one of those is dropped.

Measured: 13,880 orders and 847 redemptions go in, 14,000 rows come out. 727 touchpoints are gone, and they belong to the most active customers, because those are the ones who do two things in a day. UNION ALL is the whole fix, and the version with the bug is the one that reads as more careful.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_customer_touchpoints
