defects.title: NOT IN over a column containing nulls returns nothing, always
defects.why:
Which Cross River customers the Silverback bridge never matched, so the integration team can work through them. The query reads exactly like the question.

legacy.customer_map.customer_id is null for the 36 Silverback customers that matched nothing. NOT IN against a list containing a null is never true: for any candidate the answer is unknown, because SQL cannot rule out that the null is the value being tested.

Measured: the view returns 0 rows. It would return 0 rows if every customer were unmatched, and 0 rows if the bridge were perfect. The honest answer, written as NOT EXISTS, is 1,956 customers. What the integration team see is an empty list, which they read as the bridge being complete.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_unmatched_customers

defects.title: The next-day dispatch deadline is written as 24 hours
defects.why:
Next-day dispatch, as the contract words it. The deadline is written as placed_at + interval '24 hours', which is the same thing all but two days a year.

Cross River is a UK business and a London day is 23 hours in March and 25 in October. An interval of 24 hours is an exact duration and adds the same number of seconds whatever the calendar is doing. An interval of 1 day, added in the local zone, lands on the same clock time the next day, which is what the contract means.

Measured: 68 orders in this view sit across a transition and carry a deadline an hour away from the one the customer was promised. In March the warehouse gets an hour less than it should and misses; in October it gets an hour more and the report calls it late when it was not. Twice a year, for one day, and then it goes away on its own.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_dispatch_sla WHERE dispatch_due_at <> ((placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London') + interval '1 day') AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London'

defects.title: DISTINCT ON picks the latest message with no ORDER BY that says which is latest
defects.why:
The last message on each ticket, for the list screen. DISTINCT ON is the PostgreSQL way to write one row per group and this is how it is usually written.

DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each group as the ORDER BY presents them, so the ORDER BY has to say which row is wanted. This one orders by ticket_id alone, which only groups the rows; within a ticket the order is whatever the plan produces. PostgreSQL does not warn, because the statement is legal and nothing tells it that "first" was meant to mean "latest".

600 of the 1,800 messages sit on a ticket that has more than one, so 600 tickets can show an arbitrary message as their most recent. The choice is stable while the plan is stable, which is why it survives testing, and it moves when the table is vacuumed, when the statistics change, or when the plan goes parallel. ORDER BY ticket_id, sent_at DESC is the fix and sent_at is not in the statement at all.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 FROM support.ticket_messages GROUP BY ticket_id HAVING count(*) > 1) s) * (CASE WHEN regexp_count(substring(a FROM ':sortClause \((.*?)\) :limitOffset'), '\{SORTGROUPCLAUSE') <= regexp_count(substring(a FROM ':distinctClause \((.*?)\) :sortClause'), '\{SORTGROUPCLAUSE') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM (SELECT ev_action::text FROM pg_rewrite WHERE ev_class = 'support.v_ticket_latest_message'::regclass AND rulename = '_RETURN') AS q(a)

defects.title: The incident index covers one quarter of four and every future partition misses it
defects.why:
Created at two in the morning during an incident. The customer history screen was timing out on the current quarter, an index on customer_id fixed it, and the change was made where the problem was.

An index created on the partitioned parent is built on every partition and on every partition added afterwards. This one was created on a single partition. Measured: 1 of the 4 partitions has it. The screen is fast for the quarter that was on fire and scans every row for the other three, which is the shape of the original problem and the reason nobody reopened the ticket.

Nothing reports it. psql's \d on the parent lists no index at all, and \d on each partition has to be read one at a time to see that three of the four differ. Every partition created from now on will be missing it too.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_inherits i JOIN pg_index x ON x.indrelid = i.inhrelid JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = i.inhrelid AND a.attnum = x.indkey[0] WHERE i.inhparent = 'archive.page_views_archive'::regclass AND a.attname = 'customer_id'

defects.title: ON DELETE SET DEFAULT writes a carrier id that does not exist
defects.why:
When a carrier is retired its service levels are meant to fall back to the house carrier, which the 2017 plan said would be carrier 9. ON DELETE SET DEFAULT with a column default of 9 says exactly that.

Carrier 9 was never created. PostgreSQL cannot check a SET DEFAULT action against the key it belongs to, because the parent row could always be inserted later, so this was accepted and has sat there since.

Retiring a carrier now fails. Measured: deleting a carrier that nothing else references fires the action, the action writes 9, and the same foreign key rejects 9 with "Key (carrier_id)=(9) is not present in table carriers". The error names the foreign key on the child table, which sends whoever reads it looking for a bad service level rather than at a default that points at nothing.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE contype = 'f' AND confdeltype = 'd' AND conrelid = 'fulfilment.carrier_service_levels'::regclass

defects.title: An expression index built on a function that is only declared immutable
defects.why:
The purchasing screen sorts supplier lines by what the product currently sells for, and the sort was slow, so an expression index was created. PostgreSQL allows an expression index only on an immutable expression, and this function is declared IMMUTABLE, which is the only thing it checks.

The function reads storefront.products, and prices change. An expression index stores the value the expression had when the row was written and never recomputes it, so the index holds each product's price as it stood when its supplier line was last touched. A query the planner answers from the index and the same query forced to read the table return different answers, and neither reports anything wrong.

REINDEX rebuilds it from today's prices, so a routine reindex silently changes what the purchasing screen shows. So does a restore, which builds the index from whatever the price list holds at restore time. Two copies loaded from the same dump on different days disagree.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid WHERE c.relname = 'ix_supplier_products_current_price' AND i.indexprs IS NOT NULL

defects.title: The reporting role is exempt from row security on every table in the cluster
defects.why:
The reporting role could not read support.ticket_messages, because that table has row security on and no policy. The ticket said reporting cannot see the data it needs. BYPASSRLS made it work in one statement and the ticket was closed the same afternoon.

BYPASSRLS is not a grant on a table. It is an attribute of the role and it switches off row security on every table in every database in the cluster, including tables that get policies later. The 2020 review that asked for per-team visibility on tickets can no longer be satisfied by writing a policy, because this role will not be subject to it.

Nothing about the support tables records this. It is one boolean in pg_authid, it is not in any schema dump, and a review of who can read tickets that starts from the table finds no answer and stops.

detect.sql: SELECT rolbypassrls::text FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'reporting_ro'

defects.title: The merge-chain view does not return for the six tickets that point at each other
defects.why:
Follows merged_into_ticket_id up to the ticket a duplicate was finally merged into, so the agent screen shows one conversation instead of a chain. The recursive CTE is the standard shape and it terminates on any chain that ends.

Six tickets are in a merge cycle: a points at b and b points at a, which the self-reference permits and nothing checks. This query has no CYCLE clause and no depth guard, so on those six it does not return. It allocates until the session is killed or the machine runs out of memory, and it takes the connection pool with it.

Every other ticket works. The view was tested on a chain, because a chain is what it is for, and the cycles were made later by two agents merging in opposite directions within a minute of each other. PostgreSQL has had the CYCLE clause since version 14 and this was written in 2020.

detect.sql: SELECT (WITH RECURSIVE c(t, n, path, cyc) AS (SELECT ticket_id, merged_into_ticket_id, ARRAY[ticket_id], false FROM support.tickets WHERE merged_into_ticket_id IS NOT NULL UNION ALL SELECT c.t, t.merged_into_ticket_id, c.path || t.ticket_id, t.ticket_id = ANY (c.path) FROM c JOIN support.tickets t ON t.ticket_id = c.n WHERE NOT c.cyc) SELECT count(DISTINCT t) FROM c WHERE cyc) * (CASE WHEN a ~ ':cycle_clause <>' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM (SELECT ev_action::text FROM pg_rewrite WHERE ev_class = 'support.v_ticket_merge_root'::regclass AND rulename = '_RETURN') AS q(a)

defects.title: A search_path attached to the database that no dump carries
defects.why:
Set during the 2025 cloud migration so the old reporting scripts, written against an era when everything lived in one schema, would keep working without being edited. It worked, and they were never edited.

The setting is attached to the database, not to a session or a role, so it applies to every connection that does not override it: the application, the migration tool, psql, a restore, and anyone debugging at two in the morning. public is no longer first, so an unqualified CREATE TABLE lands in storefront, and an unqualified reference to a name that exists in both schemas resolves to the storefront one without saying so.

It appears in no schema dump and in no migration anyone reads, and psql shows it only if you know to ask pg_db_role_setting. A restore into a fresh database does not carry it, so the scripts it exists for break on the restored copy and work on the original, which is the hardest version of this to diagnose.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_db_role_setting s JOIN pg_database d ON d.oid = s.setdatabase WHERE d.datname = current_database() AND s.setconfig::text LIKE '%search_path%'

defects.title: Revenue by day grouped by the microsecond, so every order is its own day
defects.why:
Revenue by day. The GROUP BY names placed_at, which is the column the day comes from, and the query runs and returns rows that look like a rollup.

placed_at is a timestamptz to the microsecond, so grouping by it groups by the instant. Measured: the view returns 12,145 rows, which is exactly the number of distinct placed_at values, so it is one row per order and not one per day. Each aggregate is correct for the group it was given and the group is wrong.

The output has the right column names and the right types. A chart drawn from it looks like a busy day-level chart, because twelve thousand points at microsecond resolution render as a dense line. date_trunc('day', placed_at) is the fix and the difference in the statement is nine characters.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_daily_revenue

defects.title: The SKU index cannot answer the prefix search it was created for
defects.why:
The warehouse screen looks products up by the start of the SKU, because that is what is printed on the shelf label and what people type. A B-tree index on sku was added for it and the screen stayed slow.

This database runs under en_US.utf8. A B-tree built in a non-C collation orders values by the collation's rules, which do not agree with byte order, so rows sharing a prefix are not guaranteed to be adjacent in it and the planner cannot use it for LIKE 'CR-01%'. Measured: the index exists and the plan for that query is still a sequential scan of all 2,000 products.

The fix is an opclass, varchar_pattern_ops, which builds a second index in byte order for exactly this case. Nothing about the CREATE INDEX suggests one is needed, and the identical statement is correct in a C-collation database, which is what the developer who wrote it had locally.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid JOIN pg_opclass o ON o.oid = i.indclass[0] WHERE c.relname = 'ix_products_sku' AND o.opcname NOT LIKE '%pattern_ops'

defects.title: Every erasure request since 2021 reports success and changes nothing
defects.why:
Customer records must not be hard deleted, so the privacy work added a trigger that was to blank the personal fields instead. Returning NULL from a BEFORE DELETE trigger cancels the delete, which is the documented way to do this.

It cancels it silently. Measured: deleting a customer that exists reports DELETE 0 and no error, which is also exactly what deleting a row that is not there reports. The erasure tool cannot tell the two apart, so it records the request as completed either way.

The blanking half was left for a follow-up ticket and never written, so the row is neither deleted nor anonymised. The only way to find that out is to read the row back afterwards, which the tool has no reason to do.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger t WHERE t.tgrelid = 'storefront.customers'::regclass AND t.tgname = 'trg_customers_soft_delete' AND NOT t.tgisinternal

defects.title: The purchase order reference sequence wraps instead of stopping
defects.why:
Purchase order references are PO- and six digits, so the sequence behind them was given a maximum of 999999 to match the format. CYCLE was added in the same statement to stop it erroring at the end, which read as making it more robust.

NO CYCLE makes an exhausted sequence raise an error on the next call. That is loud, it stops purchasing, and it is fixed in a minute by widening the column. CYCLE makes it wrap silently to 1 and reissue references that already exist on purchase orders going back to 2018. Measured: setting the counter to 999999 and calling nextval returns 1.

reference is UNIQUE, so the first reissued value is rejected and every purchase order after it fails too, with a unique violation naming a row from eight years earlier. Nothing in that error points at the sequence.

detect.sql: SELECT cycle_option FROM information_schema.sequences WHERE sequence_schema = 'supply' AND sequence_name = 'purchase_order_ref_seq'

defects.title: CREATE on schema public granted back to PUBLIC after PostgreSQL 15 removed it
defects.why:
The cloud migration moved the database to PostgreSQL 16 and a batch of scripts stopped working, because PostgreSQL 15 took CREATE on schema public away from PUBLIC. Granting it back was the smallest change that made them run.

It gives every role in the cluster, including ones created later for a service or a contractor, the right to create objects in public. Combined with the search_path set on this database, an object created there is reachable by an unqualified name from every connection, so any role can introduce a table, view or function that shadows one the application expects to resolve elsewhere.

Measured: has_schema_privilege('public', 'public', 'CREATE') is true. The grant is one line in a migration nobody rereads, and the default it reverses was a deliberate hardening change.

detect.sql: SELECT has_schema_privilege('public', 'public', 'CREATE')::text

defects.title: The only description of the refund amount column says the opposite of its CHECK
defects.why:
Written by the person who designed the chargeback flow, describing what the column was going to mean once that flow shipped. The flow never shipped and the comment stayed.

amount_cents carries CHECK (amount_cents > 0), so a negative value cannot be stored at all. The comment says it is negative for chargebacks, and it is the only description of this column anywhere: it is what psql shows, what a schema browser shows, and what the data dictionary was generated from.

The chargeback importer was written against it and has been failing on every chargeback since it was switched on, with a check violation that reads as bad input from the payment provider. The team maintaining it have been chasing the provider rather than the column, because the column's own documentation agrees with them.

detect.sql: SELECT (col_description('payments.refunds'::regclass, (SELECT attnum FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'payments.refunds'::regclass AND attname = 'amount_cents')) ILIKE '%negative%')::text

defects.title: A rule re-evaluates the sequence, so the audit row points at the wrong receipt
defects.why:
Goods-in was going to keep an audit copy of every receipt, written in the style the author knew, which was rules rather than triggers.

A rule is not a trigger. It is a query rewrite: PostgreSQL substitutes the rule's statement into the submitted one and replaces every reference to NEW with the expression that produced it, not with the value it produced. receipt_id comes from a sequence default, so NEW.receipt_id in the rule body is a second nextval call.

Measured: inserting one receipt produces a receipt with id 1 and an audit row claiming to describe receipt 2, and the sequence advances twice. Nothing errors. The audit table fills with plausible rows pointing at receipts that do not exist. supply.receipts has never held a row, so this has never run, and it is waiting for the day goods-in is finally built.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_rules WHERE schemaname = 'supply' AND tablename = 'receipts'

defects.title: Concatenating a null carrier URL blanks the whole tracking link
defects.why:
The despatch note prints a tracking link per shipment, built by concatenating the carrier's tracking URL with the consignment's tracking code. Both parts are in the database and the view reads correctly.

Concatenation is null-propagating: anything || NULL is NULL, not the other operand. SameDay Couriers were onboarded without a tracking portal, so their tracking_url is null, and every shipment they carry produces a null link rather than a link missing its prefix. The tracking code beside it is present and correct on all of them.

Measured: 3,542 of the 10,622 shipments print a blank where the link should be. Nothing errors, because a null renders as an empty string on the page. concat() would return the prefix it has, and coalesce on the URL would make the gap visible.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.v_shipment_labels WHERE tracking_link IS NULL AND tracking_code IS NOT NULL

defects.title: A CASE with no ELSE files every cancelled order under null
defects.why:
The lifecycle column on the operations dashboard maps an order's status onto the three words the business uses. The CASE lists every status its author had in front of them.

'cancelled' is not one of them, and a CASE with no ELSE returns null for anything that matches no branch. PostgreSQL does not require an ELSE and does not warn that one is missing.

Measured: 1,735 cancelled orders come back with a null lifecycle. The dashboard groups by that column, so they arrive as a fourth bucket with no name and are read as orders the pipeline has not classified yet. They are counted in the total and excluded from every band, so the bands do not sum to the total.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_order_lifecycle WHERE lifecycle_band IS NULL

defects.title: The purchase line audit is FOR EACH STATEMENT, so a 147-row update logs one row
defects.why:
Goods-in asked for the audit trail that orders have had since 2020. The row trigger on storefront.orders was the slowest thing in the nightly import, so this one was written FOR EACH STATEMENT on the reasoning that it would be cheaper.

It is cheaper, because it fires once per statement rather than once per row. A statement trigger has no NEW record, so it cannot record which line changed, and the function logs the table and the operation and nothing else.

Measured: an UPDATE touching 147 purchase order lines writes exactly one row to ops.event_log, saying only that an update happened. The audit trail has rows in it and cannot answer the question it was built for. FOR EACH ROW is the fix, and it is in the CREATE TRIGGER rather than in the function.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'supply.purchase_order_lines'::regclass AND NOT tgisinternal AND (tgtype & 1) = 0

defects.title: BETWEEN two dates ends at midnight, so the year-end extract loses 31 December
defects.why:
The year-end extract finance reconciles against the bank, written once for 2024 with the two ends of the calendar year exactly as finance wrote them on the ticket.

A bare date compared against a timestamptz is midnight on that date. BETWEEN includes both ends, so the upper end is 2024-12-31 00:00:00 and the year runs to the first instant of its last day rather than through it.

Measured: 4 orders placed after midnight on 31 December 2024 fall outside the extract. It balances against nothing and the four are found by hand every January, which is now part of the year-end checklist. The fix is < '2025-01-01', and the reason nobody has made it is that the view looks like it already says what it means.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.orders o WHERE o.placed_at >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND o.placed_at < DATE '2025-01-01' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM analytics.v_finance_year_2024 v WHERE v.order_id = o.order_id)

defects.title: Adding one month clamps to the shorter month, so month-end invoices fall due early
defects.why:
Supplier terms are net one month from the date the order was raised, and this is the view the purchase ledger ages against. Adding an interval of one month is the obvious way to write 'a month later'.

Interval arithmetic works in months rather than days and clamps to the last day of the target month when the source day does not exist in it. An order raised on 31 January falls due on 28 February; one raised on 31 March falls due on 30 April.

Measured: 11 of the 600 purchase orders are clamped, each by one to three days. All of them are month-end orders, which is where the volume is, and the supplier's own ledger holds the date the terms give. The aging report marks those invoices overdue before the supplier believes they are due.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.v_purchase_order_terms v JOIN supply.purchase_orders p USING (purchase_order_id) WHERE extract(day FROM v.payable_on) <> extract(day FROM p.raised_at)

defects.title: count(*) over a LEFT JOIN reports one ticket for every customer who has none
defects.why:
Tickets per customer, for the support load report. The LEFT JOIN is deliberate and correct: a customer who has never raised a ticket has to appear, because the report is read to find out who is not using the desk.

count(*) counts rows, and the row a LEFT JOIN manufactures for an unmatched customer is still a row. count(t.ticket_id) counts non-null values and would return zero, which is the whole difference between the two forms.

Measured: 2,520 of the 3,120 customers have never raised a ticket, and all 2,520 are reported with a count of one. The report totals 3,120 tickets against the 600 rows in support.tickets, and it has never been checked against that table because it is read as a report about customers.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_customer_ticket_counts v WHERE v.ticket_count = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM support.tickets t WHERE t.customer_id = v.customer_id)

defects.title: A leftover join to order_items multiplies every order total in the spend view
defects.why:
Lifetime spend per customer, for the loyalty tiers. The join to order_items is there because an earlier version also reported the number of items bought; that column was dropped when the tier rules changed and the join was left behind.

A join to a child table multiplies the parent row. An order with four lines appears four times and sum(o.total_cents) adds that order's total four times. The aggregate is correct for the rows it was given and the rows are wrong, and the statement looks ordinary because the sum names a column from the table it is grouped by.

Measured: 2,730 of the 3,120 customers are reported as having spent more than they have, by a factor that varies with how many lines their orders carry, so the inflation is not a constant anyone could spot as one. Tiers have been assigned from this view since 2024, and the customers who buy many cheap items are promoted hardest.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_customer_spend v WHERE v.lifetime_spend_cents <> (SELECT sum(o.total_cents) FROM storefront.orders o WHERE o.customer_id = v.customer_id)

defects.title: placed_at::date renders in the session timezone, so the daily counts depend on who ran them
defects.why:
Orders by day, for the operations standup. placed_at is a timestamptz, which is the right type, and ::date is the shortest way to get a day out of it.

A timestamptz has no day of its own. Casting one to date renders the instant in the session's TimeZone setting and takes the date part, so the view returns a different answer to two sessions with different settings. The server runs UTC, psql on the analyst's laptop inherits Europe/London, and the reporting pool sets nothing at all.

Measured: 342 of the 13,880 orders fall on a different day under Europe/London than under UTC, being everything placed between midnight and 01:00 local during British Summer Time. The daily counts disagree by a handful of orders depending on who ran the query, which reads as a race with the nightly load rather than as a timezone. The detection query asserts the shape, because the wrong answer only appears when the two sessions are compared.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_views WHERE schemaname = 'analytics' AND viewname = 'v_orders_by_day' AND definition NOT LIKE '%AT TIME ZONE%'

defects.title: The headline product reads element zero of a one-based array, so every row is null
defects.why:
The campaign list shows one headline product per campaign, taken as the first element of the featured array, written by somebody whose last ten years were in application code where the first element is element zero.

SQL arrays are one-based, and PostgreSQL does not treat a subscript below the lower bound as an error: reading outside an array returns null, the same as reading a null column. The statement runs, the column is typed correctly, and every row comes back empty.

Measured: all 60 campaigns have featured products and all 60 report no headline product. The list screen renders the blank as 'none selected', which is a state the campaign tool can genuinely produce, so the page looks like a marketing problem rather than a query one. Changing the 0 to a 1 fixes every row.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.v_campaign_headline WHERE headline_product_id IS NULL

defects.title: Reconciliation compares a double precision amount with =, so 1,304 matching transactions do not match
defects.why:
Finance reconciles card takings against orders: a transaction is matched when the amount captured equals the total on the order it paid for. The amount is in major units and the order total is in cents, so one side is multiplied by a hundred and the two are compared.

amount is double precision. 213.64 is not representable in binary floating point, and multiplying the nearest value by a hundred does not land on 21364. It lands a fraction away, and = is exact.

Measured: 1,304 of the 12,145 transactions fail to match an order whose total is the same money, and all 1,304 match once the amount is rounded to two decimal places as numeric first. They reach the unreconciled report every month, in a different set each month as new transactions are written, and they clear themselves the moment somebody re-keys the amount by hand.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.v_transaction_reconciliation WHERE NOT reconciled

defects.title: The receipt sanity check joins its two halves with OR, so no quantity can fail it
defects.why:
A stocktake found receipt lines with a negative received quantity and lines claiming more received than were ordered. The constraint was written in the review that followed, by somebody listing the two conditions the way they had just said them out loud.

The word between them has to be AND. With OR the constraint asks whether either half holds, and for any quantity one of them does: a received quantity of -5 is not negative and over-ordered, it is merely negative, and -5 <= quantity_ordered is true, so the row passes.

Measured: a line with 20 ordered and -5 received inserts successfully, and so does one with 20 ordered and 10,000 received. The constraint is listed on the table and appears in every schema review as covering this exact problem. Only a value that is both negative and over the order is refused, and no number is both.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint c WHERE c.conname = 'purchase_order_lines_receipt_sane' AND (xpath('/row/ok/text()', query_to_xml(format('SELECT coalesce((%s), true) AS ok FROM (SELECT 20 AS quantity_ordered, -5 AS quantity_received) x', pg_get_expr(c.conbin, c.conrelid)), false, true, '')))[1]::text::boolean

defects.title: app_writer has INSERT on orders and no USAGE on the sequence behind its key
defects.why:
The checkout service was moved off the owner account onto a role of its own, which is what the 2025 security review asked for. The grants were written from the list of tables the service writes to.

A serial primary key is a default that calls nextval on a sequence, and a sequence is a separate object with its own privileges. INSERT on the table does not carry USAGE on the sequence behind its key.

Measured: as app_writer, inserting an order fails with 'permission denied for sequence orders_order_id_seq'. The role can read, update and delete, so a smoke test that touches an existing row passes and the failure is confined to new orders. Nothing in the grants names the sequence, so a review of who can write to storefront.orders shows the role correctly provisioned.

detect.sql: SELECT (has_table_privilege('app_writer', 'storefront.orders', 'INSERT') AND NOT has_sequence_privilege('app_writer', 'storefront.orders_order_id_seq', 'USAGE'))::text

defects.title: viewed_at was added to the key to get past the error, so page_view_id may repeat
defects.why:
The archive needed a primary key and PRIMARY KEY (page_view_id) was refused: PostgreSQL requires every unique constraint on a partitioned table to contain the partition key, because it can only enforce uniqueness inside one partition. Adding viewed_at made the error go away and the deploy went out.

The key that resulted promises something nobody asked for. It makes the pair unique and leaves page_view_id free to repeat, so the same archived page view can exist once in each quarter.

Measured: the same page_view_id inserts cleanly into two quarters. That is exactly what the archive loader produces when it is re-run over a window it has already copied, which is how it recovers from a failed night, and it is the one case the key was added to stop. The constraint is listed as the primary key, the column everybody joins on is in it, and the duplicate surfaces as a doubled row count in a report rather than as an error at load time.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'archive.page_views_archive'::regclass AND contype = 'p' AND cardinality(conkey) = 2

defects.title: archive.orders_base is an inheritance parent, so its primary key and bounds constrain nothing
defects.why:
A third approach to the archive, from the 2025 attempt to make the two hand-made year tables queryable as one. Table inheritance predates declarative partitioning, it is still in PostgreSQL, and it is what the tutorial open at the time described.

An inheritance parent is not a partitioned table. A query naming it reads the children too, which is the effect that was wanted, and nothing else carries down. The primary key on the parent constrains only the parent's own rows, and there is no partition bound to say which year a row belongs in.

Measured: the parent holds no rows of its own and returns 2,924 from the children, and an order_id already present in orders_2024 inserts into orders_2023 with the parent then returning two rows for it. Nothing stops a 2024 order being written into the 2023 table. Every tool that reports table sizes shows the parent as empty, and the difference between that and what a count returns is the whole trap.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_inherits i JOIN pg_class p ON p.oid = i.inhparent WHERE p.relkind = 'r' AND i.inhparent = 'archive.orders_base'::regclass

defects.title: The rewritten checkout posts an empty gift message, so 884 orders count as gifts
defects.why:
The 2023 checkout rewrite posts every field on the form whether or not it was filled in. An untouched gift message arrives as an empty string and the column takes it, because an empty string is a perfectly good varchar.

A null says no gift message was asked for. An empty string says one was asked for and is blank. Every count of gift orders is written as gift_message IS NOT NULL, because that is what the column meant from 2012 until the rewrite.

Measured: 884 orders carry an empty gift message and those same 884 are every order the IS NOT NULL test finds. The packing screen prints a blank gift card for each of them, which the warehouse has reported as a printer fault for three years, and the gifting report shows a step change in 2023 that was read as the rewrite's own success.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.orders WHERE gift_message = ''

defects.title: The order total trigger fires on INSERT only, so edited and deleted lines never update it
defects.why:
orders.total_cents is kept in step with the lines by a trigger, added when the basket service started writing lines directly and the totals stopped agreeing. It was written against the one case that was failing, which was a new line arriving.

A line can also be changed or removed, and neither fires this trigger. There is no second job that recomputes the total, and support edit lines every day, which is what the support desk screen is for.

Measured: adding five units to an existing line leaves the order total at 17,492, and inserting one new line then recomputes it to 61,722. The column still looks maintained, because it moves whenever anyone is watching a new order, and the orders that drift are the ones corrected after the fact. Adding OR UPDATE OR DELETE to the CREATE TRIGGER is the fix.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'storefront.order_items'::regclass AND tgname = 'trg_order_items_sync_total' AND (tgtype & 28) = 4

defects.title: Two fn_current_price functions, and search_path decides which one an unqualified call gets
defects.why:
The 2026 pricing rewrite moved the current-price lookup into storefront, next to the tables it reads, and gave it the behaviour the pricing team wanted: the last price the pricing job recorded, falling back to the catalogue price for products never repriced. The old one in catalog was left alone because the purchasing screen calls it by name.

Both are called fn_current_price and both take one integer. Nothing collides, because they are in different schemas, and an unqualified call is resolved against search_path at parse time. The database-level search_path puts storefront first, so every unqualified call in every application query reaches the new one, including calls written years before it existed.

Measured: the two return different prices for 333 of the 2,000 products; for product 6 the unqualified call returns 321 and catalog.fn_current_price returns 421. The difference between the two queries is a schema name written in neither of them, and changing search_path on one connection moves the answer again with no code changing.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.products p WHERE storefront.fn_current_price(p.product_id) <> catalog.fn_current_price(p.product_id)

defects.title: Stock reservation reads, decides and writes with nothing holding the row
defects.why:
Stock reservation at checkout: read what is available, refuse if there is not enough, otherwise write the new figure. Three statements in the order anyone would write them.

Nothing holds the row between the read and the write. Two checkouts for the same product read the same availability, both decide there is enough, and both write a figure computed from that read. The second UPDATE waits for the first to commit, because the row lock is taken then, and it then writes an absolute value calculated from a number that is already stale.

Measured: two concurrent transactions each reserving 5 units of product 3 both return true, and stock falls from 26 to 21 rather than to 16. One reservation is lost. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the read, or an UPDATE written as quantity_available - p_quantity with the check in its WHERE clause, fixes it. The function is correct under any test that runs one checkout at a time, and the symptom in production is a stock count that will not reconcile at the end of a sale day.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%INTO v_available%' AND prosrc NOT LIKE '%FOR UPDATE%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'storefront.fn_reserve_stock'::regproc

defects.title: storefront.box_number_seq outlived the product that used it
defects.why:
Box numbers are printed on the label and have to be unique across every box ever sent, so they came from a sequence rather than a per-table serial. It was created in storefront rather than subscriptions, because the despatch tooling that reads it lives there.

That choice is what makes it survive. DROP SCHEMA subscriptions CASCADE in 2021 takes everything inside the schema, and a default that merely references a sequence in another schema is a dependency in the wrong direction, so dropping the table removed the default and left the sequence standing.

Measured: the sequence exists, is owned by no column, and is referenced by no default, which distinguishes it from the other standalone sequences in this database. It appears in every pg_dump, in every schema diff, and in every object list, named for a product shut down five years ago.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c WHERE c.relkind = 'S' AND c.oid = 'storefront.box_number_seq'::regclass AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_depend d WHERE d.objid = c.oid AND d.deptype = 'a') AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_depend d WHERE d.refobjid = c.oid AND d.classid = 'pg_attrdef'::regclass)

defects.title: The spec feed uses -> instead of ->>, so every value carries its JSON quotes
defects.why:
The catalogue feed reads this view for the spec fields the marketplace wants as columns. -> is the operator everybody reaches for, because it is the one that navigates a document.

-> returns jsonb and ->> returns text. A string pulled out with -> keeps its JSON quoting, so the origin of a product made in the UK is the four characters "UK" rather than the two anybody wants, and the column's type is jsonb rather than the text the feed declares.

Measured: all 500 products with a spec compare equal to '"UK"' and none of them compare equal to 'UK'. Nothing errors, because the view never compares anything itself. The marketplace rejects the quoted values as unknown countries and the feed logs them as rejected rows, which reads as the marketplace being strict about a country list. The fix is one extra angle bracket, three times.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.v_product_spec_fields WHERE origin::text = '"UK"'

defects.title: The Silverback volume report counts the 100 orders their application had deleted
defects.why:
Silverback order volumes, for the acquisition review. The table is read whole, because it is an archive of a closed system and an archive does not change.

Silverback never deleted a row. Their application set is_deleted and their own reports filtered on it, which is a convention Cross River does not use anywhere else and which nothing in the column name makes mandatory. The import kept the flag; the convention did not come with it.

Measured: the view reports 100 more orders than the table holds undeleted. They are cancellations and test orders, so they are the small ones, and the volume is 2.5% high in a report read to judge whether the acquisition paid for itself. The same query written by anyone who worked at Silverback would carry the filter, and the same query written by anyone at Cross River will not.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT sum(order_count) FROM analytics.v_legacy_order_volumes) - (SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.orders WHERE NOT is_deleted)

defects.title: Every table created in analytics from now on is readable by PUBLIC before anyone sees it
defects.why:
The analysts kept asking for SELECT on each new rollup table as it was built, and each request was a ticket. ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES was the answer: every table created in analytics from then on is readable without anybody being asked.

It grants to PUBLIC, which is every role that exists and every role created later, and it applies at creation, to tables that do not exist yet, so there is no moment at which somebody reviews the grant against the data the table turned out to hold.

Measured: a table created in analytics is readable by PUBLIC the instant it exists. Nothing in the table's own grants records a decision, because the ACL is attached at creation and looks exactly like an explicit grant somebody made. The rule itself lives in pg_default_acl, which no schema comparison tool anybody here runs reports on.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_default_acl a JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = a.defaclnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'analytics'

defects.title: The customer import skips every conflicting row and reports only what went in
defects.why:
The customer feed used to abort on the first duplicate email and lose the rest of the batch, so ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING was added and the overnight failures stopped. The job logs what this function returns and has reported a clean run every night since.

DO NOTHING with no conflict target does not mean 'skip the duplicate emails'. It means skip any row that violates any unique or exclusion constraint on the table, present or future. ROW_COUNT afterwards counts the rows that went in, not the rows that were offered.

Measured: offering two rows, one of them an email already present, returns 1. There is nowhere the other row is written down. The rows skipped are the ones worth looking at: the case variants of an address already there, which the unique index treats as new and a person would call the same customer. ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE, or no clause at all with a rejects table beside it, would keep them.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'ops.fn_import_customers'::regproc

defects.title: The receipt check raises a notice and returns true, so it refuses nothing
defects.why:
Goods-in calls this before writing a receipt, to stop a line being received in a larger quantity than it was ordered in. It was written by somebody debugging the receipt flow who wanted to watch the over-receipts go past before deciding what to do about them, and the decision was never taken.

RAISE NOTICE prints and continues; RAISE EXCEPTION stops the transaction. Nothing about a notice makes the function refuse anything, and it returns true whatever it was given, so the caller writes the receipt.

Measured: a receipt of 99,999 against a line of 20 ordered returns true, with a notice. The notice reaches the client, where the driver discards it, and the server log, where it is one line among the day's several thousand with no error level on it. Goods-in have no reason to think the check does anything other than pass.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%RAISE NOTICE%' AND prosrc LIKE '%RETURN true;%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'supply.fn_check_receipt'::regproc

defects.title: Card takings by month count only the transactions with a stored payment method
defects.why:
Card takings by month, for the finance pack. count(*) was in the first draft and came back from review with a note saying count(*) is vague about what is being counted, so it was changed to name a column.

count(column) counts the rows where that column is not null. It agrees with count(*) only on a column that is never null, and payment_method_id is null on every transaction taken from a customer who did not store the card: guest checkout, one-off orders, everything taken over the phone.

Measured: 6,940 of the 12,145 transactions have no stored payment method, so the count is 57% low and has been since the review. It is the same shape as the correct query, it returns a plausible number, and it moves with the business every month, which is why the gap against the bank statement was put down to settlement timing. The amount column beside it is summed correctly, so the pack disagrees with itself.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.transactions) - (SELECT sum(transaction_count) FROM analytics.v_transactions_by_month)

defects.title: The top-sellers view takes ten rows in no order at all
defects.why:
The ten best-selling products, for the front of the merchandising dashboard. The aggregate is right, the grouping is right, and the limit is the ten the dashboard has room for.

There is no ORDER BY. LIMIT without one returns whatever ten rows the plan produces first, which is not an order: it is a side effect of the scan, the grouping strategy and the number of workers the planner chose. SQL defines no default ordering and PostgreSQL does not warn, because the statement asked for ten rows and got ten rows.

Measured: the definition carries a LIMIT and no ORDER BY. The dashboard has shown ten products under a Top sellers heading since 2024 and they are not the top ten. They are stable enough to look deliberate, because the plan is stable while the table is, and they change when it is vacuumed or when the row count crosses a parallel threshold, which reads as the bestsellers moving.

detect.sql: SELECT (a !~ ':limitCount <>' AND a ~ ':sortClause <>')::text FROM (SELECT ev_action::text FROM pg_rewrite WHERE ev_class = 'analytics.v_top_products'::regclass AND rulename = '_RETURN') AS q(a)

defects.title: The archived branches of the order index put the store in the customer column
defects.why:
One list of every order the business has ever had, live and archived, for the reconciliation that runs against the payment provider. UNION ALL of three branches, written in one sitting.

The second and third branches list customer_id and store_id the other way round. A UNION matches its branches by position, never by name, so the archived rows arrive with the store in the customer column and the customer in the store column. Both are integer, so there is nothing to object to: no type error to raise, and no name to disagree with, because the result's column names come from the first branch alone.

Measured: 1,456 of the 1,460 archived 2023 rows carry a customer id that is not the order's customer. The four that agree are the ones where the two numbers happen to match. The values are integers in the right range, so they look like customers, and the reconciliation matches most of them against a real customer who did not place the order. The live branch is correct and is most of the rows, so any spot check starting at the top passes.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_order_index v JOIN archive.orders_2023 a ON a.order_id = v.order_id WHERE v.source = 'archive-2023' AND v.customer_id IS DISTINCT FROM a.customer_id

defects.title: report_reader has three of the ten ticket columns, so SELECT * is refused
defects.why:
The reporting role was given the ticket columns it needs and not the ones it does not. Ticket bodies and customer identifiers stay out of reach, which is what the 2025 review asked for, and a column list is the precise way to say it.

A column grant is not a table grant. SELECT * expands to every column in the table, including the seven this role was deliberately not given, so any query written with a star is refused: permission denied for table tickets, naming the table the role can plainly read. The message names no column, because the check stops at the first one the role cannot see.

Measured: the role holds privileges on three of the ten columns. Selecting those three by name works; SELECT * fails. Every tool that writes its own SQL writes a star, so the schema browser, the ad hoc query window and the dashboard's preview all fail while the hand-written dashboards work, and that mixture reads as the role being intermittently broken rather than as a grant that is exactly as narrow as it was written to be.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.column_privileges WHERE grantee = 'report_reader' AND table_schema = 'support' AND table_name = 'tickets'

defects.title: The order balance is null for every order that was never refunded
defects.why:
Order total minus everything refunded against it. The subquery is right and the arithmetic is right on any order that has been refunded.

sum() over no rows returns null, not zero. An order with no refunds makes the subquery null, and anything minus null is null, so the function returns a number for the orders that were partly refunded and null for the ones still owed in full. A coalesce around the sum is the fix, and it is the one everybody forgets, because it only shows on the empty case and the empty case is not the one anyone tests.

Measured: 13,638 of the 13,880 orders return null. The billing job reads a null balance as nothing outstanding, so those orders are never chased. The 242 that were partly refunded are chased correctly, which is why the function has never looked broken to the people who watch it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.orders o WHERE payments.fn_order_balance(o.order_id) IS NULL

defects.title: Cancel and confirm take the same two tables in opposite orders
defects.why:
Two routines that touch the same two tables. fn_cancel_order releases the stock first and then marks the order cancelled, because stock is what customers are waiting on. fn_confirm_order marks the order confirmed first and then takes the stock, because the status is what the checkout screen reads back.

Each is correct alone and each was reviewed alone. An UPDATE holds its row lock until the transaction ends, so a cancel holding the inventory row and a confirm holding the order row are each waiting for the row the other holds. PostgreSQL finds the cycle after deadlock_timeout and aborts one of them.

Measured: two sessions running the two statement orders against the same order and the same product deadlock, and one is aborted. It needs the pair to overlap on the same product, so the rate tracks how busy the store is: never in testing, several times a day at Christmas. The error names the two queries and neither function, and a retry succeeds, so it has been absorbed by a retry in the caller since 2024. Making both take the two tables in the same order removes it outright.

detect.sql: SELECT ((SELECT prosrc FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'storefront.fn_cancel_order'::regproc) ~ 'inventory[\s\S]*orders' AND (SELECT prosrc FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'storefront.fn_confirm_order'::regproc) ~ 'orders[\s\S]*inventory')::text

defects.title: The provider file prints the month where the minutes belong
defects.why:
Order timestamps as a string, for the file the payment provider takes. They want the minute rather than the second, in that exact layout.

In a to_char mask MM is months. Minutes are MI. The two sit four lines apart in the manual's format table and the mask reads correctly in English, so it survived review by the person who wrote it and the person who checked it against the provider's specification. The date half is right, because MM is months and that is where months belong; the time half prints the hour and then the month again.

Measured: 13,656 of the 13,880 orders carry a time that is not the time they were placed. The 224 that agree were placed in a minute that happens to match their month. Every value is a real two-digit number in the right position, so the file parses and the provider accepts it, and the disagreement surfaces only when somebody matches a disputed transaction to an order by timestamp.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_order_timestamps v JOIN storefront.orders o USING (order_id) WHERE right(v.placed_at_label, 2) <> to_char(o.placed_at, 'MI')

defects.title: ix_orders_covering holds a second copy of the orders table
defects.why:
Index-only scans were the answer to the 2024 reporting load, and an INCLUDE list is how a btree carries the columns a query needs without putting them in the key. The list was written by taking every column the reports touched, which turned out to be every column there is.

The index is now a second copy of the table. Every insert writes both and every update to any column writes both. Heap-only tuple updates are no longer possible on this table at all, because they require that no indexed column changed and every column is indexed.

Measured: the index covers all 12 columns of a 12-column table. It does what the planner says it does, which is why it has never been questioned: index-only scans on orders did get faster. The cost is paid on the write side, by checkout, and reads as the orders table bloating and taking twice as long to vacuum.

detect.sql: SELECT cardinality(i.indkey) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid WHERE c.relname = 'ix_orders_covering'

defects.title: The heavy-items list drops everything from ten kilos up
defects.why:
Heavy items need a two-person lift, so the warehouse asked for a list of everything over five kilos. weight_kg is one of the attributes, the filter is the number they asked for, and the view was signed off against a sample of ten products that all came back correct.

attribute_value is text. Comparing text to text compares character by character, so '14.5' is less than '5' for the same reason 'ab' is less than 'b', and every weight that does not begin with a digit above five falls out. The ten sampled products were all single-digit weights, which is the range where the two comparisons agree.

Measured: the view lists 36 products. 250 weigh more than five kilos. The 214 missing are the ones from ten kilos up, so the list omits exactly the items it exists to flag, and the heavier the item the more certain it is to be left off. Casting the value to numeric fixes it, and makes the view fail on the rows whose value is not a number, which is the other half of what this column allows.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.v_heavy_products

defects.title: No trigger in this database fires on TRUNCATE, so an emptied table is unaudited
defects.why:
The audit triggers are FOR EACH ROW, which is the only level that can see the row being written. A row trigger cannot be declared on TRUNCATE at all: TRUNCATE removes every row without producing one, so only a statement-level trigger can observe it.

Nothing in this database has one. A TRUNCATE on an audited table empties it and writes no audit row, so the log's last entry for that table is whatever ordinary write came before, and it reads as a table that went quiet rather than one that was emptied.

Measured: truncating support.tickets removes all 600 rows and leaves the audit log at the 606 entries it already held. The nightly reload uses TRUNCATE because it is faster than DELETE and needs no vacuum afterwards, which is the advice everybody follows and is the same property that makes it invisible here. A DELETE of the same rows is fully audited.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE NOT tgisinternal AND (tgtype & 32) <> 0 AND tgrelid IN ('storefront.orders'::regclass, 'support.tickets'::regclass)

defects.title: An order line's product check is evaluated once and never again
defects.why:
An order line must name a product that exists. A foreign key says so and there is one, but the 2025 catalogue work needed the rule to mean sellable rather than merely present, and a CHECK calling a function was the way to express something a foreign key cannot.

A CHECK is evaluated when the row it sits on is written, and at no other time. Nothing re-checks the existing lines when a product changes, so the constraint holds for the instant of the insert and says nothing afterwards, which is the opposite of what a constraint is read as guaranteeing.

The function is also not immutable, and PostgreSQL trusts a CHECK to be. A dump and restore evaluates it against whatever the products table holds at that point in the restore, which is nothing until the products data is loaded, so a restore that loads order_items first fails on every row. That is the failure that finds this, and it finds it during a recovery.

Measured: the constraint exists and calls a function that reads another table. It has never rejected anything, because the catalogue has never deleted a product, and that is the only reason it looks like it works.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint c WHERE c.conrelid = 'storefront.order_items'::regclass AND c.contype = 'c' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM regexp_matches(c.conbin::text, ':funcid (\d+)', 'g') m JOIN pg_proc p ON p.oid = m[1]::oid WHERE p.pronamespace <> 'pg_catalog'::regnamespace AND p.provolatile <> 'i')

defects.title: The supplier cost feed sets every product to one price
defects.why:
The supplier cost feed lands in the staging table and this applies it. The UPDATE names both tables and sets the cost from the staged row, which is the shape everybody writes.

There is no condition tying the source to the target. UPDATE ... FROM with nothing joining the two pairs every target row with every source row, and PostgreSQL updates each target row once, from an arbitrary one of them. It is not an error and it is not ambiguous to the parser: a missing join condition in an UPDATE looks exactly like a deliberate cross join.

Measured: one staged cost line sets all 2,000 supplier products to that cost, and the function reports 2,000 rows. The WHERE clause that is present filters the staging rows, so the statement reads as though it is scoped, and the number it returns is the number of supplier products rather than the number of staged lines, which is the number anybody would check it against.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%FROM ops.import_staging s%' AND prosrc !~ 'WHERE[\s\S]*sp\.')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'ops.fn_apply_supplier_costs'::regproc

defects.title: Any role can call the audit purge with the owner's rights
defects.why:
SECURITY DEFINER was added so the nightly purge could run as a role that owns nothing else. That half of the change was reviewed and is right.

A new function is executable by PUBLIC. That is the PostgreSQL default, and it is the one default that surprises people, because every other object starts closed. Nothing revokes it, so every role in the database -- the reporting role, the checkout role, any role created next year -- can call a function that deletes from the audit log with the owner's privileges.

Measured: this is the only SECURITY DEFINER function in the database and its privileges have never been touched, so its access list is null, which means the default, which means PUBLIC. The argument is a timestamp, so the caller chooses how much of the log to remove, and the function returns the number of rows it took, which is the only record that it ran at all. REVOKE EXECUTE ... FROM PUBLIC is the fix and is one line.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = p.pronamespace WHERE p.prosecdef AND p.proacl IS NULL AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')

defects.title: Ten thousand shipments dispatched and none recorded as delivered
defects.why:
delivered_at was added with the rest of the table, for the delivery confirmation the carriers send back. The webhook that would write it was the next sprint's work and the warehouse launched without it.

Nothing has ever written the column. dispatched_at is set by the picking system, which is inside the building, so the shipment lifecycle looks complete right up to the last step. There is no error and no gap: the column is nullable, which is correct for a shipment that has not arrived yet, and a column that is empty because nothing fills it is indistinguishable from one that is correct and merely waiting.

Measured: 10,622 shipments dispatched, none delivered. Every report that filters on delivery returns nothing, which reads as a report with a bug rather than a column with no data, and the delivery performance figure the carriers are paid against has been taken from the carriers' own files since 2016 for exactly this reason.

detect.sql: SELECT count(delivered_at) FROM fulfilment.shipments

defects.title: A blank staging line is discarded and the insert reports success
defects.why:
A blank line in a feed file used to become a staging row with nothing in it, which the import then failed on. This trigger throws those away before they land, and the import stopped failing.

A BEFORE trigger that returns NULL cancels the write. The row is not inserted, no error is raised, and the statement reports a row count of zero for a statement it was given a row for. A client driver reads that as success, because the INSERT did not fail.

Measured: inserting a staging row with an empty raw_line inserts nothing and says nothing. The condition catches genuine blank lines, which is what it was written for, and it catches any line the feed sends as an empty string for its own reasons: a supplier sending an empty field rather than omitting it, a file whose last line is a terminator. Those rows are gone, and the only trace is that the staged count is lower than the file's line count, which nobody compares.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger t JOIN pg_proc p ON p.oid = t.tgfoid WHERE t.tgrelid = 'ops.import_staging'::regclass AND NOT t.tgisinternal AND (t.tgtype & 2) <> 0 AND p.prosrc LIKE '%RETURN NULL%'

defects.title: The staff-note audit cannot see a note being written for the first time
defects.why:
Staff notes are the one field an agent can write freely, so the 2025 review asked for a record of every change to one. The WHEN clause keeps the trigger off the updates that do not touch the note, which is almost all of them, and that is the only reason it is affordable on this table.

<> returns null when either side is null, and a WHEN clause fires on true and not on null. staff_note is null until somebody writes one, so the change that matters most -- the first note going on to an order -- is the one the clause cannot see. Removing a note is invisible for the same reason.

Measured: the trigger is declared with <> where IS DISTINCT FROM was meant, and writing a first note on an order produces no audit row. Every order in this database has a null staff_note, so the trigger has never fired and the audit it was added for has recorded nothing at all. It is present in every catalogue, enabled, and correct-looking.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger t WHERE t.tgname = 'trg_orders_staff_note_audit' AND NOT coalesce((xpath('/row/f/text()', query_to_xml(format('SELECT (%s) AS f FROM (SELECT NULL::text AS staff_note) old, (SELECT ''added''::text AS staff_note) new', substring(pg_get_triggerdef(t.oid) FROM 'WHEN \((.*)\) EXECUTE')), false, true, '')))[1]::text::boolean, false)

defects.title: The validated email type covers two agent rows and no customers
defects.why:
A domain is the way to say that a value has a shape wherever it is stored. This one was written during the 2025 data quality work and applied to the column the work started on.

It was applied to that column and no other. storefront.customers.email, legacy.customers.email_address and supply.suppliers.contact_email are all plain varchar and all accept anything. The domain exists, so a schema review finds a validated email type in the database and reads the estate as covered; the coverage is one column in one table holding two rows.

Measured: one column in the database uses the domain. The rule itself is correct, which is what makes it worse: it shows that somebody knew what the constraint should be, wrote it down, and left every column holding a real customer address outside it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE domain_name = 'email_address'

defects.title: Campaign targeting is a comma separated string, so LIKE matches the wrong segments
defects.why:
Campaign targeting moved from one segment per campaign to several. A second table was the obvious answer and would have taken a fortnight of application work, so the ids went into the existing row as a comma separated string and the campaign tool split them on the client.

Nothing in the database knows this column holds a list. It cannot be joined to the segments it names, it cannot be constrained to ids that exist, and membership has to be asked with LIKE, because that is the only operator that looks inside a string. LIKE '%1%' matches segment 1, segments 10 through 19, and segment 21.

Measured: asking for the campaigns targeting segment 1 with LIKE returns all 60 campaigns where the true answer is 20, so 40 are pulled in by a digit appearing inside another id. The counts are plausible and the campaigns are real, so the spend lands against the wrong segments in every report built on this column and none of them look empty or broken.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.campaigns WHERE target_segments LIKE '%1%') - (SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.campaigns WHERE '1' = ANY(string_to_array(target_segments, ',')))

defects.title: The archive index was created on the parent and never attached, so it is invalid
defects.why:
An index on viewed_at across the whole archive, added when the retention report started timing out. On a partitioned table the parent index is a template: it is created ON ONLY the parent and becomes usable once a matching index exists on every partition and has been attached to it.

The attaching was to be done partition by partition out of hours, and the first one was never done. An index in that state is marked invalid, and an invalid index is ignored by the planner while still being listed by every catalogue query, every schema browser and every dump.

Measured: one invalid index in the database. It answers nothing, so the retention report still times out, and the ticket was closed as fixed in 2025. Building a matching index on each partition and attaching it turns the parent valid on its own.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'archive.page_views_archive'::regclass AND NOT indisvalid

defects.title: The supplier code format check matches anywhere in the value
defects.why:
Supplier codes are three letters and three digits. The check was added after a supplier was created as 'tbc' and a purchase order went out against it.

The pattern has no anchors. ~ asks whether the pattern matches anywhere in the value, not whether it matches the whole of it, so the constraint accepts any string with SUP and three digits somewhere inside it: a code with trailing whitespace, a code with a pasted line break, a code with a second code appended to it. ^ and $ are the whole of the fix.

Measured: the constraint exists and is unanchored. It rejects 'tbc', which is the case it was written for and the case anybody tests, and accepts every malformed code that has actually been entered, because those are typing and paste errors around a real code rather than something instead of one.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint c WHERE c.conname = 'suppliers_code_format' AND (xpath('/row/ok/text()', query_to_xml(format('SELECT coalesce((%s), true) AS ok FROM (SELECT ''not a code: SUP123, trailing''::text AS code) x', pg_get_expr(c.conbin, c.conrelid)), false, true, '')))[1]::text::boolean

defects.title: order_items references orders twice, under two names
defects.why:
order_items already referenced orders. The 2025 constraint review worked from a list of the references the application relies on, found no constraint of the name it expected, and added one.

PostgreSQL does not object to a second foreign key over the same columns to the same table. There are now two, with different names and identical meaning, and both are enforced: every insert and every update of order_id takes a row lock on the parent order twice and runs the check twice.

Measured: two foreign keys from order_items to orders. Nothing is wrong with the data and nothing ever will be, which is why this survives. The cost is a doubled check on the busiest write path in the database, and dropping either one is a change with no visible benefit to whoever has to approve it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'storefront.order_items'::regclass AND contype = 'f' AND confrelid = 'storefront.orders'::regclass

defects.title: Three tables cannot have an update or a delete replicated
defects.why:
Replica identity is what a logical replication stream sends to say which row an UPDATE or a DELETE applies to. The default is to use the primary key.

Three tables here have no primary key and no replica identity set, so the default resolves to nothing. Those tables can be replicated for INSERT and cannot be replicated for UPDATE or DELETE: the publisher raises an error on the statement, when the statement runs, on a table that has worked for years.

Measured: three tables are in this state. Nothing warns while no publication exists, so the warehouse team's first change data capture pilot is the event that finds them, and it finds them as a production error rather than a configuration one. REPLICA IDENTITY FULL is the one-line answer and makes every update on those tables send the whole old row.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c WHERE c.relreplident = 'd' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint k WHERE k.conrelid = c.oid AND k.contype = 'p') AND c.oid IN ('ops.import_staging'::regclass, 'supply.contract_price_reviews'::regclass, 'conformance.rate_usage'::regclass)

defects.title: The shipment count joins on status as well as order, so it is always zero
defects.why:
How many shipments an order has. NATURAL JOIN is shorter than naming the key and reads as though it means the obvious thing.

A NATURAL JOIN joins on every column the two tables share by name, and nothing in the statement says what those are. orders and shipments share order_id, which is intended, and status, which is not: both have a status column, with different value sets meaning different things.

Measured: the two status vocabularies do not overlap at all -- an order is paid or cancelled, a shipment is picked or dispatched -- so this returns zero for every one of the 13,880 orders, including the ones among the 10,410 matched shipments that plainly have one. Zero is a plausible answer for an order with nothing shipped yet, so it reads as an order problem rather than a join, and the result moves again the moment either table gains or loses a column name.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.orders o WHERE storefront.fn_shipment_count_for_order(o.order_id) <> (SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.shipments s WHERE s.order_id = o.order_id)

defects.title: The variant list is aggregated in whatever order the plan produces
defects.why:
The variant codes for a product, as one value, for the feed the marketplace takes. array_agg is the right function and the grouping is right.

An aggregate with no ORDER BY inside it consumes its rows in whatever order the plan delivers them, so the array's order is a property of the plan and not of the data. The feed writes the array out as a joined string and the marketplace stores that string as the product's variant list, comparing it against the one it holds to decide whether anything changed.

Measured: the definition aggregates with no ordering. Nothing changes and the string changes anyway, whenever the plan does: after a vacuum, after the statistics move, when the scan goes parallel. Every product is then republished and re-reviewed at the marketplace's end, which has been put down to their side being flaky. ORDER BY variant_sku inside the aggregate makes it stable and is four words.

detect.sql: SELECT (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM regexp_matches(a, '\{AGGREF :aggfnoid (\d+) .*?:aggorder (<>|\()', 'g') m JOIN pg_proc p ON p.oid = m[1]::oid WHERE p.proname = 'array_agg' AND m[2] = '<>'))::text FROM (SELECT ev_action::text FROM pg_rewrite WHERE ev_class = 'catalog.v_product_variant_skus'::regclass AND rulename = '_RETURN') AS q(a)

defects.title: Every product against every campaign, 108,000 rows
defects.why:
Campaigns and the products they feature, for the merchandising export. The comma between the two tables is the old join syntax and means the same thing as CROSS JOIN: the predicate that ties them together belongs in the WHERE clause, and this WHERE filters campaigns and joins nothing.

There is no error and no warning. Comma syntax cannot distinguish a join somebody forgot to write from a cross join somebody wanted, and the plan is correct for what was asked.

Measured: 54 campaigns pass the filter and there are 2,000 products, so the view is 108,000 rows. The export reads as a campaign featuring the whole catalogue, which is what a sitewide sale looks like, so the first people to see it assumed the campaigns had been set up that way. The join belongs through marketing.promotion_products and is one line.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.v_campaign_products

defects.title: A LEAKPROOF function quotes the row it was given back in an error
defects.why:
Ticket search was slow once row security went on support.ticket_messages. The planner will not push a filter below a security barrier unless the function in it is LEAKPROOF, and marking it so made the search fast again.

LEAKPROOF is a promise that the function reveals nothing about its arguments beyond its return value: no error message quoting them, no timing difference, nothing. This one raises an exception containing the message body it was given. The planner takes the promise at face value and evaluates it before the row security filter, so a caller who cannot read a row can make the database quote that row's contents back at them.

Measured: calling it with an empty search term returns the ticket body in the error text, and it is the only LEAKPROOF function in the database. Only a superuser can mark one, so it was set deliberately, by somebody who read the speed-up as the point of the flag. Removing LEAKPROOF restores the barrier and puts the search back where it was.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = p.pronamespace WHERE p.proleakproof AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')

defects.title: The checkout role runs with no statement timeout at all
defects.why:
The checkout role's nightly reconciliation kept being killed at the database's ten second statement timeout. Raising the timeout for that one job needed a code change, so the timeout was turned off for the role instead, which needed none.

A role setting applies to every session the role opens, not to the job that prompted it. This is the role the storefront connects as, so every checkout query now runs without a time limit: a query that would have been killed at ten seconds holds its locks, its connection and its share of work_mem until it finishes or the client gives up.

Measured: one role has statement_timeout set to zero. It lives in pg_db_role_setting, which no schema comparison reads and no migration reproduces, so a database rebuilt from the repository behaves differently from the one in production and nothing in the repository says why.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_db_role_setting s JOIN pg_roles r ON r.oid = s.setrole WHERE r.rolname = 'app_writer' AND s.setconfig @> ARRAY['statement_timeout=0']

defects.title: A search for a percent sign returns the whole catalogue
defects.why:
How many products match what the customer typed, for the result count above the grid. The term is passed as a parameter, so there is no SQL injection here and a review looking for one finds nothing.

The term is concatenated into a LIKE pattern, and a LIKE pattern has metacharacters of its own. A term containing % or _ is not searched for, it is interpreted: a bare % matches everything, and an underscore matches any one character, so a part code written with underscores returns far more than it should.

Measured: searching for a single percent sign returns all 2,000 products. The grid below the count is built from the same pattern, so the two agree and neither looks wrong; the count is simply the wrong number for what was typed. Escaping the term fixes it.

detect.sql: SELECT catalog.fn_product_search_count('%')

defects.title: A quarter of purchase orders are expected on the first of January 1900
defects.why:
The buyers' screen requires an expected date before a purchase order can be raised, and for a quarter of orders the supplier has not given one. The convention that grew up is to type the earliest date the screen accepts.

1900-01-01 is a real date to the database and to every query written over it. It is not null, so nothing checking for a missing date finds one, and it sorts before every genuine date, so it wins every min() and every earliest-first ordering in the purchasing reports.

Measured: 150 of the 600 purchase orders carry it. The overdue report counts them as 126 years late, which is loud enough that people have learned to ignore the top of that list and quiet enough that the orders genuinely overdue are ignored along with them. Nothing in the schema records the convention: expected_on is a nullable date that is never null.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.purchase_orders WHERE expected_on = DATE '1900-01-01'

defects.title: outcome_code is "char", so every three-letter code is stored as its initial
defects.why:
A short outcome code beside the job status, so the operations dashboard can colour a row without parsing the detail text. The codes are OK, ERR and RUN, and the column was declared "char" because that reads as the character type with nothing wasted.

"char" in double quotes is not char. It is a one byte internal type PostgreSQL uses in its own catalogues, and it truncates anything longer without an error. char(3) was meant and would have held the codes.

Measured: writing 'ERR' stores 'E' and reports success, and all 1,024 existing rows hold a single character. The three codes still differ from each other, because their initials happen to, so the dashboard colours correctly and nothing looks wrong. The next code anybody adds beginning with O, E or R is silently a value already in use.

detect.sql: SELECT (atttypid::regtype::text = '"char"')::text FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'ops.job_runs'::regclass AND attname = 'outcome_code'

defects.title: The shipping weight view asks for a key the document does not have
defects.why:
Shipping weight out of the spec document, for the carrier rate card. The operator is right this time and the cast is right; the key is 'weight' and the document calls it 'weight_kg'.

A jsonb lookup for a key that is not there returns null. It cannot be an error: a document type has no schema, so there is nothing against which a missing key is wrong. The view compiles, runs, and returns a column of nulls.
