Measured: all 500 products with a spec have a null shipping weight here, and every one of them has a weight_kg in the document. The rate card reads a null weight as the lowest band, so every parcel is quoted at the cheapest rate and the carrier invoices the real one. The difference has been booked as a carrier billing discrepancy since 2019.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.v_product_shipping_weight WHERE weight_kg IS NULL

defects.title: DISTINCT hid the fan-out and 2,041 real orders with it
defects.why:
Customer order values, for the finance extract. The join to order_items was there to exclude orders with no lines, and it returned one row per line, so the duplicates were removed with DISTINCT and the counts looked right again.

DISTINCT removes duplicate rows, not duplicate joins. It collapses the fan-out, and it collapses anything else identical in the selected columns, so two genuine orders by the same customer for the same amount become one row. Adding order_id would keep them and would bring the fan-out back, which is why it is not there.

Measured: the extract holds 11,839 rows against 13,880 orders. The 2,041 missing are real orders, concentrated on the customers who order the same thing repeatedly, so the extract understates exactly the customers finance cares most about. Nothing about the output looks duplicated or short, which is what DISTINCT was added to achieve.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_customer_order_values

defects.title: The currency exposure report drops every order with no currency
defects.why:
Everything not priced in dollars, for the currency exposure report. <> is the operator for is not, and it is the one everybody reaches for.

<> against a null is null, and a WHERE clause keeps only the rows where it is true. Every order whose currency_code is null is therefore excluded, even though a null currency is certainly not USD. The filter reads as removing one currency and it removes one currency plus everything unknown.

Measured: the view covers 4,420 of the 13,880 orders. The 9,460 it drops have no currency_code, because the column was added in 2023 and only orders after the backfill carry one, and the report is presented as covering the book. currency_code IS DISTINCT FROM 'USD' includes them.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_non_usd_orders

defects.title: The job count returns 1,024 whatever status it is asked for
defects.why:
How many job runs finished in a given state, for the operations dashboard. The parameter was named after the thing it holds, which is what naming advice says to do everywhere else.

A parameter sharing a column's name is ambiguous, and PostgreSQL refuses the query rather than guess. That error is what the pragma at the top of the function is for: it picks a winner. use_column makes the column win, so `j.status = status` is the column compared to itself, which is true for every row. The pragma was added to clear the error and nobody re-read the query it was clearing it inside.

Measured: the function returns 1,024 for every argument, including one that matches nothing. The dashboard shows the same number in all three panels, which was read as the job queue being evenly loaded. Renaming the parameter fixes it and makes the pragma unnecessary.

detect.sql: SELECT ops.fn_count_jobs_by_status('no-such-status')

defects.title: Paging the ticket queue by opened_at alone can show a ticket twice or not at all
defects.why:
A page of tickets, oldest first, for the queue screen's paging. LIMIT and OFFSET are how paging is written and the ordering is the one the screen shows.

opened_at is not unique, and OFFSET counts rows in an order that is only partly determined. Rows tied on opened_at may be arranged differently by the query for page two than they were by the query for page one, so a ticket can appear on both pages and another on neither. Nothing errors, and each page is individually correct.

Measured: 390 of the 600 tickets share an opened_at with another ticket, so more than half the queue sits on a tie. Agents have reported tickets vanishing from the queue and being worked twice, which has been put down to the other agent. Adding ticket_id as a second sort key makes the order total and the paging exact.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%ORDER BY t.opened_at%' AND prosrc LIKE '%OFFSET%' AND prosrc NOT LIKE '%opened_at, t.ticket_id%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'support.fn_ticket_page'::regproc

defects.title: A CHECK naming three kinds accepts every value there is
defects.why:
value_kind says how an attribute's value is meant to be parsed. It was advisory for seven years, and the 2025 data quality work set out to make it mean something, starting with a constraint naming the three kinds. The trailing NULL is in the list because the column is nullable and the author wanted the constraint to permit a null, which a list membership test does not obviously do.

It does not do it that way, and it does something else entirely. IN with a null in the list returns true on a match and null on anything else, never false. A CHECK rejects only what is false, so this one accepts every value there is: the three it names, a typo, an empty string, the whole of a pasted email. It is the most permissive constraint the syntax allows and it reads as the most restrictive.

Measured: the constraint exists, names three kinds, and accepts a value_kind of 'zzz'. Everything in the table today is one of the three, because the catalogue feed only writes those, so the constraint has never been tested by anything other than the code that does not need it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint c WHERE c.conname = 'product_attributes_value_kind_known' AND (xpath('/row/ok/text()', query_to_xml(format('SELECT coalesce((%s), true) AS ok FROM (SELECT ''zzz''::text AS value_kind) x', pg_get_expr(c.conbin, c.conrelid)), false, true, '')))[1]::text::boolean

defects.title: 3,020 receipts print hashes where the total should be
defects.why:
Money formatted for the receipt renderer. to_char with an explicit mask is how every formatted column in this schema is written, and the mask was sized in 2024 against an order book where nothing had gone past 999.99.

to_char does not widen a mask and does not error when the number will not fit. It returns a string of hashes the width of the mask, and the renderer prints what it is given.

Measured: 3,020 of the 13,880 receipts show ####### instead of a total. They are the largest orders in the book, so the fault lands on the customers most likely to query it. Widening the mask, or dropping it and letting to_char size itself, fixes every one.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_order_receipt_lines WHERE total_formatted LIKE '%#%'

defects.title: The largest order per customer returns 3,339 rows for 2,730 customers
defects.why:
One row per customer, holding their largest order, for the account manager screen. The window function is the right tool and the partition is right.

rank() and row_number() are not interchangeable. row_number() is arbitrary between tied rows but always returns one per partition; rank() gives tied rows the same rank, so filtering to rank 1 returns every order tied on the top value. The screen reads the view expecting one row per customer and renders whichever arrives last.

Measured: 3,339 rows for 2,730 customers. The 609 extra rows are second and third copies of a customer whose largest orders came to the same money, which is common here because the catalogue has fixed prices and people re-order the same basket. Changing rank() to row_number() returns 2,730 rows and needs no other edit.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_largest_order_per_customer

defects.title: The weekend report has never included a Sunday
defects.why:
Weekend trading, for the staffing model. Saturday and Sunday were written as 6 and 7, which is how the week is numbered on a calendar, in ISO 8601, and by extract(isodow).

extract(dow) numbers the week 0 to 6 with Sunday at 0. 7 is not a value it can return, so half the filter matches nothing. Sunday is missing rather than duplicated, and no error says so.

Measured: the view returns 1,985 orders where the real weekend is 3,967. Every Sunday in fourteen years of trading is absent, which is 1,982 orders. The staffing model reads the weekend as half its true size, and the number is consistent year on year, so the trend looks sound. extract(isodow) numbers the week 1 to 7 and makes the filter as written correct.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_weekend_orders

defects.title: Casting the partition key to date makes every partition scan
defects.why:
Recent page views out of the archive. The partition key is viewed_at and the filter is on viewed_at, so this is the query partitioning was introduced to make fast.

Pruning matches the filter against the partition bounds, and it can only do that when the key appears on its own. Casting it to date produces an expression the planner cannot compare to a timestamptz bound, so nothing is excluded. The cast is there because the report compares against a date and the mismatch was removed on the wrong side of the operator.

Measured: the plan for this view appends a sequential scan of all four partitions, including the two that end before the filter starts. The same filter written as viewed_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00+00' prunes to two partitions and returns identical rows. Only the plan shows the difference, so the archive gets slower with every quarter added and nothing reports it.

detect.sql: SELECT (pg_get_viewdef('archive.v_page_views_recent'::regclass) LIKE '%::date%')::text

defects.title: The supplier loader writes the email into the name and the name into the email
defects.why:
Loads new suppliers from the procurement feed. The INSERT has no column list, so columns are matched by position. The feed exports code, then contact address, then trading name, and the SELECT was written in the order the feed arrives; the table declares name before contact_email.

Both columns are character varying and neither carries a constraint, so nothing objects. The contact address is written into name and the trading name into contact_email.

Measured: loading SUP901 as 'Acme Fixings Ltd' with 'buying@acme.invalid' stores the address as the supplier's name and the name as the address. Every screen showing a supplier shows an email where the name goes, and mail to a new supplier is addressed to a string that is not an address. A positional INSERT breaks a second way too: adding a column to supply.suppliers shifts every value one place right. Naming the columns fixes both.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%INSERT INTO supply.suppliers%' AND prosrc NOT LIKE '%(supplier_id%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'supply.fn_load_supplier_feed'::regproc

defects.title: A UNIQUE constraint containing the primary key enforces nothing
defects.why:
One line per product per order. The rule is real: two lines for the same product on one order are a double charge.

order_item_id is the primary key and is already unique on its own, so any constraint containing it is satisfied by it and can never be violated, whatever else is listed alongside. This one accepts two lines for the same product on the same order as readily as no constraint at all.

The key is in the column list because the constraint was refused without it: the table already held six such duplicates, the two-column form failed on existing data, and adding the key made it succeed. The success was read as the rule being delivered.

Measured: the constraint exists and is listed as UNIQUE in every catalogue, the six duplicates it was written to stop are still there, and inserting a seventh is accepted. It maintains an index on every write and enforces nothing.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'storefront.order_items'::regclass AND conname = 'order_items_one_line_per_product' AND 1 = ANY(conkey)

defects.title: The cancellation rate has reported zero since 2024
defects.why:
The cancellation rate for the board pack. Both counts are integers, because count() returns bigint, and the multiplication by 100 sits at the end where it reads naturally.

Dividing one integer by another in SQL is integer division: the remainder is discarded before anything else happens. The division runs first and gives zero for every rate under a hundred per cent, and the multiplication then scales zero. There is no warning and no rounding. The result is exactly zero and looks like a measurement.

Measured: 1,735 of the 13,880 orders are cancelled, which is 12.5 per cent, and the view reports 0. It has reported 0 every month since 2024, and a rate that never moves reads as a well run business rather than a broken column. Multiplying by 100 before dividing, or making either side numeric, gives 12.5.

detect.sql: SELECT cancelled_pct FROM analytics.v_cancellation_rate

defects.title: 342 orders are filed under the wrong trading day
defects.why:
Orders bucketed into UK trading days. placed_at is timestamptz, so it has to be converted to a local time before a date can be taken, and 'GMT' was chosen because the business is in the UK and GMT is what the UK clock is called.

GMT is a fixed offset of zero. Europe/London is a zone that spends about half the year an hour ahead of it. From late March to late October the conversion runs an hour early, so anything placed in the first hour of a British day is booked to the day before.

Measured: 342 orders sit under the wrong trading day. They are the ones placed between midnight and one in the morning British time during British Summer Time, so the error is invisible in a monthly total and moves revenue across a month end twice a year. AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London' is right in both halves of the year.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_orders_by_gmt_day v JOIN storefront.orders o USING (order_id) WHERE v.trading_day <> (o.placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London')::date

defects.title: The dispatch chase list holds every order in the database
defects.why:
Orders with nothing dispatched, for the fulfilment chase list. The shape is the standard anti-join: outer join to shipments, keep the rows where the shipment side is null.

The test is on delivered_at rather than on the joined key. delivered_at is null on every shipment in this database, so it is null both when there is no shipment and when there is one that has not been marked delivered, and the filter cannot tell those apart. Testing s.shipment_id IS NULL is an anti-join; testing a nullable payload column is not.

Measured: the chase list holds all 13,880 orders. 3,470 genuinely have no shipment; the other 10,410 have one and are listed anyway. Fulfilment have treated the list as unusable since it was built, which is why nobody has raised it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_orders_awaiting_dispatch

defects.title: The rollup mutex is never released and outlives the transaction
defects.why:
Stops two copies of the nightly rollup running at once. An advisory lock is the right mechanism and the constant key is what makes it a mutex.

pg_advisory_lock takes a session lock, not a transaction lock. It is held until released by name or until the session ends, and committing does not touch it. This function never calls pg_advisory_unlock.

Measured: after calling the function and committing, the lock is still held by the backend. On a pooled connection the session does not end, so the connection returns to the pool still holding the mutex and the next night's run blocks on it against a backend that is idle and shows nothing wrong. The job does not fail, it waits, so the alert that fires is for a job that has not finished rather than one that crashed. pg_advisory_xact_lock releases at commit and is what this wanted.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%pg_advisory_lock(%' AND prosrc NOT LIKE '%pg_advisory_unlock%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'analytics.fn_begin_rollup'::regproc

defects.title: The role whose access was revoked inherits more than it lost
defects.why:
report_reader is the newsletter reconciliation account. The 2025 access review revoked its direct grants, confirmed it could no longer read the tables it had been given, and closed the finding.

The same review made report_reader a member of reporting_ro, so that one role would hold the reporting grants instead of two. Membership is inherited by default, so report_reader holds everything reporting_ro holds, which is more than it ever had directly.

reporting_ro also carries BYPASSRLS, and that is inherited as well. The one account in this database whose access was deliberately narrowed now has the widest reach of any of them. Nothing in the revoke, the grant, or either role's own definition shows the two statements together.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_auth_members m JOIN pg_roles r ON r.oid = m.roleid JOIN pg_roles g ON g.oid = m.member WHERE g.rolname = 'report_reader' AND r.rolname = 'reporting_ro'

defects.title: Deleting an order does two different things depending on which column names it
defects.why:
fulfilment.returns points at storefront.orders twice: the order being returned, and the replacement order raised for it. The 2025 tidy-up made the replacement reference cascade, so that cancelling a replacement would not leave a return pointing at nothing.

The other reference to the same parent was left as NO ACTION. Deleting an order now does two different things depending on which column happens to name it: it is refused when the order is the one being returned, and it silently deletes the return record when the order was the replacement. The return row is the only record that the customer sent goods back.

Measured: of the two foreign keys from fulfilment.returns to storefront.orders, one cascades and one does not. They are ordinary foreign keys to the same table, one line apart in every catalogue listing, and nothing puts the two actions side by side unless both definitions are read.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'fulfilment.returns'::regclass AND contype = 'f' AND confdeltype = 'c'

defects.title: Every job duration on the dashboard is zero
defects.why:
Records a job run and how long it took. now() is the ordinary way to stamp a row and it is used correctly at the start.

now() returns the time the current transaction began, not the time it is called, and it returns the same value however often it is called inside that transaction. This function opens no transaction of its own, so both stamps come from one and the finish is recorded as the start.

Measured: running the function returns an elapsed time of 00:00:00 for a job that scans the whole order table. Every duration on the operations dashboard is zero, which reads as a rounding problem or a dashboard bug rather than the column being wrong, and it hides the one thing the column exists to show: which jobs are getting slower. clock_timestamp() returns the wall clock at the moment of the call and is what this wanted.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%now()%' AND prosrc NOT LIKE '%clock_timestamp%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'ops.fn_run_job'::regproc

defects.title: Every retry worker queues behind the same row
defects.why:
Claims the oldest failed job for retry. FOR UPDATE is there so two workers cannot claim the same row, which is exactly what it does.

What it also does is make every other worker wait. FOR UPDATE blocks on a locked row rather than passing over it, so a second worker running this query queues behind the first on the same row and a third queues behind the second. The pool serialises onto one job at a time however many workers are started, and adding workers makes the queue slower rather than faster.

Nothing errors and nothing times out, because the wait is an ordinary lock wait on a row that is about to be updated. It shows as idle workers and a queue that drains at a fixed rate whatever the fleet size. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED passes over the locked row and gives each worker a different job.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%FOR UPDATE%' AND prosrc NOT LIKE '%SKIP LOCKED%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'ops.fn_claim_failed_job'::regproc

defects.title: The attempt counter returns the value from before it incremented it
defects.why:
Bumps a job's attempt count and returns the new value. The UPDATE and the read are in one statement, done deliberately so nothing could change between them.

Every part of one statement sees the same snapshot, taken before the statement ran. The UPDATE in the CTE does its work, and the SELECT in the main query reads the row as it was before it, so the value handed back is the old count. The row on disk is right; the return value is one behind.

Measured: on a job run whose attempt is 1, the function returns 1 and leaves 2 in the table. The retry logic compares the returned count against the limit, so every job gets one more attempt than it is allowed. Reading from the CTE's own RETURNING clause gives the new value and is a shorter query.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%RETURNING job_run_id%' AND prosrc NOT LIKE '%RETURNING attempt%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'ops.fn_bump_attempt'::regproc

defects.title: A column dropped in 2021 is still stored on every customer row
defects.why:
The packing notes went with the subscription product in 2021. DROP COLUMN is the right statement and it returned immediately, which is what made it look like the space went with it.

DROP COLUMN does not touch the rows. It marks the attribute dropped in the catalogue and leaves every stored value in place, because avoiding a rewrite of a large table is the point of the instant form. The values are still on disk, still read with every page, and still in every base backup, and no query can reach them, which also means no query can redact them.

The attribute number is not reissued either. PostgreSQL allows 1,600 attributes per table over the table's whole life rather than at any one moment, so each add-and-drop cycle spends one permanently.

Measured: storefront.customers carries one dropped attribute. Any statement that rewrites the table reclaims it; nothing prompts for one and nothing reports the space.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'storefront.customers'::regclass AND attisdropped

defects.title: The sign-in lookup scans the customer table on every call
defects.why:
Finds a customer by email whatever the case, which is necessary here because the unique constraint on email is case-sensitive and the same address exists in more than one casing.

An index on email cannot answer a filter on lower(email). The planner matches an index to the whole expression, not to the column inside it, so the only index that helps is one declared on lower(email). There is none, so every lookup scans the table.

Measured: no index on storefront.customers mentions lower(). This is the sign-in path, so it runs on every session and gets slower in proportion to the customer table for as long as nobody reads the plan. CREATE INDEX ON storefront.customers (lower(email)) is the whole fix and changes no query.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i WHERE i.indrelid = 'storefront.customers'::regclass AND pg_get_expr(i.indexprs, i.indrelid) = 'lower((email)::text)'

defects.title: Two status columns, two type systems, one word in common
defects.why:
An order's state is a PostgreSQL enum, storefront.order_status, added by the 2023 Meridian work. A shipment's state is a varchar with a CHECK, written in 2016 and never revisited. Both columns are called status, both say where something has got to, and they share no type, no vocabulary, and no document either list appears in.

Measured: exactly one of the seven order states appears in the shipment list. 'pending' on an order means not yet paid; 'pending' on a shipment means not yet picked. A paid order with a pending shipment and a pending order with a pending shipment are different situations that read identically on a screen showing both.

Adding a value is a type change on one side and a constraint change on the other, so no single migration can keep them in step, and nothing fails when they drift further.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_enum e CROSS JOIN pg_constraint c WHERE e.enumtypid = 'storefront.order_status'::regtype AND c.conname = 'shipments_status_check' AND c.conrelid = 'fulfilment.shipments'::regclass AND (xpath('/row/ok/text()', query_to_xml(format('SELECT coalesce((%s), true) AS ok FROM (SELECT %L::text AS status) x', pg_get_expr(c.conbin, c.conrelid), e.enumlabel), false, true, '')))[1]::text::boolean

defects.title: The de-duplication view matches every customer against themselves
defects.why:
Cross River customers who also appear in the Silverback import, for the de-duplication work. The subquery was written from memory of the legacy table's shape.

legacy.customers has no column called email; it is email_address. A name a subquery cannot resolve is looked for in the enclosing query and found there, so the subquery becomes "select this customer's own email, once per legacy row" and the test compares each customer's email with itself. It is true for every customer, and it never reads the legacy table's data at all.

PostgreSQL cannot object: outer references are how correlated subqueries work, and this is indistinguishable from a deliberate one. Measured: the view returns all 3,120 customers where the real answer is 789. Qualifying the inner column as l.email turns the silent success into the error that should have been raised.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_customers_also_in_silverback

defects.title: The unknown-currency branch can never be taken
defects.why:
A readable currency label for the finance extract, with a branch for the orders that predate the currency column.

Nothing is equal to null, including null. The first branch evaluates to null rather than true for exactly the rows it was written for, so those rows fall through to the ELSE and are labelled as a foreign currency instead of as unknown. The branch is unreachable: no row can take it.

Measured: not one of the 13,880 orders is labelled unknown. The 9,460 with no currency are labelled other, sitting alongside genuine foreign-currency orders and indistinguishable from them. WHEN currency_code IS NULL takes the branch as written.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_order_currency_label WHERE currency_label = 'unknown'

defects.title: Lifetime revenue counts every legacy order at a hundredth of its value
defects.why:
Every order ever taken, across the current book and the Silverback import, for the lifetime revenue figure. The two branches line up on column count and on type, because money casts to numeric without complaint.

storefront.orders.total_cents is minor units. legacy.orders.order_total is the money type and is major units. The union puts them in one column called amount, so every legacy order is counted at a hundredth of its value, and nothing in the output says which branch a row came from.

Measured: the view totals 881,554,866. The current book contributes 880,737,046 in cents; the 4,000 legacy orders contribute 817,820 where they should contribute 8,178,200. The shortfall sits entirely in the years before the acquisition, where nobody expects much revenue anyway.

detect.sql: SELECT sum(amount)::bigint FROM analytics.v_all_order_amounts

defects.title: One side of the SKU match is in the C collation and the other is not
defects.why:
supplier_sku was moved to the C collation by the 2025 performance work, because byte-order comparison is genuinely faster than a linguistic one. The column it is matched against, storefront.products.sku, was left on the database default.

Two columns in different collations can still be compared, but they do not agree on order. C sorts every uppercase letter before every lowercase one, so a range scan, a BETWEEN and an ORDER BY over the two columns place the same row differently. An index on one side cannot serve a merge join against the other, because the planner will not assume two collations produce the same order, so the join re-sorts instead.

Equality never errors, which is how the reconciliation reading both columns kept working and got slower. The speed the change bought on one column is paid back on every join that uses it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'supply.supplier_products'::regclass AND attname = 'supplier_sku' AND attcollation <> (SELECT attcollation FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'storefront.products'::regclass AND attname = 'sku')

defects.title: Product descriptions are stored uncompressed and always will be
defects.why:
description is long free text and lives out of line in TOAST. The 2025 performance work set its storage to EXTERNAL because uncompressed TOAST can be read in slices and the product page reads only the first paragraph.

EXTERNAL stores the value out of line and uncompressed. The slice read it was chosen for is faster; everything else is larger. The column no longer compresses at all, so the TOAST table, every page read of it, the write-ahead log for each change, and every base backup carry the full text.

Measured: the column's storage mode is e. The setting lives on the column rather than in any configuration file, and it applies only to values written after the change, so the table holds a mixture and grows as rows are rewritten. Nothing reports it and no query behaves differently.

detect.sql: SELECT attstorage::text FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'storefront.products'::regclass AND attname = 'description'

defects.title: The outstanding purchase order total is one line, not all of them
defects.why:
Adds up what has been ordered from suppliers and not yet received. The loop is right, the accumulator is right, and the arithmetic is right.

The RETURN is inside the loop. PL/pgSQL returns at the first RETURN it reaches, so the loop runs one iteration and the function hands back the first line's value as the total. A RETURN inside a loop is legal and common, and the indentation puts it in line with the accumulation, so nothing about it reads as misplaced.

Measured: the function returns 10,040 where the real outstanding value is 25,936,200. The number that comes back is the right magnitude for a single line, which is what has kept it from being questioned, and the purchasing dashboard shows about four hundredths of one per cent of the commitment it exists to report. Moving the RETURN below END LOOP is the whole fix.

detect.sql: SELECT supply.fn_outstanding_order_value()

defects.title: A status test in the ON clause filters nothing
defects.why:
Shipments raised against cancelled orders, for the write-off report. The condition on the order's status sits in the ON clause because that is where the other join conditions are, and putting it there is what keeps the outer join outer.

It keeps the join outer for the wrong rows. A condition in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN decides which rows of the right table are matched; it cannot remove rows of the left table, because a left join preserves those whether they match or not. An order that was never cancelled is still in the result, carrying nulls where the shipment should be.

Measured: the report returns all 13,880 orders, 12,145 of which were never cancelled. No cancelled order in this database has a shipment at all, so the report it was written to produce is empty and the one it produces is the order book. Moving the status test to the WHERE clause filters orders; leaving it in ON filters shipments, and the two read almost identically.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_cancelled_order_shipments

defects.title: Two ids joined into one string are not a key
defects.why:
A single-column key for each order line, for the export the warehouse system reads. That system has no composite key support, so the two ids are joined into one string.

Concatenating two variable-length numbers without a separator is not injective. Order 1 product 23 and order 12 product 3 both produce '123'. The export loses one of them silently, and which one survives depends on the order rows arrive in.

Measured: 27,761 order lines reduce to 27,753 distinct pairs of ids and to 27,751 distinct keys. Six of the lost lines are the duplicate pairs the table already permits; the other two are lines the concatenation cannot tell apart. Any separator that cannot appear in a number makes the key injective again.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT line_key) FROM analytics.v_order_line_keys

defects.title: The open ticket queue holds every ticket there is
defects.why:
Tickets that are neither resolved nor closed, for the open work queue. The negation was written once, around both tests, and the connective inside it was left as the and of the sentence it came from.

NOT (a AND b) is true whenever either test fails. A ticket has one status, so it can never be both resolved and closed, and the condition is therefore true for every row including the ones it was written to remove. NOT (a OR b), or the IN form, says what was meant.

Measured: the queue holds all 600 tickets, 300 of them resolved or closed. It has been twice its true size since it was built, and the screen's own paging is what has kept that from being obvious.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_open_tickets

defects.title: A line with no coupon comes back with no price
defects.why:
The price after a coupon. STRICT was added because the function does arithmetic and a null would only propagate anyway, which is true of the arithmetic and not of the function.

STRICT means the function is not called at all when any argument is null: PostgreSQL returns null without entering the body. A basket line with no coupon passes null for the discount, so the price comes back null rather than unchanged, and the caller writes that null into the line total.

Measured: the function returns null for a price of 1000 with no discount. The body already handles that case, with coalesce on its first line, and that line can never run. Removing STRICT makes the function do what it was written to do, and it reads as correct either way.

detect.sql: SELECT (marketing.fn_price_after_discount(1000, NULL) IS NULL)::text

defects.title: 955 of 1,024 job runs are reported as not existing
defects.why:
Describes a job run for the operations screen, with a guard for an id that does not exist.

IS NOT NULL on a composite value is not the opposite of IS NULL. A record is NOT NULL only when every one of its fields is non-null, so a single null column makes the guard false for a row that was found. ops.job_runs leaves detail null on anything that did not fail and finished_at null on anything still running.

Measured: 955 of the 1,024 job runs report as 'no such job run', including every job currently running, which is the state the screen is watched for. The guard is correct for a failed job with a detail message, so it passes every test written against one. IF FOUND is the test this wanted.

detect.sql: SELECT ops.fn_job_summary(1)

defects.title: The order table must bloat by forty per cent before autovacuum looks at it
defects.why:
Raised during the March 2025 incident, when an autovacuum of the order table ran through the evening peak and the immediate fix was to make it run less often. The incident was closed and the setting stayed.

The scale factor is the fraction of the table that must change before autovacuum considers it. At 0.4 the order table has to accumulate dead rows equal to forty per cent of itself before anything reclaims them, against the default of two per cent. Between runs the table carries the bloat, every scan reads the dead pages, and the statistics feeding the planner are twenty times staler than the database's own default assumes.

Measured: the setting is on the table. It is not in postgresql.conf, so it is invisible to anyone reading the server configuration to work out why this one table behaves differently from every other.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'storefront.orders'::regclass AND reloptions::text LIKE '%autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor=0.4%'

defects.title: The running revenue total advances a day at a time, not an order at a time
defects.why:
A running revenue total, one row per order, for the cumulative chart. The window is ordered, which is what makes the sum cumulative.

A window with ORDER BY and no frame clause defaults to RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and RANGE treats every row tied on the ordering expression as occupying the same position. The ordering here is the date, so every order placed on a day already has the whole of that day added, including the orders placed after it.

Measured: 13,880 orders produce 5,030 distinct running totals, one per trading day. The cumulative line is a staircase, and any reading taken from it mid-day overstates revenue by up to a full day. ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is one clause and advances one order at a time. Nothing warns, because the default is the SQL standard's and it is right whenever the ordering is unique.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT running_total) FROM analytics.v_order_running_revenue

defects.title: The reconciliation gains 212 rows with no order
defects.why:
Orders against their shipments, for the fulfilment reconciliation. FULL was chosen over LEFT so nothing could be missed, which is a reasonable thing to want and not what FULL does.

A full join adds the unmatched rows from both sides. The unmatched rows on the shipment side are shipments whose order_id points at no order, and they arrive with a null order_id, a null status and a shipment attached. Any count of rows here is a count of orders plus those, and any sum grouped by order_id gets a group for null.

Measured: the view returns 14,092 rows, 212 with no order_id. Those are the orphan shipments, and the reconciliation that exists to find discrepancies now carries them as rows instead of reporting them as a number.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_order_shipment_reconciliation WHERE order_id IS NULL

defects.title: The quarterly pack has returned no rows since it was written
defects.why:
First quarter trading, for the quarterly pack. The dates are right and they are the right way round in the sentence the query was written from, which reads from the end of the quarter back.

BETWEEN is low AND high and is not commutative. This expands to x >= '2026-03-31' AND x <= '2026-01-01', which nothing can satisfy. PostgreSQL does not object, because both bounds are valid dates and an empty range is a legal range.

Measured: the view returns no rows. 36 orders were placed in the quarter. An empty pack was read as a quiet quarter, which the first quarter of 2026 was in any case.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_first_quarter_2026_orders

defects.title: An empty copy of the product table sits in public
defects.why:
Created by the cloud migration's restore script, which ran an unqualified CREATE TABLE before the database's search_path had been set. It landed in public, nothing ever wrote to it, and the restore was declared successful because the application connects with storefront first and reads the real table.

Anything whose search_path starts with public reads this one and gets nothing. That covers a restore into a fresh database, a session started before the database setting applies, a tool that sets its own path, and any role carrying its own. The failure is an empty result rather than an error, so it reads as a database with no products in it.

Measured: public.products exists and holds no rows. The two tables share a name and an owner and have no relationship; the only thing telling them apart in a listing is the schema column.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'public' AND c.relname = 'products'

defects.title: Order ids jump a thousand at a time and no longer follow time
defects.why:
Raised to 1000 during the 2025 load testing, because every nextval was a write to the sequence and the order table was the hottest thing in the database. It worked: the writes went away.

A cache is per session. Each backend claims a thousand values at once and hands them out from memory, so two connections inserting at the same time produce order ids a thousand apart in an order that has nothing to do with when the orders were placed. Every value a session does not use is gone for good, and a pool that recycles connections discards most of them.

Measured: the sequence's cache is 1000. Every report treating order_id as a proxy for time is now wrong, as is every test assuming consecutive ids, and the sequence is consumed about a thousand times faster than the order count suggests.

detect.sql: SELECT seqcache FROM pg_sequence WHERE seqrelid = 'storefront.orders_order_id_seq'::regclass

defects.title: One subtransaction per staging row
defects.why:
Counts the staging rows whose customer id will not parse, so the import can report them before it runs. The exception block is there because a bad cast raises, and catching it per row is what stops one bad row ending the count.

A PL/pgSQL block with an EXCEPTION clause is a subtransaction. Entering one assigns a transaction id, takes a snapshot and pushes a stack entry, and it happens on every iteration whether or not anything is caught. A loop with a handler inside it opens one subtransaction per row.

ops.import_staging is empty between imports and holds the whole feed during one, so the function returns 0 today and the cost arrives with the data. Past about sixty-four subtransactions open at once the server stops tracking them in shared memory and every other backend starts reading pg_subtrans on every visibility check, which is the failure that takes the database down rather than this query. Moving the handler outside the loop removes the subtransaction entirely.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%LOOP%' AND prosrc LIKE '%EXCEPTION WHEN%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'ops.fn_count_unparseable_staging'::regproc

defects.title: Nine and a half thousand picking slips print blank
defects.why:
The picking slip line, built by concatenating the order reference, the currency and the amount. The warehouse prints one per order.

Concatenation with || returns null when any operand is null. Not the empty string, and not the rest of the line with a gap in it: the whole expression is null, order reference included. currency_code has been nullable since 2023 and is unset on every order the old checkout wrote.

Measured: 9,460 of the 13,880 labels are null. The slip prints blank and the picker has nothing to match against the shelf, and the one field that would identify the order is the field that disappeared with the others. concat() ignores nulls and would have printed the rest of the line; coalesce on the currency would have printed a gap. Neither is here.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_order_picking_label WHERE picking_label IS NULL

defects.title: A write through the view succeeds and the row is invisible from it
defects.why:
The large-order desk writes through this view: it is simple enough to be automatically updatable, and the desk was granted it instead of the table. WITH CHECK OPTION was added after the first row went missing, which is the right fix, and LOCAL was chosen because it sounded narrower and safer.

LOCAL checks this view's own WHERE clause and stops there. CASCADED also checks the views underneath, and it is what you get when neither word is written. So the amount is enforced and the currency is not.

Measured: inserting a 60,000-cent order in dollars through the view succeeds, the row lands in storefront.orders, and the view returns nothing for it, because storefront.v_gbp_orders filters it out on the way back. Inserting a 100-cent order in sterling is rejected, so the check option looks like it is working. The desk sees a successful insert and an empty re-read, and no object it can read will show the row.

detect.sql: SELECT ('check_option=local' = ANY(reloptions))::text FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'storefront.v_gbp_large_orders'::regclass

defects.title: The application role can grant the customer table to anyone
defects.why:
app_writer is the application's role. During the cloud migration it also had to create the read-only roles the reporting stack connects with, and the migration ran as app_writer, so it could not grant what it did not hold with the option to pass on. WITH GRANT OPTION got the script through, and the script is the only thing anyone remembers it being for.

The option is permanent and it is close to invisible: \dp shows one asterisk after the privilege letters, and every grant listing generated from information_schema drops it unless someone selects is_grantable explicitly.

Measured: one grantable privilege, SELECT on storefront.customers, held by app_writer. It can hand that to any role in the database including PUBLIC, and nothing in the audit trail distinguishes such a grant from one the owner made. Revoking the option later does not revoke what was granted under it, and the database does not record which grants those were.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.role_table_grants WHERE grantee = 'app_writer' AND is_grantable = 'YES'

defects.title: Every carrier scan is stored one second after it happened
defects.why:
The carrier scan feed arrived with sub-second timestamps and the column was declared timestamptz(0), because a parcel scan is not a measurement anyone needs milliseconds of and the narrower type was tidier.

A precision of 0 does not truncate the fraction. PostgreSQL rounds it, so .7 of a second becomes the next whole second and the stored value is later than the value that was written. Nothing reports the adjustment; the insert succeeds and returns the rounded value.

Measured: the 2025 backfill loaded the 6,000 scans then on file with a fraction of .7, which is what the carrier's exporter emits, and all 6,000 are stored exactly one second after the instant they record. Scans in the same second now share a timestamp, a scan at 23:59:59.7 is filed on the following day, and any check that a scan happened before dispatch sees a second that was never real.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.shipments WHERE scanned_at = dispatched_at + interval '1 second'

defects.title: The load audit is silent on every night the loader ran
defects.why:
One audit line per load, not one per row, which is why it is FOR EACH STATEMENT: the load moves millions of page views and a row trigger on that is not affordable. It was created on the partitioned parent, because that is the table the schema is written around and the table every catalogue lists.

Row triggers on a partitioned parent are cloned onto every partition and fire wherever the row lands. Statement triggers are not cloned. A statement trigger on the parent fires only for a statement whose target is the parent, and a statement naming a partition never reaches it.

The nightly loader names the partition, because writing to the parent made the planner route every row and the loader was faster once it addressed the quarter directly.

Measured: the parent carries one statement trigger and the four partitions carry none. An insert into archive.page_views_2026q2 writes no audit line; the same insert through the parent writes one. Nothing errors and no data is missing -- the archive fills correctly. The only symptom is a gap in the log that exists to prove the archive was loaded, and the reading of a gap is that the loader did not run.

detect.sql: SELECT (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'archive.page_views_archive'::regclass AND NOT tgisinternal AND (tgtype & 1) = 0) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_trigger t JOIN pg_inherits i ON i.inhrelid = t.tgrelid WHERE i.inhparent = 'archive.page_views_archive'::regclass AND NOT t.tgisinternal))::text

defects.title: The batch loader's safety line does nothing and leaks into the caller
defects.why:
Applies a delivery to a purchase order, line by line. The first version failed halfway through a delivery and left the order half-received, so the author reached for SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED to push the checks to the end and let the whole batch stand or fall together.

It does not do that, in either direction. SET CONSTRAINTS only moves constraints declared DEFERRABLE. A CHECK constraint can never be one, nor can NOT NULL, and every foreign key in this schema but one was written without the word. The constraints that actually reject a bad receipt line still fire on the statement that breaks them.

Measured: a check violation raised in a transaction that had already called this function failed on the statement, not at commit. Every deferrable constraint the statement can reach is already INITIALLY DEFERRED, so today the line changes nothing at all -- a no-op that reads, to everyone who has looked at the function since, as the thing making the batch atomic. The batch is not atomic and never was.

What it will do is leak. SET CONSTRAINTS is transaction-scoped, not function-scoped, and does not end when the function returns. The first constraint anyone adds as DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE stops being checked per statement for the rest of any transaction that called this function, in callers that never asked for deferral and have no handler for an error arriving at COMMIT with no statement attached to it.

detect.sql: SELECT (position('SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED' in prosrc) > 0)::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'supply.fn_apply_receipt_batch'::regproc

defects.title: A BRIN index on a column with no physical order
defects.why:
The 2026 index review was asked to cut index size, and BRIN answers that question: one summary per range of blocks instead of one entry per row. The saving is real and it is the only thing measured before this shipped.

BRIN summarises each block range by the minimum and maximum value in it, and can skip a range only when the value looked for falls outside that pair. storefront.order_items is written in order of order, and the product on a line has no relation to when the order was placed.

Measured: the physical correlation of product_id is 0.004, where 1.0 is a perfectly ordered column. At the default range size of 128 blocks this table is two ranges, and both summarise as min 1, max 2000 -- the entire catalogue. There is no product for which this index excludes a single block.

It is not even reached: the unique constraint on the table leaves a btree on the same column that the planner prefers every time. What was added is 24 kB of index written on every insert, rebuilt on every restore, carried in every backup, and unable to answer a question. Nothing in the index name says BRIN, and the review's report says index size went down, which it did.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid JOIN pg_am a ON a.oid = c.relam WHERE i.indrelid = 'storefront.order_items'::regclass AND a.amname = 'brin'

defects.title: A hash index on the timestamp every query filters by range
defects.why:
The same index review replaced the btree on sent_at with a hash index, for the same reason: a hash index on a timestamp is smaller, and the ticket asking for it said the report "looks messages up by date".

A hash index supports exactly one operator, equality. It cannot answer >=, <, BETWEEN or ORDER BY, and it cannot enforce uniqueness. Every query the support SLA report runs filters sent_at over a range of dates, and nothing anywhere asks for a message by its exact sent_at to the microsecond.

Measured: a range query over sent_at plans as a sequential scan; an equality query on the same column uses the index. So it is maintained on every insert into a table that grows with every reply, it occupies space in every backup, and it has never been used and cannot be. Nothing errors and nothing warns -- the index is valid, the planner simply never picks it. The access method appears only in the catalogue; the name reads like any other index on a timestamp.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid JOIN pg_am a ON a.oid = c.relam WHERE i.indrelid = 'support.ticket_messages'::regclass AND a.amname = 'hash'

defects.title: One payment per order, enforced by a constraint that reads as correct
defects.why:
A retry loop in the payment service double-charged eleven customers over one weekend in 2026. The fix went in at the database, where it could not be got around: one transaction per order, enforced by a unique constraint.

It stops the double charge. It also makes four ordinary things impossible. A failed authorisation followed by a successful one is two rows for one order, and it is the most common sequence in card payments. A capture following an authorisation is two rows. A part payment on a split order is two rows. A fresh authorisation after a refund is two rows. All four now raise a unique violation, which the payment service catches and reports to the customer as "duplicate transaction", because from its side that is the only thing this error has ever meant.

Measured: an insert of a second transaction against an order that already has one is rejected by transactions_order_id_key. Nothing in the data contradicts the constraint today -- 12,145 transactions against 12,145 distinct orders -- so it reads as a correct statement about the business, and will keep reading that way until the first failed card of the day.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'payments.transactions'::regclass AND contype = 'u' AND conkey = ARRAY[(SELECT attnum FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'payments.transactions'::regclass AND attname = 'order_id')]

defects.title: The contact extract hands every customer to a function it never returns
defects.why:
The reporting role needs contact details for the customers who opted in to marketing and must not see the rest. A view with a WHERE clause, granted to the role with no grant on the table, is the standard way to write that: 750 of the 3,120 customers are visible through it.

A view is not a security boundary unless it says so. Without WITH (security_barrier = true) the planner may push a qualifier from the outer query underneath the view's own WHERE, and it will when that looks cheaper. A function or operator not marked LEAKPROOF therefore runs against every row of storefront.customers, including the 2,370 the view exists to hide.

Measured: a query of the form SELECT ... FROM the view WHERE f(email), with f an ordinary plpgsql function, returned the 750 rows the view permits and handed all 3,120 email addresses to f on the way. With security_barrier set, the same query hands f 750.

The leak needs no exotic function: an error message that quotes its input, a RAISE NOTICE, or a function that writes what it saw are each enough, and the reporting role can create functions in its own schema. The hidden rows never appear in the result set, so nothing in the query output shows anything wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT (NOT coalesce('security_barrier=true' = ANY(reloptions), false))::text FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'storefront.v_customer_contact'::regclass

defects.title: A column with a default that is null on every phone order
defects.why:
The sales report wanted takings split by channel, so the column was added with a default, which is the change that needs nothing else to change: every existing row gets 'web', every insert that does not mention the column gets 'web', and the column can be read as never empty.

A default fills a column an INSERT does not name. It does nothing for an INSERT that names the column and passes NULL, because a named NULL is a value and not an absence. The phone desk's importer builds its column list from the table, so it names every column, and it has no channel to send.

Measured: 632 of 13,880 orders have no channel. They are the phone orders, taken in sterling over the desk, and that is the one channel the report was added to measure. They land in a null bucket the report prints as a blank row, and they disappear altogether from the version that joins a channel lookup table, because that join is an inner one. Neither output says a row is missing.

No report coalesces the column, and there is no reason any of them should: the DDL says it has a default, and a column with a default does not come back null.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.orders WHERE channel IS NULL

defects.title: The retirement job reports one coupon retired, every night, whatever happened
defects.why:
Retires every live coupon on a campaign and returns how many it retired. The nightly job writes that number into its run log, and the marketing team read the log to know a campaign is closed.

GET DIAGNOSTICS ... = ROW_COUNT reports the row count of the most recent SQL statement, not of the statement the author had in mind. There is an INSERT into the event log between the UPDATE and the read, so ROW_COUNT is the INSERT's, and an INSERT of one VALUES row always affects exactly one row.

Measured: with twenty live coupons on the campaign the function retired all twenty and returned 1; with none it retired nothing and returned 1. Every coupon in this database is already expired, so the UPDATE touches no rows on any call made today and the log still reads "1 coupon retired" every night, which is a plausible number for this job and has never been questioned.

The case that costs something is the third: a campaign whose coupons were never retired, because the id was wrong or they had already expired, is indistinguishable in the log from one that was. Moving the GET DIAGNOSTICS above the INSERT fixes it and changes nothing else.

detect.sql: SELECT (position('INSERT INTO ops.event_log' in prosrc) < position('GET DIAGNOSTICS' in prosrc))::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'marketing.fn_retire_campaign_coupons'::regproc

defects.title: A NOT NULL domain with 800 null values in it
defects.why:
The domain was created so a received quantity carries its own rules wherever it goes: an integer, never negative, never unknown. NOT NULL is in the type rather than on the column, which was the point -- every column of the type gets the rule without anyone remembering it -- and the design note says NULL is now impossible for a received quantity anywhere in the database.

A domain's NOT NULL is checked when a value is stored. It is not a guarantee about values of that type in a result set, and an outer join manufactures one out of nothing: the columns of the unmatched side come back NULL, typed as the domain, with nothing checking them. The same is true of a full join, a grouping set, and a scalar subquery that finds no row.

Measured: the coverage view returns 2,600 rows, 800 of them with a NULL quantity_received -- one for each catalogue product that has never appeared on a purchase order line. The type of that column says it cannot happen.

The consumer is the reordering report, which keeps a line when quantity_received > 0 and drops it otherwise. NULL > 0 is NULL, which is not true, so all 800 products that have never been ordered are dropped from the report that exists to find products that have never been ordered. Nobody wrote a coalesce, because the type says there is nothing to coalesce.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.v_product_receipt_coverage WHERE quantity_received IS NULL

defects.title: A function priced at nothing is evaluated before the filter that would have skipped it
defects.why:
The escalation dashboard shows priority-one tickets that have had a reply. "Has had a reply" comes from a function, so the agent screen can reuse the definition.

COST tells the planner what a function is worth. The default for a plpgsql function is 100 units, already an understatement for a function that runs a query. This one was given 0.0001 by someone tuning a different query, where the function sat in the SELECT list and the low cost stopped the planner materialising a subquery.

In a WHERE clause, cost decides the order the qualifiers are evaluated in: the cheapest runs first. At 0.0001 this function is, as far as the planner knows, cheaper than comparing a smallint to a constant.

Measured: the plan puts the function first, and it is called 600 times -- once per ticket in the table -- to return the 120 that are priority one, each call running its own query against support.ticket_messages.

Nothing in the view is wrong. The dashboard returns the right tickets and does five times the work it needs to, and the multiple is the ratio of the table to the filter, so it grows as the ticket table does. Raising the cost to the default reorders the plan and changes no result. plpgsql is what makes it stick: a one-statement SQL function is inlined during planning and costed on what it actually does, which is how the same mistake in a SQL function comes to nothing.

detect.sql: SELECT procost::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'support.fn_ticket_has_replies'::regproc

defects.title: Anti-wraparound vacuum pushed to the hard limit on the dispatch table
defects.why:
During the March 2025 incident an anti-wraparound autovacuum started on fulfilment.shipments in the middle of the afternoon and held the table for four hours. Anti-wraparound vacuums cannot be skipped and are not cancelled by a lock conflict, so the dispatch screens waited on it. The setting that decides when one is forced was raised to its maximum and the incident was closed.

autovacuum_freeze_max_age is the transaction age at which PostgreSQL stops asking and freezes the table whether anyone is using it or not. The default is 200 million. At 2 billion this table is never force-frozen until it is at the hard limit the whole database shares, and the wraparound machinery has nothing left to give: the first warning arrives with around 11 million transactions of headroom, the database refuses new writes shortly after, and the cure by then is a vacuum that must run to completion on the largest table in the schema with the site down for the duration.

Nothing looks wrong in the meantime. Ordinary autovacuum still runs and the table is still cleaned of dead rows. The setting is visible only in pg_class.reloptions, where it reads as a number somebody chose on purpose.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'fulfilment.shipments'::regclass AND reloptions::text LIKE '%autovacuum_freeze_max_age=2000000000%'

defects.title: The audit log's changed_by is the same value on every row
defects.why:
The column is called changed_by and the log is the answer to "who changed this". current_user is the role the statement runs as, which for every write reaching this trigger is the single role the connection pool logs in as.

Measured: there is one distinct changed_by across all 30,090 rows of ops.event_log. No part of this database records which person or which service made a change, so the log answers what and when and never who.

The application knows. It has a signed-in user on every request and never passes it down, because the column looked like it was already handling that. SET LOCAL of an application setting, read here with current_setting, is the usual way to carry it, and it was never added.

The log is complete in every other respect, which is what makes it worse: it is produced in evidence, it looks like an audit trail, and the one question an audit trail is asked is the one it cannot answer.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT changed_by) FROM ops.event_log

defects.title: An upsert that treats every unique violation as a duplicate email
defects.why:
Inserts a customer and returns the id, or returns the id of the customer already here. The importer calls it once per row of the nightly phone-desk file and attaches the order to whatever comes back.

The handler catches unique_violation, which is one SQLSTATE for every unique constraint on the table, and then acts on one of them: it looks the customer up by email, because email is the key the author had in mind.

storefront.customers has two unique constraints. The other is the primary key, and the importer supplies customer_id from the phone system's own numbering, which has overlapped Cross River's since the two systems were joined. When the id collides and the email is new, the handler runs a lookup that matches nothing and the function returns NULL.

Measured: called with an existing id and a new email it returns NULL; called with a new id and an existing email it returns the right customer, which is the case it was written for and the case that is tested.

NULL is not an error here. It is returned, and the importer carries it to the next statement, where storefront.orders.customer_id is NOT NULL and the insert fails with a not-null violation naming the orders table. The night's log reports a problem with an order, in a job whose customer step reported success, and the actual event -- two systems numbering customers the same way -- is named nowhere.

detect.sql: SELECT (prosrc LIKE '%WHEN unique_violation THEN%' AND prosrc LIKE '%WHERE email = p_email%')::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'storefront.fn_ensure_customer'::regproc

defects.title: A privilege that is recorded, correct, and unusable
defects.why:
The grant that makes the contact extract available to the reporting role was the only thing the change ticket asked for. It was applied, it succeeded, and the ticket was closed.

Reaching an object in PostgreSQL needs two permissions: the privilege on the object and USAGE on the schema containing it. report_reader has never had USAGE on storefront.

Measured: the role holds SELECT on the view and does not hold USAGE on the schema. The grant is recorded, information_schema lists the privilege, and every query the role runs against the view fails with "permission denied for schema storefront", which reads as though the grant was never applied and sends whoever is debugging it to the table privileges, where everything is in order.

GRANT does not warn, because a privilege can legitimately be granted before a schema is opened up. Nothing reconciles the two halves, so the extract has been unreadable by the role it was built for since the day it shipped.

detect.sql: SELECT (has_table_privilege('report_reader', 'storefront.v_customer_contact', 'SELECT') AND NOT has_schema_privilege('report_reader', 'storefront', 'USAGE'))::text

defects.title: Composite index direction cannot satisfy the mixed ORDER BY it was built for
defects.why: The dispatch board orders by carrier_id ascending and dispatched_at descending. A btree holds one direction and can be read either way, so it satisfies an ordering only when every key runs the same way. The index declares both columns ascending, so the plan is an Incremental Sort over an index scan: the top 50 rows cost 3,540 rows read and sorted, across three carriers and 10,622 shipments. Declaring the second column DESC makes it a plain index scan that stops at 50.

detect.sql: SELECT ((i.indoption[0] & 1) = (i.indoption[1] & 1))::text FROM pg_index i WHERE i.indexrelid = 'fulfilment.ix_shipments_carrier_dispatch'::regclass

defects.title: n_distinct pinned by hand overrides what ANALYZE measures
defects.why: n_distinct set in a column's options replaces the measured value permanently. support.ticket_messages holds 1,800 rows across 600 tickets; the pin says 5. GROUP BY ticket_id is estimated at 5 groups and returns 600, and every plan built on that aggregate is costed for a hundredth of the rows it gets. pg_stats reports the pinned 5 as though ANALYZE had found it; the override is visible only in pg_attribute.attoptions.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'support.ticket_messages'::regclass AND attname = 'ticket_id' AND attoptions::text LIKE '%n_distinct=5%'

defects.title: REPLICA IDENTITY FULL on a table that already has a primary key
defects.why: storefront.inventory has a primary key, so DEFAULT already gave logical replication the identity it wants. FULL writes the entire old row into the WAL on every UPDATE and DELETE and makes the subscriber match each change by sequential scan over every column. This is the table the reservation path updates row by row and the one already carrying fillfactor 100. Nothing fails; the cost lands on WAL volume, archive size, standby replay and subscriber CPU, from one letter in pg_class that no schema dump shows.

detect.sql: SELECT relreplident::text FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'storefront.inventory'::regclass

defects.title: DELETE names the inheritance parent and empties the children too
defects.why: archive.orders_base is both a staging table and the top of an inheritance tree. A statement naming a parent reaches its children unless it says ONLY, and DELETE follows the same rule as SELECT. The parent holds no rows of its own; archive.orders_2023 and archive.orders_2024 hold 1,460 and 1,464, the only copy of those years. Called with 2026-01-01 the clean-up reports 2,924 rows deleted and leaves both year tables empty, and the number it returns is correct.

detect.sql: SELECT ((prosrc LIKE '%DELETE FROM archive.orders_base%') AND (prosrc NOT LIKE '%ONLY%'))::text FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'archive.fn_purge_staged_orders'::regproc

defects.title: Permission gate written with = ALL is vacuously true for a token with no scopes
defects.why: The gate asks whether a table is on a token's scope list, which is an ANY question written with ALL. On a single-scope token the two agree, which is every token that was tested. A two-scope token is refused both of its tables. An empty array makes the comparison vacuously true, so the 16 of 25 tokens issued before the scopes column existed pass the gate for every table name. The mechanism is strictest on the tokens with the most scopes and absent on the tokens with none.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.api_tokens t WHERE cardinality(t.scopes) = 0 AND ops.fn_partner_may_read(t.api_token_id, 'payments.transactions')

defects.title: Rows modified before they were created
defects.why: 87 of the 1,200 imported Silverback customers carry an updated_at earlier than their created_at, because the exporter took the two columns from two parts of their application. No constraint in this database compares two timestamps on the same row. An age report returns a negative duration, a filter written as updated_at > created_at silently drops all 87, and a watermark that takes the later of the two re-imports them every run.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.customers WHERE updated_at < created_at

defects.title: Identity column loaded with explicit ids, so its sequence never advanced
defects.why: The codes were numbered in a spreadsheet and loaded with their numbers intact so the print run and the database would agree, which is why the column is GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY rather than ALWAYS. An explicit value does not advance the sequence and nothing reconciles the two afterwards. 600 rows are numbered 1 to 600 behind a sequence whose last_value is still 1, so the next insert that lets the column default collides with an existing row, and so do the 599 after it.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT max(code_id) FROM marketing.campaign_codes) - (SELECT last_value FROM marketing.campaign_codes_code_id_seq)

defects.title: LIKE pattern built from a prefix containing an underscore, which is a wildcard
defects.why: The routine counts codes in a wave by putting the caller's prefix into a LIKE pattern unescaped. Underscore is LIKE's single-character wildcard, so 'AUTUMN_2026' matches AUTUMN-2026 as readily as AUTUMN_2026. The call returns 600 where the wave holds 300; the other 300 are the legacy loader's hyphenated codes, which carry a different supplier and a different reconciliation. Equality, or an escaped pattern, returns 300.

detect.sql: SELECT marketing.fn_codes_in_wave('AUTUMN_2026')

defects.title: HAVING with no GROUP BY filters the single aggregate row, not the customers
defects.why: The view is meant to count customers with more than ten orders. With no GROUP BY the query already produces exactly one aggregate row, so HAVING asks whether the whole table has more than ten orders. It has 13,880, the row survives, and the count in it is every customer who has ever ordered. The view returns 2,730 where the answer is 30, and it has been in the board pack as 'repeat customers' for two quarters.

detect.sql: SELECT repeat_customers FROM analytics.v_repeat_customer_count

defects.title: AND binds tighter than OR, so half the review queue has no status test
defects.why: The queue is meant to hold pending orders that are either large or carry a gift message. Without parentheses the clause means (pending AND large) OR (has a gift message), and the second branch tests no status at all, so every order with a gift message is queued whatever its status, shipped and cancelled included. The view returns 1,695 rows where the intended filter returns 922, and the queue is worked top-down.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.v_orders_for_review

defects.title: Self-join on postcode with no b.id <> a.id, so every address matches itself
defects.why: Fraud review wanted addresses used by more than one customer, which is a self-join on postcode. The predicate excluding the row itself is missing, so an address whose postcode is unique in the table still produces a pair that reads exactly like a shared one. The view returns 1,260 pairs of which 60 are real; the other 1,200 are the 1,200 addresses each matched with itself, so the dashboard figure tracks the size of the address table rather than anything about fraud.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.v_shared_postcodes

defects.title: Materialised view indexed but not uniquely, so CONCURRENTLY refresh cannot run
defects.why: The rollup was given an index at creation so its nightly refresh could be CONCURRENTLY and the dashboard would keep serving. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY requires a UNIQUE index, not merely an index, because it diffs old contents against new. This is a plain B-tree on product_id, which is in fact unique here, so the index the job needs could be created today without changing a row. pg_matviews reports hasindexes = true, so anything checking only that the view is indexed is satisfied while the refresh still fails and the fallback plain refresh takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'analytics.mv_product_revenue'::regclass AND indisunique

defects.title: Physical row location saved as an identifier, because the table has no key
defects.why: supply.contract_price_reviews has no primary key, so the nightly export recorded its position using the only thing available, the row's ctid. A ctid is a block number and a slot, and an update writes a new version of the row elsewhere, so the saved pointer silently stops matching. 148 pointers were captured and 50 no longer resolve to the row they came from, because a reviewer name was corrected on those rows. A VACUUM FULL, a CLUSTER or a restore would invalidate all 148 at once and log nothing. A stale pointer either finds no row or finds whichever row occupies that slot now, so the export silently re-sends or silently skips.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.export_cursors c LEFT JOIN supply.contract_price_reviews r ON r.ctid = c.row_pointer WHERE r.supplier_id IS DISTINCT FROM c.supplier_id OR r.product_id IS DISTINCT FROM c.product_id

defects.title: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE assigns EXCLUDED, overwriting stock instead of adding to it
defects.why: Goods-in calls the routine once per delivery line, and the ON CONFLICT clause is what makes a top-up work. EXCLUDED is the row that was proposed, not the row already there, so on_hand = EXCLUDED.on_hand replaces the stock level with the size of the delivery. Two waves of 10 units then 5 units across 200 products should total 3,000 and total 1,000, which is the second wave alone. The error is invisible on a first delivery and whenever consecutive deliveries are the same size, and it surfaces as shrinkage, which the DC already has a process for absorbing.

detect.sql: SELECT sum(on_hand) FROM supply.warehouse_stock

defects.title: array_agg over an unmatched outer join returns {NULL}, not an empty array
defects.why: Tags are optional, which is what the LEFT JOIN is for. When nothing matches, the outer join still produces one row with a NULL in it and array_agg aggregates that row, so the result is an array of length 1 containing NULL rather than an empty array. 2,340 of the 3,120 customers have no tags and every one is reported with a one-element array, so anything counting tags by array_length sees 3,120 tagged customers and no untagged ones. array_remove, or array_agg with a FILTER clause, returns the empty array that was meant.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_customer_tags WHERE array_length(tags, 1) = 1 AND tags[1] IS NULL

defects.title: Function carries SET enable_seqscan = off, which the caller cannot override
defects.why: The call was slow once when the planner chose a sequential scan, and the session-level workaround was made permanent by attaching it to the function. A SET clause on a function applies for the whole call and cannot be overridden by the caller: it is not a hint but a prohibition, and it survives every change in data volume, statistics and PostgreSQL version that would have let the planner choose correctly. It is the only routine in the database carrying proconfig enable_seqscan=off, and it does not appear in the function body, so reading the SQL tells you nothing. Single-day calls are fast, which is how it is always tested; the month-end routine calls it in a loop.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'analytics' AND p.proname = 'fn_revenue_for_day' AND 'enable_seqscan=off' = ANY(p.proconfig)

defects.title: Lookup bands share their boundaries, so a boundary value joins to two rows
defects.why: The bands were typed in from a carrier rate card that prints them as 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, where each boundary belongs to one band. BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends, so every boundary value belongs to two bands, and a lookup that matches twice is a join returning two rows. 27,761 order lines produce 50,895 rows through the view: every line of 2 units and every line of 3 units is counted twice, and only the 4,627 lines of 4 units are counted once. The surcharge total is therefore close to double and is reconciled against the carrier invoice by a correction factor somebody derived empirically in 2024.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.v_order_item_surcharge

defects.title: Row trigger refreshes an entire materialised view, once per row
defects.why: The dashboard was stale between nightly refreshes and the request was to update it when stock changed. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW rebuilds the whole view, so in a FOR EACH ROW trigger a delivery note of two hundred lines aggregates every order line in the database two hundred times inside the transaction recording the delivery, taking an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the view each time. It is the only trigger in the database whose function refreshes a materialised view. Nothing has gone wrong yet only because the trigger was created after this migration's own load.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger t WHERE NOT t.tgisinternal AND t.tgfoid = 'supply.fn_refresh_product_revenue'::regproc

defects.title: rank() with no PARTITION BY ranks across every store at once
