defects.why: The view groups by store and product to give merchandising the top products in each store. rank() OVER (ORDER BY ...) with no PARTITION BY ranks over the whole result, so the store column is correct and the rank beside it has nothing to do with it; a store's best seller can carry rank 4,000. Filtering to revenue_rank <= 10 returns 10 rows, all from the busiest store, where ranking within each of the three stores returns 40. The report nearly agrees with the truth for the busiest store, which is the one people check.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_store_product_rank WHERE revenue_rank <= 10

defects.title: Spend grouped by customer name, so same-named customers become one
defects.why: The report groups by the column a human reads, the name, rather than the one that identifies the row. Two customers with the same name become a single row whose spend is the sum of both and which is attributed to a person who does not exist. The view returns 64 rows where 2,730 customers have ordered. The seed data draws names from a small pool so the effect is extreme here, but the shape is the point: a name is not a key and the report cannot tell you it merged. It feeds the top-customers list, which is why the same handful of names is always at the top.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_spend_by_customer_name

defects.title: Invoice dates kept as day-first text, so they sort as strings
defects.why: The register was loaded straight from a spreadsheet: every column text, every date in the supplier's day-first format with no leading zeros. A date in a text column sorts as text, so '9/8/2026' is greater than '22/12/2026' because '9' beats '2'. max(invoice_date) returns '9/8/2026' while the latest invoice is dated 22 December 2026. Nothing errors, because text comparison is well defined; it answers a different question from the one asked. The month-end cut-off uses a range over this column, which is why December accruals are short every year.

detect.sql: SELECT max(invoice_date) FROM supply.supplier_invoices

defects.title: coalesce on the null-producing side makes never-ordered look like zero spend
defects.why: The outer join is right and the coalesce was added because the report looked untidy with blanks in it. A null on the null-producing side means the customer has no orders; zero means the customer has orders that came to nothing. Replacing the first with the second destroys the only distinction the report needed to make and it cannot be recovered downstream. 390 customers report zero spend and all 390 have never ordered, so there is not one genuine zero among them. The win-back campaign targets customers whose spend fell to zero and has been mailing all 390.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_customer_spend_zero_filled WHERE spend_cents = 0

defects.title: AS MATERIALIZED fences a CTE, so filters on the view cannot reach the tables
defects.why: Written on PostgreSQL 11, where every CTE was an optimisation fence. From 12 onwards a CTE referenced once is inlined and a filter on the view reaches the tables, so the 2026 upgrade to 18 would have changed the plan; the author added AS MATERIALIZED to keep it the same. The plan they kept is the slow one: the CTE is executed in full and stored, so a caller selecting one store's lines still builds the whole 27,761 row join and filters afterwards. It is the only view in the database that forces materialisation, and it is correct, so it has never been looked at in any investigation of why the merchandising screens are slow.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_rewrite r WHERE r.ev_class = 'analytics.v_recent_order_lines'::regclass AND r.rulename = '_RETURN' AND r.ev_action::text ~ ':ctematerialized 1 '

defects.title: Random v4 and time-ordered v7 uuids share one key column
defects.why: The log was built on PostgreSQL 14 with gen_random_uuid(), which is version 4 and random. After the upgrade to 18 the default became uuidv7(), which carries its creation time in its leading bits. Both are uuids, both unique, and the column accepted the change without comment. Ordering by the key is therefore chronological for rows written after the upgrade and meaningless for rows written before. 400 of the 1,000 keys are version 4 and 600 are version 7, nothing in the schema records which is which, and the retention job deletes the oldest deliveries by ordering on the key.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.webhook_deliveries WHERE substring(delivery_id::text, 15, 1) = '4'

defects.title: BEFORE UPDATE trigger returns OLD, so the write applies and changes nothing
defects.why: Closed tickets were made immutable in the obvious place, a BEFORE UPDATE trigger. Returning OLD does not reject the update; it replaces the proposed row with the existing one, so the write is applied and changes nothing. No error is raised, no exception is available to catch, and the command tag still counts the row as updated. A bulk repriorisation set every ticket to priority 3: 600 rows were reported updated and 120 closed tickets still hold their old priority. Raising an exception would have told the caller; returning OLD tells nobody, and this is the failure mode that makes a retry loop run forever without progressing.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.tickets WHERE status = 'closed' AND priority <> 3

defects.title: Partial unique index names one state where the rule covers two
defects.why: A ticket may be claimed by one agent at a time, and the index is partial because released claims are kept for the audit trail rather than deleted. The predicate names 'active' and the application has two live states: a claim being handed between agents is written as 'reassigning', which the index does not see. 30 tickets carry two live claims, each an active claim and a reassigning claim held by different agents. The index is doing exactly what it was asked; the predicate matched the rule as it stood in 2024, before handover was added.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT ticket_id FROM support.ticket_claims WHERE state IN ('active', 'reassigning') GROUP BY ticket_id HAVING count(*) > 1) t

defects.title: VAT rounded on every line then summed, where the invoice rounds the sum
defects.why: The view rounds each line's VAT and adds the rounded figures up, which is what the order screen shows, so screen lines and screen total agree. They do not agree with the invoice, because rounding before summing and rounding after summing are different operations. 925 of 13,880 orders have a per-line VAT total that differs from VAT on the order total, and the drift across the table is 925 pennies, all in the same direction. Either method is permitted provided one is used consistently; Cross River uses both, and the reconciliation carries an unexplained line called rounding that grows with order volume.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_order_vat v JOIN (SELECT order_id, round(sum(line_total_cents) * 0.20) AS t FROM storefront.order_items GROUP BY order_id) x USING (order_id) WHERE v.vat_cents <> x.t

defects.title: Change-log trigger has no UPDATE OF, so every column writes a lead time row
defects.why: Purchasing wanted lead time changes recorded and the log stores old and new lead time, which is what was asked for. The trigger has no UPDATE OF clause, so it fires for every update of every column: changing an email address writes a lead time change row in which the lead time did not change. The log grows at the rate of all writes rather than the writes anybody cares about. An email normalisation touched all 40 suppliers and produced 40 rows, every one with old_lead_time_days equal to new_lead_time_days, so the whole log is currently noise. UPDATE OF lead_time_days, or a WHEN clause, is the fix and costs nothing.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.supplier_change_log WHERE old_lead_time_days = new_lead_time_days

defects.title: GIN index built with jsonb_path_ops, which cannot serve ? key existence
defects.why: The event store is queried by containment and by key existence. The index uses jsonb_path_ops because a benchmark showed it smaller and faster, which it is. jsonb_path_ops indexes only the paths to values: it supports @> and does not support ?, ?| or ?&, so every key existence query falls back to a sequential scan of the whole table. It is the only jsonb_path_ops index in the database, and the default jsonb_ops opclass would serve both operator families at the cost of more space. Nothing reports this, because the queries return correct answers and the index shows as used by the containment half of the workload.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_opclass o ON o.oid = i.indclass[0] WHERE o.opcname = 'jsonb_path_ops' AND i.indrelid = 'ops.integration_events'::regclass

defects.title: numeric(4,2) silently rounds four-decimal tax rates to two
defects.why: Suppliers quote tax at four decimal places and the column holds two, sized from the whole percentages in use when it was created. numeric(4,2) does not reject a value with more precision: it rounds and stores the result silently on every insert, with no warning, no error and no record of the original, so the loss is undetectable from inside the database once the statement commits. Five distinct rates were loaded, 0.175 through 0.179, and the column holds one value, so every invoice in the register now claims the same tax rate.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT tax_rate) FROM supply.supplier_invoices

defects.title: count() over a CASE with ELSE 0 counts every row in the group
defects.why: Fulfilment rate per store, written as count the orders and count the ones that shipped. The CASE was given an ELSE because the author had been told a CASE without one is a defect, which it usually is. count() counts non-null values and zero is not null, so ELSE 0 turns an expression that was null for the rows that should not count into one that is never null, and the second count counts every row in the group. Every store reports a fulfilment rate of 100%. 3,470 of the 13,880 orders have actually shipped. Either sum(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) or count(*) FILTER (WHERE ...) is correct; count() with an ELSE 0 is the one combination that is not, and it is the one that looks most careful.

detect.sql: SELECT sum(shipped_orders) FROM analytics.v_store_fulfilment_rate

defects.title: lag() with no PARTITION BY takes its previous value from the previous product
defects.why: Stock movements and the change since the last count. lag() over an ORDER BY naming the product first and the date second gives every row the row before it, which within a product is the previous count for that product. At the first row of each product there is no previous count for that product and lag() does not know that, because the window is the whole result, so it returns the last row of the product before it. The delta is a real number computed from two real rows belonging to two different products. 149 of the 900 rows report a change that crosses a product boundary, the largest a 135 unit swing between two products whose own counts never move by more than 5 units at a time. PARTITION BY product_id is the whole fix.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT product_id, change_units, lag(product_id) OVER (ORDER BY product_id, moved_at) AS prev FROM analytics.v_stock_movement_deltas) x WHERE change_units IS NOT NULL AND prev <> product_id

defects.title: The same half, rounded as numeric and as double precision, gives two answers
defects.why: The deposit is half the invoice, rounded to the penny, and the view computes it twice: once as the current report does it and once the way the 2019 report did, which finance still reconcile against. round() on numeric rounds a half away from zero. round() on double precision rounds a half to the nearest even integer, because that is what the C library does. An odd number of pennies halves to an exact half, so the two rules disagree on exactly those rows. 60 of the 240 invoices differ by a penny; 120 invoices have an odd amount, so half the candidates disagree. Nothing in either expression says which rounding rule it gets: the difference is the literal 0.5 being numeric in one and the cast making the arithmetic double in the other.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_supplier_invoice_deposits WHERE deposit_cents <> deposit_cents_legacy

defects.title: nullif(settled_cents, 0) drops the claims the carrier rejected in full
defects.why: Average settlement per carrier. The nullif was added after a division by zero elsewhere in the same report and applied here too, on the reasoning that a zero is not a real settlement. A zero settlement is the most real one there is: it is a claim the carrier rejected in full. avg() skips nulls, so every rejected claim is dropped from both the total and the divisor and the figure reported is the average of the claims that were paid. 30 of the 120 claims were settled at zero. The view reports 9,200 pennies; the average across every claim raised is 6,900. A carrier that rejects everything it can and pays the rest in full scores better here than one that negotiates, which is the opposite of what the review is for.

detect.sql: SELECT max(avg_settled_cents) FROM analytics.v_carrier_claim_average

defects.title: CHECK length() <= 40 does not hold the label inside a 40 byte field
defects.why: The campaign label is printed into a fixed 40 byte field in the voucher file the fulfilment house consumes, and the constraint was written to hold it inside. length() on text returns characters, not bytes. The two agree for as long as every label is ASCII, and the French campaign labels are not: an accented character costs two bytes and an em dash costs three, so a label of 35 characters is 43 bytes and the constraint is satisfied. 200 labels pass the check and exceed 40 octets. The constraint has never rejected anything. octet_length() is the function that answers the question that was asked.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.campaign_codes WHERE octet_length(display_label) > 40

defects.title: A trailing space defeats the unique key on a varchar phone number
defects.why: Supplier contacts keyed by supplier and phone number so the same number cannot be entered twice. The table was loaded twice from the same spreadsheet: once from the export that trims its cells and once from the one that does not. varchar comparison does not ignore trailing spaces; char(n) does, which is where the expectation comes from, and this column is varchar. '01772 880003' and '01772 880003 ' are two different values to the unique index and one phone number to everybody else, so the constraint accepted the second load in full. 53 contacts, of which 13 duplicate another row by a trailing space. Trimming the column collapses the table to 40 rows, one per supplier.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) - count(DISTINCT (supplier_id, btrim(phone))) FROM supply.supplier_contacts

defects.title: The redaction removes the first phone number in a note and leaves the rest
defects.why: Notes are shown to an outsourced support desk with phone numbers removed, and the redaction was checked against a note containing one number, which it redacts perfectly. regexp_replace replaces the first match only; the 'g' flag is what makes it replace all of them, and leaving it off is not an error. 400 of the 600 notes still contain a full phone number after redaction, every one of them a note that carried two. The field visibly contains the string [redacted], so the redaction is assumed to have worked.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_ticket_notes_redacted WHERE body ~ '07700[0-9]{6}'

defects.title: A YY date mask puts the 1960s warranty registrations in the 2060s
defects.why: The warranty register came off a service system retired in 2001 and stored dates as six digits, which the import parsed with a YY mask. to_date with YY picks the century by a fixed rule: 00 to 69 become 2000 to 2069 and 70 to 99 become 1970 to 1999. That rule is right for a file written today and wrong for one written before 2000. 55 of 240 registrations now carry a date after 2030, and the source text stored beside the date disagrees with it on every one. Nothing rejected them, because a date in 2065 is a valid date, and the warranty expiry report reads the date column.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.warranty_registrations WHERE registered_on > DATE '2030-01-01'

defects.title: The top ten customers by spend are ordered by name, not spend
defects.why: The view was written with two columns, the name and the spend, and an ORDER BY 2 DESC over the spend. The email was added in front of the name later, to tell apart two customers who share a name. An ordinal in ORDER BY names a position in the select list, so adding a column in front moved every position by one and the view now sorts by full_name. It still returns ten rows and still calls them the top ten by spend; they are the last ten customers in the alphabet. The last name in the alphabet, Taylor Smith, belongs to 49 customers, so the view returns ten of them, and which ten depends on how the sort happens to run. None of the ten belongs in the list: the real top ten spend 40,042,348 pennies between them, and all ten rows the view returns are outside it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_top_customers_by_spend v WHERE v.email NOT IN (SELECT c.email FROM storefront.orders o JOIN storefront.customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.email ORDER BY sum(o.total_cents) DESC LIMIT 10)

defects.title: 0.80 and 0.8 are one rate and two groups once the column is cast to text
defects.why: The rate card is grouped by rate to show how many lanes sit on each one. The rates came from two spreadsheets, one writing 0.80 and one writing 0.8. numeric keeps the scale it was given, so the two are equal as numbers and different as text, and the view casts to text before grouping. The view reports six rate bands over three distinct rates, with the lanes split between the two spellings of each, so no band holds all the lanes charged at its rate. The cast was added to control how the rate printed, which it does.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_freight_rate_bands

defects.title: Empty audience segments report a null size and drop out of the under-ten review
defects.why: Audience segments hold their members in an array and the size report calls array_length on it. array_length returns null for an empty array rather than zero, because an empty array has no dimensions to measure. A null is not less than ten, so the review that lists every segment with fewer than ten members never sees the segments with no members at all. Eight of the 40 segments are empty and report a null size; the review lists 21 segments and none of them are the empty ones. cardinality() returns zero and is the function that was wanted.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_audience_segment_sizes WHERE members IS NULL

defects.title: age() measures in calendar months and the comparison converts a month to thirty days
defects.why: Resolution time is measured against a one month service level with age(), which returns months and days, and compared to INTERVAL '1 mon'. Comparing two intervals converts a month to thirty days, because an interval alone has no calendar. age() has one, and returns 1 mon 0 days for the whole of a thirty-one day month, so a ticket open thirty-one real days compares as thirty and passes; in February the same arithmetic breaches a thirty day ticket. 36 of the 600 resolved tickets are classified the opposite way round from a plain comparison of elapsed days against thirty. The view measures in calendar months and then compares in thirty day units, so the verdict depends on the month the ticket opened in.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_ticket_sla_breaches WHERE breached_sla <> (resolved_at - opened_at > INTERVAL '30 days')

defects.title: A missing slash gives every direct debit line a reference cut from the front of the line
defects.why: The parser lifts out the pair of codes either side of a slash: an eight wide window starting four characters before it. position() returns zero when it does not find the slash, and the direct debit file has none, so the start is minus four. A negative start is not an error in PostgreSQL: substring returns the part of the window that overlaps the string, which is the first three characters of the line. 60 of the 300 lines have no slash and every one of them carries a three character reference rather than a null. The matching job then fails to find the payment, which sits unallocated with a reference beside it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.remittance_lines WHERE position('/' IN line_text) = 0 AND reference_code IS NOT NULL

defects.title: The same supplier alias is stored twice, once precomposed and once decomposed
defects.why: Supplier aliases are unique so a trading name cannot be recorded twice. The list was merged from two systems, one writing an accented letter as a single character and one as a letter followed by a combining accent. PostgreSQL does not normalise text, so the two spellings are different strings to the unique index and the same word to a reader: equal under normalize(..., NFC) and not equal under =. 20 of the 60 aliases duplicate another row once normalised, and they render identically on screen. A search by name finds one row or the other depending on which keyboard typed the query.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) - count(DISTINCT normalize(alias, NFC)) FROM supply.supplier_aliases

defects.title: NaN weights outrank every real weight in the heaviest products report
defects.why: The supplier feed sends the string NaN when it has no weight, and numeric accepts it. NaN is not null, so nothing is missing as far as the database is concerned, and numeric sorts NaN above every real number and treats it as equal to itself. 86 products carry NaN; all ten rows of the heaviest products report are products with no weight and the heaviest real product is not on it, and max() over the column returns NaN. A null would have been skipped by every aggregate and sorted last by default.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_heaviest_products WHERE weight_kg = 'NaN'

defects.title: The search vector is built with simple and queried with english, so nothing stemmed ever matches
defects.why: The help centre vector is built with the simple configuration, chosen while the author was checking the index worked at all, and the application searches with english, which is the default to_tsquery uses. simple lowercases and splits on word boundaries and does nothing else, so it keeps returning as returning, while english stems it to return. 60 of the 120 articles say returning and a search for return matches none of them; it finds the other 60, which spell the word as return and need no stemming. The index is populated and used, and the failures look like missing articles rather than a broken index.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.help_articles WHERE to_tsvector('english', title || ' ' || body) @@ to_tsquery('english', 'return') AND NOT (search_vector @@ to_tsquery('english', 'return'))

defects.title: The share denominator is a running total, so the first category is 100% of sales
defects.why: The denominator is the total across every category, written as a window sum so each row can carry the whole, and an ORDER BY was added so the rows came back in category order. A window function with an ORDER BY and no frame clause gets the default frame, from the start of the partition to the current row, so the ORDER BY did not sort the output: it turned the denominator into a running total. The shares add up to 327.8% instead of 100%, and the first category is reported at 100.0% of sales while holding 11.6% of them. Removing the ORDER BY gives the total; an ORDER BY outside the window gives the row order that was wanted.

detect.sql: SELECT round(sum(share_pct), 1) FROM analytics.v_category_share

defects.title: A remittance settled in three parts holds the amount of one of them
defects.why: The settled amount was backfilled from the settlement events with an UPDATE ... FROM, which is the idiomatic way to copy a value across from another table. UPDATE ... FROM joins, and when the join matches more than one row the target is updated once from one of them, chosen by whatever the plan happened to do, with no error and no warning. The parts were meant to be added together. 133 of the 400 remittances were settled in more than one part and every one of them holds less than it was paid, leaving the register 697,850 pennies short against the events it was built from. The statement ran once and reported 400 rows updated.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.remittances r WHERE r.settled_cents <> (SELECT sum(e.amount_cents) FROM payments.settlement_events e WHERE e.remittance_id = r.remittance_id)

defects.title: The ROLLUP total row and the store that has no id both come back as null
defects.why: Returns by store with a total row, written with ROLLUP, which marks the total by putting null in the grouped column. The grouped column is already nullable, because an order placed before the second store opened has no store. The view returns two rows with a null store, one meaning the original store and one meaning every store, and nothing in the result tells them apart. The two hold 347 and 49 returns, so a filter on store_id IS NULL adds up to 396 returns from a table that holds 347. GROUPING(o.store_id) is the function that distinguishes them and is the reason it exists.

detect.sql: SELECT sum(returns) FROM analytics.v_returns_rollup WHERE store_id IS NULL

defects.title: A job scheduled at 01:30 on the spring forward night is stored as 02:30
defects.why: The overnight schedule came off cron, which ran on local time, so the times are kept as local wall clock text and converted on load with AT TIME ZONE. On the night the clocks go forward, local time jumps from 00:59 to 02:00 and the hour between does not exist. AT TIME ZONE neither rejects a time in that hour nor warns: it resolves forward, so 01:30 becomes 02:30. 1 of the 61 scheduled runs no longer round trips back to the local time it was loaded from, the run on 2026-03-29, and it is an hour later than the screen shows. A job that reconciles the day's takings at 01:30 runs after the cutover it was meant to precede.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.scheduled_jobs WHERE (run_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London')::text <> local_text

defects.title: The index leads with the carrier, and the only lookup supplies the reference
defects.why: Dispatch notes are looked up by their reference, which is unique and is what the carrier quotes back. The index was created on carrier and reference in that order, because the operations screen lists notes per carrier. A btree can only use a column when every column to its left is constrained, so the lookup, which supplies the reference and not the carrier, cannot use the index at all. carrier_id takes three distinct values across 1,200 rows, so the leading column divides the table into thirds and the lookup reads one of them end to end. Swapping the columns serves both queries, because a prefix of a composite index is itself usable, and the index shows as used because the listing screen uses it.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT attname FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'fulfilment.dispatch_notes'::regclass AND attnum = i.indkey[0]) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid WHERE c.relname = 'ix_dispatch_notes_ref'

defects.title: Three months of scans sit in the default partition and nothing reports it
defects.why: The scan feed is partitioned by month, and a default partition was added after a night when next month's partition did not exist and the inserts failed. That hid the thing it fixed: rows for months with no partition are accepted silently and land in the default, so nothing fails and nothing reports a missing partition. 900 of the 1,800 scans are in the default partition, covering April, May and June, and only January to March have partitions of their own. Creating April's partition now fails, because ATTACH scans the default and refuses while rows belonging to the new partition are still in it, so the fix costs a lock and a move and gets more expensive every month.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.delivery_scans_default

defects.title: Subtracting two YYYYMMDD integers reports 98 days for a 26 day gap
defects.why: Service visits from the system that ran until 2001 store the date as the eight digit number a human would write. The gap between visits is computed by subtracting one from the other, which is right within a month and reads correctly on screen. 20260301 minus 20260228 is 73: the value is an integer that looks like a date, so the difference is an integer that looks like a number of days and is not one. 171 of the 200 gaps cross a month end and are overstated; every visit in the table is 26 days after the one before it and the largest gap the view reports is 98 days. Casting through to_date and subtracting dates is exact.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_service_visit_gaps WHERE days_since_last_visit <> (to_date(visit_date::text, 'YYYYMMDD') - to_date(previous_visit_date::text, 'YYYYMMDD'))

defects.title: Homepage slots hold a rank number that the next refresh reassigns
defects.why: The homepage features products by their position in a materialised ranking, and the slots store that position. row_number() is a position in a result, not an identity: a refresh computes it again from whatever the data says, so a product that moves up takes the number of the product that was there before. After one score revision and one refresh, 19 of the 20 slots point at a product other than the one captured in them. Nothing is orphaned and no constraint is violated, because the number is not a key and no foreign key could be declared on it. The slot should hold product_id and read the rank when it needs it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.featured_slots s JOIN analytics.mv_product_ranking r ON r.rank_id = s.rank_id WHERE r.product_id <> s.product_id_at_capture

defects.title: Commission rates are stored as percentages in one era and fractions in another
defects.why: The 2019 agreements were typed in as the percentage people say out loud, so two and a half per cent is 2.5. The 2024 agreements were loaded from a feed that sends a fraction, so the same rate is 0.025. The column holds both and cannot tell them apart: 20 of the 60 agreements are fractions and the other 40 are percentages, and 20 suppliers hold one of each. Anything that multiplies by the column is out by a hundred for one convention or the other. The check constraint only says the rate is positive, and both spellings are perfectly good commission rates, so nothing in the database can detect it. One convention and a column name that carries it, rate_fraction or rate_percent, is the fix.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.commission_rates WHERE rate < 1

defects.title: The label print log has a smallint key and 2,767 labels of headroom
defects.why: The key was made a smallint when the first version printed a few hundred labels a week. The log has filled at about a hundred and twenty a day since the second warehouse opened and the counter stands at 30,000, which leaves 2,767 before the column's limit of 32,767, or about 23 days. The identity sequence stops at the column's maximum, so the failure is not a wrapped key: it is an insert that raises out of range for every label printed after that day, and the warehouse cannot dispatch. Widening the column rewrites the table and takes a lock on the busiest table in the warehouse, which costs a quiet hour now and the same hour with the warehouse stopped later.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'ops.label_prints'::regclass AND attname = 'print_id' AND atttypid = 'int2'::regtype

defects.title: Weighbridge tickets are keyed by a float that cannot hold the number the yard sent
defects.why: The yard system builds the ticket number from the site code and the millisecond the bridge settled, so it is sixteen digits, and it exports every number as a floating point value. The column was created to match the file. A double holds integers exactly only up to about nine thousand million million; above that the representable values are two apart, so an odd ticket number becomes its neighbour. All 600 keys differ from the number kept beside them in ticket_source: the smallest is sent as 9007199254740997 and stored as 9007199254741000. Two consecutive yard tickets can also land on the same key, which the primary key then rejects as a duplicate of a ticket it is not a duplicate of. Nothing failed at load, every join works, and the key matches nothing in the yard's own system.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.weighbridge_tickets WHERE ticket_no::numeric(16,0) <> ticket_source

defects.title: The contact view's INSTEAD OF trigger silently drops the phone column
defects.why: The contact screen writes through a view, and the INSTEAD OF trigger sets the columns the screen sent when it was written. A column added later is not in the trigger body, so an update that changes it succeeds, reports one row updated, and leaves the column exactly as it was. A cleanup lowercased every email and reformatted every phone number through the view: all 780 emails changed and none of the 780 phone numbers did. There is no error, the row count is right, and reading the row back through the same view is the only thing that would show it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.customer_contacts WHERE phone NOT LIKE '0161%'

defects.title: An unsubscribed address cannot subscribe again
defects.why: The list never deletes a row, because the unsubscribe has to be provable for as long as the marketing rules say. The unique index on the email covers every row including the unsubscribed ones, so an address that has unsubscribed cannot subscribe again: the insert raises a unique violation and the row blocking it is one the application considers deleted. 80 of the 400 rows are unsubscribed and each holds its address against a new signup. A unique index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL enforces the rule that was meant. Every report on this table already filters the deleted rows out, so the index is the only thing left that treats them as live.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'marketing.subscriber_list'::regclass AND indisunique AND NOT indisprimary AND indpred IS NULL

defects.title: Bundle labels print fewer components than the count beside them
defects.why: The picking label joins the component skus with a plus and prints the number of components beside it. array_to_string drops null elements: it does not render them and does not put a gap where they were unless it is given the optional third argument. A bundle whose component was discontinued has a null in the array, so 30 of the 120 bundles print a label with two components beside a count of three. The label is the part the picker reads. The third argument renders nulls as whatever it is given, and the honest fix is not to keep nulls in the array at all.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_bundle_labels WHERE array_length(string_to_array(label,' + '),1) <> component_count

defects.title: The console's admin check passes every account that has no role
defects.why: The console asks whether the user's roles contain admin, and the containment operator was written round the wrong way. ARRAY['admin'] @> roles asks whether every role the user holds is admin, which is true for two groups: users who hold admin, and users who hold nothing at all, because the empty array is contained in everything. 80 accounts are shown as administrators, 10 of them hold the admin role, and the other 70 hold no role, which is how every account starts. A real admin passes either way round, so the check is not broken for the people it was tested with. roles @> ARRAY['admin'] is the check that was meant, and 'admin' = ANY(roles) says it more plainly.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.v_console_admins

defects.title: The overdrawn accounts report sorts by distance from zero
defects.why: The report lists the twenty most overdrawn accounts, worst first, and selects the balance through abs() so it prints without a minus sign. The alias was kept as balance_cents. ORDER BY resolves a bare name as an output column before it looks for an input column, so the sort is over abs(balance_cents), which is distance from zero: ascending, that is the accounts closest to square. None of the twenty accounts listed are overdrawn at all, the worst account in the ledger owes 90,910 pennies and is not on the report, and the largest figure the report prints is 39 pennies. Qualifying the column as b.balance_cents in the ORDER BY sorts by the table column. The report has twenty rows, sorted, with amounts in them, which is what it is checked for.

detect.sql: SELECT max(balance_cents) FROM analytics.v_overdrawn_accounts

defects.title: Weekly picks are grouped by an ISO week and a calendar year
defects.why: The picking report groups by extract(year) and extract(week) so the warehouse can compare a week against the same week last year. extract(week) is the ISO week number and ISO weeks belong to ISO years, which disagree with the calendar year at the turn of it: the first days of January can fall in week 52 or 53 of the year before. The report carries a row for week 53 of 2027, a year that has no week 53, holding 1,242 picks over the 3 days that belong to week 53 of 2026, which appears separately as 2,426 picks over 4 days. extract(isoyear) is the year that goes with an ISO week, and to_char with IYYY-IW gives both from one call. It hides for fifty-one weeks of the year and shows up in the week the year-on-year comparison is run for.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_weekly_picks WHERE year_no = 2027 AND week_no = 53

defects.title: Callback numbers are stored as integers and lost their leading zero
defects.why: The numbers came off a spreadsheet where they were already numbers and the column was created to match. A phone number is not a quantity: its digits are positional and the first of them is a zero a numeric type has no way to keep. 832 of the 1,040 numbers are ten digits long and were eleven in the file they came from; the 208 written in international form survive because those start with a 4. The desk dials what the screen shows. varchar is the type for a phone number and also holds the spacing, the extension and the plus. Nothing rejected the load and the column validates as a number, because that is what it is now.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.callback_requests WHERE length(phone_number::text) = 10

defects.title: A NULLS NOT DISTINCT key collapses every bulk line on a purchase order
defects.why: Goods-in lines are keyed by the purchase order reference and the batch code, and bulk goods have no batch. The unique constraint was declared NULLS NOT DISTINCT because two rows with no batch looked like duplicates when the table was designed, so every bulk line on an order collides with the first one. The load runs with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, added so a rerun of the file would be safe, so the collisions are not errors: 600 of the 900 staged lines reached the table and 300 were dropped, all of them bulk lines on an order that had more than one. The default is NULLS DISTINCT, which is what this table needed. The staging table still holds the file, so the difference is visible to anybody who counts both, and nothing counts both.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.goods_in_staging) - (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.goods_in_lines)

defects.title: Correcting one brand code rewrites every product row that carries it
defects.why: Brands are keyed by the brand code, which is the value the catalogue team edit, and the products reference it with ON UPDATE CASCADE so a correction does not orphan anything. The cascade works, and that is the cost: correcting one character of one code rewrites every product row carrying it, takes a row lock on each, writes a new version of each and leaves the old ones for vacuum. One code correction moved 500 of the 20,000 product rows, and the team make that edit whenever a brand is renamed. A surrogate brand_id in the child rows makes the correction a one row update. Nothing here is incorrect and nothing shows as an error: it shows as a statement that takes minutes and blocks the catalogue while it runs.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'catalog.brand_products'::regclass AND contype = 'f' AND confupdtype = 'c'

defects.title: The blocklist filter keeps every blocked address
defects.why: Marketing may not mail certain domains, and the mailable list excludes them with <> ANY against the blocklist. ANY means at least one: x <> ANY (list) asks whether there is at least one entry x differs from, which is true for every x the moment the list holds two different entries. All 300 subscribers are mailable according to the view and 90 of them are on a blocked domain. With a single-entry blocklist the filter works, which is what it was tested against, and a second entry disabled it silently. ALL is the quantifier for the question being asked, and NOT IN or NOT EXISTS say it without a quantifier at all. The filter is present, it is in the WHERE clause, and it has never removed a row.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.v_mailable_subscribers v JOIN marketing.blocked_domains b ON b.domain = v.email_domain

defects.title: A failed concurrent build left a unique index that enforces nothing
defects.why: Agent logins are unique by email and the index was rebuilt with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY during a release, which failed part way through. A failed concurrent build leaves the index behind marked invalid and not ready: nothing removes it, nothing reports it, the planner will not use it, and it enforces nothing. The uniqueness the table is meant to have stopped existing the moment the build failed, and the index is still listed when anybody looks at the table. 60 accounts now share an email address with another account, across 30 addresses. A password reset sent to a duplicated address updates one of the two, chosen by whichever row the query reached first. DROP INDEX and a fresh build is the fix, and it has to happen before the duplicates are cleaned up rather than after.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'support.agent_accounts'::regclass AND indisunique AND NOT indisvalid

defects.title: Retiring a department moved its aisles to the front of the shop
defects.why: The category tree references itself with ON DELETE SET NULL, so retiring a category does not take its children with it. A null parent does not mean orphaned in this table: it means top level, and the homepage lists every category with a null parent. Retiring three departments in June therefore did not leave their aisles dangling, which would have been visible. It promoted them: 16 categories now have no parent, one is the real root and the other 15 are those aisles. ON DELETE RESTRICT would have refused the delete and made somebody decide where the children go. The retirement ran, reported success, and the shop rearranged itself overnight with no error anywhere.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.v_top_level_categories

defects.title: The delivery preference backfill wrote nothing to three quarters of the orders
defects.why: The migration that added a delivery preference set it with jsonb_set. jsonb_set creates a missing last key, which is what the author tested, and will not create a missing parent: given a path of two keys where the first does not exist it returns the document exactly as it was. It does not raise and does not return null, and the UPDATE reports every row as updated because every row was written, with the value it already had. 2,082 of the 2,776 orders have no delivery preference, which is every one whose document had no delivery object, and the statement reported all 2,776 updated. Creating the parent first, or merging with ||, sets it on every row. The rows that took the value are the ones that already had the object, so the new preference is present exactly where it was least needed.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.order_preferences WHERE preferences -> 'delivery' ->> 'leave_safe' IS NULL

defects.title: The agent notes policy is never consulted for the connection that reads them
defects.why: A policy restricts each agent to their own notes. It is written, it is enabled, and it is correct. Row security does not apply to the owner of the table unless the table is also set to FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and the application connects as the owner, so the policy is never consulted for the connection that does all the reading: every agent screen can read all 300 notes across the 6 agents who wrote them. Nothing about the table looks wrong, because row security is on and a policy exists and psql shows both. ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is the missing line, and the application should not be connecting as the owner either. Whichever is fixed first, the policy starts applying that day, which is the reason neither has been.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_policy p ON p.polrelid = c.oid WHERE c.oid = 'support.agent_notes'::regclass AND c.relrowsecurity AND NOT c.relforcerowsecurity

defects.title: A replayed webhook put a hundred shipments back to accepted
defects.why: The carrier sends shipment events over a webhook and the current status is kept in its own table, maintained by an upsert that takes whatever arrives last. The carrier does not promise order, and after an outage it replays, so the earlier events arrive after the later ones. 100 of the 400 shipments hold a status older than their latest event, and every one of those reads accepted on the tracking page after being delivered. The event table is complete and correct because it keeps everything; the status table is what the tracking page reads. A WHERE clause on the DO UPDATE comparing the stored timestamp against the proposed one discards the late arrival. Without it the table records arrival order rather than what happened, and the two agree for as long as the carrier's queue is empty.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.shipment_state s WHERE s.occurred_at <> (SELECT max(e.occurred_at) FROM fulfilment.shipment_state_events e WHERE e.shipment_ref = s.shipment_ref)

defects.title: 248 order lines are booked onto fewer pallets than the goods fill
defects.why: Pallets required is the quantity over the units a pallet holds, cast to integer because a pallet count is whole. A numeric to integer cast rounds to the nearest whole number: it neither truncates nor rounds up, so a line needing two and a bit pallets is booked as two and the remainder is left on the dock. 248 of the 600 lines report fewer pallets than the goods need, every one of them short by one, and 23 lines report zero pallets for goods that still have to go on the lorry. ceil() is the function for a count of containers. The figure is a plausible small whole number on every line and is only ever wrong by one, which is the amount that gets blamed on the loaders.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_pallets_required v JOIN supply.pallet_plans p USING (plan_id) WHERE v.pallets_required < ceil(p.qty::numeric / p.pallet_size)

defects.title: rtrim ate part of the part number, not just the size suffix
defects.why: The catalogue groups the sizes of one part together by stripping the size suffix, and does it with rtrim and the suffix as the second argument. That argument is a set of characters, not a suffix: rtrim removes every trailing character in the set, repeatedly, until it meets one that is not. So it strips the suffix from the parts that carry it and keeps going into the parts that merely end in one of those letters. 300 of the 900 part numbers produce a root that is not the one the printed catalogue holds; CRT-4001L becomes CRT-4001 and is grouped with a part it has nothing to do with. Removing a known suffix is an anchored regexp_replace or a length test. Every root rtrim produces still looks like a part number.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_part_number_roots v JOIN supply.part_numbers p USING (part_id) WHERE v.root <> p.catalogue_root

defects.title: 250 addresses have a postcode that is present and blank
defects.why: Addresses arrive from the depot handhelds as one pipe delimited line and the import splits them with split_part, which returns an empty string when the field is not there rather than null. A line sent with two fields instead of three produces an address whose postcode is present and blank. 250 of the 1,000 imported addresses have no postcode and not one of them is null, so a count of missing postcodes written as postcode IS NULL returns 0 and the delivery run sorts by the empty string. nullif(split_part(...), '') belongs in the import rather than in every query downstream. The distinction between absent and empty is what the import threw away, and nothing in the database can get it back.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_delivery_addresses WHERE postcode = ''

defects.title: 624 people who opted out are on the campaign list
defects.why: The campaign goes to the newsletter segment or the catalogue segment, restricted to customers who can be mailed: three selects, a UNION and an INTERSECT, no parentheses. INTERSECT binds tighter than UNION the way multiplication binds tighter than addition, so the restriction applies to the catalogue branch alone and the newsletter branch passes through untouched. 1,560 customers are on the target list and 624 of them are not mailable. Parentheses round the UNION are the fix and belong there whether or not they change the result, because a reader cannot tell without looking the precedence up. Nothing errors, the list is not short, and the people on it who should not be are the ones who asked not to be.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.v_campaign_targets t WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM marketing.campaign_audiences a WHERE a.customer_id = t.customer_id AND a.segment = 'mailable')

defects.title: Every machine on the estate reads as installed this month
defects.why: Install age in days is taken with age() and the day field pulled out of the result. age() returns an interval broken into years, months and days, so its day field is what is left after whole months and never exceeds thirty. All 400 installs report an age under 31 days and 388 of them disagree with the real gap; the oldest machine was installed 810 days before the report date and reports 18. Subtracting one date from another gives the number of days and is the whole answer. Every age on the screen is a small plausible number, every machine looks recently installed, and the warranty report reads from this view.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_install_age WHERE age_days <> (DATE '2026-09-01' - installed_on)

defects.title: A wireless settings push deleted the proxy from every handheld
defects.why: Handheld settings are one jsonb document per device and a push applies the change by concatenating a fragment onto the stored document. The jsonb concatenation operator merges at the top level only, so a fragment carrying a nested object replaces the whole object of that name and every sibling key under it is gone. The push that set the network name removed the proxy setting from all 240 devices that had one; no device on the estate now has a proxy configured and none was meant to change. jsonb_set writes one path and leaves the rest of the document alone. The statement reports the rows updated, the document is still valid jsonb, and the two operators read the same in a diff.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.device_profiles WHERE NOT (settings->'network' ? 'proxy')

defects.title: 299 manifest references each name two different orders
defects.why: The carrier takes a fixed width file, so every order reference is padded to fourteen characters with lpad. lpad pads a short value and truncates a long one, without raising or warning, and it keeps the leading characters, so a reference carrying what distinguishes it at the end loses exactly that. 600 of the 900 manifest lines carry a reference that is not the reference on the order, and 299 of the references the file prints name two different orders each. A field narrower than the value it carries is a format problem rather than a padding one, and the honest response is to raise instead of printing something the carrier will quote back. Every line in the file is fourteen characters and the carrier reconciles against it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_carrier_manifest v JOIN fulfilment.carrier_manifest_lines m USING (line_id) WHERE btrim(v.manifest_ref) <> m.order_ref

defects.title: 100 picking lines print a component with no quantity
defects.why: A kit is a list of component skus and a parallel list of quantities, and the picking list pairs them by unnesting both in the select list. Two set returning functions in one select list run in lockstep and the shorter is padded with nulls to the length of the longer, so a kit whose arrays disagree in length neither errors nor drops a row: it prints a component with no quantity beside it. 100 of the 500 kits have arrays of different lengths and the picking list prints 100 component lines with nothing in the quantity column. The pairing belongs in one array of composite values or in a child table with one row per component, which is what makes the lengths impossible to disagree. Two parallel arrays are two facts kept in step by hand and nothing here checks that they are.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_kit_component_quantities WHERE qty IS NULL

defects.title: The March refresh blanked the tax code for 1,040 customers
defects.why: The March refresh set every customer's tax code from the registry, with the new code written as a scalar subquery on the region. A scalar subquery that matches nothing is not an error and does not skip the row: it evaluates to null and the UPDATE writes that null over the code that was there. The registry covers 4 of the 6 regions, and the two it does not cover are the ones whose codes were typed in by hand and existed nowhere else. 1,040 of the 3,120 customers now have no tax code and every one of them had one before the statement ran. A WHERE EXISTS on the same subquery leaves the unmatched rows alone. The statement reported 3,120 rows updated, which is what it was checked against.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.customer_tax_codes WHERE tax_code IS NULL

defects.title: 351 ledger entries appear on no page of the finance screen
defects.why: The finance screen pages the ledger by date and entry id, carrying the last row of a page as the cursor, and asks for everything after it with two comparisons joined by AND. Two separate comparisons are not the same as comparing the pair: the pair is ordered lexicographically, so a row on a later date qualifies whatever its id, while the ANDed form also demands a larger id and drops every later row whose id happens to be smaller. 351 of the 1,051 entries after the cursor are missing from the page, and they are not on the page before it either. Row comparison, (entry_date, entry_id) > (cursor_date, cursor_id), is the expression this needed and the btree index on the same pair serves it. The page is full and in order, so nothing on the screen shows the gap.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.ledger_pages WHERE (entry_date, entry_id) > (DATE '2026-03-01', 500)) - (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_ledger_page)

defects.title: The trade counter search finds 180 valves and misses 720
defects.why: The trade counter searches part descriptions with LIKE and a pattern lowercased on the way in so the search is not fussy about capitals. LIKE is case sensitive, so lowercasing the pattern and not the column is worse than doing neither: it matches only the descriptions somebody happened to type without a capital, and the catalogue is in title case. The search returns 180 parts, so it looks like it works, and 720 more parts have valve in the description and are not returned. ILIKE, or lower() on both sides, matches what was meant, and a trigram index makes either fast. The part that is missing is the one the customer is standing at the counter asking for, and the counter tells them it is not stocked.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.part_descriptions WHERE description ILIKE '%valve%') - (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_part_search_hits)

defects.title: The archive copy of the invoice lines enforces nothing
defects.why: The archive copy of the invoice lines was created from the live table with LIKE so the two would stay the same shape. LIKE copies the columns, the types and the not null constraints and nothing else unless asked: no primary key, no unique constraint, no check constraint, no default, and a foreign key it will not copy at all. The copy therefore carries 0 primary key, check or unique constraints while describing itself identically in any column listing. The archive holds 60 lines with a negative amount and 80 line ids that appear on more than one row, both of which the live table rejects, and the reconciliation reads the archive. INCLUDING ALL copies the constraints, the indexes and the defaults; the foreign key still has to be written by hand.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM archive.invoice_lines_copy WHERE amount_cents < 0

defects.title: 360 deliveries passed the goods-in check on questions nobody answered
defects.why: A goods-in check is three yes or no questions per delivery and the delivery passes when all three are yes, which the view asks with bool_and. bool_and ignores nulls the way every aggregate does, so a question nobody answered is not counted and the verdict comes from the questions that were answered: one yes and two blanks is indistinguishable from three yes. 360 of the 900 deliveries pass with an unanswered question on them and 180 of those pass on a single yes out of three. bool_and(coalesce(answer, false)) treats an unanswered question as a failure, which is what a check sheet is for. The screen shows a pass and the supervisor signs it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_goods_check_status s WHERE s.passed AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM supply.goods_checks c WHERE c.delivery_no = s.delivery_no AND c.answer IS NULL)

defects.title: The stock audit has no record of any transfer between warehouses
defects.why: Stock moves are partitioned by warehouse and every change is audited by a row trigger on UPDATE. An update that changes the partition key moves the row between partitions, which Postgres implements as a delete followed by an insert, and the UPDATE trigger does not fire for it. 720 updates ran against the table and the audit holds 600; the 120 missing are exactly the ones that changed warehouse, which is the only change anybody would look for. Triggers on DELETE and INSERT catch the movement at the price of telling a real delete from half of a move. A trigger declared on the parent is inherited by every partition and still does not see this, which is why the audit was believed complete.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.stock_moves) + (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.stock_moves WHERE warehouse = 'leeds') - (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.stock_move_audit)

defects.title: Eight saved campaign filters return nothing at all
defects.why: Campaigns carry a list of tags and the filter keeps the campaigns whose tags contain every tag asked for, using array containment. Containment answers false whenever either side holds a null, because the comparison it is built from is null and null is not true. A saved filter with a blank row in its tag list matches no campaign at all, whatever else is in it. 8 of the 20 saved filters hold a null and return 0 campaigns each; with the nulls removed the same filters return 11,200 campaign rows between them. An array cannot declare its elements NOT NULL, so the guard is a check constraint or stripping nulls with array_remove before comparing. The filter runs and reads as a segment with no members.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.tag_filters f WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM analytics.v_tagged_campaigns v WHERE v.filter_id = f.filter_id)

defects.title: 300 contacts with no email are reported as one duplicate
defects.why: The duplicate contact report groups trade account contacts by email and keeps the groups holding more than one row. GROUP BY puts every null in one group, because grouping treats nulls as equal even though comparison does not, so every contact with no email address is reported as a single large duplicate. The report names 4 groups; the largest holds 300 contacts that have nothing in common but a blank field, and the 3 real duplicates are the rest of it. A HAVING clause excluding the null group, or a filter on email IS NOT NULL, leaves the report with the duplicates it was written to find. The null group is the biggest thing on the report, so it is the one worked first.

detect.sql: SELECT coalesce((SELECT contacts FROM analytics.v_duplicate_contacts WHERE email IS NULL), 0)

defects.title: 297 settlements over the review threshold went through unreviewed
defects.why: The settlement run applies the feed to the batches with MERGE, using two matched clauses: one marks a batch settled and the one after it marks a batch over the review threshold for review instead. MERGE takes the first clause whose condition holds and stops, and the clauses are in the order they were written rather than from the most specific outwards, so the general one takes every row and the review clause never runs. Postgres rejects a clause made unreachable by an unconditional one before it, but cannot see that one condition implies another, so this passes. 297 batches over the threshold are marked settled and none is marked for review. Ordering the clauses from the narrowest condition outwards is the whole fix.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.settlement_batches WHERE amount_cents > 200000 AND status = 'settled'

defects.title: 320 ticket subjects are cut short on the queue screen without a mark
defects.why: The queue screen shows a short subject line, so the view casts the subject to varchar(40) to fit the column it renders into. A cast to varchar(n) truncates without complaint, where the same value going into a varchar(40) column would raise, which is what anybody who has loaded a too long value expects. 320 of the 800 subjects are cut short on the screen, losing between 49 and 51 characters each. left(subject, 37) || '...' truncates on purpose and says so, which is the honest version. A silent cast makes a short subject and a truncated one look the same, and the reply quotes the short one back to the customer.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_ticket_subject_lines v JOIN support.ticket_subjects s USING (subject_id) WHERE v.subject_line <> s.subject

defects.title: Every meter read flag matches a reading in both years
defects.why: Meter reads are partitioned by year, the parent has no key of its own, and each partition declares a primary key on the read id, so the read ids start again at one every year. The flags table's foreign key names a partition rather than the partitioned table, because a partitioned table could not be referenced when it was written. The constraint is satisfied by the 2025 read with that id whatever year the flag was about, and 400 flags join to 800 meter reads, one in each year. A foreign key onto the partitioned table needs the partition key in the child, which is the column that was left out: a flag is about a read in a year, and the year is what makes the id mean anything. The constraint is present, valid, and checking the wrong table.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM archive.meter_read_flags f JOIN archive.meter_reads r USING (read_id)) - (SELECT count(*) FROM archive.meter_read_flags)

defects.title: The margin cache holds one copy per rebuild the connection has run
defects.why: The margin cache rebuild stages its working rows in a temporary table created IF NOT EXISTS, because the first version failed on the second call of the day saying the relation already existed. A temporary table lives for the session, not the call, so IF NOT EXISTS stopped the error and kept the rows: the second call stages on top of the first one's working set and every call after that adds a copy. Two calls in one session leave 2,000 rows in the cache where there are 1,000 products. ON COMMIT DROP, a TRUNCATE at the top of the function, or no temporary table at all each fix it. Every call reports success, so anything reading one product is right and anything summing the cache is out by the number of calls.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.margin_cache

defects.title: 60 products have two current prices and the screen picks one
defects.why: Prices are versioned and the counter screen shows the row flagged current, with nothing in the table saying only one version of a product may carry the flag. The application clears the old row and sets the new one in two statements, so a run that fails between them, or two price loads overlapping, leaves both flagged. 60 of the 600 products have more than one current version and the screen shows whichever of the two the planner reaches first, which is stable enough to look deliberate and changes the day the plan does. A unique index on (product_id) WHERE is_current makes the second row impossible and costs nothing. Without it the table holds a contradiction and the only place it shows is the price the customer is quoted.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT product_id FROM catalog.price_versions WHERE is_current GROUP BY product_id HAVING count(*) > 1) x

defects.title: The catalogue team review 600 items that did not change
defects.why: The price feed is applied with an upsert and a BEFORE INSERT trigger queues a notification for every new item so the catalogue team can review it. A BEFORE INSERT trigger fires for every row the statement attempts, including the ones that go on to conflict and become updates, because Postgres cannot know which will conflict until it tries. The feed carried 900 rows of which 300 were new and the queue holds 900 notifications, so 600 of them name items that did not change and are indistinguishable from the real ones. The notification belongs in an AFTER trigger, where the row that survived the conflict is known. Nothing about the queue looks wrong: every notification names a real item and the count matches the size of the feed.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.price_feed_notifications

defects.title: 240 webhook payloads are absent from the item view entirely
defects.why: Webhook payloads are stored whole and the line items are read out by expanding the items array in the FROM clause. Expanding a set returning function there is an inner join against it, so a payload with no items array expands to no rows and is not in the result at all: not with a null item, not as a row with nothing beside it. 240 of the 1,200 payloads carry no items array and none appears in the view, which reports 2,880 item rows from 960 payloads. LEFT JOIN LATERAL keeps the payload and leaves the item null, which is the difference between a delivery with no lines and a delivery that never arrived. The reconciliation counts what the view returns, and the payloads it cannot see are the ones that failed to parse upstream.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.webhook_payloads p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM analytics.v_webhook_items v WHERE v.payload_id = p.payload_id)

defects.title: Device report deduplication keeps every report twice
defects.why: Device reports arrive as json and the duplicate suppression groups them by the payload cast to text, because json has no equality operator. json keeps the text it was given, key order and spacing included, so two reports that say the same thing in a different order are different text and are not duplicates: the cast added to make the GROUP BY work is what makes it compare formatting. The estate sent 900 reports carrying 80 distinct states and the deduplicated view returns 160 rows, every state once per key order. jsonb normalises on the way in and has an equality operator. The column was made json to keep the payload exactly as the device sent it, which is a reasonable thing to want and the reason the deduplication cannot work.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_distinct_device_reports) - (SELECT count(DISTINCT payload::text::jsonb) FROM ops.device_reports)

defects.title: Two documents share the short digest printed on the cover sheet
defects.why: Every scanned document carries a digest of its reference cut down to four hex characters so it fits the cover sheet and can be typed back in. Four hex characters is 65,536 values and there are 3,000 documents, so collisions are a certainty rather than a risk: the 3,000 references produce 2,920 distinct digests, 159 documents share one with another document, and 79 of the codes somebody can type return more than one document. The column carries no unique constraint because it was never meant to be a key, and the lookup treats it as one anyway. A short typed key is allocated from a counter and checked for uniqueness. A hash prefix is stable, looks like an identifier, and is only wrong when two of the documents that share a value are in front of the same person.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT digest_short FROM ops.document_digests GROUP BY digest_short HAVING count(*) > 1) x

defects.title: Supplier note export splits sentences at the commas inside them
defects.why: Supplier notes are exported one row per supplier with the individual notes joined by a comma, and read back by splitting on the comma. Buyers write notes in prose and prose contains commas, so a note carrying one comes back as two fields and every field after it shifts along. 600 notes across 200 suppliers read back as 960 fields, 720 of which are half a sentence, and 120 suppliers have at least one note affected. Nothing errors: the export is well formed text and the split returns strings. A delimiter has to be one the data cannot contain, or the values have to be quoted and escaped, which is what a CSV writer does and string_agg does not. A jsonb array or a child table keeps the boundary in the structure instead of in a character.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_supplier_note_lines) - (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.supplier_note_items)

defects.title: Consignments that were never delivered count as delivered on time
defects.why: A consignment counts as on time if it finished on or before its due date, and the finish is taken as greatest(dispatched_on, delivered_on). greatest() ignores nulls and returns the largest argument that is not null, so a consignment dispatched and never delivered does not produce an unknown finish date, it produces the dispatch date, and if that was before the due date the consignment scores as on time. 420 of the 900 consignments count as on time and 180 of those were never delivered at all. The one category of failure the report exists to find is the one it counts as a success. The finish date of an unfinished consignment is unknown and the expression has to propagate that. greatest() is the standard's least surprising name for its most surprising null rule.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_consignment_last_seen v JOIN fulfilment.consignment_milestones c ON c.consignment_id = v.consignment_id WHERE v.on_time AND c.delivered_on IS NULL

defects.title: Only one supplier part with a blank code survives the trade file load
defects.why: Supplier part codes are unique and the column is not nullable, because a missing code is written as the empty string. A nullable unique column permits any number of unknowns, since no null equals another; a NOT NULL column defaulted to the empty string permits exactly one, since every blank equals every other blank. The trade file load inserts with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING so a rerun is safe, which makes the collision silent: 900 staging rows produce 601 part codes, the 299 missing parts are the ones whose supplier code was blank, and the load reported no errors. Unknown is null and a unique constraint is built to tolerate it. The empty string is a value that here behaves as a key with one slot, and the rows it discards are the ones that most needed looking at.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.supplier_part_staging s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM catalog.supplier_part_codes c WHERE c.part_no = s.part_no)

defects.title: Summer shift handovers redisplay an hour after they happened
defects.why: Shift handovers are recorded as the wall clock time on the depot board in a timestamp column with no zone, and the board redisplays them by casting to timestamptz and rendering in Europe/London. A timestamp without a zone carries none, so the cast assumes the server's, and this server runs in UTC while the depot runs in London. London is UTC through the winter and an hour ahead of it between the last Sunday in March and the last Sunday in October, so every handover recorded in British Summer Time redisplays an hour late and every winter one is right: 840 of the 1,200 handovers differ from what was recorded, all by exactly an hour, the earliest on 29 March and the latest on 24 October. The column should be timestamptz written by a client that knows its own zone. A bare wall clock time means whatever the machine reading it decides, and the handover log is what a dispute over a missed collection is settled with.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_shift_handover_times WHERE board_time <> handover_at

defects.title: Closing a pick wave writes no audit row
defects.why: Closing a pick wave stamps the wave and writes an audit row, with the audit write placed in a CTE in front of the UPDATE so the two happen in one statement. PostgreSQL evaluates a plain CTE only if the rest of the statement reads from it, and nothing reads from this one. A data modifying CTE, one whose body is itself an INSERT or UPDATE, runs regardless; a SELECT calling a function that writes does not. The two forms look alike and the statement is valid either way. 400 waves are closed and the audit table holds 0 rows: every wave shows a close time and none shows who closed it. The audit write belongs on a trigger or in its own statement, where whether it runs does not depend on whether anything reads its output. Nothing failed and nothing raised; the trail was simply never written.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.pick_waves WHERE closed_at IS NOT NULL) - (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.pick_wave_audit)

defects.title: Commission rates are rounded to a whole percent by a cast meant to trim decimals
defects.why: Commission is sales times the agent's rate, and the view normalises the rate to numeric(3) before multiplying, meaning three decimal places. numeric(3) is numeric(3,0): the number in the brackets is the precision, the total count of digits, and a precision with no scale means a scale of zero. The cast therefore rounds the rate to a whole percent rather than trimming its decimals, so 1.50 and 2.25 both become 2 and 2.75 becomes 3. Across 800 runs on seven distinct rates between 1.50 and 3.00 percent, 571 are paid at a rate the agency agreement does not carry and the statement totals 108,946 pounds against the 100,905 earned. numeric(6,3) is three decimal places. The precision and the scale read in the opposite order from the way people say them, and the resulting rate is still plausible, so nothing on the statement looks wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_commission_due v JOIN payments.commission_runs c ON c.run_id = v.run_id WHERE v.commission_pounds <> c.sales_cents * c.rate_pct / 10000

defects.title: The daily meter report keeps only the pulses recorded at midnight
defects.why: The daily energy report joins meter pulses to the working calendar with the pulse timestamp equated to the calendar date. Comparing a timestamp to a date promotes the date to midnight on that day, so the equality holds only for a pulse recorded at exactly midnight and every pulse taken during the day fails the join. The report is not empty, because the overnight pulses match, and it charts a plausible curve built from one reading a day: 2,400 pulses carrying 1,438,800 units produce a report totalling 59,600 units from the 100 midnight pulses. The join wanted pulsed_at::date = cal_date, or a range test if the index matters. A predicate between two types PostgreSQL will promote for you neither errors nor warns, and what it does instead is nearly always wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT sum(units) FROM ops.meter_pulses) - (SELECT coalesce(sum(units), 0) FROM analytics.v_daily_pulse_totals)

defects.title: Accounts due on the 31st are collected on the 28th for the rest of the year
defects.why: The standing charge diary is built by adding one month at a time to the previous due date. Adding a month to the 31st lands on the last day of the next month when that month is shorter, and PostgreSQL clamps rather than overflowing. Because each date is computed from the one before it rather than from the start date, the clamp is permanent: an account due on the 31st is pulled back to the 28th in February and stays there. 600 accounts produce 7,200 due dates, 2,200 of which fall on a different day of the month from the one the account was set up on, and the 200 accounts due on the 31st are collected three days early for eleven months of the year. Computing each date as first_due plus n months clamps only in the short months and recovers afterwards, which is what a monthly schedule means. Every date in the diary is a real date on a plausible day and the direct debit goes out on it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_standing_charge_dates d JOIN payments.standing_charges s ON s.charge_id = d.charge_id WHERE extract(day FROM d.due_on) <> extract(day FROM s.first_due)

defects.title: Barcode cleanup strips one stray character and leaves the rest
defects.why: The barcode lookup strips everything that is not a digit or a capital before matching, with regexp_replace and an empty string in the flags position. regexp_replace replaces the first match only; the g flag is what makes it replace all of them. So the first stray character is removed, every one after it stays, and the cleaned code still does not match the catalogue. Of 1,200 scans, 900 carry more than one stray character and all 900 still contain one after the cleanup has run, so every one of them comes back as an unknown item. The flag is one character and its absence is invisible in review, which is why the argument is better left off entirely when no flags are wanted. An empty string in the flags position reads as deliberate and does nothing.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_cleaned_barcodes WHERE cleaned_code ~ '[^0-9A-Z]'

defects.title: A support case with no watchers reports one watcher
defects.why: The watcher list on a support case is built by aggregating watchers over a left join so cases with nobody watching still appear. array_agg does not skip nulls the way sum() and count() do: a case with no watchers produces one row from the left join with a null on the right, and array_agg turns that into an array of length one holding a null rather than an empty array.
