So cardinality reports one watcher on a case that has none. 100 of the 500 cases have no watcher at all, all 100 report a watcher count of 1, and the screen listing cases with nobody assigned returns nothing. array_agg(w.watcher) FILTER (WHERE w.watcher IS NOT NULL) gives an empty array. count() over the same left join would have given zero, which is why two figures on the same screen disagree and the wrong one is the one in the list.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_case_watcher_lists WHERE watcher_count = 1 AND watchers[1] IS NULL

defects.title: The quote export still carries the four columns that existed in March
defects.why: The quote export the buying system imports is a view over the quotes table, written as SELECT * so it would follow the table. A view does not follow the table: PostgreSQL resolves the star once, at creation, and stores the column list it resolved to, so columns added later are not in the view until somebody replaces it. The table now has 6 columns and the export has 4. The currency and expiry columns added in June are missing, and 300 of the 900 quotes are priced in euros and exported with no currency beside the number. Naming the columns makes the omission visible, and CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW is the step that was missed. The export validates, the row count is right, and the buying system reads every price as sterling because that is all it has ever been sent.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'catalog.vendor_quotes'::regclass AND attnum > 0 AND NOT attisdropped) - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'analytics.v_vendor_quote_export'::regclass AND attnum > 0 AND NOT attisdropped)

defects.title: Three hundred courier bookings share a booking number with another booking
defects.why: A resync procedure keeps the booking number sequence level with the data after a restore, by taking the highest booking number and calling setval with a third argument of false. That argument is is_called, and false means the value given has not been handed out yet, so the next nextval returns it rather than the one after. The maximum is also taken from a filtered query, the bookings made before June, so the sequence is not set level with the data at all but back to where the data stood two months earlier. 1,200 bookings now hold 900 distinct numbers and 300 numbers are on two bookings each, with no unique constraint to stop it because a booking number was never meant to be a key. setval with is_called at its default sets the last value used, and the maximum has to be taken over the whole table. Both bookings quote the same number to the courier.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT booking_no FROM fulfilment.courier_bookings GROUP BY booking_no HAVING count(*) > 1) x

defects.title: Brand aliases that differ only in case cannot both be stored
defects.why: The brand alias column was given a case insensitive collation to make the search box easy, and a unique constraint to keep the list tidy. A non-deterministic collation does not only change comparison, it changes what equal means for the unique index, so two aliases differing only in case are the same value and the second cannot be stored. The load uses ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so it does not fail: 600 staged aliases produce 400 rows and the 200 dropped are the ones whose spelling differs from an existing alias only in case. Case insensitive searching is what the collation is for; case insensitive uniqueness is a separate decision and was made here by accident. The list looks complete, the search works, and the capitalisation the brand owner asked for is the one that is missing.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.brand_alias_staging s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM catalog.brand_aliases b WHERE b.alias::text COLLATE "C" = s.alias COLLATE "C")

defects.title: Every pallet label carries the depot prefix and no batch number
defects.why: A pallet label carries a batch prefix and a depot prefix, each applied by its own BEFORE INSERT trigger so the two changes stayed in separate reviews. Several BEFORE triggers on one table fire in alphabetical order by trigger name, each seeing what the previous one left in NEW, and both of these assign the whole label rather than adding to it. So trg_label_depot, which sorts later, wins outright and trg_label_batch may as well not exist: all 1,000 labels carry the depot prefix and none carries the batch number. Nothing in either trigger's own code says so and each is correct read on its own. One trigger that applies both parts is the shape this wanted, and a second trigger must append to what it was given. The printed label is well formed and scans, which is the whole of what was tested, and the batch number is what a recall is traced on.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.goods_labels WHERE printed_label LIKE batch_no || '/%'

defects.title: Order size bands still reflect the boundaries that were replaced in June
defects.why: Orders carry a size band held as a stored generated column so it can never disagree with the total, computed by a function that reads a lookup table and had to be marked IMMUTABLE for the generated column to be accepted. A function that reads a table is not immutable, and marking it so does not make it so, it only stops PostgreSQL from checking. A stored generated column is computed once at write time and never again, so when the bands were re-cut in June every order written earlier kept its old band: 305 of the 1,200 orders now carry a band the lookup table no longer agrees with, and the commercial report groups on the stored column. A view or a plain expression recomputes on every read. Marking the function IMMUTABLE was not an optimisation, it was the only way to get the definition past the parser, which is the point at which the design was already wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.order_bands WHERE band <> catalog.fn_band_for(total_cents)

defects.title: Write-offs add stock to the on-hand figure instead of removing it
defects.why: A write-off is posted as a negative quantity, which is the convention the warehouse system has used since it was written and which is recorded nowhere. The on hand view was written later by somebody who read the column name and took the quantity for a magnitude with the direction held in the reason, so it sums abs(quantity) and every write-off adds stock instead of removing it. Across 2,400 adjustments covering 200 skus the real net movement is 274,740 units and the view reports 378,060, a difference of 103,320 units that was written off and is counted as if it had arrived. A comment on the column, a separate direction column, or a check that the reason and the sign agree would each have made this impossible. The figure the view produces is positive and plausible and reconciles against nothing, because the only other place the number appears is the same view.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT sum(on_hand) FROM analytics.v_stock_on_hand) - (SELECT sum(quantity) FROM supply.stock_adjustments)

defects.title: A cycle in the merchandise tree makes the rollup count categories twice
defects.why: The category page rolls up every descendant of a node with a recursive walk carrying a depth limit, added when the page once hung. A merge in March pointed a node at one of its own descendants, so two nodes now point at each other. The depth limit means the walk terminates rather than hanging, which is why the bug was closed: it does not terminate because it has finished but because it has run out of allowance, and it revisits the nodes in the cycle once per lap until then. The tree has 300 nodes, the rollup emits 935 rows, and 44 of the root and node pairs in it appear more than once, every one of them reachable through the cycle. Those categories report their item counts several times over. A cycle is what the walk has to detect, by carrying the path and stopping when a node appears in it twice. The depth limit turned a hang, which somebody would have investigated, into a wrong number, which nobody did.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT root_id, node_id FROM analytics.v_merchandise_rollup GROUP BY root_id, node_id HAVING count(*) > 1) x

defects.title: The throughput refresh locks the dashboard out every ten minutes
defects.why: Depot throughput is a materialized view refreshed by a procedure the scheduler calls every ten minutes during the working day. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY requires a unique index on the view and this one carries 0 unique indexes and 1 plain index on the depot, so the refresh cannot be concurrent and the procedure does a plain refresh, taking an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for its whole duration while every dashboard query blocks behind it. A unique index over the grouping columns is the whole fix and it is what makes the CONCURRENTLY keyword usable. The refresh procedure reads as ordinary, the view is correct after it runs, and the dashboard does not report an error when it blocks: it reports a slow page, which is attributed to the network roughly every other time.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'analytics.mv_depot_throughput'::regclass AND indisunique

defects.title: The contract audit records note edits and no rate changes
defects.why: Contract terms are audited by a trigger declared AFTER UPDATE OF notes, from when the notes field was the only thing anybody edited by hand. A trigger with a column list fires only when one of those columns appears in the UPDATE's SET clause, and the rate has since become the thing that changes. So the annual rate review ran against all 600 contracts and the audit recorded none of them, while the 50 rows the audit does hold are note edits, which is what makes it look like it is working. The trigger is enabled, on the right table, and correct when it fires. Dropping the column list audits every update, which is what an audit trigger is for, and lets the function decide what is worth recording. A column list is a filter written in the trigger definition rather than in the function, and the function is where the review went.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.contract_term_audit WHERE change_kind = 'rate'

defects.title: Quick order lines are written and their ids are never returned
defects.why: The quick order screen writes through a view with an INSTEAD OF INSERT trigger doing the real insert, and the loader captures the new line id from RETURNING so it can attach the delivery note. An INSTEAD OF trigger has to return the row for RETURNING to have anything to return, and this one returns NULL. The insert still happens, because the trigger body does it, but the statement reports zero rows affected and RETURNING produces nothing: 400 lines were written through the view and 0 ids captured. The trigger has to RETURN NEW, reading the assigned id back into NEW first if the base table allocates it. The screen shows the order and the line is on it, so the failure sits in a table nobody opens until a delivery has to be traced.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.quick_order_lines) - (SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.quick_order_ids)

defects.title: Every till on a day shows the same running takings figure
defects.why: Running takings are summed over an ORDER BY on the date with no frame given. A window frame defaults to RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and under RANGE the current row means every row that ties with it on the ORDER BY. Four tills share a date, so all four show the whole day's total rather than the running figure up to their own line: all 800 rows show a running total that at least one other row on the same date also shows. The column is still monotonic and the last row of each day is right. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts rows rather than peers, and an ORDER BY that includes the till number makes the order total anyway. The final balance is correct, which is what gets reconciled, and every intermediate figure on the screen is wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_running_takings v WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM analytics.v_running_takings o WHERE o.took_on = v.took_on AND o.taking_id <> v.taking_id AND o.running_total = v.running_total)

defects.title: A bank line sent twice reconciles against a ledger that holds it once
defects.why: The morning reconciliation lists the bank feed lines that are not in the ledger, written as one SELECT EXCEPT another. EXCEPT removes duplicates from both sides before subtracting, so a line the bank sent twice and the ledger holds once is reconciled: the duplicate collapses into the single row the ledger matches and the pair leaves no trace. Of 1,200 feed lines, 100 were sent twice and the unreconciled list is empty, so the second copy of each of those 100 is money the ledger has never seen. EXCEPT ALL subtracts by multiplicity, which is what a reconciliation means, and counting both sides per reference says the same thing more plainly. The report is clean every morning, which is exactly what a reconciliation is supposed to tell you.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT feed_ref FROM payments.bank_feed_lines GROUP BY feed_ref HAVING count(*) > 1) x) - (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_unreconciled_lines)

defects.title: The support leaderboard lists ten agents who have never been scored
defects.why: The leaderboard is the ten highest scoring agents, ordered by score descending with a limit. PostgreSQL sorts nulls as larger than any value, so descending order puts them first and an agent who has never been surveyed outranks every agent who has a score. Of 60 agents, 12 have never been scored, all 10 rows on the board are unscored agents, and the highest scoring agent in the company is not on it. The board is full, the names are real agents, and the blank number beside each reads as a rendering problem rather than as the wrong ten people. NULLS LAST on the ORDER BY, or a WHERE that excludes the unscored, and the choice between them is a real one: an unscored agent is not a low scoring agent. The board was correct for the first twelve weeks, because nobody was unscored yet.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_top_agents WHERE score IS NULL

defects.title: The credit note screen shows a depot a sixth of its own credits
defects.why: The view was written to keep the credit note screen quick: the two hundred most recent credits, newest first. The LIMIT is inside the view, so it is applied before anything the caller adds. A manager who filters the view to their own depot is filtering a result that has already been cut to two hundred rows for the whole company, and the rest of their depot's credits are not in the view at all to be found. Measured: 1,200 credit notes across 6 depots, 200 rows in the view, and 34 of DEP-A's 200 credit notes visible to a manager at DEP-A. The fix is to take the LIMIT out of the view and let the caller apply its own after its own WHERE. Nothing marks the rows that are missing, and 34 recent credits for one depot is a plausible enough number that the screen reads as correct.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_recent_credits WHERE depot_code = 'DEP-A'

defects.title: Every field the tariff loader wrote is the empty string
defects.why: The customs broker sends a pipe separated tariff file and the loader splits each line into one row per field. The split is a regular expression split and the pattern is a bare full stop, which in a regular expression matches any character. Every character in the line is therefore a separator and every field between two separators is empty. The loader does not fail, it writes more rows than it read, all of them blank. Measured: 600 feed lines produced 11,331 field rows and 0 of them are non-empty, so none of the commodity codes the broker sent are in the database. The delimiter wanted escaping, or split_part, or string_to_array, which takes a literal delimiter rather than a pattern. A loader whose output is twenty times its input reads as one that is working hard rather than one that has lost every value it was given.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.tariff_feed_fields WHERE field_value <> ''

defects.title: Every payout report row reads zero while the payout run reads correctly
defects.why: A payout run is inserted gross and a constraint trigger works out the net amount after the processor's fee. It was declared DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED so a run could be corrected inside the same transaction before the net was settled. A second trigger writes the finance report row, and that one is an ordinary AFTER INSERT trigger, so it runs immediately while the deferred one waits for commit. The report row is written from the net amount as it stands at insert time, which is the column default of zero. Measured: 400 payout runs, all with a net amount above zero once the transaction commits, and 400 report rows all reading zero. Nothing errors. Both triggers need the same timing and the report one needs to be the later of the two. Deferring a trigger moves it past every other AFTER trigger on the table, which is not what deferred until commit sounds like it means.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.payout_report WHERE net_cents = 0

defects.title: The schema change log the auditors asked for has never recorded a change
defects.why: The auditors asked for a record of every schema change and an event trigger was added to write one. Its tag filter carries the commands from the example the pattern was copied out of, which is about foreign data wrappers: CREATE SERVER and CREATE FOREIGN TABLE. This database has never had either. Every ALTER TABLE, CREATE INDEX and CREATE TABLE since goes unrecorded, and because the trigger exists and is enabled, a check that the audit is in place passes. Measured: 0 rows in the change log, against 3 ALTER TABLE statements in the migration that introduced it. The filter wants the tags that actually occur, or no tag filter at all with the decision made inside the function. An empty audit table reads as a quiet quarter rather than as an audit that has never once fired.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_event_trigger t WHERE t.evtname = 'trg_ddl_change_log' AND t.evtenabled <> 'D' AND t.evtevent = 'ddl_command_end' AND t.evttags IS NOT NULL AND NOT ('ALTER TABLE' = ANY (t.evttags)) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ops.ddl_change_log)

defects.title: Half the loading bay diary is dropped at load because each booking touches the next
defects.why: Loading bay bookings must not overlap, which is an exclusion constraint over the bay and the booked period. The period is built with inclusive bounds at both ends, so a booking that ends at ten and a booking that starts at ten share the instant of ten o'clock and count as overlapping. The yard books bays back to back all day. The nightly load runs with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so the rejected bookings are reported nowhere; they are simply absent from the diary the next morning. Measured: 900 staged bookings, 450 loaded, 450 dropped, and every dropped booking is one that starts at the exact minute another ends. The range wants half open bounds, which is what tstzrange gives by default and what every other period in this schema uses. The yard telephones the office about the bookings that vanished and the office re-enters them, which works, because by then the neighbouring booking has moved.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.bay_reservations

defects.title: The partitioned usage table has no statistics, only its partitions do
defects.why: Usage samples are partitioned by quarter and the maintenance job analyses each partition after loading it. Analysing the partitions gives the partitioned table itself nothing, and autovacuum never analyses a partitioned parent either, so a parent has statistics only when somebody asks for them by name. Every query the capacity report runs is written against the parent, and every plan for it is made from the planner's defaults rather than from the data. Measured: 4 partitions carry column statistics, the parent carries none, and the parent's estimated row count is -1 against 4,000 rows present. That is not a stale estimate, it is no estimate at all. ANALYZE on the parent is the whole fix and the job's loop over the partitions will never do it. The report stays correct and only gets slow, which is attributed to volume.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT tablename) FROM pg_stats WHERE schemaname = 'analytics' AND tablename LIKE 'usage_samples%'

defects.title: Every Sunday's counter takings are reported against the week before
defects.why: The trading week at Cross River runs Sunday to Saturday, because the tills are cashed up on Saturday night. The weekly report buckets with date_trunc on week, which is the ISO week and starts on Monday, so every Sunday's takings land in the week that has just finished rather than the week that has just started. Measured: 53 week buckets in the report and all 53 begin on a Monday, and 214 of 1,500 counter sales are reported a week early. The annual total is right and each weekly total is plausible, so the error only shows when a Sunday promotion is judged against a week it was not in. PostgreSQL has no Sunday-start week truncation; the bucket has to be worked out from the day of week. Reviewers check totals rather than boundaries, which is why this has survived a year of weekly reporting.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_trading_week_sales WHERE extract(isodow FROM week_start) = 1

defects.title: A clerk can write a case note to a team they cannot read
defects.why: Case notes are restricted by team: the policy on the table is FOR ALL and covers only the northern team, for reading and for writing alike. A second policy was added for INSERT when a bulk import needed to run, and its check is simply true. Permissive policies are combined with OR, so the second policy is sufficient on its own and the clerk can insert a note against any team at all. Reading is still restricted, so a note saved against the wrong team vanishes from the clerk's own screen the instant it is saved, which reads as a failed save. Measured: 600 case notes written by the clerk role, of which 180 carry a team the clerk cannot read back. The import policy wants restricting to the import role, or expressing as RESTRICTIVE, which is combined with AND rather than OR. The clerks re-type the notes that vanished, which is where the duplicates in the northern team come from.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.case_notes WHERE team <> 'north'

defects.title: The rate card archive is emptied by the loader every night
defects.why: The rate card loader clears its staging table at the start of every run. The archive keeps every version the buying desk has loaded and carries a foreign key back to the staging row it came from, which is how a version is tied to its source file. TRUNCATE will not run against a referenced table, so the loader was changed to TRUNCATE ... CASCADE and the error stopped. CASCADE on TRUNCATE does not delete the matching referencing rows, it truncates the referencing tables as well, so every run empties the archive. Measured: 2,400 archive rows loaded historically, none left after the nightly run, and 300 written by the run that followed, which is the whole of the history the archive now holds. The foreign key does not belong on an archive, and a DELETE with a WHERE is what the loader wanted. The archive is read once a year, at audit.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.rate_card_archive

defects.title: Manufacturers whose name starts lowercase are listed after Z
defects.why: The A to Z manufacturer index on the trade site is ordered with an explicit COLLATE "C", added to make the ordering the same on a developer's machine as on the server. The C collation orders by byte value, so every capital letter sorts before every lowercase one and a manufacturer whose name begins lowercase lands after the whole alphabet rather than under its own letter. The index on the column carries the database collation, so it cannot serve the ordering either and the page sorts from scratch every time. Measured: 400 manufacturers, 23 of them with a lowercase first letter, occupying positions 378 to 400; the first of them is a de la Roche, which belongs in the D section and sits below Yarrow. The stability that was wanted is a tie-break on the primary key, not a different collation. Nobody reports a missing entry on an A to Z page, they report that a supplier is not listed, and support tells them to use search.

detect.sql: SELECT min(list_position) FROM analytics.v_manufacturer_index WHERE name ~ '^[a-z]'

defects.title: Only the last line of the depot file matches the depot register
defects.why: The haulier sends a depot list every morning. The file is written on Windows, the import splits it on the newline, and the carriage return before each newline stays on the end of every value except the last one in the file. A depot code with a carriage return on the end is not equal to the same code without one, so the join to the depot register matches nothing for those rows. The import does not fail and the codes look correct in every screen that shows them, because a carriage return is invisible. Measured: 500 imported rows against 40 registered depots, 20 matched and 480 unmatched, and the 20 are the last line of each day's file. Both the register and the import are correct; only the comparison between them is not. The import wants trimming, and the check on it wants writing against the byte length rather than against what the value looks like.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.depot_code_import WHERE matched_depot IS NOT NULL

defects.title: Till events recorded during a rollup run are never rolled up by any run
defects.why: The till rollup reads every event newer than the stored watermark, writes its rollup rows, and then stores the current time as the new watermark. The current time at the end of the run is later than the newest event the run actually read, by however long the run took, so every event recorded during the run falls between the two and the next run starts after it. Those events are rolled up by no run at all, and since each run reports the number of rows it wrote, every run looks healthy. Measured: 3,000 till events over three runs, 2,916 rolled up and 84 lost in the gaps between what a run read and where it set its watermark. The watermark wants setting to the newest event the run actually read. The shortfall is a fraction of a percent, which sits inside the tolerance the cash position is reconciled to, so it is absorbed rather than found.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.till_events e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM analytics.till_event_rollup r WHERE r.event_id = e.event_id)

defects.title: Narrowing the call summary column cut 720 summaries mid-word
defects.why: Call summaries were free text until the service desk moved to a vendor package whose summary field is sixty characters, and the column was narrowed to match. A plain ALTER of the type refuses to run when a value does not fit, which is exactly the warning that was wanted; a USING clause with left() was added to get the migration through, and left() refuses nothing. Every summary longer than sixty characters was cut where it stood, in place, with no copy of the original kept. Measured: 900 call summaries, 720 of them now exactly sixty characters long and ending mid-word, and the remaining 180 were short enough to be untouched. The migration wanted a second column, or a refusal and a conversation about the vendor's field width. A summary that stops mid-sentence reads as a typist who was interrupted, which happens often enough on a service desk that nobody queried it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.call_summaries WHERE length(body) = 60

defects.title: Every shelf price audit row records a change from a price to itself
defects.why: The shelf price audit is a statement trigger with a transition table, which is the modern way to audit a bulk price change without firing once per row. It declares the new transition table and then joins it back to the base table to find the old price. By the time an AFTER trigger runs, the base table already holds the new price, so the join returns the new price twice and the audit records every change as a change from a value to itself. Measured: 600 shelf prices changed in one statement, 600 audit rows written, and 0 of them show any difference between the old price and the new one. The old transition table is what the trigger needed to declare and it is a single clause. The audit is complete, timely and full of rows, which is what an audit is judged on when anybody checks that it is working at all.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.shelf_price_audit WHERE old_price_cents <> new_price_cents

defects.title: A quarter of picking errors sits in a partition that was detached and never archived
defects.why: Picking errors are partitioned by quarter. The first quarter of the year was detached so it could be archived to cold storage and the archive step never ran. A detached partition is an ordinary table: its rows are still there, still indexed, still taking space, and no longer visible through the parent. Every report written against the partitioned table lost a quarter of the year without a single row being deleted and without an error anywhere. Measured: 2,000 picking errors recorded, 1,461 visible through the parent, and 539 in the detached table that no report reads. Either finish the archive or attach the partition back. The quarterly trend looks better than it is, which is the direction of error nobody investigates, and because the rows still exist no backup or row count check finds it either.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.picking_errors

defects.title: The night loading role is in the group and holds none of its privileges
defects.why: The night loading crew have their own role, granted membership of the warehouse writers group so that it picks up the group's privileges as those change. The role was created NOINHERIT, copied from the pattern used for the administrative roles where not inheriting is the point. A NOINHERIT role holds none of its group's privileges until it runs SET ROLE, and the night loading job does not: it connects and writes. The grant is in place, the membership is in place, and the privilege is not. Measured: night_loader is a member of warehouse_writers, warehouse_writers holds INSERT on the load sheet table, and night_loader has no INSERT on it. Dropping NOINHERIT is the fix, or the job issuing SET ROLE on connect. The failure arrives as permission denied at two in the morning and is read as a connection problem, because the job worked the night before when it ran as somebody's personal account.

detect.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN has_table_privilege('night_loader', 'ops.load_sheets', 'INSERT') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END

defects.title: The counter can correct stock at any depot in the country
defects.why: The trade counter is allowed to correct stock at its own depot, which it does through a SECURITY DEFINER function because the counter role has no write access to the stock tables directly. The function takes the depot code as a parameter and applies the correction to whatever depot it is handed. Nothing checks that the caller works at that depot, and the staff table that would answer the question is sitting in the same schema and is never consulted. Anybody who can call the function can correct stock anywhere in the country, and the log records it as a correction made by them at that depot, which reads as legitimate. Measured: 240 corrections applied, 60 of them at a depot the caller is not on the staff of. The depot belongs to the caller, not to the parameter, and the function should look it up. The counter staff are not doing this maliciously; they are correcting stock for the depot on the telephone, and it works, so it has become the way stock is corrected.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.stock_correction_log l JOIN ops.depot_staff s ON s.login_role = l.applied_by WHERE l.depot_code <> s.depot_code

defects.title: 150 delivery rounds carry the same vehicle twice
defects.why: Which vehicles run which delivery round is a join table, created without a key of any kind because a join table is just two columns. Nothing stops the same vehicle being recorded against the same round twice, and the round planner writes a fresh row every time it is saved rather than comparing against what is already there. A round with a duplicated vehicle is costed twice, and transport cost per drop, which is the number the depots are measured on, is overstated for exactly those rounds. Measured: 1,200 rows covering 1,050 distinct pairs, so 150 pairs appear twice. The primary key is the pair. Adding it now means deciding what to do with the duplicates, which is why it has not been added: the answer is obvious for 150 rows and nobody wants to be the one who deleted transport history.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT round_id, vehicle_ref FROM fulfilment.round_vehicles GROUP BY round_id, vehicle_ref HAVING count(*) > 1) d

defects.title: The gate log runs an hour fast for seven months of the year
defects.why: Gatehouse check-ins are stored with a time zone, which is right, and the reporting view renders them in London time, which gives a timestamp without a zone: a wall clock reading. The view then puts a zone back on that reading and the zone it uses is UTC. A London wall clock is not a UTC one for seven months of the year, so every check-in recorded during British Summer Time is reported an hour later than it happened, and winter check-ins are exact. Measured: 1,200 check-ins across the year, 720 an hour late in the reported column and 480 exact. AT TIME ZONE converts in whichever direction the type it is given implies, so applying it twice either reverses the first conversion or compounds it, and here it compounds. The yard manager's complaint is that the gate log runs an hour fast in the summer, which sounds like a clock on the barrier rather than a view definition.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_gatehouse_times WHERE reported_at <> checkin_at

defects.title: 240 collection notes carry a dispatch time and a status of pending
defects.why: A collection note takes its dispatch timestamp from the carrier's scan, which arrives over the feed within the hour, while the status is moved to dispatched by a nightly job that runs Monday to Friday. Anything scanned on a Friday evening or over a weekend carries a dispatch time and a status of pending until Monday night, and anything scanned in a week the job failed carries both for longer. Two columns describe the same event, they disagree, and every screen in the business trusts whichever one its author picked. Measured: 900 collection notes, 240 of them with a dispatch timestamp and a status of pending, which is the list the carrier desk chases every Monday. The status belongs in the same statement that writes the timestamp. Nobody reads this as a defect because the notes do clear in the end, so it looks like a queue rather than a contradiction.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.collection_notes WHERE status = 'pending' AND dispatched_at IS NOT NULL

defects.title: 36 colour codes are left and the buying desk allocates twenty a month
defects.why: Colour codes are two uppercase letters, enforced by a check constraint, a convention set when the catalogue carried about eighty colours. Two letters is 676 codes. The buying desk allocates roughly twenty a month across the ranges added since, and the free codes are nearly gone; when the last one is taken the allocation routine will not degrade, it will violate the check constraint on the next insert, in the middle of a supplier load. Measured: 640 codes allocated of the 676 the constraint permits, leaving 36, which is under two months of allocations. Widening the code means touching every system with the two letters hardcoded, which is why it has not been done. Nothing alerts on this and no report shows it: the number of free codes is written down nowhere.

detect.sql: SELECT 676 - count(*) FROM catalog.colour_codes

defects.title: Parallelism is switched off on the table the throughput report scans
defects.why: Scan events are the largest table the throughput report touches. During an incident two years ago parallel workers were set to zero on it to stop a report from saturating the box, and the setting stayed. Nothing else on this database limits parallelism, so the setting is invisible unless somebody reads the table's storage options. Every sequential scan of the table now runs on a single worker, the overnight aggregation included, which is the longest job in the schedule and the reason the morning figures are late twice a week. Measured: parallel_workers = 0 in the storage options of ops.scan_events, the only table in the database carrying it. Resetting the option and letting the planner decide is the fix. A table-level storage option survives every restore and every failover and is in none of the places an engineer looks when a query is slow.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'ops.scan_events'::regclass AND reloptions @> ARRAY['parallel_workers=0']

defects.title: Two attempts at one address on one day, and no way to tell which was last
defects.why: A doorstep delivery records the day it happened and not the time, because the original round sheet was paper and had a date at the top. A driver often calls twice at an address on one day: carded in the morning and delivered in the afternoon, or the other way round when the customer telephones. With only a date there is no way to tell which attempt came last, so the outcome shown against the address is whichever row the query happens to return and the outcome the customer is told is not reliably the final one. Measured: 1,800 deliveries covering 300 address and date pairs with more than one attempt, and in every one of them the two attempts have different outcomes. The column wants to be a timestamp, and the round sheet has been an app for six years. Support resolves these by telephoning the driver, which works, so the data has never been the thing that got fixed.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT address_ref, delivered_on FROM fulfilment.doorstep_deliveries GROUP BY address_ref, delivered_on HAVING count(*) > 1) d

defects.title: The median basket is 3.5 items and no basket holds 3.5 items
defects.why: The trading summary reports a median basket size worked out with percentile_cont, which interpolates between the two middle values. That is correct for a continuous measure and wrong for a count of items: the median basket is reported as a number of items no basket in the business has ever contained, and it moves by a fraction whenever a single basket is added, which reads as a sensitive metric rather than an artefact. Measured: 2,000 baskets, a reported median of 3.5 items, and 0 baskets containing 3.5 items. percentile_disc returns an actual value from the data, which is what a median basket size means. A figure ending in a half looks deliberate enough that it has been quoted in a board pack.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.basket_sizes WHERE item_count = (SELECT median_items FROM analytics.v_basket_median)

defects.title: 60 correction pairs disappear from the adjustments report
defects.why: Credit and debit adjustments live in separate tables, which is reasonable, and the reconciliation view stacks them with UNION. UNION removes duplicate rows, and two adjustments are the same row when they carry the same order, amount, date and reason. That is exactly what a correction pair looks like: a debit raised in error and the credit that reversed it, entered on the same day for the same money. The view keeps one of the two, so the report balances for the wrong reason. Measured: 900 credits and 900 debits stacked into a view returning 1,740 rows, with the 60 lost rows being the correction pairs finance most needs to see. UNION ALL is what stacking two ledgers means. Nothing fails and the totals look tidier than they should, which is why the view has never been questioned.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.credit_adjustments) + (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.debit_adjustments) - (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_all_adjustments)

defects.title: The consignment chase list is empty, not short
defects.why: The chase list is the consignments with no receipt against them, written as NOT IN over the receipt references. Receipt references are nullable, because a receipt booked in by hand at the gate sometimes has no consignment to hang off. A single null anywhere in a NOT IN subquery makes the condition unknown for every row, so the chase list comes back empty rather than short. Measured: 800 consignments, 200 of them never receipted, 12 receipts carrying a null reference, and a chase list showing 0. NOT EXISTS returns the 200. The buying desk reads an empty chase list as good news and has done for years, which is why the missing consignments surface as supplier queries instead of as a report.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.consignments c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM supply.consignment_receipts r WHERE r.consignment_ref = c.consignment_ref)) - (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_unmatched_consignments)

defects.title: Commission is rounded once per line instead of once per payment
defects.why: Agent commission arrives from the sales feed at four decimal places, because it is a percentage of a line value and that is what a percentage gives. The column it lands in is the money type, which holds two decimal places and rounds on the way in. Every line with a third or fourth decimal is rounded where it is stored, so the rounding happens once per line rather than once per payment, and an agent's total is out by however those roundings fell. Measured: 600 commission lines, 450 of them stored at a value that differs from the feed figure kept alongside. The money type also formats in dollars on this database, for a business that has only ever traded in sterling. numeric(12,4) holds what the feed sends and rounds once, at the end. Agents query their statements by a few pence every month and are told it is rounding, which is true and is not an explanation.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.commission_lines WHERE amount::numeric <> source_amount

defects.title: The suppression list can hold the same address any number of times
defects.why: Contact addresses carry a unique index so the list cannot hold the same address twice, and the index has a WHERE clause restricting it to subscribed contacts. The unsubscribed rows are precisely the ones uniqueness matters for, because the suppression check is what stops a mailing reaching somebody who asked to be left alone. Under the partial index an address can be unsubscribed any number of times, each row with its own date and reason. Measured: 1,800 contacts, 360 unsubscribed rows holding an address that is unsubscribed more than once, and 600 holding an address that appears more than once somewhere in the table. Two consequences pull in opposite directions: resubscribing a duplicated address violates the index the moment the status changes, in the middle of a preference update, and a suppression check written with one row in mind can read the copy that says the contact is still contactable.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.contact_emails e WHERE e.status = 'unsubscribed' AND (SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.contact_emails x WHERE lower(x.email) = lower(e.email) AND x.status = 'unsubscribed') > 1

defects.title: The goods in role has insert on the table and nothing on its sequence
defects.why: The goods in role was granted what a grant script usually covers: usage on the schema, and select and insert on the table. The key column is a serial, so an insert that leaves it out reads the sequence, and the role holds no privilege on the sequence. Every insert from that role fails on permission denied for sequence, naming an object the grant script never mentions and that nobody thinks of as having its own permissions. Measured: the role holds insert on supply.goods_in_notes and does not hold usage on supply.goods_in_notes_note_id_seq. An identity column takes its privilege from the table and removes the trap entirely. The warehouse works around this by booking goods in under a shared account with more privilege than it should have, which is how a permission gap turns into an audit finding.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 WHERE has_table_privilege('goods_in_writer', 'supply.goods_in_notes', 'INSERT') AND NOT has_sequence_privilege('goods_in_writer', 'supply.goods_in_notes_note_id_seq', 'USAGE')) s

defects.title: 120 contractors are in the register twice, under a unique constraint
defects.why: A contractor is identified by a national insurance number, and the column carries a unique constraint so the register cannot hold the same person twice. The number is not always known on the day a contractor starts, so the column is nullable, and a unique constraint treats every null as distinct from every other. The rows without a number are the ones most likely to be entered twice, because the agency sends the person back through the same sign up, and those are exactly the rows the constraint lets through. Measured: 900 contractor records, 300 with no number, and 120 people held twice under the same agency and the same name. UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT would allow one unknown per register, which is not what is wanted either; the register needs a key it can actually fill in. The duplicates come to light when a contractor is paid twice, about once a quarter, and are treated as a payroll error each time.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT agency_ref, contractor_name FROM support.contractor_records WHERE national_id IS NULL GROUP BY agency_ref, contractor_name HAVING count(*) > 1) d

defects.title: The 400 orders with no delivery promise cannot appear on the promise report
defects.why: The promise report is orders with their delivery promise, written as a LEFT JOIN because an order does not always have one. The WHERE clause then filters on a column from the promised side, restricting it to this quarter. An order with no promise carries nulls in those columns, the comparison is unknown, and the row is dropped, so a line written twenty lines below the join turns it back into an inner join. Measured: 1,800 trade orders, 1,400 with a promise, and a report showing 1,400. The 400 orders with no promise at all are exactly what the service desk is looking for, and they are the ones that cannot appear. The condition belongs in the JOIN clause, where a non-matching promise leaves the order in place with nulls beside it. The report has a plausible row count, which is what has kept it.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.trade_orders) - (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_orders_with_promise)

defects.title: Telephone orders are absent from the trading sheet, not a small number on it
defects.why: The daily trading sheet counts orders per day with count(channel_code). Counting a column counts the rows where that column is not null, and the channel code is null on every order taken over the telephone, because the telephone was never given a channel when the codes were introduced. Those orders are not a channel with a small number beside it, they are absent. Measured: 1,800 channel orders, 240 with no channel code, and a daily sheet totalling 1,560. count(*) counts orders. The two figures are close enough that the difference reads as a quiet day, and the telephone desk's own numbers have never been reconciled against the trading sheet.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.channel_orders) - (SELECT sum(orders) FROM analytics.v_channel_order_counts)

defects.title: An account anchored on the 31st bills on the 28th for the rest of the year
defects.why: A direct debit schedule is built by taking the last date and adding a month to it, twelve times over. Adding a month to the 31st of a month that has no 31st gives the last day that month does have, which would be harmless if the next date were worked out from the anchor. It is worked out from the date before it, so once the schedule clamps it never climbs back: an account anchored on the 31st of January bills on the 28th of February and on the 28th of every month after it. Measured: 720 schedule rows across 60 accounts anchored on month ends, 210 of them falling on a different day from the anchor plus that many months. Anchor plus n months gives each date independently and clamps only where it must. Customers on the 29th, 30th and 31st quietly move to the 28th, and being billed earlier is not what generates a call.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.billing_schedules WHERE scheduled_on <> (anchor_on + (period_no || ' month')::interval)::date

defects.title: 240 listings were withdrawn, logged as withdrawn, and are still live
defects.why: Withdrawing a supplier listing is a DELETE, and a BEFORE DELETE trigger records what was withdrawn before it goes. The function writes its log row and returns NULL, and a BEFORE trigger that returns NULL cancels the operation for that row. The log is written, the listing stays, and the DELETE reports zero rows affected, which is only visible to a caller that looks. The buying desk's withdrawal script does not look. Measured: 240 listings withdrawn, 240 rows in the withdrawal log, and the same 240 listings still live in the catalogue. A BEFORE DELETE trigger must return OLD for the delete to proceed. The log makes the withdrawal look done, so the gap surfaces only when a supplier asks why a withdrawn line is still being ordered.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.supplier_listings l WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM catalog.listing_delete_log d WHERE d.listing_id = l.listing_id)

defects.title: Job 9 is the latest repair on any unit that has reached ten jobs
defects.why: Repair job numbers are a count per unit held in a text column, because the first system printed them with a letter in front and the letter was dropped in the migration that brought them here. Text sorts a character at a time, so job 9 sorts after job 10 and after job 100. The latest job per unit is worked out with max(), so any unit that has reached ten jobs shows the wrong one, and shows it confidently. Measured: 1,260 repair jobs across 120 units, and on 66 of those units the highest job number by text is not the highest by number. An integer column sorts the way the number is meant to. Every unit with fewer than ten jobs reads correctly, which is most of them on any given day, so the report is right far more often than it is wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_latest_repair v WHERE v.latest_job_no <> (SELECT max(r.job_no::integer)::text FROM support.repair_jobs r WHERE r.unit_ref = v.unit_ref)

defects.title: The tote move sequence is at 1 and the highest key is 2,000
defects.why: Tote moves were loaded from the old warehouse system with their keys included, so the numbering would line up with the paperwork. Supplying the key explicitly does not advance the sequence behind it, so the sequence is still where the load found it. The next insert that lets the sequence pick a key will pick one already taken and fail on the primary key, and it will keep failing, once per insert, until it has counted its way past the loaded range. Measured: 2,000 tote moves loaded, the highest key 2,000, and the sequence sitting at 1. A setval after a keyed load is the whole fix, and it is one line that is easy to leave out of a migration nobody expects to run twice. Nothing reads wrong until the first write arrives.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT max(move_id) FROM ops.tote_moves) - (SELECT last_value FROM ops.tote_moves_move_id_seq)

defects.title: An index leading with a column that says UK on all 3,000 rows
defects.why: The label print log carries a two column index leading with the region. Cross River trades in one region and always has: the column was added for a European expansion that was cancelled, and every row says UK. An index leading with a column that holds one value narrows nothing on its first column, so a lookup by print time walks the whole index in region order before the second column can help, and the index is the size of the table while behaving like a sequential scan with extra steps. Measured: 3,000 label prints, one distinct region code, and the index leading with that column. Reversing the columns makes the index useful and dropping it costs nothing. An unused index still has to be maintained on every insert, and this table takes several thousand a day.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid WHERE i.indrelid = 'ops.pallet_labels'::regclass AND c.relname = 'pallet_labels_region_printed_idx' AND (SELECT a.attname FROM pg_attribute a WHERE a.attrelid = i.indrelid AND a.attnum = i.indkey[0]) = 'region_code'

defects.title: Half the settlement batches disagree with their own lines
defects.why: Card settlement lines are held in a double precision column, the default type in the tool that generated the table. Double precision is binary floating point and cannot hold most decimal amounts exactly, so each line is slightly out, the error accumulates across a batch, and the batch total does not equal the total of the same lines added in decimal. The difference is fractions of a penny per batch: enough to make the settlement file disagree with the bank, not enough to point at anything. Measured: 2,000 settlement lines across 40 batches, with 20 batches whose floating point total differs from the decimal total of the same rows, kept alongside for exactly this reason. numeric is the type for money. The reconciliation is done by a person who has learned to ignore differences under a penny, which also hides the real ones.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT batch_ref FROM payments.settlement_lines GROUP BY batch_ref HAVING sum(amount) <> sum(amount_exact)::double precision) b

defects.title: A constraint forbidding blank contacts has accepted 180 of them
defects.why: The supplier site register requires a contact name and there is a check constraint on the column saying so. The constraint tests that the trimmed length is zero or more, and every string has a length of zero or more, the empty one included, so it accepts everything the column can hold and has never rejected a row. It was meant to say greater than zero. It is in the schema, it is in the review that signed the schema off, and it does nothing. Measured: 900 supplier sites, 180 with a blank contact name, every one of them accepted by a constraint written to forbid exactly that. A constraint that cannot fail is worse than no constraint, because the next person to read the table sees the guarantee and writes code that relies on it. The blank names surface when a delivery needs a signature.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.supplier_sites WHERE trim(contact_name) = ''

defects.title: Retiring a van round raises a not null violation instead of keeping history
defects.why: A round stop belongs to a van round, and the foreign key is declared ON DELETE SET NULL so retiring a round leaves its history behind. The column is NOT NULL, so setting it to null is the one thing that cannot happen: deleting a van round raises a not null violation and the delete fails. The referential action and the column definition each look correct alone and contradict each other. Measured: the foreign key on fulfilment.round_stops carries the set null action against a column declared NOT NULL. ON DELETE SET NULL wants a nullable column, and keeping the history really wants the round retired by a flag rather than deleted. Rounds are retired perhaps twice a year, so the failure is rare enough to be remembered as a one off each time.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint co JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = co.conrelid AND a.attnum = co.conkey[1] WHERE co.conrelid = 'fulfilment.round_stops'::regclass AND co.contype = 'f' AND co.confdeltype = 'n' AND a.attnotnull

defects.title: The takings dashboard is missing every row written since the view was built
defects.why: The finance dashboard reads daily takings from a materialised view, built to keep a heavy aggregate off the till table. A materialised view holds the rows it held when it was last refreshed, and nothing refreshes this one: no job, no trigger, no line in the deployment touches it. It answers instantly and it answers with the data as it stood the day it was created. Measured: 2,000 till takings rows with the view accounting for 1,600, the 400 missing being every takings row written since. A refresh in the nightly schedule fixes it, and so does an ordinary view if the aggregate is cheap enough. The dashboard is read every morning and the numbers move, because the view still holds days the business is trading through, so nobody reads it as frozen.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.till_takings) - (SELECT sum(takings_rows) FROM analytics.mv_daily_takings)

defects.title: The on stop flag is spelled eight ways by three systems
defects.why: The account flag says whether an account is on stop. Three systems write it and none agrees with the others on how to spell yes. The column is text, so it takes Y, y, 1 and true from the three writers, and N, n, 0 and false for the other answer. Every reader has to know all eight, and a reader that checks for one spelling quietly treats the other three as the opposite answer: an account on stop under a spelling the credit check does not know is an account that can still order. Measured: 1,600 account flags holding 8 distinct values, four meaning yes and four meaning no. A boolean column takes one of two values, and a check constraint on text takes one of a named set. Each writer is correct by its own convention, which is why this has survived three rewrites of the code around it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT flag_value) FROM legacy.account_flags

defects.title: Payroll is run from a table crash recovery empties
defects.why: Shift clockings were moved to an unlogged table during a week when the clock in terminals were timing out, and it worked: an unlogged table skips the write ahead log and its writes are considerably cheaper. An unlogged table is also emptied on crash recovery and is not replicated, so it is absent from the standby and from any base backup taken there. Payroll is run from this table, so a crash at any point in a month costs the clockings since the last export, and the standby has never held them at all. Measured: 4,000 clockings in a table whose persistence is unlogged. A logged table with the write load spread across the terminals is the fix. The change was made under pressure, it solved the problem in front of everyone, and nothing has gone wrong since, which is the whole difficulty.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'ops.shift_clockings'::regclass AND relpersistence = 'u'

defects.title: Every refund batch delete scans all 6,000 refund lines
defects.why: Refund lines reference their refund batch and the foreign key is declared, which is more than several older tables here manage. Postgres indexes the parent side of a foreign key because the primary key is indexed already; it does not index the child side, and nothing here does either. Every delete or key update on a refund batch scans the whole of refund lines to prove no child is left behind, and so does any join from a batch down to its lines. Measured: one foreign key on payments.refund_lines with no index whose leading column is the referencing column, over 6,000 lines. One index on the referencing column removes both problems. Batches are deleted rarely enough that the scan is never the thing blamed; it shows up as the batch screen being slow, which is read as the screen.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint co WHERE co.conrelid = 'payments.refund_lines'::regclass AND co.contype = 'f' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_index i WHERE i.indrelid = co.conrelid AND i.indkey[0] = co.conkey[1])

defects.title: 600 price changes since the repricing have no audit row
defects.why: Price changes are audited by a trigger, which was disabled for a bulk repricing because the audit was doubling the time the load took, and never enabled again. A disabled trigger is still there: in the schema, in the dump, and visible to anybody reading the table as an audited table. Nothing since the repricing has been audited, and there is no gap in the audit table to notice because the rows were never written. Measured: 1,800 price changes, 1,200 with an audit row and 600 without, with the trigger still disabled. Enabling it costs nothing and the 600 cannot be recovered. This is the one defect here that a routine schema diff would catch, if the diff were run against a database rather than against the migration files.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.price_changes c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM catalog.price_change_audit a WHERE a.change_id = c.change_id)

defects.title: The three hundred largest accounts have no band at all
defects.why: Accounts are banded by annual spend on the marketing dashboard as bronze, silver or gold. The CASE expression has a branch for each band and no ELSE, and an expression matching no branch returns null, so accounts above the top band come back with no band. They are the largest accounts on the ledger and exactly the ones the banding exists to find. Measured: 1,500 accounts, 300 of them above the top band and banded as null. A final ELSE, or a top branch with no upper bound, covers the range. The dashboard groups by band and draws the null group as an empty label at the bottom of the chart, which reads as a rendering fault rather than as the three hundred best customers.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_account_bands WHERE band IS NULL

defects.title: 160 campaigns target a product group that does not exist
defects.why: A campaign targets a list of product groups, and the list is an array column on the campaign row. An array cannot carry a foreign key, so nothing stops a campaign naming a group that has been retired or one that never existed, and nothing tells the person retiring a group which campaigns point at it. The check has to be written by hand in every query that cares, and most of them do not. Measured: 400 campaigns, 160 of them naming at least one group code absent from the product group table. A campaign to group junction table makes the reference declarable and the retirement check a join. The array is easier to write from the campaign screen, which is where this design came from.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.campaign_targets t WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM unnest(t.group_codes) AS gc WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM catalog.product_groups p WHERE p.group_code = gc))

defects.title: 2,400 manifests share one received time, so nothing can be sorted by it
defects.why: The inbound manifest feed stamps each row with now() as it loads, and the received time is what the warehouse sorts by to work out which manifest arrived first. now() is the time the transaction started, not the time the row was written, and a load is one transaction, so every row carries one identical timestamp and the sort has nothing to work with. The order the warehouse sees is whatever the query happens to return, and it changes between runs of the same query. Measured: 2,400 manifests loaded in one transaction carrying 1 distinct received time between them. clock_timestamp() advances within a transaction and gives each row its own instant. The rows do arrive in the right order on the day, because the feed is written in order, which is why this has never been the explanation for a mis-sorted manifest.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT received_at) FROM supply.inbound_manifests

defects.title: Three ranges are each other's ancestor
defects.why: Ranges sit in a hierarchy, each naming its parent, and three of them name each other. A parent column with no cycle check is a graph, not a tree: the three ranges point round in a ring, and any walk that follows parents upwards runs until something stops it, whether a recursion limit, a timeout or the memory on the box. The reporting job that rebuilds range paths has a depth cap added the week the cycle was created, which is why the job finishes and those three ranges simply have no path. Measured: 303 ranges, 3 of them able to reach themselves by following parents. A check on insert, or a self-reference exclusion plus a periodic walk, keeps it a tree. The depth cap turned an outage into a silent gap, which is the trade every depth cap makes.

detect.sql: WITH RECURSIVE w(start_code, code, depth) AS (SELECT range_code, parent_code, 1 FROM catalog.range_tree WHERE parent_code IS NOT NULL UNION ALL SELECT w.start_code, t.parent_code, w.depth + 1 FROM w JOIN catalog.range_tree t ON t.range_code = w.code WHERE t.parent_code IS NOT NULL AND w.depth < 50) SELECT count(DISTINCT start_code) FROM w WHERE code = start_code

defects.title: 400 addresses are held forever by accounts that were closed
defects.why: A customer who closes an account is soft deleted: the row stays with a deleted timestamp on it. The unique index on the address covers the whole table, so a closed account holds its address forever. A customer who closes an account and comes back cannot register with the address they had, and the message they see is that the address is already in use, which is true and reads as an accusation. Measured: 3,000 registered customers, 400 closed, and 400 addresses held by a closed account and by nothing else. A partial unique index over the live rows releases the address on closure, and keeping the history is what the deleted timestamp is for. The support desk handles these by asking for a different address, which works and quietly creates a second customer for the same person.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.registered_customers d WHERE d.deleted_at IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM storefront.registered_customers l WHERE l.deleted_at IS NULL AND l.email = d.email)

defects.title: The invoice prints one total and the statement adds up another
defects.why: The invoice header carries a total and the invoice lines carry the amounts that total is made of. The header total is written when the invoice is raised; lines are amended afterwards by the credit desk correcting a price or removing a line that was never delivered, and nothing rewrites the header. The same fact is held in two places, one stops being true, and which one the customer sees depends on the document they are sent: the invoice prints the header, the statement adds up the lines. Measured: 900 invoices, 211 with a header total that does not equal the sum of their lines. The total belongs in one place, worked out from the lines when needed or maintained by the same statement that amends them. The difference is usually small, which is why it is settled by whoever argues longest.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.invoice_headers h WHERE h.total <> (SELECT coalesce(sum(l.line_total), 0) FROM storefront.invoice_lines l WHERE l.invoice_ref = h.invoice_ref)

defects.title: 300 undelivered consignments count as signed for
defects.why: The delivery signature flag is a smallint, because the terminal that writes it speaks in numbers. It sends 1 for signed, 0 for refused, and 2 when the driver could not get an answer either way. Two of those are an answer and one is the absence of one, but every reader here was written against a column described as a boolean and treats anything non-zero as signed, so the consignments that were never checked are counted as delivered and signed for. Measured: 3,000 consignment checks holding 3 distinct values, 300 of them the third. A boolean column plus a nullable timestamp says both things without inventing a third state. The proof of delivery report is 300 rows too optimistic and has been since the terminals were replaced.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.consignment_checks WHERE is_signed = 2

defects.title: The card token policy does not apply to the connection that reads them
defects.why: Card tokens are protected by row level security, with a policy restricting each merchant to its own rows. Row level security does not apply to the table's owner unless it is forced, and the application connects as the owner, so the policy is real, correct, and not consulted for the one connection that matters. The protection shows up in every review as present and applies to nobody. Measured: row security enabled on payments.card_tokens and not forced, across 1,500 tokens for 25 merchants. ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY makes the owner obey the policy, and an application role that does not own its tables is the better answer. Testing the policy as a non-owner shows it working perfectly, which is how it was signed off.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'payments.card_tokens'::regclass AND relrowsecurity AND NOT relforcerowsecurity

defects.title: Bin totals never see a correction or a removal
defects.why: The stock screen reads a bin total kept up to date by a trigger on bin movements, and the trigger is AFTER INSERT only. A movement corrected after the fact is an update, a movement entered against the wrong bin is deleted, and neither reaches the total. The total is right for a bin nobody has had to correct, which is most bins, and drifts furthest on exactly the bins that have had the most attention. Measured: 6,000 movements across 500 bins, 458 corrected or removed since, and 352 bins whose total no longer equals the sum of their movements. The trigger wants INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE with the OLD row taken off the total. The stock screen is checked against a physical count once a quarter and the differences are written off as shrinkage.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.bin_totals t WHERE t.total_units <> (SELECT coalesce(sum(m.units), 0) FROM ops.bin_movements m WHERE m.bin_code = t.bin_code)

defects.title: A summary view that selects every column, bank details included
defects.why: The supplier portal reads a summary view instead of the remittance table, because the remittance table carries bank details. The view selects every column of the table, bank details included. A view runs with the privileges of its owner, so granting select on the view gives the reader everything the view can see, and the reader needs no privilege on the table itself. The grant on the table was deliberately withheld, which is what makes this look safe in a review: the audit shows no direct access to remittance advice. Measured: the portal role holds select on analytics.v_remittance_summary and no privilege at all on payments.remittance_advice, while the view exposes the account number column. A view that lists the columns it means to expose is the fix, with a column level grant as the belt. The view is called a summary and summarises nothing.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 WHERE has_table_privilege('remittance_reader', 'analytics.v_remittance_summary', 'SELECT') AND NOT has_table_privilege('remittance_reader', 'payments.remittance_advice', 'SELECT')) s

defects.title: 120 call off orders violate a constraint every tool lists as enforced
defects.why: Call off orders were given a check constraint requiring a positive quantity, added NOT VALID because validating it would have locked the table during a working day and the rows already in it were known to be untidy. NOT VALID applies the constraint to new rows only. The plan was to fix the old rows and run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in the next maintenance window, and there was no next maintenance window. The bad rows are still there, the constraint reads as enforced in every tool that lists constraints, and any query written on the strength of it is wrong for exactly those rows. Measured: 1,500 call off orders, 120 with a quantity of zero or less under a constraint that forbids it. Fixing the rows and validating the constraint is an afternoon. A zero quantity is read as cancelled by some reports and as an error by others, and both readings are guesses.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.call_off_orders WHERE quantity <= 0

defects.title: 800 claims name a customer who cannot be found under that name
defects.why: A warranty claim copies the account holder's name onto the claim so the form prints without a join, and the copy is never updated. A holder who marries, divorces or corrects a misspelling has a new name on the account and the old one on every claim raised before the change. A record of what was true on the day is a defensible thing for a document to be, and it is not what this column is used for: the claims screen searches it, so a customer telephoning about their claim cannot be found under their name. Measured: 1,200 warranty claims and 2,000 account holders, 800 renamed since, leaving 800 claims naming somebody who no longer exists under that name. A join gives the current name and the printed document can keep its own copy of what it printed. The search is the thing that breaks, and it breaks for the customers most likely to be telephoning.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.warranty_claims c JOIN storefront.account_holders h ON h.account_ref = c.account_ref WHERE h.holder_name <> c.holder_name

defects.title: 441 stocktake dates are valid read either way round
defects.why: The handheld stocktake export writes dates as text, day first, because that is how they print on the sheet. Text is not a date: nothing checks the format, nothing orders correctly, and for any day of the month up to twelve the same string is a valid date under two different readings. A reader that assumes month first turns the third of April into the fourth of March without complaint, and the rows it gets wrong are the ones at the start of every month. Measured: 1,200 stocktake imports, 441 of them holding a date that is also a valid date read the other way round. A date column takes the parsing once, at the import, where the format is known. The stock team reconciles these by eye against the paper sheets, which is why the ambiguity has never had to be resolved in the data.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.stocktake_imports WHERE split_part(taken_on, '/', 1)::integer <= 12 AND split_part(taken_on, '/', 1) <> split_part(taken_on, '/', 2)

defects.title: Medium sorts after large in every ordering of the size band
defects.why: Garment sizes are an enum. Small and large were the original two and medium was added when the range grew. An enum sorts in the order its labels were created, so a label added later sorts last whatever it means: medium sorts after large in every ORDER BY, every MIN and MAX, and every range comparison. The size picker lists small, large, medium, which customers read as a fault in the picker, and the size mix report puts the middle of the range at the bottom of the table. Measured: 900 garment sizes, 300 of them medium, every one comparing as greater than large. Rebuilding the type in the right order means rewriting every column that uses it, which is why it has not been done. A lookup table with an explicit sort column never has this problem.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.garment_sizes WHERE size = 'medium' AND size > 'large'::catalog.size_band

defects.title: The petty cash book adds pence to pounds
defects.why: The petty cash book takes lines from two places: the till writes pence, as tills do, and the ledger clerk types pounds. The column is a plain integer with no unit anywhere near it, not in the name, not in a comment, not in a constraint. Both writers are internally consistent and the book adds them together, so a monthly total is the sum of two different units and is out by a factor of a hundred in whichever direction the month's mix leans. Measured: 1,500 petty cash lines, 600 written by the till in pence and 900 typed by the ledger in pounds. A numeric column in one unit, named for that unit, is the whole fix. The monthly figure is small enough that a wrong total looks like a quiet month rather than an error, and petty cash is the last thing anybody audits.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.petty_cash_lines WHERE amount > 500

defects.title: 400 price lines were read, not stored, and reported as loaded
defects.why: The supplier price list load inserts every line with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so a file sent twice does not fail. DO NOTHING does not distinguish a line already loaded from a line that collides for a different reason, so a supplier who sends two prices for the same product in one file has the second dropped silently, and the load reports success because the statement did succeed. The count recorded against the file is lines read, not lines stored, so the two never disagree on paper. Measured: 4,000 lines read across 40 files, 3,600 stored, and the loads table recording 4,000. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE takes the later price, and counting the rows actually written makes the gap visible either way. The prices that survive are the first of each pair, which is usually the old one.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT sum(lines_read) FROM supply.price_list_loads) - (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.price_list_entries)

defects.title: 600 yard moves have no log row and nothing recorded the failure
defects.why: The yard move trigger writes a log row, wrapped in an exception handler that catches everything and carries on so a problem with the log can never stop a move being recorded. WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL catches the failure, discards it, and returns as though the log had been written. The handler was added after a week when a full disc stopped the yard and it does what it was asked to do; it also catches the failures that are not a full disc, such as a value too long for its column. Measured: 3,000 yard moves and 2,400 log rows, the 600 without a log being the moves whose vehicle registration is longer than the log column allows. Catching the specific condition, recording the failure somewhere, or letting the write fail are all defensible. Catching everything and saying nothing is the one choice that makes the gap undiscoverable, and the log is what the yard is audited against.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.yard_moves m WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ops.yard_move_log l WHERE l.move_id = m.move_id)

defects.title: Conveyor events share a belt and a second with each other
defects.why: Conveyor events are stamped to the second, because the column was declared timestamp(0) to save space on a table expected to be large. The conveyor reads faster than one parcel a second, so two events on the same belt in the same second are indistinguishable by time, and time is what the throughput report and the jam investigation both sort by. Rounding to the second is rounding rather than truncation, so an event can be stamped a second after the event that followed it. Measured: 5,000 conveyor events, 4,994 of them sharing a belt and a second with at least one other. Microsecond precision is the default for a reason and costs nothing on disc worth having. Jam investigations are done from the belt's own logs, which is the workaround that has kept this invisible.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.conveyor_events e WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ops.conveyor_events o WHERE o.event_id <> e.event_id AND o.belt_code = e.belt_code AND o.occurred_at = e.occurred_at)

defects.title: 200 lead sources are listed twice under the same name
defects.why: Lead sources are keyed by their name, typed in by whoever set the campaign up.
