Nothing trims the name and nothing folds its case, so the same source arrives as itself, as itself with a trailing space, and as itself with a capital letter in a different place. Each is a distinct key, each accumulates its own leads, and the source report lists them as separate lines with no indication they are the same thing. Measured: 600 lead sources, with 400 rows in 200 pairs differing from each other only by case or surrounding whitespace. Trimming and folding on the way in, under a unique index over the folded value, makes the key mean what people think it means. The report reads as a long tail of small sources, which is a plausible thing for a source report to show.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.lead_sources s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM marketing.lead_sources o WHERE o.source_id <> s.source_id AND lower(trim(o.source_name)) = lower(trim(s.source_name)))

defects.title: 160 meter readings hold a reference that is not a number
defects.why: Meter readings reference their meter by a number held in a text column, because the import file has it in quotes. Most values are digits and some are not: a meter that was replaced has the old and new numbers in one field separated by a slash, and a meter nobody could find has the word unknown. Any join that casts the column to an integer fails on those rows, so the import either errors on the whole file or is written to skip them, and it was written to skip them. Measured: 2,400 meter readings, 160 holding a reference that is not a number, and 160 readings that reach no meter. The reference belongs in an integer column, with the unparseable rows held somewhere they can be worked through. The energy billing sitting in those 160 readings is under the threshold anybody investigates.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.meter_readings WHERE meter_ref !~ '^[0-9]+$'

defects.title: The daily dispatch figures add up to more than the dispatches
defects.why: The daily dispatch count takes everything from midnight to midnight and takes both ends inclusively. A dispatch stamped at exactly midnight falls in two days: the end of one window and the start of the next. The board's daily figures add to more than the number of dispatches, and the overlap is small enough to read as a good day rather than as the same parcels counted twice. Midnight is not a rare timestamp here, because the overnight trunk run stamps its manifest at exactly midnight. Measured: 3,600 dispatch events, 120 of them at exactly midnight, and daily totals overstating the period by 120. A half open window, from midnight inclusive to the next midnight exclusive, is the only version that tiles. Every calendar in the world is half open and almost every hand written date range is not.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT sum(dispatches) FROM analytics.v_daily_dispatch) - (SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.dispatch_events WHERE dispatched_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-07-01' AND dispatched_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-07-31')

defects.title: 200 weighbridge dockets are in the table twice
defects.why: Weighbridge dockets are loaded as they arrive from the weighbridge and the table has no primary key, because the weighbridge software does not promise one. Without a key there is nothing for a second load to collide with, so loading the same file again inserts every row a second time and reports success. One morning the operator was not sure the overnight load had run and ran it again. Measured: 2,600 dockets holding 2,400 distinct docket references, the 200 extra being that file. Declaring the docket reference as the key stops the second load dead and documents what the weighbridge already guarantees. The tonnage report adds both copies, and deduplicating afterwards means choosing between two rows that are identical in every column.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) - count(DISTINCT docket_ref) FROM ops.weighbridge_dockets

defects.title: 300 trade prices carry the margin of a price never charged
defects.why: Trade prices carry a margin worked out by a trigger, and seasonal lines carry an uplift applied by another trigger, both BEFORE INSERT on the same table. Triggers at the same timing fire in name order, and the margin trigger is named for what it does rather than for when it has to run, so it sorts first. It works the margin out from the price as typed and the uplift trigger then raises the price underneath it. Measured: 1,200 trade prices, 300 of them seasonal and uplifted, and on all 300 the stored margin does not equal price minus cost. One trigger doing both things in order is the fix; naming triggers for their order survives only until somebody renames one. Nothing errors and the margin is plausible, being the one the buyer originally quoted, which is also the number the buying team negotiates against.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.trade_prices WHERE margin <> price - cost

defects.title: 2,000 gate pass references are unique and nothing says so
defects.why: Every gate pass carries a reference allocated by the gatehouse system, and no two passes have ever shared one. The column has no unique constraint and no unique index. The uniqueness is real, every join written against this table relies on it, and it is held up by nothing but the habits of the system upstream. The planner does not know the column is unique either, so a join on it is estimated as though a reference could match many rows and the plan chosen is the plan for that. Measured: 2,000 gate passes, 2,000 distinct references, and no unique index over the column. Declaring the constraint costs one statement and gives the planner a number it can trust. The first duplicate will arrive the day the gatehouse system is replaced, and nothing here will stop it or notice it.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(DISTINCT pass_ref) FROM ops.gate_passes) - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indrelid JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'ops' AND c.relname = 'gate_passes' AND i.indisunique AND i.indnatts = 1 AND i.indkey[0] = (SELECT attnum FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = c.oid AND attname = 'pass_ref'))

defects.title: A contract and its current version cannot exist without each other
defects.why: A supply contract names the version of it currently in force and every version names the contract it belongs to. Both columns are NOT NULL and both carry a foreign key, so each table requires a row in the other before either can exist. The load works only because the constraints were made deferrable, closing the cycle inside one transaction. Anything that writes a contract and its first version in separate transactions fails, and so does deleting either side: the contract needs its version and the version needs its contract, so neither goes first. Measured: 300 contracts, 900 versions, and a foreign key in each direction between the two tables. Putting the current version in a nullable column, or in a flag on the version row, removes the cycle. Contracts are retired by a date rather than deleted, which is why nobody has met the delete side of this.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint a JOIN pg_constraint b ON a.conrelid = b.confrelid AND a.confrelid = b.conrelid WHERE a.contype = 'f' AND b.contype = 'f' AND a.conrelid = 'supply.contracts'::regclass AND a.confrelid = 'supply.contract_versions'::regclass

defects.title: An elevated function resolves its table names against the caller's path
defects.why: Applying a credit note runs as a SECURITY DEFINER function so that a clerk who cannot write to the ledger can still apply an approved note. The function does not set its own search_path and it is executable by everybody. It resolves the table names it uses against whatever search_path the caller happens to have, so a caller who can create a table in a schema earlier on that path chooses which table the function writes to, and it is written to with the owner's privileges rather than the caller's. The elevation is the point of the function; the unqualified names are what hand it over. Measured: one SECURITY DEFINER function in the payments schema with no search_path of its own and execute granted to everybody, over 900 credit note applications. SET search_path = pg_catalog plus schema qualified names inside the body closes it, and revoking execute from PUBLIC is the other half. The function was reviewed for what it does to the ledger, which it does correctly.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_proc p WHERE p.oid = 'payments.fn_apply_credit_note'::regproc AND p.prosecdef AND p.proconfig IS NULL AND has_function_privilege('public', p.oid, 'EXECUTE')

defects.title: 2,000 parcel scans record the word migration as the scanner
defects.why: Parcel scans gained a column recording who scanned the parcel. The column is NOT NULL, so the rows already in the table had to be given a value and they were all given the same one. That value is the word migration: not a scanner, not a person, and not a fact about any of those parcels, just a placeholder that satisfied the constraint on the afternoon the column was added. Every report that groups by the scanner shows migration as the busiest operator in the business, and every audit of who handled a parcel before that afternoon returns the same non-answer. Measured: 3,000 parcel scans, 2,000 of them recording migration, which is two thirds of the table and one value. A nullable column says honestly that the old rows do not know and lets reports exclude them. Migration reads as a system account, which is why it has never been questioned.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.parcel_scans WHERE scanned_by = 'migration'

defects.title: The brand list runs through the alphabet twice
defects.why: Brand names sit in a column declared COLLATE "C", copied from an older table where the C collation had been chosen to make an index work with a LIKE pattern. The database collates as en_US and this one column does not. C ordering is byte ordering, so every name beginning with a capital letter sorts before every name beginning with a lower case one, and the brand filter on the site runs through the alphabet twice. Measured: 600 brands, every one of which sits in a different position under the database's own collation than under the column's. Dropping the column's collation makes it sort like everything else, and the LIKE index the C collation was for wants a text_pattern_ops index instead. The brands at the bottom are the ones that spell themselves in lower case, which is a style choice new brands make more often than old ones, and nothing on screen explains why they are there.

detect.sql: WITH a AS (SELECT brand_name, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY brand_name) AS r FROM catalog.brand_names), b AS (SELECT brand_name, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY brand_name COLLATE "en_US.utf8") AS r FROM catalog.brand_names) SELECT count(*) FROM a JOIN b USING (brand_name) WHERE a.r <> b.r

defects.title: The stock audit role cannot read the third stock count table
defects.why: The stock audit role was given select on the stock count tables when it was created, one table at a time, which is the only way to grant them. A third table was added to the same schema afterwards and nothing repeats the grant for tables created later. There are no default privileges set for the schema either. Measured: three stock count tables in the ops schema and the audit role holding select on two of them. The role reads two and gets permission denied on the third, and the report it runs joins that table, so the failure is the whole report rather than a missing column. ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES makes the grant apply to tables that do not exist yet, which is what was meant. The auditors work from an export produced under somebody else's login, so the broken report is not on anybody's list.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'ops' AND c.relname IN ('stock_counts', 'stock_count_lines', 'stock_count_adjustments') AND NOT has_table_privilege('stock_reader', c.oid, 'SELECT')

defects.title: 2,800 case comment keys sit above where the sequence is
defects.why: Case comments were restored from a backup after a bad deployment, and the restore kept the original comment ids because the case threads reference them. Restoring rows with explicit keys does not move the sequence behind the column. The sequence is where it was when the backup was taken, thousands below the highest key now in the table, so every insert from here until it catches up asks for a key that already exists. Each one fails on the primary key, the application retries, and the retry asks for the next one, which also exists. Measured: 4,000 case comments with a highest id of 4,000 and the sequence sitting at 1,200, leaving 2,800 keys already taken above it. setval to the table's maximum is one statement and is the last step of any restore that keeps its keys. The failures read as a flapping application rather than as a restore that was not finished.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT max(comment_id) FROM support.case_comments) - (SELECT last_value FROM support.case_comments_comment_id_seq)

defects.title: 192 baskets show a total higher than the lines in them
defects.why: The checkout page reads a basket total from its own table, kept up to date by the code that adds a line to the basket. Removing a line takes a different code path, written later, and that path deletes the line without touching the total. The total is correct until the shopper changes their mind, and after that it is the total of everything they ever put in the basket. Measured: 500 baskets holding 2,308 lines, with 192 whose stored total no longer equals the sum of their lines. One function owning the total and called from both paths is the fix, and working the total out from the lines when the page renders removes the question entirely. The page shows the inflated figure while the payment is taken for the real one, so the shopper is charged correctly and told they were charged more, and the complaints arrive as pricing complaints and are answered by pointing at the card statement.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.basket_totals t WHERE t.total <> COALESCE((SELECT sum(l.line_total) FROM storefront.basket_lines l WHERE l.basket_ref = t.basket_ref), 0)

defects.title: 800 rate card amendments produced 4 audit rows
defects.why: Rate card amendments are audited by a trigger declared FOR EACH STATEMENT. A statement level trigger fires once per statement however many rows the statement touched, and it cannot see NEW or OLD, so the audit row records that something changed and nothing about what. An amendment made one card at a time is audited one row at a time, which is how it was tested. The yearly uplift is four statements over hundreds of cards and is audited four times. Measured: 800 rate cards amended and 4 rows in the audit table. FOR EACH ROW with OLD and NEW recorded gives the audit its subject back, and a transition table gives the same thing at statement level if the volume matters. The audit is read when a supplier disputes a rate, and the bulk uplift is exactly when that happens.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.rate_cards WHERE amended_at IS NOT NULL) - (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.rate_card_audit)

defects.title: 1,966 courier surcharges are rounded down instead of to the penny
defects.why: The courier surcharge is worked out per kilogram from a weight held in grammes: weight times rate, divided by a thousand. Every value in that expression is an integer, so the division is integer division and the remainder is thrown away. The surcharge is always rounded down, never to the nearest penny, and the amount lost is between nothing and a penny on every parcel. Measured: 2,000 courier surcharges, 1,966 of them lower than the same calculation done in decimal, which is kept alongside. Dividing by 1000.0, or casting one operand to numeric, makes the division decimal, and rounding rather than truncation decides the penny. It is charged to the courier, who is content, and it is the kind of rounding only ever noticed by whoever is on the losing side of it consistently, at two thousand parcels a week.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.courier_surcharges WHERE surcharge_pence <> surcharge_exact

defects.title: The label queue has 2,767 keys left before it stops
defects.why: The label queue was given a smallint key, because a queue was never going to be large and the table was expected to be emptied. Nothing empties it. A smallint identity stops at 32,767 and the queue has been filling since it was built, so the ceiling is a date rather than a risk. On the day it arrives every insert fails with an out of range error, the queue stops accepting work, and the labels stop printing. There is no warning before it and no degradation: the queue works perfectly until it does not work at all. Measured: 30,000 rows in the label queue and 2,767 keys left before the smallint runs out. An integer key has room for two billion, and widening an identity column is a table rewrite, which is an outage to schedule rather than one to be surprised by. Nothing reports on the headroom, and the number only becomes interesting once.

detect.sql: SELECT 32767 - max(queue_id) FROM ops.label_queue

defects.title: 1,200 return labels reference a request nothing enforces
defects.why: Every returns label belongs to a returns request and carries the request's id in a column named for it. There is no foreign key. The relationship is real, every join in the returns code relies on it, and it exists only in the naming of the column. Nothing stops a label being written against a request that was never raised, nothing stops a request being deleted out from under its labels, and no tool that draws the schema draws a line between the two tables, so the returns process looks like two unrelated tables to anybody arriving new. Measured: 1,200 return labels, every one matching a request, and no foreign key between the two tables. Declaring the key costs one statement while the data is still clean, which is the only time it is cheap. The relationship holds today because one piece of code writes both sides, and that is the whole of the guarantee.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.return_labels l WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fulfilment.return_requests r WHERE r.request_id = l.request_id)) - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE contype = 'f' AND conrelid = 'fulfilment.return_labels'::regclass)

defects.title: 1,200 archived lines belong to orders the purge removed
defects.why: Old orders and their lines were moved to the archive schema together, and a purge deletes orders past a retention date. The purge was written against the orders table only, and there is no foreign key between the archived tables, so the lines stay behind. They reference an order reference that no longer exists anywhere in the database. Any report that starts from the lines counts them, gets no order to join to, and either drops them or shows them with every order column empty. Measured: 1,200 archived orders and 6,000 archived lines, of which 1,200 belong to the 300 orders the purge removed. The purge wants to delete the lines first, or the tables want a foreign key with a cascade. The archive is read perhaps twice a year, which is why lines with no order have been sitting there since the first purge ran.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM archive.archived_order_lines l WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM archive.archived_orders o WHERE o.order_ref = l.order_ref)

defects.title: 1,500 consent changes have nothing recording them
defects.why: Marketing consent changes are logged by a trigger, because the log is what the business would produce if it were asked to show when somebody opted out. The trigger was disabled for a bulk import, so that loading two years of consent history from the old system did not write two years of log rows describing an import rather than a decision. It was never enabled again. The trigger is in the schema, it is correct, and it has not fired since. Measured: 2,500 consent changes and 1,000 log rows, leaving 1,500 changes with nothing recording them. ENABLE TRIGGER is one statement and belongs in the same script that disables it. The log looks healthy from the outside: it has rows, they are recent enough, and only counting both tables shows the gap.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.consent_changes) - (SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.consent_log)

defects.title: 900 orders predate the web site and are recorded as web orders
defects.why: Orders gained a channel column recording where the order came from, and the historic rows were backfilled by asking which channel the account uses now. The answer today is not the answer for an order placed years ago. Almost every account orders through the web site now, so almost every historic order was backfilled as web, including the orders placed before the web site existed. The column reads as a clean, complete history and it says the web site was taking orders four years before it opened. Measured: 2,400 orders, 900 of them placed before the web site opened in January 2023 and recorded as web orders. The channel was knowable at the time and is not knowable now, so the honest backfill is a null plus a note about which rows predate the column. Every channel trend built from this table shows the web growing from a base it never had, which is the shape everybody expected to see.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.order_channels WHERE placed_on < DATE '2023-01-01' AND channel = 'web'

defects.title: 180 hauliers are set up twice under different account numbers
defects.why: Haulier accounts are keyed by an account number issued by the yard, and a haulier who is set up twice gets two of them. Nothing checks the name and the postcode on the way in, and there is no reason a haulier should not have two accounts, so the duplicates are not wrong in any way the database can see. The yard books collections against whichever account is nearest to hand. Measured: 1,200 haulier accounts, 360 of them sharing a name and a postcode with another account, in 180 pairs. A unique index over the folded name and postcode stops the second setup and makes the existing pairs visible in one query. The spend report groups by account number, so a haulier over the threshold that triggers a rate review sits under it twice, and merging the pairs means deciding which account number the history moves to, which is why nobody has.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.haulier_accounts a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM supply.haulier_accounts b WHERE b.account_no <> a.account_no AND b.haulier_name = a.haulier_name AND b.postcode = a.postcode)

defects.title: 200 snapshot rows double count a depot and a day
defects.why: The nightly snapshot job writes one row per depot per day into a table with no primary key and no unique index. The job is not idempotent because nothing makes it so. It was rerun by hand on five nights when the first run looked wrong, and each rerun appended a second row for every depot on that day. Both rows are plausible, the later one is the corrected figure, and the board pack sums the column, so those five days are reported at roughly twice the truth. Measured: 4,000 snapshot rows covering 100 days and 40 depots, with 200 rows duplicating a depot and day already in the table. A primary key over the depot and the day turns the rerun into an upsert, or into a failure loud enough to notice. The double counted days are spread across a quarter and each one reads as a strong day rather than as an error.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.daily_snapshots) - (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT depot_code, snapshot_on FROM analytics.daily_snapshots) d)

defects.title: One reading per pump per day is enforced by the handheld alone
defects.why: A fuel pump is read once a day at each depot, and the pair of the pump and the day is what every query treats as the identity of a reading. No unique index says so. The rule is enforced by the handheld, which only lets an operator submit one reading per pump per day, and by nothing in the database. The consumption report subtracts yesterday's reading from today's and assumes exactly one of each; it is written with a scalar subquery, so the day a second reading arrives the report fails outright rather than reporting the wrong number. Measured: 1,800 fuel readings over 1,800 distinct pump and day pairs, with no unique index over the two columns. The unique index is the rule written down where the next query can rely on it. The handheld is being replaced this year, and nothing in the schema will notice when it is.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(DISTINCT (depot_code, pump_no, read_on)) FROM ops.fuel_readings) - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indrelid JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'ops' AND c.relname = 'fuel_readings' AND i.indisunique AND i.indnatts = 3)

defects.title: Every case state has no service level due date
defects.why: A new case gets two AFTER INSERT triggers: one creates the case state row, the other sets the service level due date on it. Triggers at the same timing fire in name order, and the trigger that sets the due date sorts first, so it runs an UPDATE against a state row that does not exist yet. An UPDATE that matches nothing is not an error; it reports zero rows and the trigger returns happily. The state row is then created by the second trigger with the due date left null. Measured: 1,000 case states and 1,000 of them with no service level due date. One trigger that inserts the state with its due date already on it removes the ordering question entirely. The service level report treats a null due date as not yet due, so every case is inside its target and the dashboard has been green since the day it was built.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.case_states WHERE sla_due_at IS NULL

defects.title: 40 pairs of products each name the other as their replacement
defects.why: A discontinued product names the product that replaces it, so the catalogue can send a shopper on to the current line. Forty pairs name each other. Each was discontinued in favour of the other, on different days, by different buyers, and nothing checks the other direction before writing the row. The catalogue follows replacements until it finds a product that is not discontinued, which for these pairs is never, so the request runs until the timeout cuts it off. Measured: 900 product replacements, 80 of them in a pair that points back at itself in two steps. Refusing a replacement that is reachable from the product being replaced keeps the chain a chain. Both products in each pair are discontinued and neither is orderable, so the only symptom is a slow page on a dead product.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.product_replacements a JOIN catalog.product_replacements b ON b.sku = a.replaced_by_sku WHERE b.replaced_by_sku = a.sku

defects.title: 320 towns fall out of the delivery zone on collation alone
defects.why: Delivery zones are cut from the town list by a range of names, which is how the rounds were described on paper and how they were written in SQL. The town column is declared COLLATE "C" and the database collates as en_US. Under C the comparison is byte by byte, so a town whose name begins with a lower case letter falls outside a range that the same comparison under the database's own collation would include. The zone query returns fewer towns than the paper round covers, and the towns it drops are the ones with unusual names rather than the ones on the edge of the map. Measured: 1,200 towns, 320 of which fall inside the round's name range under the database's collation and outside it under the column's. Leaving the column to the database's collation makes the range mean what the round means. Cutting a delivery zone by name range is the deeper problem and the collation is what makes it fail invisibly.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.town_names WHERE (town COLLATE "en_US.utf8") BETWEEN 'A' AND 'Z' AND NOT (town BETWEEN 'A' AND 'Z')

defects.title: 1,680 summer shifts are recorded an hour before they happened
defects.why: Shift start times were recorded for years as plain timestamps, in the local time of the depot. A column with a time zone was added and the old values were converted across. The conversion read every stored value as though it were UTC, because that is what a bare cast does when the session is set to UTC. The stored values were British local time, so every shift recorded during British Summer Time is now an hour earlier than it happened. Winter shifts converted correctly, which is why the conversion was signed off in February. Measured: 3,000 shift starts, 1,680 of them in British Summer Time and each an hour earlier in the converted column than the local time it was taken from. AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London' reads a local timestamp as local, and it has to be applied to the stored values rather than to the reads. Payroll rounds shifts to the nearest quarter hour, so an hour is a real difference and still lands on a plausible start time.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.shift_starts WHERE (started_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London') <> started_local

defects.title: 300 gate passes were voided by the web application's role
defects.why: Voiding a gate pass runs through a SECURITY DEFINER function, so the gatehouse terminal can void a pass without holding write access to the table. The function checks nothing about its caller. Execute on a function is granted to everybody by default and nobody revoked it, so every role in the database can void any pass and the function will do it with the owner's privileges. It records who called it, which is the only reason this is visible at all. Measured: 1,200 pass voids, 300 of them recorded against the web application's role, which has no business voiding gate passes. A check on current_user inside the function, and execute granted to the gatehouse role rather than left with PUBLIC, are both one line. The voids look ordinary in the yard's own report, which does not show who made them.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.pass_voids WHERE voided_by = 'web_app'

defects.title: 1,330 invoices carry a due date the customer never agreed to
defects.why: Trade invoices gained a due date column and the historic rows were backfilled at thirty days from issue, because thirty days is the standard term. It is the standard term and it is not everybody's term. Accounts negotiated down to fourteen days and up to sixty days both exist, and the backfill did not look at the account. Every historic invoice now claims a due date the customer never agreed to, in both directions: the fourteen day accounts look late when they were not and the sixty day accounts look current when they were overdue. Measured: 2,000 invoices against 400 accounts, and 1,330 invoices whose due date does not match the account's own terms. The terms were on the account the whole time and joining to them is the backfill that should have run. The credit control list is built from this column, so the chasing has been aimed at the wrong customers since the day it was populated.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.invoice_due_dates d JOIN payments.account_terms t USING (account_ref) WHERE d.due_on <> d.issued_on + t.terms_days

defects.title: The agency role holds select on a table it cannot reach
defects.why: The agency's reporting role was granted select on the campaign statistics table and cannot read a row. Reading a table needs usage on the schema that holds it as well as select on the table itself, and the grant only did the second. Every privilege audit shows the role holding select on exactly the table it is supposed to read, and every query it runs returns permission denied for schema marketing. The grant is present, correct and useless. Measured: the agency role holds select on marketing.campaign_stats and no usage on the marketing schema. GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA marketing is the missing line. The agency reports the failure as the report being broken, and it has been retried, rewritten and escalated as a reporting problem three times.

detect.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN has_table_privilege('agency_reader', 'marketing.campaign_stats', 'SELECT') AND NOT has_schema_privilege('agency_reader', 'marketing', 'USAGE') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END

defects.title: The reporting role can write to every storefront table
defects.why: The reporting role needs to read the shop visit log and was granted all privileges on every table in the storefront schema. ALL is shorter to type than SELECT and it was a Friday. The role can insert, update, delete and truncate every table in the schema that holds the shop, the baskets and the orders. Nothing it runs uses any of that, so nothing has gone wrong and nothing will until a report is written with a typo in it, or the role's credentials are used by something that is not a report. Measured: the reporting role holds update on both the shop visit and shop basket tables, which it is supposed to be able to read and nothing else. GRANT SELECT is the grant that was meant and revoking the rest is one statement. A privilege audit that lists roles rather than privileges shows one reporting role with access to one schema, which is exactly what was asked for at the time.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'storefront' AND c.relname IN ('shop_visits', 'shop_baskets') AND has_table_privilege('report_writer', c.oid, 'UPDATE')

defects.title: 400 trade invoices went with the suppliers that were tidied up
defects.why: Trade invoices reference their supplier with ON DELETE CASCADE, so that removing a supplier does not leave rows behind. Removing a supplier is not supposed to remove its invoices: invoices are financial records and are kept for six years whatever happens to the relationship. The cascade was written by somebody clearing up orphan rows in a test database and it does exactly what it says. A tidy up of twenty dormant suppliers deleted four hundred invoices without a word, and the only record that they existed is the load table, which counts what was loaded. Measured: 2,000 invoice lines loaded, 1,600 invoices in the table, and 20 suppliers removed. ON DELETE RESTRICT refuses the delete and makes the question visible, which is what a financial record wants. The gap was found by a total that no longer matched last year's accounts, eleven months later.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT sum(lines_loaded) FROM supply.trade_invoice_loads) - (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.trade_invoices)

defects.title: A merchant may write a payout row it cannot then see
defects.why: Merchant payouts are protected by a row policy so that a merchant sees only its own payouts. The policy has a USING clause and no WITH CHECK clause. USING filters what a statement can see; WITH CHECK decides what it may write, and when it is absent for an insert the policy allows any row at all. A merchant can therefore insert a payout attributed to another merchant, which it will then be unable to see, and that is the detail that makes this hard to find by testing: everything a merchant writes and reads back behaves exactly as it should. Measured: one policy on payments.merchant_payouts with a USING clause and no WITH CHECK, over 1,500 payouts for 25 merchants. FOR ALL wants both clauses, and the WITH CHECK is usually the same expression as the USING. The policy was reviewed by reading what a merchant can see, which is the half that is correct.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_policy p WHERE p.polrelid = 'payments.merchant_payouts'::regclass AND p.polwithcheck IS NULL AND p.polcmd = '*'

defects.title: 300 test orders are counted as real in every report
defects.why: Order status is a number: one is taken, two is picked, three is despatched, nine is cancelled, and ninety-nine means the order is a test. Ninety-nine is written nowhere. There is no lookup table, no constraint and no comment on the column; it is a convention two people in the warehouse agreed to when the system went in, and one of them has retired. Every report written since counts those orders as real, because nothing in the database suggests they are anything else, and they are indistinguishable from real orders in every other column. Measured: 3,000 order status rows, 300 of them at status ninety-nine. A lookup table with a name against each code makes the convention readable and a boolean for test orders makes it enforceable. The test orders are spread evenly through the history, so they inflate every period by about the same amount and no trend looks wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.order_status_rows WHERE status_code = 99

defects.title: An 8,000 row working table from 2024 is still backed up nightly
defects.why: A reconciliation in 2024 needed somewhere to put its working rows, so it made a table in the archive schema and filled it. The reconciliation finished and the table did not go anywhere. Nothing reads it, nothing writes to it, no foreign key points at it and no view mentions it, and it is backed up, vacuumed and replicated every day along with everything else. Its name says 2024 and its contents are a snapshot of a problem that was solved, which makes it exactly the kind of object nobody is willing to drop without asking somebody who no longer works here. Measured: 8,000 rows in the working table and nothing in the database depending on it. Dropping it is the fix and the obstacle is confidence, not effort. Creating a working table in a schema that is backed up, rather than as a temporary table, is what turns a scratch pad into an artefact.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM archive.tmp_reconcile_2024) - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_depend d WHERE d.refobjid = 'archive.tmp_reconcile_2024'::regclass AND d.deptype = 'n')

defects.title: A whole year of delivery notes is missing on a key collision
defects.why: Supplier delivery notes are keyed by their note number, and the supplier restarts its note numbers at one every January. The note number is unique within a year and the key treats it as unique for all time. The loader inserts what it can and skips what collides, so the first year loaded is complete and every year after it silently loses every note whose number was used before. The loader counts what it read, which is the only reason the loss is countable at all. Measured: 2,400 delivery note lines read across two years and 1,200 notes in the table, the missing 1,200 being the second year's. The key is the year and the number together, which is what the supplier's own paperwork means. The second year's notes are simply absent, so nothing in the table looks wrong: it looks like a year of trading that did not happen.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT sum(notes_read) FROM supply.delivery_note_loads) - (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.delivery_notes)

defects.title: The busiest table writes ten times for every row inserted
defects.why: The belt read log is the busiest table in the building and it has nine indexes. Each one was added for a query somebody needed once and none was ever removed. Every insert now writes the row and then writes nine index entries, so the table takes ten times the write work of the row itself, and the indexes are most of its size on disc. Reads are excellent. The belt does not read anything; it writes, several times a second, all day. Measured: 12,000 belt reads under 9 indexes, not counting the primary key. Two or three indexes covering the queries that actually run is the fix, and deciding which those are needs the statistics nobody has looked at. Adding an index is always a local improvement and removing one always feels like a risk, which is how a table gets to nine.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i WHERE i.indrelid = 'ops.belt_reads'::regclass AND NOT i.indisprimary

defects.title: 400 hazardous products have no data sheet on file
defects.why: Every hazardous product must have a data sheet on file and the column that holds the reference to it is nullable. Nothing at the point of entry makes it mandatory either, so a product can be set up, listed and sold with the sheet left empty, and it is: the sheet arrives from the supplier days or weeks after the product is set up and nothing comes back to fill it in. The obligation is real and the schema treats it as optional, which is exactly the kind of gap that is discovered by an inspection rather than by a report. Measured: 1,200 hazardous products and 400 with no data sheet reference. NOT NULL is the fix if the sheet can be insisted on at setup, and a status column with a deadline is the fix if it cannot. Products without a sheet trade normally and look exactly like products with one everywhere except the column itself.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.hazard_sheets WHERE sheet_ref IS NULL

defects.title: 600 null wrap charges mean two different things
defects.why: The gift wrap charge is null when the wrapping was free and null when the charge was never recorded. One column, two meanings, and nothing to tell them apart. The promotion that gave free wrapping through December wrote nulls, the counter terminal that was misconfigured for three weeks in February wrote nulls, and both look identical now. Sum skips nulls, so the wrapping revenue is understated by the February rows and correctly excludes the December ones, in one figure that cannot be decomposed. Measured: 2,000 gift wraps, 600 with a null charge, of which 400 were free and 200 were never recorded, distinguishable only by the date. Zero means free and null means unknown, and that is the whole distinction this column needs. The wrapping revenue is a small number nobody forecasts, so being understated has never raised a question.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.gift_wraps WHERE charge IS NULL

defects.title: 1,800 message ids missing from the email table, taken by the text table
defects.why: Email sends and text sends were once one table. They were split in two and both kept the original sequence, so that a message id would stay unique across the pair. It does stay unique, and neither table's ids are contiguous any more: each table holds the ids the other did not take, so both look as though they have lost most of their rows. Every check that reasons from the highest id to the number of rows, and every report that counts sends by taking a range of ids, is wrong by the share the other table took. Measured: 3,000 messages across the two tables under one sequence, a highest id of 3,000, and 1,800 ids missing from the email table alone. A single table with a type column, or two sequences and a separate business key, both give ids that mean what people read into them. The uniqueness this was built for is real and nobody has ever needed it.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT max(message_id) FROM marketing.email_sends) - (SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.email_sends)

defects.title: 800 proof of delivery scans name no courier
defects.why: Proof of delivery scans are validated by a trigger that refuses a scan with no courier reference on it. The trigger was turned off for a weekend, because the handheld firmware was sending blank references and the depot could not stop scanning while it was fixed. The firmware was fixed on the Monday. The trigger was not turned back on, and the blank references kept arriving from the two depots whose handhelds were never updated. Measured: 4,000 proof of delivery scans, 800 with a blank courier reference, every one of them written after the trigger was disabled. Enabling the trigger is one statement and the 800 rows have to be dealt with first, which is the reason it is still off. A scan with no courier on it proves delivery by nobody, which is exactly the scan that gets quoted in a dispute.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.pod_scans WHERE length(trim(courier_ref)) = 0

defects.title: 600 attachments hang off cases the attachment screen cannot find
defects.why: Support cases were split into open cases and closed cases, two tables, to keep the open list small. Attachments stayed in one table and kept pointing at the case reference. There is no foreign key, because there is no single table to point at. A case that closes moves out of the open table, and every attachment on it now references a case reference the attachment screen cannot find. The attachment is still there, still stored, and unreachable from the only place anybody looks for it. Measured: 2,000 attachments against 1,400 open cases, and 600 attachments whose case is no longer in the open table. One case table with a status column is the fix and the small open list was never the real problem. The attachments are found again when somebody reopens the case, which is the only time anybody notices they were missing.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.attachments a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM support.open_cases c WHERE c.case_ref = a.case_ref)

defects.title: 400 customers have their own address in the book twice
defects.why: A customer's address book holds one row per address, and 400 customers have the same address in it twice. Addresses are typed, not chosen, and nothing compares a new address with the ones already there. A customer who types their own address again, with the county left off or the postcode spaced differently, gets a second row, and the checkout lists both with nothing to tell them apart. Half the deliveries to those customers are booked against one row and half against the other, which splits their delivery history in two. Measured: 3,000 addresses for 2,600 customers, with 800 rows in 400 pairs holding the same postcode and house number for the same customer. Normalising the postcode and comparing it with the house number on the way in catches these at the point they are created. The duplicates are correct addresses, deliverable and never wrong, which is why nothing has ever flagged them.

detect.sql: SELECT coalesce(sum(n), 0) FROM (SELECT count(*) AS n FROM storefront.customer_addresses GROUP BY customer_id, house_no, postcode HAVING count(*) > 1) s

defects.title: 900 depot assets carry a code that is on no label
defects.why: Depot assets reference their depot by the depot code, with the foreign key declared ON UPDATE CASCADE. The depot codes were re-lettered as part of a numbering tidy up. The cascade did what it promised and rewrote the depot code on every asset in the same statement, which is correct inside the database and wrong everywhere else: the asset labels, the insurance schedule and the maintenance contracts all carry the old code on paper, and nothing outside the database was updated. There is no record in the assets table that they ever had another code. Measured: 900 depot assets carrying a re-lettered depot code and 0 carrying the code printed on their label. A stable surrogate key on the depot means a re-lettering changes one row. Cascading an update across a natural key is correct behaviour producing an outcome nobody asked for, which is the hardest kind of problem to argue about afterwards.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.depot_assets a WHERE a.depot_code NOT LIKE 'DEP-%' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint c WHERE c.conrelid = 'ops.depot_assets'::regclass AND c.contype = 'f' AND c.confupdtype = 'c')

defects.title: 1,080 evening orders are counted against the day before
defects.why: The daily order figures are cut by the UTC date, because the timestamp column is a timestamptz and casting one to a date is the obvious thing to write. Casting a timestamptz to a date uses the session's time zone, and the reporting session runs in UTC. For half the year London is an hour ahead, so the trading day the report cuts runs from one in the morning to one in the morning, and every order placed in that first hour of the British day is counted against the day before. The evening orders are the ones that move, because they sit either side of midnight. Measured: 3,000 evening orders and 1,080 whose UTC date is not the date they were placed on in London. AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London' before the cast makes the day the day the business traded. Nine orders a night land on the day before, every night of British Summer Time, and the same nine are missing from the day they were taken. Nothing goes missing in the total, so the monthly figure agrees with the bank and only the daily figures are wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.evening_orders WHERE (placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date <> (placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London')::date

defects.title: 40 rebate batches disagree about which supplier they are for
defects.why: A rebate claim belongs to a claim batch. The batch reference is on every claim row, every query groups by it, and there is no table of batches for it to point at. The batch is a key in every sense that matters: it is what the buyer works from, what the supplier is invoiced on, and what the finance team reconciles. It has no table, no primary key and no foreign key, so nothing checks that two claims filed under one batch reference agree about the supplier, the period or the rate. They do not always agree, and the group by hides it by picking whichever row the aggregate happens to reach. Measured: 2,400 rebate claims across 300 batch references, and 40 batches where the claims disagree about which supplier the batch is for. A batch table with the supplier, the period and the rate on it, and a foreign key from the claims, makes the disagreement impossible to write in the first place. Every report still runs and still returns a number, which is why the missing table has never been raised.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT batch_ref FROM supply.rebate_claims GROUP BY batch_ref HAVING count(DISTINCT supplier_ref) > 1) s

defects.title: 3,000 payout amounts are rounded and then overwritten twice
defects.why: Three BEFORE INSERT triggers on the payout lines, all of them setting the payable amount, all of them at the same timing. Triggers at the same timing fire in name order, so the one whose name sorts last is the one whose answer survives. The rounding trigger was added first and named for what it does; the commission trigger and the adjustment trigger were added later by different people and both sort after it. The rounding is applied and then overwritten twice, which means the column is rounded only when the last trigger happens to agree with it. Measured: 3,000 payout lines, every one of which holds an amount with more than two decimal places. The rounding trigger runs on all of them and its answer survives on none. One trigger that does all three things in the order the business wants is the fix, and naming them for their order is a trap that works right up until somebody adds a fourth. The unrounded amounts are pennies, so the payouts reconcile to the pound and never to the penny.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.payout_lines WHERE payable <> round(payable, 2)

defects.title: 4 depots are their own parent and 20 depots hang underneath them
defects.why: Depots roll up to regional depots through a parent column on the same table, and four depots are their own parent. Nothing stops it: the foreign key is satisfied by a row pointing at itself, and a check that a row is not its own parent was never written. The walk up the tree from any depot underneath one of those four never terminates. The recursive query that builds the regional roll up has a depth limit on it, added when the roll up first hung, so the report finishes and quietly drops everything under those four depots. Measured: 240 depots in the hierarchy, 4 of them their own parent, and 20 depots underneath the four. A check constraint that a depot is not its own parent stops the obvious case in one line, and the general cycle needs a walk on the way in. The depth limit means nobody has seen the roll up fail, only seen it come back short.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.depot_hierarchy WHERE parent_code = depot_code

defects.title: The portal role can call the totals function and read neither table it reads
defects.why: The settlement totals function reads two payments tables and is called by the merchant portal role. It runs as invoker, and that role has execute on the function and select on neither table. Execute was granted because the call failed without it. Select was not granted, because nobody wanted the portal reading the payments tables directly, which is the correct instinct and the wrong mechanism: an invoker function borrows the caller's rights, so the call still fails, just later and with a message about a table the portal was never meant to know the name of. The portal swallows the error and shows a zero. Measured: the function is SECURITY INVOKER, portal_reader holds EXECUTE on it and holds SELECT on 0 of the 2 tables it reads. SECURITY DEFINER with a pinned search_path is what this function was always meant to be, and it must be granted execute explicitly so its access list is not left empty. A zero on a portal screen looks like a merchant with nothing outstanding, which is why this has been open for a year.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'payments' AND c.relname IN ('settlement_runs', 'settlement_holdbacks') AND has_table_privilege('portal_reader', c.oid, 'SELECT') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace pn ON pn.oid = p.pronamespace WHERE pn.nspname = 'payments' AND p.proname = 'fn_settlement_totals' AND NOT p.prosecdef)

defects.title: Every ledger row in the staging table is there twice
defects.why: The ledger import lands in a staging table with no primary key and no unique index on anything. It is loaded twice a day from the same source file, morning and evening, and the evening load was meant to pick up only what changed. It picks up the whole file. With no key there is nothing to conflict against and nothing to update, so every row the morning load wrote is written again in the evening. The downstream job reads the staging table with a DISTINCT on it, which is why nobody has noticed, and the DISTINCT is over fewer columns than the table has. Measured: 9,000 rows in the staging table holding 4,500 distinct ledger references, every one of them present exactly twice. A primary key on the ledger reference and a load that conflicts against it makes the second load do what it was meant to do. Nothing downstream is wrong today, because the DISTINCT happens to cover the duplicate, and the day somebody adds a column to the SELECT it stops covering it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) - count(DISTINCT ledger_ref) FROM legacy.ledger_imports

defects.title: 480 rebate supplier names sort into a different place than every other name column
defects.why: The rebate supplier names are held under the C collation, and the supplier names everywhere else in the database are held under the database collation. The rebate report joins the two and sorts on the rebate table's column, because that is the one it selects. C sorts by byte, so every lower case letter comes after every upper case one, and a name beginning with a lower case letter, or with an accent on it, lands at the end of the list rather than where a reader expects it. The same names sorted from the other table come out in a different order, and both orders are correct for their column. Measured: 600 rebate supplier names, of which 480 sort into a different position under the database collation than under C. Dropping the COLLATE clause makes the column behave like every other name column in the database. Nobody has reported it because the list is long enough that people search it rather than read it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY supplier_name) AS a, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY supplier_name COLLATE "en_US.utf8") AS b FROM supply.rebate_suppliers) s WHERE a <> b

defects.title: 600 returns are back in stock with no credit raised
defects.why: A return puts the goods back into stock and raises a credit against the customer. Two tables, two writes, and nothing that requires the second one to happen when the first one does. The stock move is written by the warehouse handheld the moment the goods are scanned back in. The credit is raised by the returns desk afterwards, from a worklist, and the worklist is built from a query that skips returns scanned outside the desk's opening hours. Those returns are in stock, sellable, and have never been credited. The customer chases, the desk raises the credit by hand, and the ones nobody chases stay uncredited. Measured: 3,000 return stock moves and 2,400 return credits, leaving 600 returns in stock with no credit against them. One transaction that writes both, or an outbox the desk drains, makes the pairing something the database holds rather than something a worklist query has to remember. Stock is right, which is what gets checked, so the gap only shows up as customers ringing about credits.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.return_stock_moves m WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments.return_credits c WHERE c.return_ref = m.return_ref)

defects.title: 5,000 price changes produced 5 audit rows
defects.why: Every price change on a listing is audited, and the audit trigger is declared FOR EACH STATEMENT. A statement that changes one price writes one audit row, which is why it looked right when it was tested. The nightly repricing job changes prices in batches of a thousand in a single statement, and that statement also writes one audit row. The audit table holds a row per repricing run and no record of which listings moved or what they moved from, which is the only thing anyone opens it for. Measured: 5,000 listing prices loaded in 5 statements, and 5 rows in the audit table. FOR EACH ROW is the whole fix and it makes the audit table five thousand rows instead of five, which is the size it was always meant to be. The audit exists, is populated and is checked by a monitor that counts rows, so it has looked healthy every day since it was built.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.listing_prices) - (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.listing_price_audit)

defects.title: The buyer role can read the detail and not the summary
defects.why: The buyers' reader role was granted select on the returns table and not on the view that aggregates it. The grant was written against the table because that is what existed when the role was created. The view came later, in a different migration, by a different person, and a view is a separate object with its own access list. The role can read every row of the underlying table and cannot read the summary of it, which is the wrong way round from what anybody intended: the summary is what the buyers were supposed to have and the detail is what they were not. Measured: buyer_reader holds SELECT on the returns table and not on the view over it. Granting select on the view and revoking it on the table gives the role what it was built for. Nobody has complained because the buyers export the table into a spreadsheet and aggregate it there, which works and is how the numbers in two different reports came to disagree.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 WHERE has_table_privilege('buyer_reader', 'catalog.return_rate_rows', 'SELECT') AND NOT has_table_privilege('buyer_reader', 'catalog.v_return_rates', 'SELECT')) s

defects.title: 3,728 cost lines are short by 552,368 pence in total
defects.why: The cost per unit is worked out by dividing the case cost in pence by the number of units in the case, in integer arithmetic, and the line cost is that unit cost multiplied back up by the quantity. Dividing first throws away the remainder once per unit, and multiplying back up by the quantity multiplies the loss. A case of 24 costing 1,000 pence gives 41 pence a unit rather than 41.67, and a line of ten cases is short by sixteen pence before anything else happens. The error is always downwards, never rounds out, and grows with the order. Measured: 4,000 case cost lines, of which 3,728 are short against the same arithmetic done without the integer division, by 552,368 pence in total. Multiplying before dividing, or holding the unit cost as numeric, both fix it and the second is what the rest of the schema does. The shortfall is in the cost, not the price, so it overstates margin and no report has ever flagged a margin that came in higher than expected.

detect.sql: SELECT sum(case_cost_p * cases_ordered - line_cost_p) FROM supply.case_costs

defects.title: 34,999 quote references left in a six character format
defects.why: Counter quotes are numbered from a six character reference, zero padded, held as text and generated from a sequence. Six characters means the highest reference the format can hold is 999999. The sequence does not know that, because the constraint is the column width and the padding, not the sequence, and it will hand out 1000000 without complaining. The insert will fail on the column width at that point, in the middle of a counter serving a customer, with a message about a value being too long for a character varying. Measured: the highest quote reference issued is 965000, leaving 34,999 of the 999,999 the format can hold, against about 3,200 quotes a month. Widening the column and the padding to eight characters buys a hundred years and can be done any evening. It has not been done because nothing reports on headroom in a text column and the number looks like it has five digits of room left when it has one.

detect.sql: SELECT 999999 - max(quote_ref)::integer FROM storefront.quote_numbers

defects.title: 1,800 tickets were all assigned at the same instant
defects.why: Ticket ownership was added to the support system in March. Every ticket that already existed was given an owner by a backfill, and the backfill stamped the assignment timestamp with the moment it ran. Every one of those tickets now says it was assigned at the same instant on the same afternoon, years after some of them were opened. The report that measures how long a ticket waits before somebody picks it up reads that timestamp, so every backfilled ticket shows either an enormous wait or a negative one, depending on whether it was opened before or after the backfill. The averages are pulled around by rows that describe the backfill rather than the work. Measured: 3,600 ticket owners, of which 1,800 share one assignment timestamp to the microsecond. Leaving the timestamp null for rows whose real assignment time is not known lets the report exclude them, which is the honest answer. A wait time that is wrong in both directions averages out to something plausible, which is why this has survived four quarterly reviews.

detect.sql: SELECT coalesce(max(n), 0) FROM (SELECT count(*) AS n FROM support.ticket_owners GROUP BY assigned_at) s

defects.title: 900 delivery drops belong to no route
defects.why: A drop belongs to a route plan, and the foreign key is declared ON DELETE SET NULL, so deleting a route plan leaves its drops behind with no route. SET NULL was chosen so that deleting a cancelled route would not take the delivery records with it, which is a reasonable thing to want and the wrong way to get it. The drops survive, with nothing to say which route they were on, and the column is nullable because it has to be for the action to be legal. Every report that joins drops to routes loses them silently, and the count of drops made never agrees with the sum of drops per route. Measured: 4,500 route drops, of which 900 have no route plan, left behind by 60 deleted routes. ON DELETE RESTRICT plus a cancelled flag on the route keeps the history and keeps the link. The orphaned drops are real deliveries that really happened, so nothing about them looks wrong until somebody adds up two numbers that were never going to match.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.route_drops WHERE plan_id IS NULL

defects.title: Four reason codes mean different things in two schemas
defects.why: The reason a thing was done is picked from a list of reason codes. There are two lists, one in operations and one in support, and they were the same list when they were copied. They were copied because the two teams were on different release cycles and neither wanted to wait for the other. Codes have been added to each since, and not to the other. Worse, four codes exist in both lists with different descriptions, so a reason recorded in one system reads as something else in the other, and the weekly report that unions the two shows both descriptions for the same code without saying which is which. Measured: 60 reason codes in operations, 60 in support, 48 held in common, and 4 of those 48 with different descriptions on each side. One table in a shared schema, with a foreign key from both sides, is the fix and the release cycle argument stopped applying three years ago. Both lists are internally consistent and both are maintained, which is why neither team believes theirs is the copy.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.reason_codes o JOIN support.reason_codes s USING (reason_code) WHERE o.description <> s.description

defects.title: 11,940 shelf tags are rewritten nightly to the price they already hold
defects.why: The shelf tag job runs every night and sets the printed price on every tag from the current price list. It sets it on every tag, not on the tags whose price moved. Postgres writes a new row version for an update whether or not the value changed, so the job rewrites the whole table nightly, every row of it, and leaves a dead version behind for each. The table is a hundred times the size of its data and the autovacuum that would reclaim it is fighting a job that undoes the work every night. Measured: 12,000 shelf tags and 12,000 rows updated by the last run, of which 11,940 were set to the price they already held. A WHERE clause comparing the new price with the old one turns a twelve thousand row write into a sixty row write. The job finishes inside its window, so nothing has ever escalated, and the table's bloat is charged to storage rather than to the job that causes it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.shelf_tags WHERE printed_on = DATE '2026-06-02' AND tag_id % 200 <> 0

defects.title: 200 goods receipt numbers were issued twice
defects.why: The goods receipt numbers come from a sequence, and the sequence was reset by hand during a restore and set to a number that had already been issued. The receipt number column has no unique index, because the sequence was supposed to guarantee uniqueness and a second index on a heavily written table was argued against at the time. So the reissued numbers went in without complaint. Two goods receipts now share a number, on different dates, against different suppliers, and the warehouse enquiry screen shows whichever one the query reaches first. Measured: 6,000 goods receipts holding 5,800 distinct receipt numbers, with 200 numbers issued twice. A unique index on the receipt number would have refused the second issue and turned a silent duplicate into a failed restore, which is the outcome anybody would have chosen. The duplicates are eighteen months apart, so no screen shows them side by side and nobody has seen the two rows together.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) - count(DISTINCT receipt_no) FROM supply.goods_receipt_numbers

defects.title: 239 statement periods start on the day the previous one ends
defects.why: Statement periods are stored as a start date and an end date, and the statement query selects transactions BETWEEN the two. BETWEEN includes both ends. The next period starts on the day the last one ended, because that is how the periods were generated, so every transaction on a period boundary appears on two statements. The customer sees the same transaction twice across two statements, once at the bottom of one and once at the top of the next, and the statement totals add up to more than the year. Measured: 240 statement periods, 239 of which start on the day the previous one ends. Either the end date becomes exclusive and the query uses >= and <, or the periods stop overlapping. The double counted transactions are correct on both statements taken alone, which is why every query about them has been answered with "that is the one from last month".

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.statement_periods a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments.statement_periods b WHERE b.starts_on = a.ends_on)

defects.title: 2,400 vouchers hold a null code under a unique index
defects.why: Voucher codes are unique. The unique index is on a nullable column, and in SQL a null is not equal to another null, so any number of rows may hold a null code and the index will not object. The code is null while the voucher is being drafted and is filled in when the campaign is approved. Drafts accumulate. There are now more vouchers with no code than there are with one, all of them passing a unique index that reads as though it guarantees something, and the code that generates a new voucher code checks the table for a clash with a query that also compares against null and therefore never matches. Measured: 4,000 voucher rows under a unique index on the code, of which 2,400 hold a null code. Either the column is NOT NULL and drafts live somewhere else, or the index is partial and says WHERE code IS NOT NULL, which at least states what it enforces. The index exists, is unique and is on the right column, so every review of this table has passed it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.voucher_codes WHERE code IS NULL

defects.title: One pick face rebuild runs 8,000 statements
defects.why: The pick face rebuild walks the pick faces one at a time and runs a query inside the loop for each one. It was written that way because the first version had to log a line per face and a loop was the obvious shape. The logging was removed and the loop was not. The body is now a single UPDATE against a single row, repeated once per face, so a job that could be one statement is eight thousand statements, each with its own plan, its own snapshot and its own round trip through the executor. Measured: 8,000 pick faces and 8,000 statements executed by one call of the rebuild, which the function records as it goes. One UPDATE with a join against the source table does the same work in one statement. The job runs overnight and finishes before anybody arrives, so the only sign of it is a warehouse that cannot rebuild pick faces during trading hours and has stopped asking to.

detect.sql: SELECT max(statement_count) FROM ops.pick_face_rebuild_log

defects.title: 700 consignments sit at a status that was retired three years ago
defects.why: The consignment status is a text column with no constraint on it, and one of the values in it was retired from the application three years ago. The status was 'held_customs', used when consignments were routed through a third country. That route was dropped and the application stopped writing and stopped reading the value. The rows that held it were never migrated, because migrating them meant deciding what they had become and nobody could. They are still there, still saying held_customs, and every screen that switches on the status falls through to its default branch and shows them as unknown. Measured: 5,600 consignment states across 5 distinct statuses, of which 700 hold a status the application no longer knows. A lookup table with a foreign key, or an enum, makes retiring a value a migration rather than a decision nobody takes. The rows are old and closed, so they appear on no worklist, and the only place they show up is a total that does not match the sum of the statuses beneath it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.consignment_states WHERE status = 'held_customs'

defects.title: 20 agents who took no calls are reported as having taken one
defects.why: The calls per agent view left joins agents to calls and counts with count(*). A left join gives an agent with no calls one row, with every call column null, and count(*) counts rows. So an agent who took no calls is reported as having taken one. The agents who took none are the new starters and the ones on long term leave, which is exactly the population the report is opened to look at, and every one of them reads as having taken a single call. Measured: 120 agents, 20 of whom took no calls, every one of them reported by the view as having taken 1. count(c.call_id) counts calls rather than rows and gives zero, which is the answer. One call is a plausible number for a new starter, so the report has never looked obviously wrong to the person reading it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_calls_per_agent v WHERE v.calls_taken = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM support.agent_calls c WHERE c.agent_ref = v.agent_ref)

defects.title: 4,400 customer rows kept from a cutover two years ago
defects.why: The customer table was copied before the last cutover so that the old application could be rolled back to. The rollback window closed two years ago and the copy is still here. It is a full copy, rows and all, frozen at the moment it was taken. Nothing reads it, nothing writes it, and nothing references it. It is backed up every night, restored into every environment, and its rows are two years out of date, which matters because somebody looking for a customer who is not in the live table will find them in this one and believe what it says. It has the word customers in its name and it is not the customers. Measured: 4,400 rows in the pre cutover copy, 0 objects in the database referencing it, and 0 grants on it beyond the owner. Dropping it is one statement and the only argument against is that nobody wants to be the person who dropped a table with customers in the name. It costs storage in every environment and it is the reason two reports about customer counts have never agreed.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM legacy.customers_pre_cutover WHERE (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE confrelid = 'legacy.customers_pre_cutover'::regclass) = 0 AND (SELECT coalesce(array_length(relacl, 1), 0) FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'legacy' AND c.relname = 'customers_pre_cutover') = 0

defects.title: A yes or no column holds 7 different values
defects.why: The marketing opt in is a text column, and it holds four different ways of saying yes and three of saying no. The column started as text because the first import had the word Yes in it, and every later source wrote whatever it had: the web form wrote true, the till wrote Y, the call centre wrote 1, and an import from a bought list wrote YES in capitals. Every query that filters on this column picks some of the opted in customers and misses the rest, and which ones depends on which values the person writing the query happened to know about. Measured: 6,000 opt in rows holding 7 distinct values, of which 4 mean yes and cover 3,429 rows. A boolean column, NOT NULL, with the import normalising on the way in, makes the question answerable. Every query returns a number and no query returns the same number, which is why this is a long standing argument rather than a bug.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT opted_in) FROM storefront.marketing_opt_ins

defects.title: Autovacuum is off on the highest churn table in the database
defects.why: The scan queue is the highest churn table in the database and autovacuum is disabled on it. It was disabled during an incident, because autovacuum was running during the evening peak and the warehouse blamed it for the scanners timing out. The incident was something else. The setting stayed. The table takes a row per scan and deletes it when the scan is processed, so it is almost entirely dead rows, and nothing is reclaiming them. The planner's statistics are from the day it was turned off, so every query against the queue is planned for a table that no longer resembles this one. Measured: autovacuum_enabled is off on the scan queue, 24,000 rows have been written to it and 21,600 deleted, leaving 2,400 live rows in the space of twenty four thousand. Re-enabling it, with a cost delay if the peak really is tight, is one ALTER TABLE. Nobody will re-enable it because the last person who touched autovacuum on this table was blamed for an outage.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'ops' AND c.relname = 'scan_queue' AND c.reloptions @> ARRAY['autovacuum_enabled=false']

defects.title: 600 haulage bookings are costed at zero because of a trailing space
defects.why: Haulage bookings join to haulage rates on the lane code. The rate side holds the code in a char column, the booking side in a varchar, and the costing view casts the char to text to join them. char ignores trailing spaces when it is compared to another char, which is what made the original join work. Casting it to text turns off that behaviour: text compares every character, spaces included. The booking table stores the code as it arrived from the haulier's file, and for some hauliers that file carries a trailing space. Under the char comparison those matched. Under the cast they do not, so those bookings match no rate and are costed at zero. Measured: 3,600 haulage bookings against 240 rates, of which 600 bookings match no rate because their lane code carries trailing spaces. Trimming on the way in, and one type for the column on both sides, fixes it and the second half is the part that stops it coming back. The cast was added to silence a type warning and changed the answer. A booking costed at zero is a booking that never appears in a cost report, so the haulage spend has looked under budget for two years.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_haulage_costs WHERE cost = 0

defects.title: Half the bin moves were written by the trigger, not by a person
defects.why: The bin move trigger writes a balancing move into the same table it is attached to. Writing to the table fires the trigger again for the row it just wrote. The function guards against running forever by checking a flag column and returning early when it is set, which works, and means every move written by a person produces exactly one machine written move and no more. That is the intended behaviour and it is also why the table holds twice the moves anybody thinks it does: the balancing moves are indistinguishable from real ones in every report, because the flag is not selected by any of them. Measured: 4,000 bin moves, of which 2,000 were written by the trigger rather than by a person. A separate table for the balancing side, or a column every report actually filters on, makes the two kinds of move tellable apart. The stock balances, because the balancing moves are correct, so the only symptom is a move count that is exactly double what the warehouse says it did.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.bin_moves WHERE machine_written

defects.title: A three column index led by a column nothing filters on
defects.why: The despatch note index is on (note_status, despatched_on, depot_code). Every query against the table filters on the depot and a date range, and none of them filters on the status. A composite index can only be used from its leading column onwards. Filtering on the depot and the date, with nothing on the status, means the index cannot be searched at all and the planner reads the whole table. The index is a hundred megabytes of pages that are maintained on every insert and read by nothing. Measured: 30,000 despatch notes under an index whose leading column is the status, of which every row holds one of 3 statuses, and 0 queries in the application filter on it.
