(depot_code, despatched_on) is the index the queries want and it is a third of the size. The index exists and looks like it covers the columns in the query, which is why every review of the table has concluded the indexing is fine.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class ic ON ic.oid = i.indexrelid JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = i.indrelid AND a.attnum = i.indkey[0] WHERE i.indrelid = 'fulfilment.despatch_notes'::regclass AND a.attname = 'note_status' AND i.indnatts = 3

defects.title: The only documentation of the unit states the wrong one
defects.why: The bulk discount threshold column is documented as pence and it holds pounds. The comment was written when the column was added and was right at the time. The column was changed to pounds a year later, in a migration that changed the loader and the column type and not the comment, and the comment is the only documentation of the unit anywhere. Anybody who reads it and writes a query dividing by a hundred gets an answer a hundred times too small, and the number still looks like money, so it passes review. Measured: 1,800 bulk discount rows with a threshold column commented as pence and a maximum value of 4,999, which as pence would be fifty pounds and as pounds is the top of the band the business actually uses. Renaming the column to say its unit puts the fact somewhere a query writer cannot miss it, and a comment that contradicts the data is worse than no comment. The values are plausible under either reading, which is exactly why this has never been caught.

detect.sql: SELECT max(threshold) FROM catalog.bulk_discounts

defects.title: 1,200 uplifts are percentages and 1,200 are fractions in one column
defects.why: The campaign uplift is a percentage, and half the rows hold it as a whole number and half as a fraction. The campaign tool was rewritten. The old one wrote 12 for twelve percent and the new one writes 0.12, and the rows written by each are still there with nothing to say which is which except the date. A row holding 0.12 is a twelve percent uplift under one reading and a twelfth of a percent under the other, and both are plausible campaign results. Any average over the column is meaningless and any sum is worse. Measured: 2,400 campaign uplifts, of which 1,200 are below 1 and 1,200 are above, with no column saying which convention a row was written under. One unit, stated in the column name, with the old rows converted, is a day's work and settles it. The averages come out to something between the two conventions and have been reported to the board for six quarters.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.campaign_uplifts WHERE uplift < 1

defects.title: The active accounts view reports 800 where 1,500 have ordered
defects.why: The active trade accounts view selects accounts whose last order date is within the last two years, and the base table stopped populating the last order date eighteen months ago. The column was maintained by a nightly job that was retired when ordering moved to the new platform, and nothing replaced it. The column is still there, still holding the value it last held, and the view still filters on it. So the view returns the accounts that were active eighteen months ago, and it shrinks by itself every night as the two year window walks past dates that will never be updated again. Measured: 2,000 trade accounts, 800 of which the view reports as active, while 1,500 have placed an order in the last two years. Deriving the last order date from the orders rather than storing it makes the view correct and unmaintained by anybody. The view returns a number that falls slowly, which reads like a business trend rather than a broken column, and it has been explained as one in three separate meetings.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(DISTINCT account_ref) FROM storefront.trade_counter_orders WHERE placed_on >= DATE '2026-09-20' - 730) - (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_active_trade_accounts)

defects.title: 24 depots run two shifts a day and the roster holds one
defects.why: The shift roster is keyed on (depot, shift date), one row per depot per day. The depot runs two shifts a day and has done since the warehouse went to extended hours. The key allows one. The loader writes the day shift, then writes the night shift, and the second write replaces the first because the loader uses ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE. So every extended hours depot holds only its night shift, and the day shift has never been in the table at all. Measured: 3,600 roster rows across 40 depots and 90 days, where 24 of those depots run two shifts and hold one row a day. The key wants the shift code in it, which makes it (depot, date, shift) and turns the loader's upsert into two inserts. Every depot has a roster and the roster it has is a real one, so the table passes every check that asks whether a depot is covered.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.shift_rosters WHERE shift_code = 'night'

defects.title: 720 pallet receipts name a source that does not exist
defects.why: Pallet receipts referenced the pallet source by its source code, which had a unique index on it, and the index was dropped during a rebuild and the foreign key went with it. Dropping a unique index that a foreign key depends on takes the foreign key too, and Postgres says so at the time. The rebuild script ran overnight, the message went into a log nobody reads, and the index was recreated afterwards without the constraint. The column is still there, still populated, still joined on everywhere, and nothing checks it any more. Receipts have since been loaded against source codes that do not exist. Measured: 4,800 pallet receipts against 400 pallet sources, of which 720 receipts name a source that is not in the source table, and 0 foreign keys on the receipts table. Recreating the constraint takes a validation scan and a decision about the 720 rows, which is the reason it has not been done. The join is a left join in every report, so the bad rows come back with nulls in the source columns and are read as receipts from a source that was not recorded.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.pallet_receipts r WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM supply.pallet_sources s WHERE s.source_code = r.source_code) AND (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'supply.pallet_receipts'::regclass AND contype = 'f') = 0

defects.title: A commission policy exists and is applied to nothing
defects.why: There is a row security policy on the agent commissions table restricting each agent to their own rows, and row security was never enabled on the table. A policy without ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is inert: it is stored, it shows up in the catalogue, it reads correctly, and it is not applied to anything. The migration that added it did the policy and not the enable, and the test that was supposed to prove the restriction worked was written as the owner, who bypasses row security anyway. Every agent can read every agent's commission. Measured: 1 policy on the commissions table, row security not enabled on it, and 3,000 commission rows visible to every role that can select the table. ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is the missing line. The policy exists and is correct, which is why every review that looked for one found it and stopped there.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_policy p JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = p.polrelid WHERE c.oid = 'payments.agent_commissions'::regclass AND NOT c.relrowsecurity

defects.title: 8 depots report no last stocktake at all
defects.why: The last stocktake view takes the maximum stocktake date per depot. The stocktake date is nullable, and a depot whose every stocktake has a null date gets a null back. The null means the stocktake was booked and never completed, which is a real and different thing from never having been counted. max ignores nulls, so a depot with one completed count and four incomplete ones correctly reports the completed one. A depot whose counts were all abandoned reports null, and the screen that shows the overdue depots sorts nulls last and puts the worst depots at the bottom of the list. Measured: 40 depots and 8 of them reported with no last stocktake date at all, every one of which has booked stocktakes that were never completed. Counting the completed stocktakes alongside the maximum date tells the two apart in the view rather than in the head of whoever reads it. Null sorts last, so the depots that most need counting are the ones nobody scrolls to.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.v_last_stocktake WHERE last_counted_on IS NULL

defects.title: 240 pack sizes of zero under a constraint that forbids them
defects.why: The pack size must be at least one, and the check constraint that says so was added NOT VALID, so it applies to new rows and was never checked against the old ones. NOT VALID was the right call at the time, because validating it would have taken a table lock during trading hours. The VALIDATE CONSTRAINT that was supposed to follow that evening was never run. The constraint reads as a guarantee in every schema dump and in every review, and there are rows in the table that break it, including pack sizes of zero that make the cost per unit a division by zero. Measured: 2,400 pack sizes under a NOT VALID check that units_per_pack >= 1, of which 240 hold zero. VALIDATE CONSTRAINT takes a share update exclusive lock and no table rewrite, and it will fail on the 240 rows, which is the point. The constraint is in the dump and looks enforced, so nothing has ever asked whether it is.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.pack_sizes WHERE units_per_pack = 0 AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'catalog.pack_sizes'::regclass AND contype = 'c' AND NOT convalidated)

defects.title: 3,000 handover durations differ by an hour depending on who asks
defects.why: The handover row holds the time the driver arrived and the time the customer signed. One is a timestamptz and the other is a plain timestamp. The arrival is written by the vehicle tracker, which sends an instant, and the signature is written by the handheld, which sends a wall clock reading with no zone on it. Subtracting one from the other makes Postgres read the plain timestamp as being in the session's time zone, which is UTC on the reporting connection and London on the application's. The same two rows give a handover duration that differs by an hour depending on who asks, for half the year. Measured: 3,000 handover rows, of which 3,000 fall in British Summer Time, and every one gives a duration an hour longer when the signature is read as UTC than when it is read as London time. One type for both, timestamptz, with the handheld's zone applied where the reading is taken. Both columns hold plausible times and the difference between them is plausible too, which is why the discrepancy is argued about rather than investigated.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.handover_times WHERE (signed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') <> (signed_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London')

defects.title: 480 escalations hold one level in the enum and a different one in the text beside it
defects.why: Escalation levels were an enumerated list of four. A fifth was needed, adding to the enum was a schema change nobody wanted during peak, and a free text column was added beside it to hold the ones that did not fit. So the level of an escalation is in one of two columns, and which one depends on when it was raised and how far it went. The enum column is not null, so an escalation at the fifth level holds the fourth in the enum and the real level in the text, and it reads as a level four escalation to everything that does not know about the second column. The queue that the directors watch is filtered on the enum. Measured: 3,200 escalations, of which 480 hold an override level in the free text column that contradicts the enum column on the same row. One column, with the fifth value added to it, and the schema change taken. Both columns are populated and both are readable, so the contradiction is only visible to somebody who selects them together, which no screen does.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.escalation_levels WHERE level_override IS NOT NULL AND level_override <> level::text

defects.title: 1,000 euro invoices sit in a sterling total with no currency column to tell them apart
defects.why: Overseas invoices are raised in sterling and in euro. The amount column holds both and there is no currency column. The currency was going to be added when the second market opened and the invoice numbering was changed instead, so a euro invoice can be told from a sterling one by the prefix on its reference and by nothing else. Every sum over this column adds sterling to euro. The totals are wrong by the exchange rate on the euro share, they have always been wrong, and they move with the rate in a way that looks like trading performance. Measured: 4,000 overseas invoices, of which 1,000 are in euro, identifiable only by the EU prefix on the invoice reference, in a table with no currency column. A currency column, NOT NULL, with a constraint on the values it may hold, and the totals grouped by it. The reference prefix works and is used by the three people who know about it, which is why this has never been raised as a data problem rather than a reporting one.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.overseas_invoices WHERE invoice_ref LIKE 'EU-%' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = 'payments' AND table_name = 'overseas_invoices' AND column_name IN ('currency', 'currency_code', 'ccy'))

defects.title: The partial index covers the 19,200 cleared exceptions and skips the 800 anybody reads
defects.why: The exception queue has a partial index WHERE cleared_at IS NOT NULL. Every query against the queue asks for the exceptions that are not cleared. The index was written the wrong way round. It covers the cleared exceptions, which is the large and growing part of the table and the part nobody reads, and it excludes the open ones, which is the small part every screen in the warehouse polls every thirty seconds. Those polls read the whole table. The index is maintained on every clear and used by nothing. Measured: 20,000 exceptions, 19,200 of them cleared and covered by the partial index, and 800 open and excluded from it. WHERE cleared_at IS NULL is the index, and it would be eight hundred rows rather than nineteen thousand. There is an index on the column in the catalogue, so the table reads as indexed to anybody checking a list.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.exception_queue WHERE cleared_at IS NULL) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'ops.exception_queue'::regclass AND indpred IS NOT NULL)

defects.title: 1,000 search keys describe the description the item used to have
defects.why: The item search key was a generated column, derived from the description. A restore from a logical dump brought it back as a plain column holding the values it had at the time. A generated column is restored as a plain column when the dump is taken with the option that writes data for every column, which is what the restore script used. It looked identical afterwards: same name, same type, same values. It stopped updating. Every description edited since has a search key describing the old description, and there is nothing in the schema to say that column was ever supposed to maintain itself. Measured: 5,000 item search keys, of which 1,000 no longer match the description they are derived from, and the column is not generated. Recreating it as a generated column recomputes every row and puts the derivation back in the schema where it can be read. The search still finds most things, because most descriptions have not been edited, so it is a search that quietly fails on the newest products.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.item_search_keys k WHERE k.search_key <> lower(k.description) AND (SELECT attgenerated FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'catalog.item_search_keys'::regclass AND attname = 'search_key') = ''

defects.title: 180 waves are logged as closed with lines that were never picked
defects.why: The wave close function wraps its body in an exception handler that catches everything and returns the success value anyway. The handler was added because a transient lock timeout was failing the overnight run and somebody wanted the run to finish. It catches the lock timeout and it catches everything else: a wave whose lines cannot be closed because they were never picked returns closed, and the caller records it as closed, and the lines stay open. The only trace is in the wave close log, which stores the reported outcome and not the real one. Measured: 900 waves logged as closed, of which 180 still have unpicked lines against them. Catching the lock timeout by name, and letting everything else out, is the fix and it is four characters different. The overnight run has not failed in two years, which is the evidence everybody cites for it working.

detect.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT l.wave_id) FROM fulfilment.wave_close_log AS l JOIN fulfilment.picking_wave_lines AS pl ON pl.wave_id = l.wave_id AND NOT pl.picked WHERE l.outcome = 'closed'

defects.title: All 7,200 regional sales rows are discarded by an inner join to an empty lookup
defects.why: The sales by region view inner joins the sales rows to a region lookup table. The lookup table is empty. It was created by the migration that introduced the view and was to be populated by a separate load that never ran, because the load was owned by the team that was reorganised that quarter. An inner join to an empty table returns nothing, so the view returns nothing, and the report that reads it shows a blank page rather than an error. A blank report reads as a quiet period, and it has read as one for four months. Measured: 7,200 regional sales rows, 0 rows in the region lookup, and 0 rows out of the view. Populating the lookup is the fix and a left join would at least have shown the sales with an unknown region. The view compiles, runs and returns cleanly every time, which is why nothing monitoring it has ever gone red.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.regional_sales) - (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.regional_sales AS s JOIN analytics.region_lookup AS l ON l.region_code = s.region_code)

defects.title: 4,800 rate agreements are unique on a pair no constraint mentions
defects.why: A supplier has one rate agreement per effective date. That is true of every row in the table and nothing in the schema says it. The table has a surrogate key on an identity column and no constraint on the pair that actually identifies a row. The loader enforces it, in the sense that the loader has never written a duplicate, and the loader is a Python script that has been rewritten twice. Every query that picks the rate in force for a date assumes one row comes back, and the ones that use a subquery will fail loudly if two ever do, while the ones that use a join will quietly double the line. Measured: 4,800 rate agreements over 400 suppliers and 12 effective dates each, with 4,800 distinct (supplier, effective from) pairs and no unique constraint over those two columns. A unique constraint on the pair would be accepted by the data as it stands today. It has not been added because nobody is certain it holds historically, which is a question the data answers in one query.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT supplier_ref, effective_from FROM supply.rate_agreements) AS s) * (1 - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'supply.rate_agreements'::regclass AND indisunique AND indnatts = 2))

defects.title: 1,500 invoice holds store a total the row beneath it contradicts
defects.why: Two before-insert triggers on the invoice holds table. The first works out how much is being held. The second clears the released amount. They fire in name order and the second one invalidates the first one's answer. The held total is the invoice amount less whatever has already been released. The release-clearing trigger was added later, by a different change, to stop a partial release being carried into a new hold. It is named trg_b_clear_released, the total trigger is named trg_a_set_hold_total, and Postgres fires triggers of the same timing in alphabetical order. So the total is computed against a released amount that is about to be zeroed, and the row it is stored on says the released amount is zero. Measured: 3,000 invoice holds, of which 1,500 store a held total that does not equal the amount less the released figure on the same row. One trigger doing both things in the order the business wants, or the total computed in the after-insert. Every individual number on the row is a number the system once believed, which is why reconciling them has been attempted twice and abandoned twice.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.invoice_holds WHERE hold_total_p <> amount_p - released_p

defects.title: 60 report definitions name a relation that no longer exists
defects.why: The report definitions table holds the name of the table each report reads from, as text. A quarter of those names are of tables that no longer exist. The name is text because the definitions are edited by the reporting team through a screen, and a text column can hold anything, including the name of something that has been dropped. Nothing validates it on write and nothing re-validates it when a table is dropped, because a text column carries no dependency. The report fails at run time with a relation does not exist error, which is caught by the scheduler and logged as a failed run, and a failed run of a report nobody has opened in two years is not looked at. Measured: 240 report definitions, of which 60 name a relation that does not exist in the database. A regclass column carries the dependency and refuses the drop, which is the whole point of the type. The definitions look complete and well maintained because the rows are all there and all populated.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.report_definitions WHERE to_regclass(source_table) IS NULL

defects.title: 300 bundles have no lead item because the third load step never reached them
defects.why: The bundle header points at its lead item and the bundle item points at its header. Each foreign key requires the other table to be populated first. The lead item is the one shown on the listing, so the header needs it, and an item belongs to exactly one bundle, so the item needs the header. Loading a bundle means inserting the header with a null lead item, inserting the items, then going back and setting the lead. The loader does the first two steps and the third is a separate job that fails silently on any bundle whose items were rejected. The headers that come out of that have no lead item, so the listing shows a bundle with no picture and no price. Measured: 600 bundles with 2,400 items between them, of which 300 headers have a null lead item despite having items in the bundle. Deferring one of the two constraints, or dropping the lead item column in favour of a flag on the item, breaks the cycle. Both foreign keys are correct in isolation, which is why each has survived every review of its own table.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.bundle_headers AS h WHERE h.lead_item_id IS NULL AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM catalog.bundle_items AS i WHERE i.bundle_id = h.bundle_id)

defects.title: One crafted case reference reassigned all 1,200 cases to one agent
defects.why: The case reassignment function runs as its owner and builds its UPDATE by gluing the caller's arguments into a string. It is SECURITY DEFINER for the right reason: reassigning a case writes to a table agents cannot write to directly. It builds the statement with EXECUTE and string concatenation because an earlier version needed a dynamic table name, which it no longer does. Nothing quotes the arguments. A case reference containing a quote closes the literal and the rest of it runs as SQL, with the owner's rights, which are the rights the function exists to lend. One call with a crafted reference reassigns every case in the table. Measured: 1,200 case assignments, of which 1,200 were reassigned to a single agent by one call whose case reference closed the quote. format with %L, or a plain parameterised UPDATE since the table name is fixed, removes it entirely. The function has a search path set and is granted to one role, so it passes every check that is run against definer functions.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.case_assignments WHERE agent_ref = 'AGT-99999'

defects.title: 956 list memberships are exact duplicates in a table with no key
defects.why: The marketing list membership table has no primary key and holds exact duplicate rows. Membership is a list and an account and a date, and the same three were loaded twice by an import that was re-run after a partial failure. With no key there was nothing to stop it and nothing to detect it afterwards. A person asking to be taken off a list is removed with a delete on the three columns, which removes both copies and looks correct. A person whose preferences are corrected with an update gets both copies updated, which also looks correct. What does not work is any count: the list is reported larger than it is, and the send rate against it is reported lower. Measured: 6,056 list membership rows with no primary key, of which 956 are exact duplicates of another row in the table. A primary key over the three columns, after the duplicates are removed with ctid, is the fix and the duplicates are safe to remove because they are identical. Every operation the marketing team performs on this table gives the right answer, so the table has never been suspected.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) - count(DISTINCT (list_code, account_ref, joined_on)) FROM marketing.list_members) * (1 - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'marketing.list_members'::regclass AND contype = 'p'))

defects.title: 4,800 stock corrections have no audit row and the trigger is still disabled
defects.why: The audit trigger on stock corrections was disabled to let a backfill run overnight and nobody enabled it again. The backfill rewrote two years of corrections and the trigger would have written an audit row for each one, which would have taken the run past the maintenance window. Disabling it was the right call. Enabling it was a line in a runbook that the person following the runbook had already closed. Every correction made since has no audit row, and the audit table is not empty, so nothing looking at it sees a gap: it sees a table with rows in it that stops partway through last year. Measured: 7,200 stock corrections, of which 2,400 have an audit row and 4,800 do not, with the trigger present and disabled. ENABLE TRIGGER is one statement and the missing audit rows can be reconstructed from the corrections themselves, which is the argument for leaving it. The trigger shows in every listing of triggers on the table, so a review that asks whether corrections are audited gets a yes.

detect.sql: SELECT ((SELECT count(*) FROM supply.stock_corrections) - (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.stock_correction_audit)) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'supply.stock_corrections'::regclass AND tgname = 'trg_audit_stock_correction' AND tgenabled = 'D')

defects.title: 3,000 saved card rows readable through a group with 6 roles nested inside it
defects.why: Select on the saved cards table was granted to a group role. Nobody keeps a list of who is in that group. The group was created to hold the depot staff who needed read access during a stock take, three years ago. Membership is managed by adding a role to it, which anybody with the right to create roles can do, and nothing has ever removed anybody. Two of its members are themselves group roles, so the effective list is longer than the direct membership suggests and reading the grant tells you nothing about who can use it. The table holds card tokens and expiry dates. Measured: 3,000 saved card rows, readable through one group grant whose membership is 4 roles directly and 6 roles once nested membership is followed. Granting to the two application roles that need it, and dropping the group, makes the access list the grant itself. The grant is to a named role rather than PUBLIC, so it passes every review that looks for public grants.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.saved_cards) * has_table_privilege('depot_staff', 'storefront.saved_cards', 'SELECT')::int

defects.title: 1,200 cached prices disagree with the price table the bulk load wrote
defects.why: The storefront reads prices from a cache table. One of the two things that change a price writes the cache and the other does not. The cache is refreshed by the pricing service whenever a price is changed through the pricing screen. Bulk price loads go straight into the price table, because the loader predates the cache and was never told about it. The cache is otherwise correct, so nothing about it looks stale, and the rows it is wrong on are exactly the rows a bulk load touched, which are the seasonal ranges and the clearance lines. Measured: 6,000 prices with 6,000 cache rows, of which 1,200 hold a price the price table no longer agrees with. One write path, or a trigger on the price table, or dropping the cache and reading the prices. The cache has a row for every product and a recent timestamp on every row, so every check of its completeness and freshness passes.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.price_cache AS c JOIN catalog.current_prices AS p ON p.sku = c.sku WHERE c.price_p <> p.price_p

defects.title: 48,000 single-row upserts against a 40-row table for one nightly load
defects.why: The generator readings table has a per-row trigger on it and it is loaded forty eight thousand rows at a time. The trigger keeps a per-depot latest reading table up to date, which is the right thing to keep and the wrong place to keep it from. The readings arrive as a nightly file from the telemetry supplier and go in as one COPY. The trigger runs once per row, so the load does forty eight thousand single-row upserts against a forty-row table, every one of them contending on the same forty pages. The load takes hours and the only thing that has changed about it in two years is that it starts earlier. Measured: 48,000 generator readings and 48,000 trigger firings recorded against a latest-reading table of 40 rows. A statement-level trigger over the transition table does the same work once. The latest reading table is correct after every load, so the trigger is doing its job, which is why the cost of it has never been the thing anybody looked at.

detect.sql: SELECT sum(write_count) FROM ops.generator_latest

defects.title: The reporting role reads 2,400 drop notes and none of their 9,600 lines
defects.why: The reporting role can read drop notes and cannot read the lines on them. The grant was written when the notes table was the whole thing. The lines table came later, in a migration that added the table and forgot the grant, which is easy because nothing ties one to the other. A report that joins the two fails with a permission denied on the lines table, and the report that only reads the header works, so the role appears to have access. The team that owns the reports works around it by reading the header and counting the lines from a different table that happens to hold a line count. Measured: 2,400 drop notes and 9,600 lines, where report_reader holds select on the notes and not on the lines. One GRANT, and default privileges on the schema so the next table does not repeat it. The header is readable, so every check of the form can this role see drop notes returns true.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.drop_note_lines) * has_table_privilege('report_reader', 'fulfilment.drop_notes', 'SELECT')::int * (1 - has_table_privilege('report_reader', 'fulfilment.drop_note_lines', 'SELECT')::int)

defects.title: All 400 accounts have category shares that add to less than 100
defects.why: The share of spend per category is stored as a whole number of percent. The shares for an account are supposed to add to a hundred and they do not. The column is an integer because the first report rounded to whole percent and the column was made to fit the report. Each share is computed and truncated on its own, so an account whose spend splits three ways loses one percent, and an account that splits seven ways loses up to six. The total row is computed separately from the real amounts, so it says a hundred, and the category rows beneath it do not add to it. Measured: 2,800 share rows over 400 accounts, of which all 400 accounts have category shares adding to less than 100. Storing the amount and computing the share at read time, or a numeric with two decimal places, removes it. Every individual share is within one percent of the truth, which is why this reads as rounding rather than as a column that cannot hold the answer.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT account_ref FROM analytics.share_of_spend GROUP BY account_ref HAVING sum(share_pct) < 100) AS s

defects.title: 540 vehicle defects join to two vehicles because the fleet number was reused
defects.why: Vehicle defects are joined to the vehicle register on the fleet number. The register's key is the registration plate. The fleet number is the number painted on the side of the cab and it is what the driver writes on a defect card, so the defect table holds it. The register is keyed on the plate, because a plate is unique and a fleet number is reused when a vehicle leaves the fleet and a new one takes its slot. There is no foreign key, because there cannot be one. The join works for current vehicles and returns two rows for a fleet number that has been reused, and the defect history of a vehicle that left the fleet three years ago is attached to the one parked in its space. Measured: 3,600 vehicle defects against 500 register entries, where 60 fleet numbers appear twice in the register and 540 defects join to two vehicles. The defect wants the plate on it, captured once when the card is raised. The join returns a vehicle for every defect, so nothing about it looks broken, and the duplicates are in the tail of the history where nobody checks.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.vehicle_defects AS d WHERE (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.vehicle_register AS r WHERE r.fleet_no = d.fleet_no) > 1) * (1 - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'ops.vehicle_defects'::regclass AND contype = 'f'))

defects.title: 2,799 callout request numbers will collide before the sequence is clear
defects.why: The callout request sequence was reset to one during an environment refresh and the table it feeds was not emptied. The refresh script truncates the tables it knows about and resets every sequence in the schema. The callout requests table was added after the script was written, so it was not truncated, and its sequence was reset anyway. The reference column has a unique index, so the collisions are not silent: the insert fails, the application retries, and the retry fails too, until the sequence climbs past the highest reference already in the table. Every request raised during that climb is lost, and the loss looks like a transient database error in the log. Measured: 4,000 callout requests with references up to 4,000, against a sequence sitting at 1,201, leaving 2,799 values that will collide before it is clear. setval past the maximum is one statement, and the refresh script needs the table in its truncate list. The table is intact and every row in it is correct, so nothing that inspects the data finds anything wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT max(request_no) FROM support.callout_requests) - (SELECT last_value FROM support.callout_request_seq)

defects.title: 40 freight carriers are in the table twice under two names and one company number
defects.why: Several freight carriers are in the table twice, once with the trading name and once with the registered company name. Carriers are added by whoever books the first consignment with them, from whatever is on the quote. A quote from the sales office carries the trading name and a quote from the finance team carries the registered name, and the two are different strings for the same company. There is a unique index on the name, which is why nobody noticed: it is doing its job, and its job is not the one anybody thought. Spend is split across the two rows, so neither reaches the threshold at which a carrier is reviewed. Measured: 320 freight carriers holding 280 distinct companies, with 40 companies present twice under two names sharing one company number. The company number is the key and it is already on the row. Deduplicating means deciding which of the two rows the history moves to, which is a decision with an owner nobody has appointed.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT company_number FROM supply.freight_carriers GROUP BY company_number HAVING count(*) > 1) AS s

defects.title: 51,999 container references left before a varchar(6) stops accepting them
defects.why: Container references are six characters. The sequence behind them is at 948,000 and the volume is 3,000 a week. Six characters was three times what was needed when the format was agreed, and the format is in the customs paperwork, the carrier's system and two printed label templates. The column will not take a seventh character and the sequence will pass a million in about four months, at which point the insert fails with a value too long for type character varying, in the middle of a goods-in run, on the loading bay. Measured: 8,000 container references against a varchar(6) column, with the sequence at 948,000 and 51,999 values left before the format breaks. Widening the column is one statement and a lock; changing the format is a conversation with three external parties. Nothing is wrong today and the table will keep working until the week it does not.

detect.sql: SELECT (999999 - (SELECT last_value FROM supply.container_ref_seq)) * (SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = 'supply' AND table_name = 'container_refs' AND column_name = 'container_ref' AND character_maximum_length = 6)

defects.title: 7,200 null discounts cover three different things the column cannot tell apart
defects.why: A null discount on an order means no discount was offered, or one was offered and declined, or the discount engine was down. The column cannot tell them apart and neither can anybody else. The column started as the percentage taken off and nulls were the orders with no discount. The declined case arrived with the loyalty scheme and was written as null because zero would have appeared in the average. The engine failure case arrived with the engine and was written as null because there was nothing else to write. The discount take-up rate is computed as the share of orders with a non-null discount, so every engine outage looks like a drop in customer interest. Measured: 12,000 orders with 7,200 null discounts, made up of 4,800 never offered, 1,800 declined and 600 raised while the engine was unavailable. A status column beside the amount, with the three cases named, makes the question answerable and the historic rows a one-off decision. Every non-null discount is correct, so the column has never been suspected of anything.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.order_discounts WHERE discount_pct IS NULL

defects.title: 7,200 settlement advice lines sit under a cascading delete
defects.why: Deleting a settlement advice deletes the lines under it, and the lines are the record of what was paid. ON DELETE CASCADE was put on the constraint so that a mistyped advice could be removed cleanly during entry, which it does. It also means a correction to an advice from two years ago, done by deleting and re-entering it, removes the lines that the ledger reconciles against. The re-entered advice has new line identifiers, so the reconciliation that matched on them fails for that advice and is written off as a historic mismatch. Measured: 1,800 settlement advices with 7,200 lines under a cascading constraint, where deleting one advice removes 4 lines and leaves nothing behind that says it happened. ON DELETE RESTRICT, and a void flag for the entry mistake. The cascade is exactly what somebody asked for, which is why it has survived every review of the constraint.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.settlement_advice_lines AS l WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint AS c WHERE c.conrelid = 'payments.settlement_advice_lines'::regclass AND c.contype = 'f' AND c.confdeltype = 'c')

defects.title: 304 gate slots are booked twice in a table with no key on the three columns
defects.why: A gate booking is one depot, one gate and one slot. Those three columns identify a booking and there is no constraint on them, so the same slot has been booked twice. The booking screen checks for a clash before it writes, which is why this is rare rather than constant. Two users booking the same slot within the same second both pass the check and both write. The double booking surfaces on the morning of the slot, when two vehicles arrive for the same gate, and it is resolved on the yard by whoever is standing there. Nothing goes back into the table, so the same two rows are still there. Measured: 6,064 gate bookings over 5,760 distinct depot, gate and slot combinations, of which 304 combinations are booked twice, with no unique constraint on the three columns. A unique constraint on the three columns turns the race into a failed insert the screen can retry. Adding it needs the 304 duplicate slots resolved first, and resolving them means telling somebody their booking is gone.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT depot_code, gate_no, slot_start FROM ops.gate_bookings GROUP BY 1, 2, 3 HAVING count(*) > 1) AS s) * (1 - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'ops.gate_bookings'::regclass AND indisunique AND indnatts = 3))

defects.title: 960 billing lines are transfers, told apart by a prefix nothing documents
defects.why: A cost centre beginning with T is a transfer and must be left out of the depot's charge. That rule lives in one query and in one person's head. The prefix was chosen when transfers were added because it did not need a schema change, and it has worked for six years. It is not a constraint, not a comment, not a lookup table and not documented anywhere a new analyst would find it. Every report written since by somebody who did not know it charges the depots for moving their own stock between themselves, and the numbers are plausible, so the reports have been signed off. Measured: 4,800 billing lines, of which 960 have a cost centre beginning with T, on a column carrying no comment and no constraint that mentions the rule. A boolean column, or a cost centre type table, puts the rule in the schema where it can be read. The convention is reliable, which is exactly what makes it dangerous: it has never failed, so nobody has ever had to learn it.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.depot_billing WHERE cost_centre LIKE 'T%') * (CASE WHEN (SELECT col_description('ops.depot_billing'::regclass, attnum) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'ops.depot_billing'::regclass AND attname = 'cost_centre') IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 600 SLA breaches exist in the audit and were never stored
defects.why: Two before-insert triggers on the SLA breach table. The audit trigger fires first and the validation trigger, which drops invalid rows, fires second. Auditing before validating means the audit records attempts and the table records breaches, and the two were always going to differ. Nobody intended that: the audit trigger was named trg_a_write_audit so that it would be the first thing anybody saw in a listing, and that is also the order Postgres fires them in. The validation trigger returns null for a breach whose resolved time is before its raised time, so those rows never land, and the audit already has them. Measured: 3,000 attempted SLA breaches, of which 2,400 were stored and 600 were dropped by validation, against 3,000 audit rows. Validating in a before trigger and auditing in an after trigger puts them in the right order. Both tables are internally consistent, so the difference is only visible when the two are counted against each other, which happens in no report.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM support.sla_breach_audit) - (SELECT count(*) FROM support.sla_breaches)

defects.title: 880 depot months drop out of the headcount view because the agency feed stopped
defects.why: The depot headcount view adds the agency headcount to the permanent one. The agency feed stopped eighteen months ago and the column has been null ever since. The agency supplied a nightly file of who was on site. The contract ended, the file stopped, and the column was left in place because removing it meant changing the view and the view belongs to another team. Permanent plus agency is null on every row since the feed stopped, and sum skips nulls, so those rows are dropped from the total entirely. The view returns a number, it is not flagged, and it covers eight months out of thirty. Measured: 1,200 depot months over 40 depots, of which 880 have a null agency headcount and are silently left out of every depot's total. coalesce in the view is the one-line version and dropping the column is the honest one. The view returns a plausible number for every depot and the permanent headcount is correct and present on every row, which is why the source table passes every completeness check run against it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.depot_staff_counts WHERE agency_headcount IS NULL

defects.title: 1,200,000 rows scanned to write 200 reorder points
defects.why: The reorder point rebuild loops over the lines and reads the whole demand history once per line. The history has no index on the line, so each read is a full scan, and there are two hundred lines. The rebuild therefore scans one point two million rows to produce two hundred numbers. It was written when there were twelve lines and a thousand rows of history, where it was fine, and it has been scaled by adding lines rather than by changing the shape of the query. Measured: one rebuild run scanning 1,200,000 rows of demand history to write 200 reorder points, recorded by the function as it goes. One grouped query over the history writes all two hundred in a single scan. The rebuild runs weekly at two in the morning and finishes, so its cost has never appeared on anything anybody watches.

detect.sql: SELECT rows_scanned FROM supply.reorder_rebuild_log ORDER BY run_id DESC LIMIT 1

defects.title: 3,600 consent events all happened at the same instant in November 2025
defects.why: The consent events table was backfilled from an older system and every backfilled row carries the date the backfill ran. The source had the consent date in it. The backfill script wrote now() into the recorded_at column, because that is what the column default was and the script inserted without naming it. So two fifths of the consent history happened, as far as this table is concerned, on one afternoon in November 2025. Any question about when consent was given, which is the question the regulator asks, is answered wrongly for those rows, and the answer is confidently wrong rather than null. Measured: 9,000 consent events, of which 3,600 carry the identical timestamp the backfill ran at. The source file still exists and the dates can be restored from it, which is a day of work nobody has been given. The rows are present, complete and correctly ordered relative to each other, so every check of the backfill passed.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.consent_events WHERE recorded_at = TIMESTAMPTZ '2025-11-12 16:41:09.226471+00'

defects.title: Row security on 2,400 card disputes compares a column to a session setting nothing sets
defects.why: Row security is enabled on the card disputes table and the one policy compares the account reference to a session setting that nothing sets. The setting was to be set by the connection pool on checkout, from the signed in user. That pool change was scoped, estimated and never scheduled. The policy uses the two-argument form of current_setting, which returns null rather than raising when the setting is missing, and a comparison to null is not true, so the policy matches no row at all. Every non-owner role sees an empty table. The application connects as the owner, which bypasses row security entirely, so the application sees everything and nobody has noticed that the protection is not protection: the table is either fully visible or fully invisible depending on who you are. Measured: 2,400 card disputes under row security with one policy whose setting has no default at database or role level, so it evaluates to null for every session. Setting the variable on checkout makes the policy work; until then the policy is decoration. Row security shows as enabled with a policy attached, which is what every security review checks for.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.card_disputes) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_policy p JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = p.polrelid WHERE c.oid = 'payments.card_disputes'::regclass AND c.relrowsecurity) * (CASE WHEN current_setting('app.account_ref', true) IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 2,402 VAT lines hold two different VAT figures for the same net amount
defects.why: VAT is computed on the line by the storefront and on the invoice total by the finance system, and the two round in different places. The storefront rounds each line to the penny and adds them up. Finance adds the net lines, applies the rate once and rounds at the end. Both are defensible and one of them has to be the one on the invoice. The table holds both numbers on the same row, because a reconciliation project put them there to measure the gap and then ended. The gap is a penny or two per invoice and it is real money that neither system will admit to. Measured: 6,000 VAT lines, of which 2,402 hold a line VAT figure that does not match the invoice VAT figure apportioned back to the line. The fix is one of the two rounding rules, written down, with the other system reading the first one's number. Both columns are correct by their own rule, so every test of either system passes.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.vat_lines WHERE line_vat_p <> invoice_vat_p

defects.title: 30,000 chat transcripts are indexed on the timestamp and not on the case reference they are filtered by
defects.why: The chat transcript table is filtered by case reference and sorted by time, and the index is on the time. It was added after a complaint that the transcript screen was slow, and it was added on the column in the ORDER BY because that is the column somebody read off the slow query. Sorting was never the cost. The filter is on the case reference, which has no index, so every transcript load scans the whole table, and the index on the timestamp is maintained on every insert and used by nothing that matters. Measured: 30,000 chat transcript rows over 6,000 cases, with an index on the timestamp and none on the case reference. An index on (case_ref, said_at) serves the filter and the sort together. The screen did get faster after the index was added, because the table was small then, which is the evidence that closed the ticket.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM support.chat_transcripts) * (1 - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = i.indrelid AND a.attnum = i.indkey[0] WHERE i.indrelid = 'support.chat_transcripts'::regclass AND a.attname = 'case_ref'))

defects.title: Basket events carries two identical single-column indexes under two names
defects.why: There are two indexes on the basket events table over the same column in the same order, and one of them is never chosen. The first was added with the table. The second was added two years later by a migration written against a schema dump that predated the first, by somebody who checked whether the column was indexed by reading the migration history rather than the database. Postgres will happily build both. Every insert into the table maintains two identical B-trees, the planner picks one, and the other costs write throughput, disk and vacuum time for nothing. Measured: 24,000 basket events carrying 2 single-column indexes over the same column, one of which is redundant. Dropping one is a single statement with no risk, once somebody establishes that they really are the same, which needs the index definitions compared rather than the names. Both have plausible names, so a list of indexes on the table reads as two sensible entries.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'storefront.basket_events'::regclass AND indnatts = 1 AND NOT indisprimary

defects.title: The unique visitors view reports 12,000 sessions as if they were 3,000 visitors
defects.why: The unique visitors figure counts distinct sessions, and a session is not a visitor. The visitor identifier is on the row, in the visitor_ref column, and the view counts session_ref instead. A visitor who comes back the next day is two sessions and one visitor, and the figure the board sees is the first. It has been called unique visitors since it was built, it goes up when people come back more often, and coming back more often is what the marketing team is measured on, so the number moves in the direction that confirms the work. Measured: 36,000 site visits from 3,000 visitors over 12,000 sessions, where the view reports 12,000 unique visitors. count(DISTINCT visitor_ref) is the change and it will cut the headline number by three quarters, which is the real reason it has not been made. Every other figure in the same view is correct.

detect.sql: SELECT unique_visitors FROM analytics.v_unique_visitors

defects.title: 540 supplier lead times say seven days because the not null migration filled them in
defects.why: The supplier lead time column was made not null with a default of seven days, and the rows that had no lead time now say seven. Making a column not null needs the existing nulls dealt with, and the migration dealt with them by filling in the default. Seven days was chosen because it was the median. It is now indistinguishable from a real lead time of seven days, and the planning system treats it as measured rather than assumed. The suppliers whose lead time was never recorded are the small ones and the new ones, which are the ones where the true figure is most often longer than seven days. Measured: 1,800 supplier lead times, of which 540 are exactly 7 and were written by the migration rather than measured, against a column that is now not null with a default of 7. A nullable column, or a flag saying the figure is assumed, keeps the two apart. Every row has a plausible number in it and the column is not null, which is what the data quality check was asking for.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.supplier_lead_times WHERE lead_days = 7

defects.title: 60 assemblies contain a part that contains a part that contains the assembly
defects.why: Sixty assemblies contain a part that contains a part that contains the original assembly, so anything that walks the bill of materials down never reaches the bottom. The explosion table is a plain parent and child pair with a quantity, and nothing forbids a cycle because nothing can: a constraint that rejects one has to walk the whole graph on every insert. The cycles were created by engineering changes that swapped a sub-assembly for a kit containing the thing it replaced, and each change was correct on its own. The costing run recurses to a depth of eight and stops, so it returns a number rather than hanging, and the number counts the cycle parts eight times over. Measured: 2,000 parts and 6,000 explosion rows, of which 180 form 60 closed three-part loops. The fix is a cycle check when a change is posted, plus a decision about which of the sixty edges to cut, which needs an engineer for each one. The costing run completes and the totals look high rather than wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.part_explosions a JOIN supply.part_explosions b ON b.parent_part_id = a.child_part_id JOIN supply.part_explosions c ON c.parent_part_id = b.child_part_id WHERE c.child_part_id = a.parent_part_id

defects.title: A definer function hands remittance_reader the api_secret its column grants withhold
defects.why: The merchant account table grants column by column and holds the API secret back, and the function beside it returns the whole row. Column level grants were added when the reporting role was given access to merchant settlement, and they were added carefully: merchant reference, display name and settled amount, and not the secret. The summary function predates that work, is SECURITY DEFINER because it was written for a background job, and returns the table's composite type, so it returns every column the table has. Granting EXECUTE on it hands over the secret and the column grants say nothing about it, so the careful part of the permission model is bypassed by the part nobody revisited. Measured: 240 merchant accounts where remittance_reader holds SELECT on three columns and not on api_secret, and holds EXECUTE on a definer function returning all four. The function wants an explicit column list in its return type, or its own revoke. Every permission audit that reads table grants sees the secret protected, because on the table it is.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.merchant_accounts) * (CASE WHEN has_function_privilege('remittance_reader', 'payments.fn_account_summary(character varying)', 'EXECUTE') AND NOT has_column_privilege('remittance_reader', 'payments.merchant_accounts', 'api_secret', 'SELECT') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 2,400 outbox messages are in the table twice because the publisher retried
defects.why: The outbox table has no primary key and no unique index on the message key, and the publisher retries. The publisher writes the message, publishes it, then marks it sent. When the publish succeeds and the mark fails, the next run writes the message again, because the write comes first and there is nothing to collide with. The consumer is documented as idempotent, which is true of four of the six consumers; the other two send an email and adjust a balance. Measured: 14,400 outbox messages holding 12,000 distinct message keys, with 2,400 keys present twice and no primary key on the table. A unique index on the message key turns the second write into an error the publisher can ignore. Adding it now needs the 2,400 duplicates resolved first, and resolving one means deciding whether its consumer already acted.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT message_key FROM ops.outbox_messages GROUP BY message_key HAVING count(*) > 1) s) * (1 - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'ops.outbox_messages'::regclass AND contype = 'p'))

defects.title: 4,800 refund requests have no audit row because the trigger is in replica mode
defects.why: The refund audit trigger is set to fire only in replica mode, and nothing here runs in replica mode. A bulk correction was loaded with session_replication_role set to replica so that the triggers would stay out of the way, and the trigger was afterwards set with ENABLE REPLICA instead of ENABLE, which is one word away and reads as if it turns the trigger back on. It turns it on for exactly the mode nothing uses. The trigger is listed as enabled in every tool that shows a boolean, and psql marks it in a way that is easy to read past. Measured: 6,000 refund requests against 1,200 audit rows, leaving 4,800 refunds with no audit record, behind one trigger in replica mode. ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE TRIGGER is the whole fix. The missing 4,800 audit rows cannot be reconstructed, because the audit is the only place the approving user was ever written.

detect.sql: SELECT ((SELECT count(*) FROM payments.refund_requests) - (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.refund_request_audit)) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'payments.refund_requests'::regclass AND tgenabled = 'R')

defects.title: The fitting name index carries COLLATE "C" and the column and its queries do not
defects.why: The index on the fitting name was built with COLLATE "C", and the column is in the database collation and so is every query against it. The COLLATE "C" was copied from a tuning note about making a LIKE prefix search use an index, where it is the right advice, and applied to an index that serves equality and ordering instead. An index whose collation differs from the one a comparison uses cannot answer that comparison, so the planner ignores it. Nothing failed: the queries returned the same rows, more slowly, and the index has been maintained on every write since. Measured: 9,000 fitting names where the one index over the name column carries a collation the column does not. Rebuilding the index without the COLLATE clause is a concurrent build and a drop. The index exists, is valid, has a sensible name and appears in every list of indexes on the table, so the table reads as indexed.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.fitting_names) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = i.indrelid AND a.attnum = i.indkey[0] WHERE i.indrelid = 'catalog.fitting_names'::regclass AND a.attname = 'fitting_name' AND i.indcollation[0] <> a.attcollation)

defects.title: 300 section paths name node identifiers that are not in the node table
defects.why: Each section carries the path of node identifiers above it as a string, and some of those identifiers belong to nodes that were deleted. The path is written when a section is created and rewritten when it is moved, and deleting a node higher up is neither of those things. The delete removes the node and the rows that reference it by foreign key, and leaves every path string that merely names it, because a string is not a reference and the database has no way to know it was meant to be one. The breadcrumb on the catalogue page renders the identifiers it cannot resolve as an empty link. Measured: 1,200 section paths against 1,200 nodes, where 300 paths name at least one identifier that is not in the node table. The path wants rebuilding from the parent links, and the delete wants to rebuild the paths below it. Every path is well formed and parses cleanly, so the format check that runs nightly passes.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.section_paths p WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM unnest(string_to_array(trim(both '/' from p.path), '/')) AS t(id) WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM catalog.section_nodes n WHERE n.node_id = t.id::integer))

defects.title: 2,400 customers each have exactly one default address and no index says they must
defects.why: Every customer has exactly one delivery address marked as the default, and the database does not know that is a rule. The rule is enforced in the checkout service, in a transaction that clears the old default before setting the new one, and it has held for every customer since the column was added. It holds because one service owns the write path. The import that loads addresses from the trade portal is the second write path, it sets is_default from the file, and the file has a default flag on every row. Nothing has gone wrong yet because no trade customer has more than one address in the portal. Measured: 7,200 delivery addresses over 2,400 customers, every one of which has exactly one default, with no unique index expressing it. A unique index on customer_ref where is_default is the whole fix and it will apply cleanly today. Left alone, the first trade customer with two portal addresses gets two defaults and the checkout picks whichever the planner returns first.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT customer_ref FROM storefront.delivery_addresses WHERE is_default GROUP BY customer_ref HAVING count(*) = 1) s) * (1 - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'storefront.delivery_addresses'::regclass AND indisunique AND NOT indisprimary))

defects.title: 1,500 goods receipts hold a total the validating trigger passed and the next trigger changed
defects.why: One trigger checks that the receipt total is the quantity times the unit price, and a second trigger then changes the total, by which point the check has already run. Both are BEFORE INSERT triggers, so they fire in name order, and the validating one is named first by accident rather than by design. It sees the total the application sent, which is always correct, and passes. The discount trigger then takes five per cent off for bulk receipts and writes the new total, which no longer matches the columns beside it. The check was added precisely to stop the total drifting from the line, and the thing that makes it drift runs where the check cannot see it. Measured: 3,000 goods receipts of which 1,500 are bulk and hold a total that is not the quantity times the unit price, behind a validating trigger that passed every one of them. The check belongs in an AFTER trigger or a constraint, where it sees the row that is actually stored. Renaming the triggers to reverse the order makes the discount fail the check instead, which is the argument that has kept this open. Every insert succeeds, so nothing appears in any log.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.goods_receipts WHERE total_p <> qty * unit_p

defects.title: A volatile lookup function is called once for each of 24,000 range items
defects.why: The function that turns a range code into a label reads one table and returns one string, and it is declared volatile, so the planner has to call it for every row it returns. Volatile is the default when nothing is written, and nothing was written. The function is a lookup: the same code gives the same label all day. Marked stable, the planner may call it once per distinct value and may use it in an index condition. Marked volatile, it cannot cache anything, cannot push it down, and cannot reorder around it, so the report that renders twenty four thousand rows makes twenty four thousand calls, each of which is its own index lookup on a small table. Measured: 24,000 range items behind a view that calls a volatile lookup function once per row. The fix is one word in the function definition. Nobody has looked, because the function is correct, the report returns the right labels, and the cost lands as a report that takes nine seconds rather than as an error.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.range_items) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'catalog' AND p.proname = 'fn_range_label' AND p.provolatile = 'v')

defects.title: stock_reader holds UPDATE on the consignment number sequence, which is permission to call setval
defects.why: The stock reading role was granted every privilege on the consignment number sequence, and UPDATE on a sequence is the privilege that lets you call setval. The grant was written as ALL PRIVILEGES because the role needed currval to read back the number the job it watches had just allocated, and ALL was shorter than working out which of USAGE, SELECT and UPDATE that needs. It needs SELECT. UPDATE lets the role move the sequence anywhere, including backwards, at which point the next consignment number collides with one already issued and the goods leave the yard under a number that is already on a different lorry's paperwork. Measured: 9,000 consignments numbered from a sequence that stock_reader holds UPDATE on. GRANT SELECT ON SEQUENCE is what was wanted. The role has never called setval, so nothing in the audit or the data shows the privilege is there.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.consignments) * (CASE WHEN has_sequence_privilege('stock_reader', 'ops.consignment_no_seq', 'UPDATE') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 80 night shifts span seven or nine hours on the wall clock because eight hours was added to an instant
defects.why: A night shift is stored as a start instant and an end instant eight hours later, and on the two nights a year the clocks change, eight hours of elapsed time is seven or nine hours on the wall. The rota writes the start from the local 22:00 and computes the end by adding an interval of eight hours, which is eight hours of absolute time and is the right answer for pay. It is the wrong answer for the rota, which is read as a clock time: the October shift shows as ending at 05:00 and the March one at 07:00, and the depot manager reads those as a mistake and corrects the rota by hand. Adding eight hours to a local time and adding eight hours to an instant are different operations and this system needs both, in different places. Measured: 14,600 night shifts across 40 depots, of which 80 span a local clock difference that is not eight hours. The rota wants the local end time computed in the local zone, and pay wants the instants, which means storing both. Every row is correct as an instant, so every check that subtracts the timestamps passes.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.night_shifts WHERE (ended_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London') - (started_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London') <> INTERVAL '8 hours'

defects.title: counter_staff may update 4,800 shelf labels and may not read the rows it is updating
defects.why: The counter staff role may update the shelf label table and may not read it, and every update it writes has a WHERE clause. The grant was written to the letter of the request, which said the counter staff need to correct a shelf label and must not be able to list prices. An UPDATE with a WHERE clause reads the rows it is choosing between, so it needs SELECT on the columns in that clause, and without it the statement fails with a permission denied on the table the role was just granted. The till software catches the error, shows could not save, and the staff rewrite the label by hand on a sticker. Measured: 4,800 shelf labels where counter_staff holds UPDATE and does not hold SELECT. Column level SELECT on the key alone is enough and keeps the prices hidden. The grant reads correctly in every listing: the role has update on the table, which is exactly what the request asked for.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.shelf_labels) * (CASE WHEN has_table_privilege('counter_staff', 'catalog.shelf_labels', 'UPDATE') AND NOT has_table_privilege('counter_staff', 'catalog.shelf_labels', 'SELECT') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 9,600 transit legs are stored short because minutes were divided by sixty in integers
defects.why: The transit time is stored as a whole number of hours, computed by dividing minutes by sixty in integer arithmetic, so every part hour is thrown away. The column was added for a report that grouped legs into hour bands, where whole hours are the right unit, and the value was written by the same query that filled the bands. The carrier service level agreement is also written in whole hours, and it is measured against this column. A leg that took forty eight hours and fifty minutes is stored as forty eight and counts as inside a forty eight hour agreement, so the carrier is never charged for it. Every leg is short by up to fifty nine minutes and never long by any. Measured: 12,000 transit legs, of which 9,600 hold an hour count that does not match the interval between the two timestamps. The two timestamps are on the row and the interval between them is the real answer, so the column can be dropped and computed. Every stored value is within an hour of the truth, which is why comparing a handful of rows by hand has never found it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.transit_times WHERE arrived_at - left_at <> hours * INTERVAL '1 hour'

defects.title: 1,200 audience tags still hold the sentinel the backfill was meant to replace
defects.why: The audience tag backfill ran in batches ordered by a column the backfill itself was updating, so some rows moved out of the window before it reached them. The script selected the next ten thousand rows ordered by the tag column, updated them, and repeated until nothing came back. Each batch changed the value it was ordering on, so rows shifted position between batches, and the loop terminated when a batch returned nothing rather than when every row was done. It exited on the first gap. The rows that were missed still carry the sentinel the column was created with, and the segment builder treats the sentinel as a real audience, so those contacts are in every campaign that targets everybody and no campaign that targets anybody. Measured: 18,000 audience tags of which 1,200 still hold the UNSET sentinel the column was created with. Re-running the backfill over the sentinel rows alone is a single statement. The script reported success, because it did what it was written to do, and the count it logged was the number of rows it updated rather than the number it should have.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.audience_tags WHERE tag_value = 'UNSET'

defects.title: 2,400 cases carry a current status that is not the status of their latest history row
defects.why: Every case carries its current status in one table and its status history in another, and one transition writes the history and not the column. There are three ways a case changes status: an agent does it in the console, the escalation job does it on a timer, and the customer does it by replying to a closed case. The first two write both tables in one transaction. The third was added for the reply handler, which appends to the history and was never given the update to the current status table, because whoever wrote it read the history table and assumed the current status was a view over it. It is not. The console shows the status column and the audit export shows the history, so the two disagree in front of two different audiences. Measured: 9,000 cases with 27,000 history rows, of which 2,400 carry a current status that is not the status of their latest history row. The current status wants to be derived, or the reply handler wants the second write. Both tables are internally consistent and each one is right about the thing it records, so neither has ever failed a check of its own.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.case_current_status c JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT ON (case_ref) case_ref, status FROM support.case_status_history ORDER BY case_ref, changed_at DESC) h ON h.case_ref = c.case_ref WHERE c.status <> h.status

defects.title: 1,800 deleted asset transfers left no audit row because the trigger omits DELETE
defects.why: The asset transfer audit trigger fires on insert and on update, and deleting a transfer leaves no trace at all. The trigger was written when transfers were append only, so INSERT OR UPDATE covered everything that could happen. Deletion arrived later, with a screen that lets a depot clerk remove a transfer raised in error, and the screen was tested against the table rather than against the audit. The audit is the record the insurer asks for when an asset cannot be found, and for a deleted transfer it shows the asset arriving somewhere and never shows it leaving, because the row that said it left is gone and nothing recorded its going. Measured: 9,000 audited transfers against 7,200 transfers still in the table, a gap of 1,800 deletions, behind one trigger that does not cover DELETE. Adding OR DELETE to the trigger and a row type to the audit is small. The audit table is complete for every operation it covers, so a check that reads the audit alone finds nothing missing.

detect.sql: SELECT ((SELECT count(*) FROM ops.asset_transfer_audit) - (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.asset_transfers)) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'ops.asset_transfers'::regclass AND NOT tgisinternal AND (tgtype & 8) = 0)

defects.title: 2,400 staff have a null badge number under a unique index that permits every one of them
defects.why: The badge number is unique and nullable, and two thousand four hundred staff have no badge number, about which the unique index has nothing to say. The uniqueness was declared because a badge number identifies one person. The column was left nullable because contractors and new starters do not have one on their first day. Postgres treats nulls as distinct in a unique index by default, so the constraint that was meant to say one person per badge says nothing at all about the two fifths of the table where the badge is missing. The door system looks a person up by badge number and finds one row or none, which is why the gap has never shown as a duplicate. Measured: 6,000 staff badge rows of which 2,400 hold a null badge number, under one unique index that permits every one of them. Either the column is NOT NULL with a placeholder scheme, or the identity lives somewhere else and the badge is an attribute. The index is valid and enforced, so every schema review has seen a unique constraint and moved on.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.staff_badges WHERE badge_no IS NULL) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'ops.staff_badges'::regclass AND indisunique AND NOT indisprimary)

defects.title: 8,000 tariff lines sit under a foreign key that discards the reference when the code is renamed
defects.why: The tariff line points at the tariff code with ON UPDATE SET NULL, so renaming a tariff code detaches every line that used it, in silence. The action was chosen because ON UPDATE CASCADE had rewritten nine hundred rows overnight once before and somebody wanted the opposite of that. SET NULL is not the opposite: it is the same write, with the reference thrown away instead of carried across. Tariff codes are renamed by the customs team about twice a year, when the commodity schedule changes. Each rename leaves the lines that used the old code pointing at nothing, and the export paperwork prints an empty tariff, which the freight forwarder fills in from memory. Measured: 8,000 tariff lines under a foreign key whose update action is SET NULL, against 400 tariff codes. The fix is a surrogate key on the tariff code so that a rename is not an update to the referenced column at all. No rename has happened since the constraint was written, so the action has never fired.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.tariff_lines) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'supply.tariff_lines'::regclass AND contype = 'f' AND confupdtype = 'n')

defects.title: The lookup code index is built under the default operator class, so the prefix search scans 15,000 rows
defects.why: The picking terminal searches by typing the first few characters of a code, the column is indexed, and the index cannot answer that search. A B-tree on a text column is built under the database collation, and the comparisons that collation defines are not the byte-order comparisons a prefix match needs. Postgres will only use an index for LIKE 'ABC%' when the index is built with text_pattern_ops, and this one is not. So the terminal scans fifteen thousand rows for every keystroke after the third, and the index sits beside it being maintained and never chosen. The column was indexed because somebody asked whether it was indexed, and the answer was yes. Measured: 15,000 product lookup codes behind one non-primary index on the code, built under the default operator class rather than text_pattern_ops. A second index with text_pattern_ops serves the prefix search and the first one still serves equality. The search returns the right products, the terminal is merely slow, and slow on a handheld reads as the wireless.
