detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.product_lookup_codes) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_opclass o ON o.oid = i.indclass[0] WHERE i.indrelid = 'catalog.product_lookup_codes'::regclass AND NOT i.indisprimary AND o.opcname = 'text_ops')

defects.title: 720 of 18,000 drop references in the manifest string match no drop point
defects.why: The drops on a round are held as a comma separated list of references in one column on the round, so nothing can join to them and nothing checks them. The manifest was built to be printed, and a printed manifest is a line of text, so a line of text is what was stored. Reporting then needed the drops individually and got them by splitting the string, which works until a reference is mistyped, at which point the split produces a value that looks like a drop reference and matches no drop. There is no foreign key because a foreign key cannot be declared on a substring, and there is no constraint because whatever the loader writes is by definition well formed text. Measured: 3,600 round manifests naming 18,000 drop references, of which 720 match no row in the drop point table. The list wants to be a table with one row per drop and a foreign key. The manifest still prints correctly, because printing is concatenation and the bad references print exactly as well as the good ones.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.round_manifests m CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(string_to_array(m.drop_refs, ',')) AS t(ref) WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fulfilment.drop_points d WHERE d.drop_ref = t.ref)

defects.title: 60 of 240 scheduled jobs name a function that is not in the catalogue
defects.why: The scheduler reads the job table and calls what it finds there by name, and sixty of the two hundred and forty rows name a function that was dropped. Jobs are added to the table by whoever writes the function and removed from it by nobody. Dropping the function is a migration; deleting the row is a data change in a table no migration touches, and the two were never done together. The scheduler builds the call with EXECUTE, so a missing function is a runtime error rather than something the database could have refused when the job was written. The error is caught by the scheduler's retry loop, which retries it every fifteen minutes for ever. Measured: 240 job definitions of which 60 name a function that does not exist in the catalogue. The names want resolving to regprocedure at write time, or the table wants to hold nothing but jobs the scheduler has proved it can call. Every row is well formed and the enabled flag is true, so the table reads as a list of two hundred and forty working jobs.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.job_definitions WHERE to_regprocedure(routine_name) IS NULL

defects.title: The largest ledger balance is 2,060,000,000 pence against an integer ceiling of 2,147,483,647
defects.why: The running ledger balance is held in pence in a four byte integer, the largest balance is two thousand and sixty million, and the ceiling is two thousand one hundred and forty seven million. Pence in an integer is a sound choice up to about twenty one million pounds, which was comfortable when the ledger held one trading company. It now holds the group, the balance is cumulative and never resets, and it has grown by about a hundred and forty million pence a year for the last three years. The overflow is not a wrong answer: it is an error at insert time, in the overnight ledger run, which stops the run and leaves the day half posted. Measured: 1,200 ledger balances whose maximum is 2,060,000,000 pence against an integer ceiling of 2,147,483,647. The column wants to be bigint, which is a rewrite of a small table and an hour of downtime nobody has scheduled. Nothing is wrong today and every balance in the table is correct.

detect.sql: SELECT max(balance_p) FROM payments.ledger_running_totals

defects.title: 600 wholesale accounts name a merge target and are still active, so the customer appears twice
defects.why: Six hundred wholesale accounts were merged into another account, the merge wrote the target on the losing row and left it active, and nothing since reads that column. The merge was designed in two halves: mark the loser, then move its history and deactivate it. The second half was a separate job that was run once, on a sample, and then the project moved to another team. Every screen that lists accounts filters on the active flag, which is still true on all six hundred, so the same customer appears twice in the account picker with two credit limits, and which one a salesperson picks decides how much that customer can order. Measured: 4,800 wholesale accounts of which 600 name a merge target and are still marked active. Deactivating the marked rows is one statement, and it is one statement nobody will run without knowing which of the two accounts the open orders are on. Both rows are valid accounts with valid histories, so no integrity check has ever objected.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.wholesale_accounts WHERE merged_into IS NOT NULL AND is_active

defects.title: The market price table holds one region of the eight the extract is documented as loading
defects.why: The market price extract was written with a region filter so that it could be tested against one region, and the filter is still there. It was in the WHERE clause of the source query, hard coded to the north west because that was the smallest region and the test ran in a minute. It was never taken out, and the load has run nightly ever since, reporting the number of rows it loaded, which is a real number and is consistent night to night. The pricing team compares Cross River's prices against the market and the market it compares against is one region of eight. Where that region is cheap, the whole estate is repriced down. Measured: 1,800 market price rows covering 1 region of the 8 the extract is documented as loading. Removing the filter is a one line change and it will multiply the table by eight, which is why it needs a conversation about what happens to the comparisons already published. The table is complete and correct for the region it holds, so every check of its contents passes.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.market_prices) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(DISTINCT region_code) FROM analytics.market_prices) = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 9,000 newsletter signups are unique on the lowercased address under no unique index at all
defects.why: No two signups share an email address once case is ignored, and nothing in the schema says that. The signup form lowercases what it is given before it looks for an existing row, so the rule holds for every row the form has written, which is all of them. The rule lives in one JavaScript function and one Python handler and nowhere else. The unsubscribe link matches on the address exactly as typed, so an address that arrives capitalised through the import route would unsubscribe nothing and would also be a second signup, and both halves of that would look like the system working. Measured: 9,000 newsletter signups holding 9,000 distinct lowercased email addresses, with no unique index on the column or on any expression of it. A unique index on lower(email_address) applies cleanly today and moves the rule into the database. Every row is distinct as stored, so any check for duplicates that compares the column to itself finds none.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT lower(email_address) FROM marketing.newsletter_signups) s) * (1 - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'marketing.newsletter_signups'::regclass AND indisunique AND NOT indisprimary))

defects.title: 36,000 telemetry samples sit in a replicated table whose replica identity resolves to a key that does not exist
defects.why: The telemetry table has no primary key and its replica identity is the default, which means the primary key. There is not one, so an update or a delete on this table cannot be replicated at all. The table was built for inserts only, which is true of the hardware feed and was true of the table until the correction screen arrived. Logical replication carries inserts happily and raises an error on the first update, which stops the whole subscription rather than just this table. The downstream warehouse then stops receiving every table in the publication, and the first sign of it is a report that is a day stale, then two days, then a week. Measured: 36,000 telemetry samples in a table with no primary key and a replica identity of d, which resolves to a primary key that does not exist. A primary key on the identity column is the fix and it is one statement. REPLICA IDENTITY FULL is the other, and it makes every update carry the whole old row. Inserts replicate perfectly today, which is all anybody has tested.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.telemetry_samples) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c WHERE c.oid = 'ops.telemetry_samples'::regclass AND c.relreplident = 'd' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint k WHERE k.conrelid = c.oid AND k.contype = 'p'))

defects.title: 2,400 exported leads carry no score because the export trigger sorts before the scoring trigger
defects.why: Two after-insert triggers sit on the lead table. The first copies the lead to the export table and the second works out its score, so every exported lead is unscored. The export trigger was written first and named for what it does. The scoring trigger was added a year later, named for what it does, and the two names put them in the wrong order, because triggers at the same timing fire alphabetically and nobody chose that. The scoring trigger writes the score back onto the lead, so the lead table is right. The export table took its copy a moment earlier and holds a null where the score should be. The agency that reads the export treats a null score as cold and works the list from the bottom. Measured: 6,000 lead captures of which 2,400 carry a score, against 2,400 exported copies of those same leads that carry none. Renaming the triggers fixes it, or the export moves to a deferred constraint trigger that runs at the end of the statement. Both tables are populated, both look healthy, and the disagreement is only visible by joining them.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.lead_exports e JOIN marketing.lead_captures c ON c.lead_id = e.lead_id WHERE c.score IS NOT NULL AND e.score IS NULL

defects.title: 4,800 batch releases went unaudited behind a trigger that is enabled and does nothing
defects.why: The batch release audit trigger is enabled and fires on every insert, and its body returns without writing anything. During an incident the audit insert was deadlocking against the release itself, and the fastest way out was to replace the function body with a return and get the releases flowing again. That was the right call at two in the morning. The follow-up ticket to put the body back was closed as a duplicate of the incident, which was closed when the releases resumed. The trigger still exists, is still enabled, and still runs, which is what every check looks at. Measured: 6,000 batch releases against 1,200 audit rows, all of them written before the incident, behind a trigger that is enabled and does nothing. Putting the body back is a repeatable migration and the deadlock it caused needs the lock order fixed first. Nothing about the trigger's definition, timing or enabled state looks wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.batch_releases) - (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.batch_release_audit)

defects.title: 12,000 consignment labels draw from a sequence no tool can associate with the column
defects.why: The label number comes from a sequence that is not owned by the column it feeds, so anything that walks a table's sequences does not find it. The sequence was created by hand, before the table, and the default on the column names it by string. That is a working arrangement and the numbers come out right. It also means pg_get_serial_sequence returns null for the column, so the environment refresh, which resets every sequence it can find by walking the tables, walks straight past this one. Refreshed environments therefore carry a sequence from whenever it was last touched, against a table that has just been reloaded, and the first label printed collides. Measured: 12,000 consignment labels numbered from a sequence that pg_get_serial_sequence cannot associate with the column. ALTER SEQUENCE ... OWNED BY is one statement and changes nothing about the numbering. The sequence works, the default works, and every label printed so far is unique.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.consignment_labels) * (CASE WHEN pg_get_serial_sequence('fulfilment.consignment_labels', 'label_no') IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 47,600 of 48,000 item versions repeat the long copy of the version before them
defects.why: Editing one field on an item writes a complete new row carrying every field, and four hundred items have produced forty eight thousand rows. The table was designed to be append only so that any past state could be reconstructed, which it can. What it was not designed for is the merchandise team's workflow, which is to open an item, change one attribute, save, and repeat. Each save copies the description, the long copy, the dimensions and the care instructions unchanged into a new row. The table is now the largest in the schema by bytes and the current view of it is a window function over every version ever written, which is the query every product page runs. Measured: 48,000 item versions over 400 items, of which 47,600 carry a long copy character for character identical to the version before it. Storing the changed field alone, or a current table beside the history, turns the product page query into a primary key lookup. Every version is a true record of the item at that moment, so the table is correct and it is only its shape that is wrong.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT long_copy, lag(long_copy) OVER (PARTITION BY item_ref ORDER BY version_no) AS prev FROM catalog.item_versions) s WHERE s.prev = s.long_copy

defects.title: 200 price lists sit in fifty rings where four supersede steps return to the start
defects.why: Each price list names the list it supersedes, and two hundred of them are arranged in fifty rings of four, so the walk back to the original never reaches one. The rings came out of a reissue. A batch of lists was reissued under new numbers, and the script that wired up the supersedes column was run twice with the batch ordered differently each time, which pointed the oldest list in each group at the newest. The foreign key is satisfied, because every list named exists. The pricing tool walks the chain to find what a product used to cost and stops after twenty hops, which it calls a deep history, and returns whatever it was holding. Measured: 4,000 price lists of which 200 sit in a ring where four supersede steps return to the list they started from. A recursive check with a cycle clause finds them in a second and the rings want breaking by hand, because which of the four is the original is a pricing question. Every row passes its foreign key and the chain looks perfectly ordinary from any single list.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.price_list_chain a JOIN catalog.price_list_chain b ON b.list_id = a.supersedes_id JOIN catalog.price_list_chain c ON c.list_id = b.supersedes_id JOIN catalog.price_list_chain d ON d.list_id = c.supersedes_id WHERE d.supersedes_id = a.list_id

defects.title: 600 lowercase season codes satisfy a range check written to allow only capitals
defects.why: The season code is constrained to the range A to Z so that codes are always capitals, and six hundred lowercase codes are in the table satisfying that constraint. A range comparison on text is answered by the database collation, and in en_US.utf8 the letters interleave, so b through z all fall between A and Z. The constraint therefore rejects almost nothing. It was written by someone reasoning in ASCII, where the range would have held, and it was tested with codes that were already capitals. The season code is the join key to the buying system, which is case sensitive, so a lowercase code matches no season there and the product drops out of the buy. Measured: 3,000 season codes under one check constraint, of which 600 are not equal to their own uppercase form. The constraint wants to be code = upper(code), or a regular expression, both of which are collation independent. The constraint is declared, valid and enforced, so it appears on every schema report as a column that is constrained.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.season_codes WHERE code <> upper(code)) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'catalog.season_codes'::regclass AND contype = 'c')

defects.title: 2,400 price overrides sit behind a definer function whose EXECUTE is held by PUBLIC
defects.why: The price override function runs as its owner and its execute privilege is held by PUBLIC, so every role in the database can set the selling price of anything. The function was written so that the merchandising application could override a price without holding write access to the price tables, which is the right shape. The grant was the last line of the migration and it was written to PUBLIC because the migration ran before the application role existed and PUBLIC made it work that morning. The function records the caller in the override row, so the audit is honest, and it has never recorded a caller nobody expected, which is the only thing anybody checks. Measured: 2,400 price overrides behind one SECURITY DEFINER function whose access control list grants EXECUTE to PUBLIC. Revoking from PUBLIC and granting to the application role is two statements and nothing legitimate loses access. The function is owned correctly, sets its search path, and does exactly one well scoped thing.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.price_overrides) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_proc p WHERE p.oid = 'catalog.fn_apply_price_override(varchar,integer)'::regprocedure AND p.prosecdef AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM aclexplode(p.proacl) a WHERE a.grantee = 0 AND a.privilege_type = 'EXECUTE'))

defects.title: 1,200 promotions hold a whole-percent discount of zero against a real basis point rate
defects.why: The promotion rate arrives in basis points and is stored as a whole percentage, so twelve hundred promotions with a real rate are stored as no discount at all. Basis points were chosen upstream so that a rate could be finer than a percent, which is the whole reason the unit exists. The column here was declared as an integer percentage because every promotion at the time was a round five or ten percent, and the load divides by a hundred in integer arithmetic. A rate of eighty five basis points, which is a real promotion the pricing team ran, becomes zero. The basket applies it, takes nothing off, and the promotion reports a hundred percent redemption with no cost. Measured: 4,800 promotion discounts of which 1,200 hold a whole percent of zero against a basis point rate above zero. The stored percentage wants to be the basis points, or numeric, and the source column is already on the row so nothing needs re-importing. Every promotion is present, active and internally consistent, and a zero is a legitimate value for the column.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.promo_discounts WHERE discount_pct = 0 AND discount_bps > 0

defects.title: 1,500 historic refunds were multiplied into pence a second time
defects.why: Historic refunds were held in pounds and converted to pence, and the conversion was run twice over an overlapping range, so fifteen hundred refunds are a hundred times what they should be. The first run covered everything up to the end of the month. The second run was written to cover the same month again because the first was believed to have failed part way, and it had not: it had finished and reported nothing, because the log was going to a file nobody had opened. Multiplying by a hundred is not idempotent and nothing on the row records whether it has been converted. The refunds are historic and are read only by the annual return, which is where a fifteen thousand pound refund on a forty pound order will eventually be read out loud. Measured: 6,000 historic refunds of which 1,500 exceed a million pence against a genuine maximum of 6,499. Dividing the affected rows by a hundred is safe only because the genuine rows are two orders of magnitude away, which is luck rather than design. Every amount is a positive integer in the right column and no total has ever failed to balance, because the refunds balance against themselves.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.historic_refunds WHERE amount_p >= 1000000

defects.title: The buying role may select a margin view whose function it may not execute
defects.why: The buying role has SELECT on the margin band view, and the view calls a function the buying role may not execute, so every select fails. The function had its execute privilege revoked from PUBLIC during a tightening exercise, which was correct, and the grants that were meant to follow covered the roles that called the function directly. Nobody called this one directly. It is called from inside a view, and a view runs its body as whoever selects from it, so the privilege that matters belongs to the caller and not to the view's owner. The grant on the view is real, recorded and visible in every privilege report, which is why the access review passes and the buying team cannot open the report. Measured: 6,000 margin band rows behind a view the buying role may select and a function the buying role may not execute. One GRANT EXECUTE fixes it, or the view becomes security_invoker = false and runs as its owner. The table grant is correct, the view grant is correct, and the missing privilege is on an object no grant report lists beside them.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.margin_bands) * (CASE WHEN has_table_privilege('buyer_reader', 'analytics.v_margin_bands', 'SELECT') AND NOT has_function_privilege('buyer_reader', 'catalog.fn_margin_band(integer)', 'EXECUTE') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 1,800 cancelled pallet moves never fired an audit trigger that tests for capitals
defects.why: The audit trigger on pallet moves carries a WHEN clause testing the status against CANCELLED in capitals, and the application writes it in lower case, so the trigger has never fired. The WHEN clause was added to keep the audit table small, which was a reasonable thing to want, and the value in it was copied from the specification rather than from the code. The specification was written in capitals because the whole document is. Nothing failed: a trigger whose condition is false is a trigger that did its job and decided there was nothing to record. The cancellations are the only pallet moves anybody ever asks about, because a cancelled move is a pallet that is somewhere it is not recorded as being. Measured: 7,200 pallet moves of which 1,800 are cancelled, against an audit table holding none of them, behind one trigger with a WHEN condition. Comparing on upper(NEW.status) fixes it, and the audit for the moves already made cannot be reconstructed. The trigger is present, enabled, correctly owned and syntactically fine.

detect.sql: SELECT ((SELECT count(*) FROM ops.pallet_moves WHERE upper(status) = 'CANCELLED') - (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.pallet_move_audit)) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'ops.pallet_moves'::regclass AND NOT tgisinternal AND tgqual IS NOT NULL)

defects.title: 9,000 gate events sit in a partitioned table with no primary key, so nothing can upsert
defects.why: The gate event table is partitioned by month and has no primary key, because the key the application needs does not include the partition column. A primary key on a partitioned table must contain every partitioning column. The natural key here is the badge and the sequence number the gate controller emits, which says nothing about the month. Rather than widen the key, whoever partitioned the table dropped it, and nothing complained, because partitioning was done to make the archive job cheaper and the archive job does not care. The loader was written to upsert on that key. An upsert needs a unique index, so the loader now deletes by badge and sequence and inserts again, in two statements, with no lock between them. Measured: 9,000 gate events across three monthly partitions with no primary key on the partitioned table. Widening the key to include the event month makes the constraint legal and the upsert possible. Every partition is attached, every row routes correctly, and the archive job runs in seconds.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.gate_events) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c WHERE c.oid = 'ops.gate_events'::regclass AND c.relkind = 'p' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint k WHERE k.conrelid = c.oid AND k.contype = 'p'))

defects.title: The agency reporting role holds CREATE on the supply schema
defects.why: The agency reporting role holds CREATE on the supply schema and was meant to hold nothing but USAGE and SELECT. The grant was written as ALL PRIVILEGES ON SCHEMA supply, which on a schema is USAGE and CREATE and nothing else, so it reads as a small grant and is not one. CREATE on a schema is permission to add objects to it, and an object added to a schema that sits early on somebody's search path is consulted before the object it shadows. The agency connects from outside the estate over a pooled connection shared with the buying application, and the buying application's search path starts with supply. Measured: 3,600 buying notes in a schema where the agency reporting role holds CREATE. REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA supply FROM agency_reader is one statement and the role loses nothing it uses. The role has never created anything, every object in the schema is owned by the migration user, and the privilege report shows a grant that was requested and approved.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.buying_notes) * (CASE WHEN has_schema_privilege('agency_reader', 'supply', 'CREATE') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: A full walk of 300 pages scans 9,030,000 rows to return 60,000
defects.why: The portal activity export pages with OFFSET, so page three hundred reads the first three hundred pages and throws away all but the last. OFFSET does not skip rows: it produces them and discards them, so the cost of a page grows with how far into the result it sits. The function was written against a table with four hundred rows, where two pages is the whole thing, and it has been correct and fast ever since. The table is now sixty thousand rows and the export walks every page in order, so the walk costs the square of the pages rather than the count of the rows. It is also not stable: a row inserted during the walk shifts the boundary and a row is either exported twice or not at all. Measured: one full walk of 300 pages scanning 9,030,000 rows to return the 60,000 that are in the table. Keyset paging, carrying the last key forward instead of a page number, makes every page cost the same and fixes the shifting boundary at the same time. Every page returns exactly two hundred rows in the right order and the export has never produced a wrong total.

detect.sql: SELECT sum(rows_scanned) FROM ops.event_page_log

defects.title: 9,600 case attachments sit under two permissive policies combined with OR
defects.why: Case attachments carry two row security policies, both permissive, so they are combined with OR and the second one grants back everything the first was written to withhold. The first policy limits an agent to the attachments on cases in their own team. The second was added so that the complaints team could see attachments flagged as complaints, whatever team the case belongs to. Written as a permissive policy, that is not an exception: it is an alternative. A row satisfies the table's security if it satisfies either one, so every attachment flagged as a complaint is readable by every agent, and every attachment is flagged as a complaint by the form's default. Measured: 9,600 case attachments under two permissive policies and no restrictive policy on one table. The second policy wants to be RESTRICTIVE, or the two want folding into one expression. Both policies are enabled, both are correct in isolation, and row security is on.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM support.case_attachments) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_policy WHERE polrelid = 'support.case_attachments'::regclass AND polpermissive) = 2 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_policy WHERE polrelid = 'support.case_attachments'::regclass AND NOT polpermissive) = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 3,000 summer clock-ins are an hour adrift from the gateway instant on the same row
defects.why: The clock-in terminal writes local wall clock time into a column with no time zone, and everything downstream reads that column as UTC, so between March and October it is an hour out. The terminal is a fixed device in a depot and it reports what its own clock says, which is British time. The column was declared without a time zone because the value has no offset on it, which is true and is exactly the problem: nothing on the row says what it is local to. The gateway also records a proper instant on the same row, which is where the discrepancy can be seen, and nothing compares the two. Payroll reads the wall clock column, so a summer shift starting at six is paid from five. Measured: 6,000 clock-ins of which 3,000 fall in British Summer Time and disagree by an hour with the gateway instant on the same row. Storing the instant and rendering the wall clock when it is needed is the fix, and the gateway column already holds it. Every timestamp is a real reading from a working clock and no row is internally malformed.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.depot_clock_ins WHERE clocked_at <> (device_utc AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')

defects.title: 4,800 vehicle check edits are unaudited because the trigger names a single column
defects.why: The vehicle check audit trigger is declared UPDATE OF odometer, so every other edit to the row passes without a word. Naming the column was a deliberate narrowing, done when the audit table was growing faster than the table it audited, and the column chosen was the one being edited at the time. The defect note is the column that matters. It is the free text a driver writes when something is wrong with the vehicle, it is edited by the workshop after the fact, and it is the column an insurer reads. A trigger declared on one column does not fire for a statement that does not mention it, so those edits leave nothing behind, not even a timestamp. Measured: 6,000 vehicle checks against 1,200 audit rows, a gap of 4,800, behind one trigger scoped to a single column. Dropping the column list restores the audit and doubles the audit table, which is the trade that was made. The trigger fires correctly for every statement it was written to cover.

detect.sql: SELECT ((SELECT count(*) FROM ops.vehicle_checks) - (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.vehicle_check_audit)) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'ops.vehicle_checks'::regclass AND NOT tgisinternal AND array_length(tgattr::int2[], 1) = 1)

defects.title: 4,000 accounts each hold exactly one active rate and no index says they must
defects.why: Each account has exactly one active rate, which is the rule the billing run depends on, and there is nothing in the schema that says it. Rates are superseded rather than replaced, so the table holds the history and one live row per account. The activation is done by a stored procedure that deactivates the old row and inserts the new one in the same transaction, which is why the rule has held. A partial unique index on the account where the row is active would say the same thing in the schema and would take a second to build. The billing run selects the active rate into a scalar, so a second active row is not a double charge: it is an error that stops the run part way through a batch of four thousand accounts. Measured: 12,000 account rates of which 4,000 are active, one per account, under no unique index other than the primary key. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE is_active applies cleanly against the data as it stands. Every account has its one live rate and the history behind it, and the table has never held a second active row.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.account_rates WHERE is_active) * (1 - (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'payments.account_rates'::regclass AND indisunique AND NOT indisprimary))

defects.title: 600 supplier scorecards report 20 open claims against the 8 that are open
defects.why: The supplier scorecard holds a count of open claims, the count is incremented when a claim is raised, and nothing decrements it when one is settled. The scorecard was built as a fast read for the buying screen, which shows sixty suppliers at once and cannot join to a claims table with a hundred thousand rows in it. Incrementing on raise was written into the claim creation path on day one. Settling a claim happens in a different service, which posts to the finance ledger and updates the claim, and was never told the scorecard existed. Buyers are scored on open claims against their suppliers, so the number only ever gets worse, and suppliers who fix things quickly look identical to suppliers who do not. Measured: 600 supplier scorecards, every one of which reports 20 open claims against the 8 the claims table holds open for that supplier. The count wants to be a view, or the settlement path wants the matching decrement. Every claim is correctly marked and the scorecard is a perfectly accurate count of the claims ever raised.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.supplier_scorecards s WHERE s.open_claims <> (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.supplier_claims c WHERE c.supplier_ref = s.supplier_ref AND c.is_open)

defects.title: 3,600 dispatch notes carry a hash of a reference that was rewritten a moment later
defects.why: Two BEFORE INSERT triggers sit on the dispatch note. The first hashes the dispatch reference and the second folds it to upper case, so the hash on the row is a hash of a value the row does not hold. Normalising the reference was added months after the hash, to stop the same dispatch being received twice under two capitalisations, and it was named for what it does. Triggers of the same timing run in name order, so the normaliser runs second, which nobody chose and nothing warns about. The hash is what the courier's acknowledgement is checked against. An acknowledgement carrying the hash of the stored reference does not match the stored hash, and the reconciliation job writes those off as unacknowledged and dispatches them again. Measured: 9,000 dispatch notes of which 3,600 carry a hash that does not match a hash of the reference stored beside it. Renaming the triggers fixes every row written from then on, and the existing hashes want recomputing in a one-off statement. Both triggers do exactly what they say, every reference is normalised, and every hash is a real hash of a real value.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.dispatch_notes WHERE ref_hash <> md5(dispatch_ref)

defects.title: 800 manufacturer part numbers sit on more than one catalogue line
defects.why: Eight hundred manufacturer part numbers are in the catalogue twice, once plain and once with a revision suffix on the catalogue's own reference. A revision is a change to the drawing, not to the part, and the buying team handle it by adding a new catalogue line so that the old drawing stays orderable while stock lasts. The catalogue reference carries the suffix and the manufacturer part number does not, because it is the manufacturer's and it has not changed. Nothing says the manufacturer part number is unique, because under this working practice it is not meant to be. Stock is held against the catalogue reference, so the same physical part is counted in two places, and the reorder point is calculated per line, so both lines reorder. Measured: 4,800 catalogue lines holding 800 manufacturer part numbers that appear on more than one line. A part table with a revision table beneath it separates the drawing from the part. Every line is a legitimate catalogue entry with its own reference, its own stock and its own history.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT mfr_part_no FROM supply.part_catalogue GROUP BY mfr_part_no HAVING count(*) > 1) s

defects.title: 2,400 delivery attempts carry a status the lookup no longer holds
defects.why: The delivery attempt status is a string matched against a lookup table, the lookup's values were renamed, and the rows that already existed were not. There is no foreign key, because the status column was there first and the lookup was added later to drive a dropdown. Renaming the lookup values was done to make the dropdown read better on the driver's handheld, which it does. The rename was a data change in the lookup and touched nothing else. Reporting joins the attempts to the lookup to get the label, with an inner join, so two thousand four hundred attempts fall out of every report of how deliveries went, and the totals still add up to a plausible number. Measured: 12,000 delivery attempts of which 2,400 carry a status that is not in the 8 row lookup table. A foreign key and an update of the historic rows closes it, in that order. Every status was valid when it was written and the lookup is a complete and correct list of the statuses in use today.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.delivery_attempts a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fulfilment.attempt_statuses t WHERE t.status_code = a.status_code)

defects.title: 200 framework contracts are above ninety million in a numeric(10,2) column
defects.why: Framework contract values are held in numeric(10,2), which stops at 99,999,999.99, and two hundred contracts are already above ninety million. Ten digits with two after the point was chosen when the largest framework was eleven million, and it is a sensible shape for money: exact, no rounding, no floating point. What it is not is open ended. Numeric with a declared precision raises an error on overflow rather than rounding, so the day a framework is signed at a hundred million the insert fails, in the contract management screen, with a message about field overflow that means nothing to the buyer typing it. Group turnover has trebled since the column was declared and frameworks are being consolidated deliberately. Measured: 1,200 framework contracts of which 200 exceed ninety million pounds, in a column declared numeric(10,2). Widening to numeric(14,2) is a rewrite of a small table and nothing else changes. Every value in the column is exact and correct, and no contract has ever been refused.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.framework_contracts WHERE value_gbp > 90000000) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'supply.framework_contracts'::regclass AND attname = 'value_gbp' AND atttypmod = 655366)

defects.title: Thirty daily imports each hold exactly one page of one thousand rows
defects.why: The supplier portal import reads the first page of the API's response and stops, so every daily import holds exactly one thousand rows. The API pages at a thousand and returns a continuation token beside the rows. The client reads the rows, ignores the token, and reports the number of rows it loaded, which is a number that looks like a healthy import and is the same every day, which looks like a stable feed. It went unnoticed because for the first year the supplier portal held fewer than a thousand records a day. The rows that are missing are the ones the API sorts last, which is by supplier reference, so the back half of the alphabet has been invisible to the buying report since the volume crossed the page size. Measured: 30 daily imports of which every one holds exactly 1,000 rows, the page size of the source API. Following the continuation token is a small change to the client and will multiply the table by an unknown factor, which is the point. Every row that was loaded is correct, and the import has never failed or reported an error.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT imported_on FROM analytics.api_imports GROUP BY imported_on HAVING count(*) = 1000) s

defects.title: The callback slot sequence will hand back the key the table's newest row holds
defects.why: The callback slot sequence was reset to the highest key in the table with the is_called flag set to false, which means the next value it hands out is that same key. Resetting a sequence after a restore is routine and the shape of the call is setval(sequence, max(id)). The third argument defaults to true, meaning the value has been used and the next one will be one higher. Passing false makes the sequence hand out the value itself, which is the right thing after setval(sequence, 1, false) on an empty table and is wrong after a restore. The restore was a rehearsal that was kept, so this is the live sequence. The next callback booked collides with the newest row in the table, and the insert fails on the primary key, which will read as the booking screen being broken. Measured: 6,000 callback slots whose highest key is 6,000, against a sequence sitting at 6,000 with is_called false. One setval with the default third argument puts it right, before the next booking rather than after it. The sequence is owned, attached and working, and the table is intact.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT max(slot_id) FROM support.callback_slots) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT last_value FROM support.callback_slot_seq) = (SELECT max(slot_id) FROM support.callback_slots) AND NOT (SELECT is_called FROM support.callback_slot_seq) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 900 depot stock lines name a depot and product pair that is in no stock profile
defects.why: A depot stock line names a depot and a product. The product has a foreign key and the pair has nothing, so a line can name a product the depot has never stocked. The stock profile, which says which products a depot holds, is keyed on the pair. The stock line was built first, against the product catalogue, and the profile arrived a year later when depots started specialising. Declaring the foreign key on the pair would mean the profile row has to exist before the stock line, which is true of the real process and was not true of the overnight load, so it was left off for now. Replenishment reads the stock line, orders against it, and the goods arrive at a depot with no bay set up to receive them. Measured: 9,000 depot stock lines of which 900 name a depot and product pair that is not in the 8,000 row stock profile table. The foreign key wants declaring on the pair and the nine hundred lines want resolving first. Every line names a real depot and a real product, and every single column foreign key on the table is satisfied.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.depot_stock_lines l WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM supply.depot_stock_profiles p WHERE p.depot_code = l.depot_code AND p.sku = l.sku)

defects.title: 1,200 case histories hold 200 events in one column rewritten on every append
defects.why: The case history is one text column holding every event on the case, and adding an event reads the column, appends to it and writes the whole thing back. It was built that way so that the case screen is one row read, which it is, and it is the fastest case screen in the estate. Writing is the other half of the trade and nobody measured it. A case with two hundred events has had its history column written two hundred times, at an average of half the final size, so a twelve kilobyte history has cost well over a megabyte of writes and two hundred TOAST round trips. It is also not concurrent: two agents adding a note at once means one of the notes is not there. Measured: 1,200 case histories each holding 200 appended events in a single 12,200 character column. An events table with one row per event makes the write a single insert and the read a cheap ordered scan. Every history is complete, in order, and renders correctly on the case screen.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.case_histories WHERE event_count = 200 AND length(history_text) > 10000

defects.title: 1,200 seal numbers were rejected by a unique index over a substring of the reference
defects.why: The seal number is unique on its first eight characters, seal numbers are fourteen characters, and the first eight are the manufacturer and batch. The index was written as an expression over a substring because the loader was matching on a truncated reference printed on the old paper log, and making that match unique seemed like the way to stop the same seal being entered twice. It stops far more than that: every seal in a batch shares its first eight characters, so the second seal from any batch is refused. The loader catches the error, writes the row to a rejects table, and carries on, which is why nothing has ever alerted. A trailer with no seal recorded cannot be signed off at the far end. Measured: 1,800 seal numbers loaded against 1,200 rejected by a unique index declared over the first eight characters of the reference. The index wants to be on the whole reference. It is valid, it is enforced, and it does exactly what it was declared to do.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.seal_number_rejects) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i WHERE i.indrelid = 'ops.seal_numbers'::regclass AND i.indisunique AND NOT i.indisprimary AND i.indexprs IS NOT NULL)

defects.title: 1,200 key accounts sit in a three table foreign key cycle with no load order
defects.why: A key account names a depot, the depot names an account manager, and the account manager names a key account, so the three tables reference each other in a ring and there is no order in which they can be loaded. Each constraint was added on its own and each is defensible: the account must have a home depot, the depot must have somebody accountable for it, and the manager must have a lead account, which is the account their bonus is measured on. Nobody drew the three together. Every referencing column is nullable, which is the only reason the data loaded at all, because the loader inserts with nulls and fills the references in afterwards in a second pass that is in no migration and in no schema. A restore into an empty database looks for a dependency order, finds there is not one, and either fails or loads the three tables with their references empty. Measured: 1,200 key accounts whose home depot names a manager whose lead account is a key account again, under three foreign keys forming a cycle. One of the three references wants moving to a table of its own, most naturally the manager's lead account. Every constraint is valid, every row satisfies it, and the cycle is invisible unless all three tables are drawn at once.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM storefront.key_accounts k JOIN ops.account_depots d ON d.depot_code = k.home_depot JOIN ops.account_managers m ON m.manager_ref = d.manager_ref JOIN storefront.key_accounts k2 ON k2.account_ref = m.lead_account) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE contype = 'f' AND (conrelid, confrelid) IN (('storefront.key_accounts'::regclass, 'ops.account_depots'::regclass), ('ops.account_depots'::regclass, 'ops.account_managers'::regclass), ('ops.account_managers'::regclass, 'storefront.key_accounts'::regclass))) = 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 480 part codes were exported twice or not at all because the pages were cut in byte order
defects.why: The part finder export cuts its pages at boundaries computed under the C collation and then fetches each page under the database collation, and the two orders are not the same, so codes fall through the seams. The boundary list comes from a nightly job that sorts with an explicit COLLATE "C", because the job was written to match a fixed width file the printer sorts in byte order. The export then selects each page with a BETWEEN against those boundaries in the default collation, where case interleaves and punctuation is weighted differently. Every page still returns rows and every page is the right size, so the export looks healthy from the job log. Codes that sit near a boundary either land on two pages or on none, and a part on no page cannot be ordered from the printed catalogue at all. Measured: 12,000 part codes exported over 241 pages, of which 240 appear on two pages and 240 appear on none, 480 between them. Both halves want the same collation named explicitly, or keyset paging on the primary key rather than on the text. Every page is internally sorted, and the export row total equals the table row total exactly, which is the only check anybody runs.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT part_code FROM catalog.part_finder_exports GROUP BY part_code HAVING count(*) > 1) x) + (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.part_finder_index i WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM catalog.part_finder_exports e WHERE e.part_code = i.part_code))

defects.title: 4,800 rebate applications sit behind a definer function whose search path names public first
defects.why: The rebate function runs as its owner and its search path names public ahead of its own schema, so anyone who can create a table in public decides what the function reads and writes. Setting a search path on a SECURITY DEFINER function is the right habit and this one has it, which is why it passes every review that checks for the setting rather than its contents. The order is the problem. Name resolution takes the first match, public comes first, and CREATE on public is held by PUBLIC in this database. A table called rebate_applications created in public is read by this function in preference to the real one, with the owner's rights, and the function writes its result back through the same unqualified name. Measured: 4,800 rebate applications behind one SECURITY DEFINER function whose search path is public ahead of supply. Putting the function's own schema first, with pg_catalog ahead of that, is a one line change. The function is owned correctly, sets a search path, takes typed arguments, builds no dynamic SQL, and its execute privilege is granted to one named role rather than to PUBLIC.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.rebate_applications) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_proc p WHERE p.oid = 'supply.fn_apply_rebate(varchar,integer)'::regprocedure AND p.prosecdef AND p.proconfig @> ARRAY['search_path=public, supply'])

defects.title: Two of the five marketing spend tables are unreadable by the portal reporting role
defects.why: The portal reporting role was granted SELECT on all tables in the marketing schema, and two of the five spend tables were created afterwards, so the role cannot read them. GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA is a loop over the tables that exist when it runs, not a standing rule, and it was run once during the handover week. The two tables added since are the daily and the annual rollups, which are the two the portal's spend page reads first. A default privilege would have covered them and there is not one on this schema. The page catches the permission error per panel and renders that panel empty, so the spend page shows three populated charts and two blank ones, which reads as no spend rather than as no access. Measured: 5 marketing spend tables of which 2 are unreadable by the portal reporting role, holding 987 rows between them. ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES makes the rule standing and the two tables want granting now. Every grant that was made is intact, correct and visible in every privilege report, which is why the access review passes.

detect.sql: SELECT ((SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.spend_daily) + (SELECT count(*) FROM marketing.spend_annual)) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'marketing' AND c.relname IN ('spend_weekly', 'spend_monthly', 'spend_quarterly', 'spend_daily', 'spend_annual') AND NOT has_table_privilege('portal_reader', c.oid, 'SELECT')) = 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 600 load lines are character for character identical to another line in a table with no key
defects.why: The load line table has no key of any kind and six hundred lines are identical in every column to another line, while the loading screen deletes a line by matching every column. A load line is a product, a quantity and a trailer, and the same product can legitimately be loaded twice onto the same trailer, as two pallets from two separate picks. Nothing on the row tells the two apart, because the table was built by a copy out of a spreadsheet and the spreadsheet had no line number either. Removing one line therefore removes both, the trailer goes out a pallet short, and the shortage is found at the far end and put down to a picking error. Measured: 9,600 load lines of which 600 are exact duplicates of another line, in a table with no primary key and no unique index. A generated identity column is one statement and makes a line addressable. Every line is a true record of something that was loaded and the totals on the trailer manifest are correct, because the manifest sums the quantities rather than counting the lines.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT trailer_no, sku, qty, loaded_on FROM fulfilment.load_lines GROUP BY trailer_no, sku, qty, loaded_on HAVING count(*) > 1) x) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'fulfilment.load_lines'::regclass AND indisunique) = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 7,200 shift export rows sit on a table the stock reporting role may truncate
defects.why: The stock reporting role was granted ALL PRIVILEGES on the shift export table, and ALL includes TRUNCATE. The grant was written while chasing a permission error in a nightly job that turned out to be about a sequence, and ALL made the error go away. TRUNCATE is not a lot of deletes: it is one statement that empties the table, it takes an access exclusive lock, and it fires no row triggers, so the audit trigger on this table records nothing at all about it. The table is the source for the shift productivity figures the depot managers are measured on, and it is rebuilt weekly, so an accidental truncate on a Tuesday would be noticed the following Monday at the earliest and would look like a failed rebuild. Measured: 7,200 shift export rows on a table where the stock reporting role holds TRUNCATE. GRANT SELECT is what was meant and is one statement. The role has never issued anything but a select, the grant was made deliberately by somebody entitled to make it, and it appears in every privilege report as a grant that exists rather than as a grant that is too wide.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.shift_exports) * (CASE WHEN has_table_privilege('stock_reader', 'ops.shift_exports', 'TRUNCATE') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 9,000 axle weight tickets are unaudited because the trigger sits on one partition
defects.why: The axle weight audit trigger was created on one partition instead of on the partitioned table, so three quarters of the tickets are written with nothing recorded. The trigger was added during an overload investigation that concerned only the quarter then open, and CREATE TRIGGER was pointed at that quarter's table because that is the table the investigator was reading. A trigger created on the partitioned parent is cloned onto every partition, including partitions created later, which is what was wanted and is a few characters different to write. Routing an insert through the parent fires the triggers belonging to the partition the row lands in, so the audit runs for one quarter and stops dead at the quarter boundary. Nothing announces it: the audit table grows while that quarter is open and simply stops when it closes, which reads as a quiet quarter rather than as a broken audit. Measured: 12,000 axle weight tickets across four quarterly partitions, of which 3,000 are audited and 9,000 are not, under a trigger that exists on exactly one partition and not on the parent. Dropping the partition trigger and creating the same trigger on the parent covers every partition, present and future. The trigger function is correct, the audit rows it did write are complete and accurate, and the partitioning itself is sound.

detect.sql: SELECT ((SELECT count(*) FROM ops.axle_weights) - (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.axle_weight_audit)) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger t WHERE t.tgrelid IN (SELECT inhrelid FROM pg_inherits WHERE inhparent = 'ops.axle_weights'::regclass) AND NOT t.tgisinternal) = 1 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'ops.axle_weights'::regclass AND NOT tgisinternal) = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 6,000 haulier ratings are read through a pure function marked parallel unsafe
defects.why: The haulier rating function does nothing but arithmetic on its arguments and is marked parallel unsafe, which is what a function is when nobody says otherwise, so every query that calls it is planned without parallelism. PARALLEL UNSAFE is the default and it is the right default, because the planner cannot know that a function is safe to run in a worker. The cost of leaving it is not local to the function. One unsafe call anywhere in a query makes the whole plan serial, including the sequential scan underneath it that would otherwise have been divided between workers, so the penalty lands on the scan rather than on the function and is invisible in the plan as anything but a missing parallel node. The rating is selected in the haulier performance view, which is the slowest report in the estate and has been explained several times without anybody reading the function's markings. Measured: 6,000 haulier ratings read through a function that is immutable in fact and marked parallel unsafe in the catalogue. Adding PARALLEL SAFE is one word and the function genuinely is safe: it reads no table, writes nothing and touches no setting. It is already marked IMMUTABLE, takes typed arguments, and returns the right answer every time.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.haulier_ratings) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'analytics.fn_haulier_rating(integer,integer)'::regprocedure AND proparallel = 'u' AND provolatile = 'i')

defects.title: 12,000 trunk legs sit on a table whose catalogue still names a clustering index
defects.why: The trunk leg table was clustered on the depot index once and the catalogue still records that index as the clustering one, while nothing has re-clustered it since and every row written afterwards was appended wherever there was room. CLUSTER rewrites the table in index order and marks the index it used. It is a one time rearrangement, not a property the table keeps, because the next insert goes wherever the free space map points. The mark it leaves is the trap: it reads as a table that is clustered, and it is quoted as such in the tuning notes for the depot report. That report's plan assumes a correlated heap and chooses an index scan, which was right the week after the cluster ran and is wrong now that a quarter of the table was written after it, each row landing in a page unrelated to its depot. Measured: 12,000 trunk legs on a table whose catalogue marks one index as the clustering index, 3,000 of them written after the one and only CLUSTER. Either re-cluster on a schedule and say so, or clear the mark so nobody reads it as a standing property. Every row is present, the index is valid and used, and the cluster that ran did exactly what it was asked to do.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.trunk_legs) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'ops.trunk_legs'::regclass AND indisclustered)

defects.title: 3,000 hub scans took a partition's own column default instead of the table's
defects.why: One hub scan partition carries its own default for the scan source and the overnight load inserts straight into that partition rather than through the parent, so three thousand scans are recorded as coming from nowhere. A partition may hold column defaults of its own and they win for an insert addressed to the partition by name. This one was set during a cutover, when the handheld fleet was being swapped and the source genuinely was not known, and it was never cleared. The load targets the partition by name because the loader builds the table name from the date, which is faster and which was the recommendation at the time. A scan routed through the parent takes the parent's default and the same scan written directly takes the partition's, so one handheld produces two different answers depending on which door the row came in. Measured: 9,000 hub scans of which 3,000 carry a source of UNKNOWN, on a column whose default is declared once on the parent and once on each of three partitions and reads two different ways. Dropping the partition's default and writing through the parent are each one statement. Every scan is present, every timestamp is right, and each row is in the partition its date says it belongs to.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.hub_scans WHERE scan_source <> 'HANDHELD') * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(DISTINCT pg_get_expr(d.adbin, d.adrelid)) FROM pg_attrdef d JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = d.adrelid AND a.attnum = d.adnum WHERE a.attname = 'scan_source' AND d.adrelid IN (SELECT inhrelid FROM pg_inherits WHERE inhparent = 'fulfilment.hub_scans'::regclass)) = 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 7,800 depot stock targets were overwritten by an upsert keyed on the product alone
defects.why: The stock target table is unique on the product alone while the target is set per depot per product, and the nightly upsert names that unique index as its conflict target, so every depot overwrites the depot before it. The table began as a group-wide target, one number per product, and the depot column was added when depots started setting their own. The unique index was not widened with it. The load reads a feed of eight thousand depot and product lines and upserts each one, and because the conflict target is the product on its own, every line after the first for a product updates the same row. The table ends the night holding two hundred rows, one per product, each carrying whichever depot the feed happened to visit last, which is the depot whose code sorts last rather than the depot that matters. The load reports eight thousand rows applied, which is true, and nobody counts the table afterwards. Measured: 8,000 depot and product target lines in the feed against 200 rows in the target table, whose only unique index has one key column. Widening the unique index to the depot and the product, and naming both in the conflict target, keeps every line. Every target in the table is a real number a depot really set, and the feed is complete and correct.

detect.sql: SELECT ((SELECT count(*) FROM supply.stock_target_feed) - (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.stock_targets)) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT max(indnkeyatts) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'supply.stock_targets'::regclass AND indisunique) = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 2,400 priority reviews on hold sit outside the predicate of the only status index
defects.why: The priority review index is partial on the open status and the service desk screen asks for open and on hold together, so the index answers neither half of the query. The index was correct when it was built, because on hold did not exist and a review was open or it was closed. The status was added a year later with a screen of its own, and then the two screens were merged into one queue because the desk works them as one queue. A partial index can only answer a query the planner can prove falls inside its predicate, and open or on hold is not inside open, so the merged screen scans the whole table every time it is opened. It is fast enough at twelve thousand rows, which is why it has never been raised, and it is a sequential scan that grows with the table rather than with the queue. Measured: 12,000 priority reviews of which 2,400 are on hold and outside the predicate of the only partial index on the table, against 2,400 that are open and inside it. Widening the predicate to the two live statuses, or dropping the predicate and indexing the status itself, restores an index scan. The index is valid, it is still used by the open-only report that has not been retired, and every review is correctly statused.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM support.priority_reviews WHERE status = 'ON_HOLD') * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'support.priority_reviews'::regclass AND indpred IS NOT NULL)

defects.title: 24,000 sensor readings each carry twenty one bytes of alignment padding
defects.why: The sensor reading columns alternate between a one byte flag and an eight byte value, so every row carries twenty one bytes of padding that hold nothing at all. PostgreSQL stores columns in the order they are declared and aligns each one to its own boundary, so a boolean sitting in front of a bigint costs seven wasted bytes on every row. The declaration reads well, because each flag sits beside the value it qualifies, and that is exactly why nobody reordered it. The cost is not in the flags but in the table: the padding is written to disk, copied into shared buffers, read back by every sequential scan, and carried into every backup and every replica. On this table it is about a fifth of the row. Nothing reports it, because no statistic distinguishes a padding byte from a data byte, and the table's size looks proportionate to its row count because nobody knows what the row should weigh. Measured: 24,000 sensor readings in a table whose declaration places a one byte column immediately in front of an eight byte column three times over. Declaring the eight byte columns first and the flags at the end stores the same data in fewer pages and is a rewrite of one table. Every column is the right type, every value is correct, and the table reads exactly as intended.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.sensor_readings) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT a.attalign, lag(a.attalign) OVER (ORDER BY a.attnum) AS prev FROM pg_attribute a WHERE a.attrelid = 'ops.sensor_readings'::regclass AND a.attnum > 0 AND NOT a.attisdropped) s WHERE s.attalign = 'd' AND s.prev = 'c') = 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 1,800 product titles carry a double escaped ampersand from a second escaping pass
defects.why: The import escapes ampersands for the web template, and for one supplier's feed it ran over titles that had already been escaped, so eighteen hundred products are called something with a doubled entity in the middle of the name. Escaping is not idempotent: the ampersand inside an escaped ampersand is itself an ampersand, so a second pass escapes it again. The feed in question already escaped its titles, which nobody knew, because the only sample anybody had looked at was a title with no ampersand in it. The template escapes nothing itself, on the grounds that the data arrives safe, so the double escape goes straight to the page and the customer reads the entity rather than the character. Search makes it worse: a shopper looking for the product by name matches neither the escaped form nor the plain one. Measured: 9,000 product titles of which 1,800 contain a double escaped ampersand. The affected rows want one pass of unescaping and the import wants to stop escaping what the feed has already escaped. Every title is present, in the right row, correctly associated with its supplier, and renders as valid markup.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.product_titles WHERE position('&amp;' in title) > 0

defects.title: 2,400 docket lines match no order because the reference carries a trailing space
defects.why: The docket line carries the order reference as it came off a fixed width feed, padded to the column width with a space, while the order header holds it unpadded. Varchar comparison does not ignore trailing spaces, so those lines match no order at all. The feed pads every field to its declared width, which is what fixed width means, and the loader writes the field as it finds it. That worked for years because the references filled the width and there was nothing to pad. The current numbering is one character shorter, so a single space now arrives on the end of every reference the new format writes. There is no foreign key on the column, which is the only reason the rows loaded. On screen the two forms look identical, because a trailing space does not render, so the goods-in report simply shows the line against no order and the buyer assumes the order was raised in another system. Measured: 12,000 docket lines of which 2,400 match no order header as stored and match exactly one once the trailing space is removed. Trimming on load, and a foreign key afterwards, closes it for good. Every line names a real order, the quantities are right, and the reference is correct to the character apart from the padding.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.docket_lines d WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM supply.order_headers h WHERE h.order_ref = d.order_ref) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM supply.order_headers h WHERE h.order_ref = rtrim(d.order_ref))

defects.title: 3,600 hire periods with no return date satisfy the check that was meant to cover them
defects.why: The hire period check says the return date must be after the hire date, and a row with no return date satisfies it, because the comparison is unknown and a check constraint rejects a row only when its expression is false. This is the rule of three valued logic that every review forgets. The constraint was added to stop a keying error that had put a return before a hire, and it does stop exactly that, every time. It was then written up as the guarantee that every hire has a sane return, which it is not and never was. The hire desk reads open hires off a different screen, so the two have never been cross-checked, and equipment that was never booked back in sits in the table looking exactly like equipment still legitimately out. Measured: 9,000 hire periods under one check constraint, of which 3,600 have no return date and are therefore checked by nothing. Adding NOT NULL, or spelling the rule out as a return that is either absent by design or later than the hire, makes the intent explicit and testable. The constraint is valid, enforced, and has genuinely caught the reversal it was written for.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.hire_periods WHERE returned_on IS NULL) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'fulfilment.hire_periods'::regclass AND contype = 'c')

defects.title: 40 depot totals hold one identical figure because the trigger names no depot
defects.why: The trigger that rolls a sale into the depot total updates the total table without naming a depot, so every sale is added to every depot. The trigger was written against a table that held a single row, back when the total was a group total, and the depot column was added underneath it without the trigger being reread. An UPDATE with no WHERE is perfectly legal, it reports the number of rows it touched, and forty is a plausible number to see in a log when the trigger fires thousands of times a night. The totals are wrong in a way that is hard to see, because they are all wrong identically and they all still climb through the day, which is what somebody glancing at them expects. It is the depot league table, read every morning, and it currently shows forty depots tied to the penny. Measured: 40 depot totals holding one and the same figure, rolled from 3,000 sales by a trigger whose UPDATE names no depot. One WHERE clause fixes the trigger and a single pass over the sales rebuilds the totals. Every sale is recorded correctly in the sales table, and the sum across all depots is right, which is the figure the board is shown.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.depot_totals) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(DISTINCT total_p) FROM ops.depot_totals) = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 12,000 field change rows carry one distinct user between them
defects.why: The field change audit stamps each row with the database user, and every connection arrives through a pool that logs in as one role, so twelve thousand rows all say the same thing. Defaulting the column to the current user is the obvious way to record who did something, and it is right on a database where people connect as themselves. Nobody has connected as themselves here since the application was put behind a pool. The end user is known to the application and is never passed down, so the audit faithfully records the pool. That is worse than an empty column: the column is populated, the audit looks complete, and it was signed off as meeting the record keeping requirement on the strength of looking complete. The first time it was needed was a disputed price change, and the answer it gave was the name of a service account. Measured: 12,000 field change rows carrying exactly one distinct user between them. The application user wants passing down, either through a session setting the default reads or as a column the application fills explicitly. Every row is otherwise complete: the table, the column, the old value, the new value and the time are all correct and in order.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM support.field_changes) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(DISTINCT changed_by) FROM support.field_changes) = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 2,200 imported invoices hold a date the source text does not say
defects.why: The invoice import parses the date with a month first mask and the file writes it day first, so every date whose day is twelve or under was read with the day and the month swapped. The mask was set when the feed came from an American supplier and it was never revisited when the feed was consolidated. A date such as 05/03 is accepted by both masks and answers differently, which is the whole problem: the import raises no error, because there is nothing wrong with the input. Only the dates where the day exceeds twelve would have failed under the wrong mask, and those are the ones that are right, because the parse fell back. So the errors are invisible and the successes are wrong. The invoice date drives the payment run, so those invoices are paid early or late by up to eleven months, and the original string is still on the row, which is the only reason this is provable at all. Measured: 6,000 imported invoices of which 2,400 were read month first and 2,200 hold a date that does not agree with the day first reading of the text the file supplied, the remaining 200 being the days where the day and the month are the same number. Re-parsing the stored text with the right mask corrects every row, and the import wants one mask that matches the feed. Every invoice is present, every amount is right, and the source text was kept, which is what makes the fix a single UPDATE rather than a re-import.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.invoice_imports WHERE invoice_date <> to_date(date_text, 'DD/MM/YYYY')

defects.title: 2,400 related product rows are 1,200 pairs stored once each way round
defects.why: The related products table holds a pair of products in one row, and twelve hundred pairs are in it twice, once each way round. A relationship that has no direction wants storing once, with a rule that says which of the two goes in the first column. There is no such rule here. The merchandising screen writes the pair as the buyer entered it, and the weekly import writes it as the supplier's file lists it, and the two orders disagree for about a fifth of the catalogue. Nothing rejects the second row, because the unique constraint is on the pair in the order it is stored, and the two orders are two different keys. The product page shows the same accessory twice, the count of related products is wrong, and removing the relationship from one screen leaves the other half of it behind. Measured: 6,000 related product rows of which 2,400 have a mirror row holding the same pair the other way round, being 1,200 pairs stored twice. Storing the pair with the lower product code first, under a check constraint that says so, makes the duplicate impossible. Every row names two real products and the relationship each row describes is true.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.related_products r WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM catalog.related_products m WHERE m.sku_a = r.sku_b AND m.sku_b = r.sku_a)

defects.title: 12,000 handling rates hold six values that read as twelve rate bands
defects.why: The handling rate is numeric with no declared scale, so the same rate is stored as 2.5 by one screen and 2.50 by another. The two are equal as numbers and different as text, and the rate card report groups them as text. Numeric without a scale keeps whatever scale the value arrived with, which is the right behaviour for a column that must not round anything. Equality ignores the trailing zero, so every arithmetic check passes and every join on the number matches. The rate card report builds its groups by casting the rate to text, because the heading is printed from the same expression, and the cast is faithful to what is stored. So the report shows twelve rate bands where the business has six, each one split between the screen that entered it and the file that loaded it, and the depot reading it believes two neighbouring bands apply to the same work. Measured: 12,000 handling rates holding 6 distinct values as numbers and 12 as text. Declaring the column numeric(8,2) normalises every row and the report can go on grouping however it likes. Every rate is exact, every comparison between rates is right, and no total is out by a penny.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.handling_rates) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(DISTINCT rate_gbp) FROM catalog.handling_rates) = 6 AND (SELECT count(DISTINCT rate_gbp::text) FROM catalog.handling_rates) = 12 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 1,200 exported settlement rows name a key that does not exist
defects.why: The finance export reads settlement keys through a reader that holds every number as a double, so twelve hundred keys above two to the fifty third came back changed. A double holds integers exactly up to two to the fifty third and then in steps of two, so an odd key above that line cannot be represented and is rounded to its even neighbour. The keys crossed that line eighteen months ago, when the settlement sequence was moved onto a shared range. The export is JSON and the reader is a general purpose one that parses every number the same way, which is exactly what it is documented to do. The keys still look right, because they are the same length and differ only in the last digit, and the export reconciles on totals rather than on keys, so it balances to the penny while naming settlements that were never made. Measured: 6,000 settlement keys exported, of which 1,200 name no row in the settlement table they were read from. Exporting the key as a string is a one line change and every reader handles it. The source table is correct, the totals agree, and every exported row corresponds to a real settlement.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.export_ledger e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments.settlement_keys s WHERE s.settlement_key = e.settlement_key)

defects.title: 9,000 shift plans sit behind three columns that only one spelling reaches
