defects.why: The shift plan columns were created with quoted mixed case names, so every statement that touches them must quote them in exactly that case, and any that does not fails outright. The table was generated from a spreadsheet whose headings became the column names, capitals, spaces and all. PostgreSQL folds an unquoted identifier to lower case, so the column called Shift Code can only ever be written as "Shift Code": shift_code is a different name, and Shift_Code is the same as shift_code and equally wrong. Every query against the table is therefore copied from one that worked, and the one that got it wrong failed immediately with a column not found error, which is at least honest. The cost is that nothing generic can touch this table: no view built by a tool, no ORM mapping, and no query typed from memory. Measured: 9,000 shift plans in a table with 3 columns whose names differ from their own lower case form. Renaming the columns to lower case with underscores is three statements and one pass through the queries that name them. Every column holds the right data, the table is keyed properly, and every statement that does quote the names correctly works exactly as intended.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.shift_plans) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'ops.shift_plans'::regclass AND attnum > 0 AND NOT attisdropped AND attname <> lower(attname)) = 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 3,000 parcel event keys each name an event in all three months
defects.why: The parcel event partitions were each created with a default of their own sequence, so the event key restarts at one in every month and the same key names three different events. The parent was created without a key, because a partitioned table can only be keyed on something that includes the partition column and nobody wanted a two column key. The partitions were then created one at a time by a script that set up a sequence and a default alongside each one, which looks tidy and reads as though each month is self contained. Nothing across the partitions is unique, so nothing objects. Every join to a parcel event by key alone returns one row per month, which triples the row count on the tracking report, and the support tool that looks an event up by key shows whichever month it found first. Measured: 9,000 parcel events across three monthly partitions, of which 3,000 keys appear in more than one partition, on a parent carrying no index at all. One sequence for the table, or a key that includes the month, makes an event addressable again. Every event is in the right partition for its date, every key is unique inside its own partition, and no partition has ever raised a duplicate.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT event_id FROM fulfilment.parcel_events GROUP BY event_id HAVING count(DISTINCT tableoid) > 1) x) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'fulfilment.parcel_events'::regclass) = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 300 large objects are held by a database no row can reach them from
defects.why: The attachment rows were deleted and the large objects they pointed at were not, so three hundred objects sit in the database with nothing referring to them and no way to reach them. A large object is not owned by the row that names it. Deleting the row removes the reference and nothing else, because the object lives in its own catalogue and only an explicit unlink removes it. The uploader journals every object it creates, which is how this is provable at all, and the delete path was written against the reference table alone, because that is the table the screen knows about. Nothing complains: the objects take no part in any query, no constraint refers to them, and the only sign is the size of the database, which grows at the rate uploads are made rather than at the rate attachments are kept. Restores carry them too, so the waste compounds every time the estate is copied. Measured: 900 journalled large objects of which 300 are still present in the database and named by no attachment row. Unlinking in the same transaction as the delete, or a sweep over the journal for objects nothing references, reclaims the space. Every attachment that is still referenced opens correctly, the journal is complete, and no reference points at an object that has gone.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.attachment_journal j WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM support.attachment_refs r WHERE r.loid = j.loid) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_largeobject_metadata m WHERE m.oid = j.loid)

defects.title: 600 upload digests are 64 bytes of hex text rather than a 32 byte digest
defects.why: One upload path hands the checksum to the database as a hex string and the column is bytea, so six hundred rows hold the sixty four characters of the hex rather than the thirty two bytes they spell. Casting text to bytea does not decode anything. It reads the string as bytes in the escape format, and a string of hex digits contains no escape, so every character is kept as its own byte. The result is twice the length and entirely wrong, and it is still a valid bytea, so nothing raises. The comparison that matters is against the digest of the file as computed at read time, which is thirty two bytes, and it never matches, so those uploads are reported as corrupt and re-sent. That has been happening for months and was put down to the supplier's network. Measured: 3,000 upload digests of which 600 are 64 bytes long, being the hex text of a digest rather than the digest. Decoding with decode(...,'hex') on the way in fixes the path, and the stored rows can be decoded in place because the text is still exactly what was computed. Every digest was calculated correctly, against the right file, and the rows written by the other path are the right length and match.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.upload_digests WHERE octet_length(payload_sha) = 64

defects.title: 400 hire bookings double book an asset under a constraint that skips them
defects.why: The hire bookings carry an exclusion constraint that stops one asset being booked twice over the same hours, and the four hundred bookings written by the old path have no period at all, so the constraint never considers them. An exclusion constraint compares values with an operator, and an operator against NULL is unknown, so a row with a null range conflicts with nothing and nothing conflicts with it. The period column was added when the constraint was, and the desk screen was changed to fill it. The overnight import was not, because it writes the start and the end as separate columns and always has, and both of those are still present and still correct. So the table enforces the rule for bookings made by a person and enforces nothing for bookings made by the file, and the double bookings that result are exactly the ones nobody is watching. Measured: 1,200 hire bookings of which 400 have no period, and all 400 overlap another booking of the same asset on the start and end times they do carry. Backfilling the period from the two columns and declaring it NOT NULL brings those rows under the constraint, and the import wants to write it. Every booking names a real asset, every start is before its end, and the bookings that do carry a period are provably free of overlap.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.hire_bookings a WHERE a.period IS NULL AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ops.hire_bookings b WHERE b.booking_id <> a.booking_id AND b.asset_id = a.asset_id AND b.starts_at < a.ends_at AND a.starts_at < b.ends_at)

defects.title: 600 booking notes are filed against a request number that does not exist
defects.why: The booking routine takes the key of the request it has just inserted from lastval, and an audit trigger on that table inserts a row of its own first, so lastval returns the audit key and every note is filed against a request that does not exist. lastval returns the value most recently produced by nextval in this session, whichever sequence produced it. The routine was written when the request table was the only thing with a sequence, and it was correct for two years. The audit trigger was added afterwards by a different piece of work. The identity value for the request is taken before any BEFORE trigger runs, so the trigger's own sequence is the last one moved and it is the one lastval answers with. Nothing fails: the note table has no foreign key, the numbers are the right shape, and the notes screen shows an empty list for a request rather than an error, which reads as a request nobody commented on. Measured: 600 booking notes, none of which name a request that exists, filed against 600 real requests. INSERT ... RETURNING request_id into a variable is the fix and cannot be broken by anything added later. Every request is recorded correctly, the audit is complete and points at the right request, and the text of every note is intact.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.booking_notes n WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ops.booking_requests r WHERE r.request_id = n.request_id)

defects.title: 1,500 saved searches are too short for the trigram index that covers them
defects.why: The saved searches are indexed for substring matching with trigrams, and fifteen hundred of the terms are two characters long, which is shorter than a trigram, so the index can do nothing for them. A trigram index cuts each value into three character pieces and looks a query up by the pieces it contains. A two character term contains no whole piece of the indexed value, so the index cannot narrow the search at all and the planner falls back to reading the table and matching every row. The short terms are the depot codes and the size codes, which is exactly what the counter staff type, and they are the searches run most often. The index looks healthy, it is used constantly by the long terms, and the statistics show it doing work, so the slow searches read as a busy afternoon rather than as an index that cannot help. Measured: 6,000 saved searches of which 1,500 are shorter than three characters, against a single trigram index on the term. Codes want matching by equality or by prefix against a plain index, and the free text wants the trigram index it already has. Every term is stored correctly, the index is valid and does answer the longer searches, and no search returns a wrong row.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.search_terms WHERE length(term) < 3) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_opclass o ON o.oid = i.indclass[0] WHERE i.indrelid = 'catalog.search_terms'::regclass AND o.opcname = 'gin_trgm_ops')

defects.title: 6,000 region labels are indexed under a collation version that has moved on
defects.why: The region labels are sorted under a collation the database still records at the version it was created with, and the operating system now provides a different one, so the index on the label is ordered by rules that are no longer in force. A collation is a library, not a property of PostgreSQL, and its sort order changes between releases of that library. PostgreSQL records the version it built each collation against so it can tell you when the two have parted company, and it tells you with a warning at every connection that touches it, which is exactly the kind of warning that gets filtered out of the application log. An index built under the old order is no longer in order under the new one, so an index scan can pass straight over a row that matches. Equality on a value that the two versions order differently can therefore return nothing while the row sits in the table, and a range over labels can miss its ends. Measured: 6,000 region labels behind 1 index whose column carries a collation whose recorded version does not match the one the system provides. Rebuilding the index and running ALTER COLLATION ... REFRESH VERSION is the whole fix, and it must be done in that order. Every label is present and correct, the column is the right type and length, and every query that reads the table without the index returns the right answer.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.region_labels) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = i.indrelid AND a.attnum = i.indkey[0] JOIN pg_collation c ON c.oid = a.attcollation WHERE i.indrelid = 'analytics.region_labels'::regclass AND c.collversion IS DISTINCT FROM pg_collation_actual_version(c.oid))

defects.title: 2,250 manifests print an hour that is not the hour the lorry loaded
defects.why: The manifest is printed with a twelve hour mask and no meridiem, so every load after one o'clock prints an hour that is not the hour it happened. HH in a date mask is the twelve hour clock. HH24 is the twenty four hour one, and the difference is two characters nobody reads twice. The mask was copied from a customer facing template, where it sat next to AM, and the AM was dropped here because the paper is narrow. Every morning load prints correctly, which is when the person who checks the manifests is on shift. The afternoon loads print as the morning of the same day, so the printed sheet says a lorry left at three in the morning, and the timestamp on the row, which is right, is not on the paper. The dispute that matters is always about the paper. Measured: 6,000 manifest lines of which 3,000 were loaded after midday and 2,250 print an hour that does not match the hour they were loaded, midday itself printing the same either way. HH24 in the mask fixes every print from here, and the stored timestamp is right, so the affected sheets can be reprinted exactly as they should have been. Every load time is recorded correctly, to the second, in the right time zone.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM fulfilment.manifest_prints WHERE printed_time <> to_char(loaded_at, 'HH24:MI')

defects.title: 4,800 rows sit in two tables the reporting role was never granted
defects.why: The reporting role was granted select on all tables in the schema, which grants it on the tables that existed at that moment and on nothing created afterwards, so the two tables added since carry no grant to it at all. ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA is not a standing rule. It expands to one grant per table at the time it runs, and the standing version is ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES, which is a different statement that has to be run before the tables are created. The grant was run once during the reporting rollout and written down as the way access is given, so every schema change since has shipped without it. Nothing has broken yet, and that is the trap: this database also hands PUBLIC a select on every table it creates, so the reports read the new tables through a grant nobody meant them to use. The day that public grant is withdrawn, which is on every remediation list ever written against this estate, the reporting role loses two tables it was never actually given and the overnight reports fail with permission denied. Measured: 4,800 rows across 2 tables whose access lists carry no grant to the reporting role, in a schema where 19 older tables carry one. ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES for the role that creates the tables makes it standing, and a repeat of the grant catches the two that are already here. The role is correct, its schema usage is right, and every table it was granted still reads.

detect.sql: SELECT ((SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.late_scan_counts) + (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.late_scan_reasons)) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class c WHERE c.oid IN ('analytics.late_scan_counts'::regclass, 'analytics.late_scan_reasons'::regclass) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM aclexplode(c.relacl) a WHERE a.grantee = 'manifest_reader'::regrole)) = 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 2,997 levy charges were rounded to the thousand by the column itself
defects.why: The levy amount is declared with a negative scale, so every value is rounded to the nearest thousand pence on the way in and the pence are gone. A negative scale is legal and it means the opposite of what a scale usually means: numeric(9,-3) keeps nine digits and stores the value to the nearest thousand. It was written during a modelling exercise about the size of the levy, where the figures were quoted in thousands, and it was copied into the table definition as though it described the units rather than the rounding. The rounding happens on insert, silently, exactly as a declared scale is supposed to. The source text is still on the row because the feed is kept verbatim, which is the only reason the difference can be shown. The levy is reconciled against the authority's statement, and it is out by up to five pounds per line in both directions, which nets to something small enough to be written off each month. Measured: 3,000 levy charges of which 2,997 differ from the amount the feed supplied, by up to 500 pence either way, the other 3 being the amounts that happened to land on a round thousand. Declaring the column numeric(12,0) keeps every pence and the reports can divide by a thousand where they want thousands. Every charge is against the right account, on the right date, and the text the authority sent is stored untouched.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.levy_charges WHERE amount_p <> amount_text::numeric

defects.title: 3,600 gate scans name a pass that now belongs to somebody else
defects.why: The site pass table was emptied with TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY and reloaded, so the pass numbers were handed out again from one and every scan recorded before the reload now names somebody else's pass. TRUNCATE does not reset a sequence unless it is asked to, and asking is one clause. It was added so the reloaded table would read from one again, which looked tidy in a table nobody joins to, except that the scan log joins to it. The scans keep the pass code they read at the time, because the reader writes what it scanned, and that is the only reason this is provable. The reload also changed the order, because the source file is sorted by holder now and was sorted by depot then, so the numbers did not land where they were. Every scan still resolves to a pass, which is what makes it dangerous: the gate report names a real person for every scan and names the wrong one. Measured: 3,600 pass scans, every one of which names a pass whose code is not the code the reader recorded at the gate, across 1,200 passes. Rekeying the scans from the code they recorded puts every scan back on the right pass, and the reload wants to leave the sequence alone. Every pass is valid, every holder is right, and every scan happened where and when it says.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.pass_scans s JOIN ops.site_passes p ON p.pass_id = s.pass_id WHERE p.pass_code <> s.pass_code_at_scan

defects.title: 3,000 archived cases were deleted by a purge that left every one of them
defects.why: The case archive carries a rule that turns every delete into an update, so the nightly purge reports three thousand rows deleted and the table still holds them. A DO INSTEAD rule replaces the statement it fires on. The delete never happens, the update that replaces it does, and the command tag the client receives is the tag of the rewritten statement, which reports the same row count. The rule was written to make a delete safe while an export was being proved, and the export was signed off eighteen months ago. A rule is invisible from the table: nothing in the column list or the constraints hints at it, and the only places it shows are the catalogue and a schema dump nobody reads to the end. The purge is measured by what it reports, so it has reported success every night since, while the archive has grown without bound and the retention statement the business signed is not true. Measured: 9,000 archived cases of which 3,000 were deleted by the purge, are flagged accordingly, and are still in the table. Dropping the rule and letting the delete through is one statement, after which the flagged rows can go in one pass. Every case is archived correctly, the flag records exactly which rows the purge asked for, and nothing has been lost.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM support.case_archive WHERE is_deleted) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_rewrite WHERE ev_class = 'support.case_archive'::regclass AND ev_type = '4' AND is_instead)

defects.title: 1,200 products lost every attribute they had to a null care note
defects.why: The care label backfill wrote each product's care note into the attributes document with jsonb_set, and jsonb_set returns null when any argument is null, so the twelve hundred products with no care note lost every attribute they had. jsonb_set is strict. Given a null value it does not leave the document alone, and it does not write a JSON null: it returns SQL NULL, and the update writes that over the whole column. The backfill was written against a sample where every product had a care note, because the sample came from the category that prompted the work. The column is nullable, as it has always been, so nothing raised. The product page treats a null document as a product with no attributes and renders the rest of the page normally, which is why this was not noticed for a season: the pages look sparse rather than broken. Measured: 6,000 care attribute rows of which 1,200 hold no document at all, every one of them a product whose care note was missing. Wrapping the value in coalesce, or filtering the update to rows that have a note, stops it happening again, and the lost attributes are recoverable from the catalogue feed. The 4,800 documents the backfill did write are correct and carry every attribute they had before.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.care_attributes WHERE attributes IS NULL AND care_note IS NULL

defects.title: 12,000 route legs are planned as though all 400 routes were one
defects.why: The route code column carries an n_distinct override of one, so the planner believes every leg is on the same route, and it plans as though any filter on the route returns the whole table. n_distinct can be set per column to tell the planner what ANALYZE cannot work out for itself, and it is the right tool on a column whose sampled estimate swings. It was set here during a tuning session on a table that had one route in it at the time, to stop the estimate collapsing to nothing, and it was never revisited when the other three hundred and ninety nine routes arrived. An override is not a hint, it is an assertion, and ANALYZE will not correct it: the value is taken as given every time the table is planned. So a query for one route is estimated at twelve thousand rows and gets a sequential scan and a hash join, when it returns thirty rows and wanted an index. The estimate is visible in every plan, and it is the one number in a plan that people assume ANALYZE keeps honest. Measured: 12,000 route legs across 400 route codes on a column whose declared n_distinct is 1. Resetting the option to zero returns the column to the sampled estimate, and ANALYZE does the rest. Every leg is on a real route, the distances are right, and the table is analysed on the usual schedule.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.route_legs) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT split_part(o, '=', 2)::numeric FROM pg_attribute a, unnest(a.attoptions) o WHERE a.attrelid = 'ops.route_legs'::regclass AND a.attname = 'route_code' AND split_part(o, '=', 1) = 'n_distinct') = 1 AND (SELECT count(DISTINCT route_code) FROM ops.route_legs) > 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 600 weighbridge readings are at or below zero under a check that skips them
defects.why: The weighbridge check that a net weight is positive was declared NO INHERIT, so the northern depot's table, which inherits from it, is under no check at all and holds six hundred readings at or below zero. NO INHERIT means the constraint applies to this table and to nothing that inherits from it. It exists for the case where the parent is a real table with rules of its own that the children do not share, and it was written here because the constraint was added while the parent was being backfilled and the child was in the middle of a load that would have failed. The clause was a way to get the constraint on without stopping the load, and the follow-up never happened. Selecting from the parent reads the child as well, so the bad readings are in every report the parent feeds, and the constraint is right there in the parent's definition for anyone who checks whether such a rule exists. It does exist. It just does not reach where the rows are. Measured: 5,000 tare readings visible through the parent, of which 600 are at or below zero, all of them in the inheriting table, under one check constraint marked as not inherited. Re-declaring the constraint without NO INHERIT, after correcting the six hundred, puts both tables under it. Every reading is stamped with the right depot and time, the parent's own rows all satisfy the rule, and the inheritance is set up correctly in every other respect.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.tare_readings WHERE net_kg <= 0) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'supply.tare_readings'::regclass AND contype = 'c' AND connoinherit)

defects.title: 500 card takings are banked under the day before the one they happened on
defects.why: The business day on every card taking is cut at midnight UTC, and the shops trade in London, so through the summer every taking in the first hour after midnight is filed under the day before. The timestamp is a timestamptz and is exactly right. The business day was derived from it by reading it at UTC, which is what you get if you cast without saying a zone, and for half the year UTC and London are the same, so the derivation was correct when it was written in February and tested the same week. From the last Sunday in March it is an hour out, and only for the takings between midnight and one, which is a quiet hour everywhere except the two sites with a late licence. The daily banking reconciles against the acquirer, whose day is London, and it has been out by a handful of transactions every night since spring, small enough that the difference is carried forward rather than investigated. Measured: 12,000 card takings of which 500 carry a business day that is not the London day they were taken on, summarised into 31 daily totals. Deriving the day with AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London' is the fix, and it is correct in both halves of the year. Every taking is stamped to the second with the right instant, every amount is right, and the totals are the correct sum of the rows filed under each day.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.card_takings WHERE business_day <> (taken_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London')::date

defects.title: 800 supplier names carry two characters where an accented letter belongs
defects.why: The supplier feed is UTF-8 and one loader reads it as Latin-1, so eight hundred supplier names hold two characters where an accented letter belongs. Reading UTF-8 as Latin-1 never fails, because every byte is a valid Latin-1 character. An accented letter is two bytes in UTF-8 and becomes two letters, so the name is longer than it was and looks like a typing accident rather than an encoding one. The database is correct: it was handed those characters and stored them faithfully. The loader in question is the older of the two and is used for the European suppliers, which is precisely where the accents are. Search is the visible damage: the buyer types the supplier name as it is spelled and finds nothing, then raises a second supplier record, which is how the same firm comes to be in the system twice. Measured: 4,000 supplier names of which 800 contain the byte sequence a UTF-8 accented letter takes when it is read as Latin-1. Re-reading those names from the feed as UTF-8 corrects them, and the loader wants its encoding declared rather than assumed. Every supplier reference is right, every name is against the right supplier, and the names without an accent came through both loaders identically.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.supplier_names WHERE position('Ã' in supplier_name) > 0

defects.title: 3,000 option positions disagree with the array stored on the same row
defects.why: The option positions were written by numbering the rows an unnest produced, sorted by the option name, and the position that matters is the position in the array, so half of them are wrong. unnest returns the elements of an array in order, and WITH ORDINALITY is how you keep that order. The routine that filled this table did not use it. It ordered by the option text instead, because the output looked tidier that way in the ticket that asked for it, and numbered the rows. For the products whose options were already entered alphabetically the two agree exactly, which is what made it look right in testing, and those are the products in the sample. For the rest the position is alphabetical and the array is the order the merchandiser chose, which is the order the size chart is printed in. So half the products show their sizes sorted by name, and the array on the same row says otherwise. Measured: 6,000 option positions of which 3,000 disagree with the position the option holds in the array stored beside them. unnest(options) WITH ORDINALITY gives the position directly and cannot drift from the array. Every option belongs to its product, every array is complete, and the products whose options were entered alphabetically are numbered correctly.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.option_positions WHERE recorded_position <> array_position(options, option_code)

defects.title: 9,000 works orders are numbered from a sequence that belongs to nothing
defects.why: The works order numbers come from a sequence that belongs to nothing, so nothing ties it to the column it feeds: it is not dropped with the table, not dumped with it, and not reset by anything that rebuilds it. A serial or identity column owns its sequence, and that ownership is what makes the pair behave as one object. This sequence was created on its own and named in a column default, which works perfectly and is how the column was converted off serial during a migration that wanted the sequence to survive the table being rebuilt. It did survive, and it has been unattached ever since. Restoring this schema on its own gives a table whose default calls a sequence that is not there, and every insert fails at once, which is at least loud. The quiet version is worse: a rebuild that recreates the sequence separately starts it at one and hands out numbers that are already on works orders in the field. Measured: 9,000 works orders numbered from 1 sequence that has no owning column, reached through a column default that does depend on it. ALTER SEQUENCE ... OWNED BY ops.job_numbers.job_no restores the link and changes nothing about how the numbers are handed out. Every works order has a unique number, the sequence is ahead of every number issued, and the default works exactly as intended.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.job_numbers) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_depend WHERE classid = 'pg_class'::regclass AND objid = 'ops.job_number_seq'::regclass AND deptype = 'a') = 0 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_depend WHERE classid = 'pg_class'::regclass AND objid = 'ops.job_number_seq'::regclass AND deptype = 'n') = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 16,000 route legs are planned as though the depot and the region were unrelated
defects.why: Every depot sits in exactly one region, and the planner has nothing that tells it so, so a query naming both a depot and its region is estimated at a fraction of a fraction and comes out near zero. PostgreSQL keeps statistics per column. Given a filter on two columns it multiplies the two selectivities, which is right when the columns are independent and badly wrong when one determines the other. Here one depot in forty and one region in eight multiply to one row in three hundred and twenty, and the true answer is one in forty, because naming the region after the depot excludes nothing. The reports name both, always, because the screen has both boxes and the region is filled in from the depot when the depot is picked. An estimate near zero makes the planner choose a nested loop and a plan that assumes a handful of rows, and it gets four hundred, on every leg of every route, in a join that is then executed four hundred times. CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies) on the two columns is one statement and ANALYZE picks the relationship up from the data. Measured: 16,000 route legs across 40 depot codes and 8 region codes, where the 40 distinct depots yield exactly 40 distinct depot and region pairs, on a table carrying no extended statistics object. Every leg names a real depot in its real region, the distances are right, and the table is analysed on the usual schedule.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.depot_routes) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_statistic_ext WHERE stxrelid = 'ops.depot_routes'::regclass) = 0 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT depot_code, region_code FROM ops.depot_routes) z) = (SELECT count(DISTINCT depot_code) FROM ops.depot_routes) AND (SELECT count(DISTINCT region_code) FROM ops.depot_routes) < (SELECT count(DISTINCT depot_code) FROM ops.depot_routes) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 4,000 contact cards have no mobile number and were never asked for one
defects.why: The contact card is a composite type, a mobile number was added to that type, and the four thousand cards already stored kept the shape they were written in, so every one of them holds nothing where the mobile number goes. Adding an attribute to a composite type rewrites the tables that use it and fills the new attribute with null, which is the only thing it can do. Nothing else happens: there is no default to apply, no constraint to violate, and no error. The cards captured since are complete, because the form that writes them was changed in the same piece of work. So the column is half populated along a line drawn on the day the type changed, and the line is invisible from the data, because a card with no mobile number looks exactly like a customer who did not give one. The dispatch text message goes to everyone with a mobile number on file, which is a query that returns the newer half of the book and looks entirely reasonable. Measured: 6,000 contact cards of which 4,000 hold no mobile number in the composite value, all of them captured before the attribute was added. The numbers are in the older contact table the cards were built from and can be backfilled from it. Every card names a real customer, every landline and email is correct, and the cards captured after the change carry the mobile number they were given.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.contact_cards WHERE (card).mobile IS NULL

defects.title: 12,000 reprints sit behind an index vacuum has been told to leave alone
defects.why: The reprint queue has index cleanup switched off, so vacuum reclaims the table and leaves the index alone, and the index grows without bound on a table whose whole content is replaced several times a day. vacuum_index_cleanup = off tells vacuum to skip the index pass. It exists for the case where a vacuum must finish quickly, usually to stop transaction ids wrapping around, and it is meant to be set for that vacuum and taken off again. It was set here during exactly such an incident, in the ALTER TABLE that was the fastest way to apply it, and an ALTER TABLE is permanent. Every vacuum since has been a partial one. The table stays small, which is the number anyone looks at, and the index does not, so the queue screen gets slower every week on a table of twelve thousand rows. Reindexing fixes it for a month and it has been done twice. Measured: 12,000 reprints on a table whose storage options carry vacuum_index_cleanup switched off. Resetting the option returns vacuum to its normal behaviour and one REINDEX recovers what has already been lost. Every reprint names a real consignment and printer, the printed timestamps are right, and the queue is emptied correctly.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.reprint_queue) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'ops.reprint_queue'::regclass AND reloptions @> ARRAY['vacuum_index_cleanup=off'])

defects.title: 6,000 products over twenty kilos are freighted as heavy because bulk is unreachable
defects.why: The banding rule tests for heavy before it tests for bulk, and heavy is the wider test, so the bulk branch can never be reached and the band has never once been assigned. A CASE takes the first branch that matches. Over ten is checked first and over twenty is checked second, and everything over twenty is already over ten, so the second branch is dead code that the database will not warn about, because it is a perfectly legal expression. The bulk band was added later, appended below the rule that was there, which is where a new branch naturally goes and is the one place it cannot go. Bulk carries a different carrier and a different rate, so six thousand products are quoted at the heavy rate and shipped on the heavy contract, which is cheaper per consignment and wrong for the pallet space they take. The carrier invoices for the space. The difference has been absorbed as a surcharge for a year. Measured: 9,000 freight bands of which 6,000 weigh more than twenty kilos and carry the heavy band, and 0 carry bulk. Reordering the branches heaviest first fixes every future row, and the six thousand can be rebanded in one update. Every weight is correct, every product reference is real, and the light and heavy boundary at ten kilos is applied exactly as the tariff states.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.freight_bands WHERE weight_kg > 20 AND band_code <> 'bulk'

defects.title: 1,800 pallet notes stop at 120 characters under a check nobody removed
defects.why: The pallet note column was widened from a hundred and twenty characters to four hundred and the check constraint that caps it at a hundred and twenty was left in place, so the extra room does not exist and every long note is cut to fit. Widening a varchar is one statement and it is the statement everybody remembers. The check was added separately, years earlier, to make the limit explicit for a client that read constraints rather than types, and it is not part of the column's type, so nothing about the widening touched it. The loader was changed at the same time to allow the longer note, and it truncates rather than fails, because a rejected pallet note stops a goods receipt and a truncated one does not. So the schema says four hundred, the type says four hundred, and the rows stop dead at a hundred and twenty, which is exactly where a damage description stops being useful. Measured: 1,800 pallet notes exactly 120 characters long, on a column declared to hold 400, under 1 check constraint that caps the length at 120. Dropping the constraint is the whole fix, and the full notes are still in the goods receipt files they were loaded from. Every note is against the right pallet and every note under the limit is stored in full.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.pallet_notes WHERE length(note) = 120) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT atttypmod FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'supply.pallet_notes'::regclass AND attname = 'note') = 404 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'supply.pallet_notes'::regclass AND contype = 'c') = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 300 intake rows are the column headings of the files they came from
defects.why: Every intake file starts with a row of column headings and the loader was pointed at the whole file, so each file contributed one row whose supplier reference is the words supplier ref and whose quantity is the words qty text. A COPY that is not told the file has a header treats the first line as data, and it will succeed whenever the columns it lands in accept text, which these do because the quantity is stored as text and parsed later. Storing the quantity as text was itself a decision to survive bad files, and it is what lets the bad row through. Nothing fails at load and nothing fails afterwards either: the quantity parse is wrapped so an unparseable value is skipped, so the header rows are counted in the row count of the intake, reported to the supplier as received, and silently dropped from the quantity total. The intake report and the quantity report therefore disagree by one row per file, every day, which reads as a rounding difference. Measured: 9,000 intake rows across 300 files, of which 300 are the header line of their file. HEADER on the COPY skips it, and the three hundred rows already stored can be removed by the value they hold. Every real row is against the right supplier and file, the quantities parse correctly, and the received dates are right.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.intake_rows WHERE supplier_ref = 'supplier_ref' AND qty_text = 'qty_text'

defects.title: 9,000 gate tickets are numbered above a sequence that still starts at one
defects.why: The gate tickets were loaded with their old numbers using OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE, which tells the identity column to accept the supplied value, and nothing moved the sequence afterwards, so the column that is supposed to generate the number has never generated one and still begins at one. OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE exists for exactly this load: a table is being migrated and the keys must come across unchanged. It does the job and it does nothing else. The sequence is only advanced when the column is allowed to generate, so after a load of nine thousand rows it is exactly where it was. Two things follow. Every ticket issued from now is numbered from one, so the printed ticket number is in a range the gate staff have not seen since the old system, and a ticket number is how a driver is identified at the barrier and on the paperwork. And when the sequence eventually reaches the range that was loaded, every insert fails on the primary key until somebody intervenes, with no warning before the first failure. Measured: 9,000 gate tickets, all of them numbered at or above the value the identity sequence would next hand out. setval on the identity sequence to just above the highest ticket is the fix and takes one statement. Every ticket is unique, carries the vehicle and gate it was issued at, and is stamped with the right arrival time.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.gate_tickets WHERE ticket_id >= (SELECT last_value FROM ops.gate_tickets_ticket_id_seq)

defects.title: 1,500 charges were dropped by the UNION that combines the two files
defects.why: The day file and the late file are combined with UNION rather than UNION ALL, so fifteen hundred charges that are genuinely separate and happen to be identical in every stored column were folded into one row each and are not billed. UNION removes duplicate rows. That is its definition and it is why it is slower than UNION ALL, and it is the wrong operator whenever the rows carry no key. These rows carry no key: the combined table holds an account, a date and an amount, because that is all the acquirer's file gives and nothing was added to tell one line from another. Two charges to the same account on the same day for the same amount are ordinary for a customer with two deliveries, and there is no column that distinguishes them, so the database cannot tell them apart and neither can anyone reading the table. The loss is invisible from the combined table and the daily total is short by the amount of the folded lines, which is why the reconciliation against the acquirer is out by a few hundred pounds a month. Measured: 9,000 charges across the two source files and 7,500 in the combined table, so 1,500 lost. UNION ALL keeps every line, and a line identifier from the source file makes the pair distinguishable for good. Both source files are complete, every account reference is real, and every amount is correct as sent.

detect.sql: SELECT ((SELECT count(*) FROM payments.charge_lines_day) + (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.charge_lines_late)) - (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.charge_lines_combined)

defects.title: 20,000 weigh events sit behind a BRIN index on an uncorrelated column
defects.why: The weigh events carry a BRIN index on the time they were weighed, and the rows are not stored in time order, so the index can exclude almost nothing and every query that uses it reads the whole table anyway. A BRIN index stores the smallest and largest value in each block range and skips a range when the value being looked for falls outside it. That is enormously cheap and it works only when the physical order of the rows follows the indexed column, which is the normal case for an append-only log. This table is not append-only: it is loaded from the six weighbridges in the order their files arrive, so every block range spans nearly the whole period and none of them can be skipped. The index is tiny, which is what makes it attractive and what stops anyone noticing it: it costs almost nothing to build, it is reported as used, and it returns the right answer. It just returns it after reading everything. Measured: 20,000 weigh events on a column whose statistical correlation with physical order is under 0.01, behind 1 BRIN index. A btree index on the same column answers the same queries properly, and BRIN becomes right again if the table is ever clustered on the timestamp and kept that way. Every event names a real weighbridge, the weights are correct, and the timestamps are right to the second.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.weigh_events) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class ic ON ic.oid = i.indexrelid JOIN pg_am am ON am.oid = ic.relam WHERE i.indrelid = 'ops.weigh_events'::regclass AND am.amname = 'brin') = 1 AND abs((SELECT correlation FROM pg_stats WHERE schemaname = 'ops' AND tablename = 'weigh_events' AND attname = 'weighed_at')) < 0.01 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 1,200 depot contracts name a depot that does not exist and pass the key anyway
defects.why: The contracts reference the depot terms by depot and term together, and the foreign key is MATCH SIMPLE, which is the default, so a row with one of the two columns null is not checked at all and twelve hundred contracts name a depot that has never existed. MATCH SIMPLE means the key is checked only when every column in it is non-null. MATCH FULL means it is checked unless every column is null. The difference matters only for composite keys and only when one column can be null, which is why it is almost never thought about, and the default is the permissive one. The term column is nullable because a contract can be signed before its terms are agreed, which is a real case and happens on about one contract in five. So one contract in five is admitted with no check on the depot either, and the depot code on those rows came from a spreadsheet column that was never validated. The contract list joins to the terms and those rows simply do not appear, which reads as contracts awaiting terms rather than contracts naming nothing. Measured: 6,000 depot contracts of which 1,200 have no term code and name a depot that appears nowhere in the terms table. MATCH FULL on the key rejects the mixed rows outright, and the twelve hundred depot codes can be corrected from the signed contracts. Every contract reference is unique, every signing date is right, and the 4,800 contracts with both columns filled reference terms that exist.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.depot_contracts c WHERE c.term_code IS NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM supply.depot_terms t WHERE t.depot_code = c.depot_code)

defects.title: 2,400 leaflets are missed by a search the index cannot answer
defects.why: The leaflet text is indexed with the simple text search configuration and the search screen queries it with the english one, so the index holds whole words where the query holds stems and the two never meet on any word that inflects. A text search configuration decides how a document is cut into searchable words, and the english one reduces a word to its stem, so returns and returning and returned all become return. The simple configuration does no stemming at all and stores returns as returns. The index was created with simple because simple was the example in the note the work was copied from, and the query uses english because english is the default configuration of the database. Searching for return therefore finds nothing in the index, and worse, the planner cannot use the index for that query at all, so it falls back to a sequential scan that recomputes the vector with english on every row and returns the right answer slowly. The index is never wrong; it is simply never used. Measured: 6,000 leaflets of which 2,400 match a stemmed english search that the simple vector does not match. Rebuilding the index with the english configuration, which is what the query uses, is the whole fix. Every leaflet names a real product, the text is stored intact, and the search returns the correct rows today.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.leaflet_text WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'return') AND NOT (to_tsvector('simple', body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'return'))

defects.title: 3,000 cycle counts are dated the day the table was created
defects.why: The count date has a fixed date as its default rather than CURRENT_DATE, so every count from the handheld, which does not send a date, is filed on the day the table was created. A default is an expression evaluated at insert. CURRENT_DATE evaluates to the day the row is written; a written-out date evaluates to itself, forever. The literal was put there during the build to make the first day of counts land somewhere sensible, and it reads as a sensible default to anyone scanning the table definition, because it is a real date in the right format and it is in the past. The stock system supplies its own date and is unaffected, which is two thirds of the rows and all of the rows anyone looked at. The handheld counts are a third of the table and they all claim to have happened on one day in February. Stock variance is measured by comparing consecutive counts of the same location, and three thousand counts stacked on a single date make that comparison meaningless for every location the handheld covers. Measured: 9,000 cycle counts of which 3,000 carry the default date while the row itself was created on a different day. DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE is the fix, and the three thousand can be re-dated from the creation timestamp, which is correct on every row. Every count names a real depot and counter, and the 6,000 counts that carry their own date are right.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.cycle_counts WHERE counted_on = DATE '2026-02-02' AND created_at::date <> DATE '2026-02-02'

defects.title: 2,400 specification lines were folded away by the document that holds them
defects.why: The specification document for each product is built by aggregating the source lines into a JSON object, and two of the ten lines per product repeat a key the first sheet already supplied, so the second value overwrites the first and two thousand four hundred lines are gone. A JSON object cannot hold the same key twice. Given two, the aggregate keeps the last one it saw, silently, because that is what a key means and there is nothing else it could do. The two sheets were never meant to overlap: the second was added for the attributes the first sheet does not carry, and eight of its keys are new. Two of them were reused by a supplier who filled in the wrong column, and nothing in either sheet or the aggregate complains. Which of the two survives depends on the order the rows are read, which is not fixed, so the same rebuild can produce a different document. The product page shows the attribute, with a value, so the page looks complete and the value is simply the wrong one. Measured: 12,000 specification lines aggregated into 1,200 documents holding 9,600 keys between them, so 2,400 lines lost. Grouping by product and key first, and raising the pairs that appear twice, surfaces the conflict rather than resolving it by accident. Every source line is stored intact, every product has a document, and the eight keys that appear once are correct.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.spec_source) - (SELECT sum((SELECT count(*) FROM jsonb_object_keys(d.doc))) FROM catalog.spec_documents d)

defects.title: 1,200 tip offs were accepted by the system and never stored
defects.why: The screening trigger on the tip off table returns NULL for anything under twenty characters, and a BEFORE INSERT trigger that returns NULL cancels the insert, so twelve hundred short reports were journalled, acknowledged and never stored. Returning NULL from a BEFORE ROW trigger is the documented way to suppress a row. It is not an error and it is not reported as one: the INSERT succeeds, the client is told zero rows were affected, and almost nothing checks that number. The rule itself was deliberate, written to stop empty test submissions filling the table, and twenty characters was a guess made in an afternoon. A real tip off is often short, because the useful ones are a pallet number and a time, and the form does not tell the reporter their report was dropped. The journal exists because the same trigger writes it before it decides, which is the only reason this is provable at all. The reports are anonymous, so nobody can be asked to resend. Measured: 6,000 tip offs submitted and journalled, 4,800 stored, so 1,200 dropped by the trigger. Rejecting with an error, or storing the row and flagging it for review, both make the outcome visible; returning NULL cannot. The 4,800 stored tip offs are complete and carry the depot and the time they were raised.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.tip_off_journal j WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ops.tip_offs t WHERE t.depot_code = j.depot_code AND t.body = j.body AND t.raised_at = j.raised_at)

defects.title: 3,000 prices did not move because the upsert keeps the older row
defects.why: The price upsert was meant to apply a change only when the incoming row is newer, and the comparison is written the wrong way round, so it applies a change only when the stored row is newer, which it never is, and three thousand price changes were discarded. The WHERE on an ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE decides whether the update happens. When it is false the conflicting row is skipped in silence: no error, no count, nothing to distinguish it from a row that was already correct. Written as stored newer than incoming, it is exactly backwards, and the two column references are easy to transpose because one is qualified by the table name and the other by EXCLUDED, and both read naturally. The insert half works perfectly, so a genuinely new product gets its price and only changes to existing products are lost. That is the half nobody tests, because a price that does not change is the normal outcome for most of the catalogue on most days. Measured: 9,000 prices in the feed, 3,000 of which differ from the stored price and carry a later timestamp than the row that was kept. Reversing the comparison to EXCLUDED newer than stored is the whole fix, and the three thousand can be reapplied from the feed as it stands. Every sku exists, every price in the feed is correct, and the 6,000 prices the feed did not change are right.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.price_updates u JOIN supply.price_feed f USING (sku) WHERE u.price_p <> f.price_p AND f.updated_at > u.updated_at

defects.title: 18,000 picking slots are indexed with no room left for the next update
defects.why: The index over the time a picking slot was last touched was built with fillfactor set to a hundred, so every page was packed solid at build time, and the column it indexes changes on every pick. A btree index defaults to ninety for exactly this reason: the ten per cent left free absorbs the entries that arrive after the build without splitting a page. Packed to a hundred, the first new entry on a full page splits it, and a split is a page allocation, two page writes and a parent update. The setting was applied because the index is read far more than it is written, which is true, and because a denser index is a smaller index, which is also true, and both are reasons that apply to a static table. This table is the opposite of static: the touched time is rewritten every time a picker takes a unit, which is the highest write rate in the warehouse. So the index is now a long chain of half full pages, larger than it would have been at ninety, and it is rebuilt by hand every few months. Measured: 18,000 picking slots behind 1 index whose storage options pin fillfactor at 100. Dropping the option and reindexing returns it to the default and the rebuilds stop. Every slot names a real aisle and sku, the unit counts are right, and the index answers every query correctly.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.picking_slots) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'ops.idx_picking_slots_touched'::regclass AND reloptions @> ARRAY['fillfactor=100'])

defects.title: 7,284 pack yields drop the part pack the division leaves behind
defects.why: The number of packs is a stored generated column that divides the total units by the pack size, both of them integers, so the division truncates and the part pack at the end of every run is not counted. Integer division in PostgreSQL discards the remainder. It does not round and it does not warn, and the expression reads as ordinary arithmetic to anyone reviewing the table. It is a generated column, which makes it worse in one specific way: the value is computed by the database and stored, so it carries the authority of a column rather than the suspicion of a report, and nothing downstream recomputes it. The part pack is real product. It is packed, labelled and shipped, and it is the pack that makes a promotion run short, because a promotion is quoted in packs and picked in units. Measured: 9,000 pack yields of which 7,284 have units left over after the division and therefore understate the packs by one. Casting one side to numeric and applying ceil gives the number of packs that actually leave the line, and the column can be redefined in place. Every total and every pack size is correct, and the 1,716 products whose run divides exactly are right.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.pack_yields WHERE total_units % pack_size <> 0

defects.title: 4,800 margin rates are a hundred times the rates beside them
defects.why: Two loaders write the margin rate into the same column and they disagree about the units, so four thousand eight hundred rows hold a percentage and the rest hold a fraction, and nothing in the column says which is which. The column is a plain numeric and both values are valid numerics. A rate of 0.32 and a rate of 32 are the same margin, and the only way to tell them apart is to know which system wrote the row, which is recorded but is not something any report consults. The finance sheet has always quoted percentages and the margin service has always quoted fractions, and they were pointed at the same table when the reporting was consolidated, on the assumption that a rate is a rate. Every consumer picks one convention and is wrong about two rows in five. The category comparison is the visible damage: a category loaded by the sheet appears to out-earn one loaded by the service by a factor of a hundred, which is large enough that the chart is dismissed as broken rather than read. Measured: 12,000 margin rates of which 4,800 are greater than 1 and therefore cannot be fractions. Dividing the percentage rows by a hundred and constraining the column to the range a fraction can take stops it recurring. Every rate names a real category and period, and each loader's rows are internally consistent and correct in its own units.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.margin_rates WHERE margin_rate > 1

defects.title: 5,787 inspection findings were destroyed by a purge of the visits above them
defects.why: The visit purge keeps two years of depot visits, the findings underneath them are on a seven year retention, and the foreign key cascades on delete, so purging the visits took nearly six thousand findings with them. ON DELETE CASCADE is a property of the child table and it is applied without reference to why the parent is being deleted. It was declared so that deleting a visit entered in error would not leave findings pointing at nothing, which is a real and reasonable need, and it is indistinguishable from the purge as far as the database is concerned. The two retention periods were set by different people for different reasons: visits are operational and short lived, findings are evidence and are kept because a regulator can ask for them. Nothing connects the two rules, and the purge job was written against the visits table alone because that is the table the retention policy names. The findings are gone, the purge reports the number of visits it removed and nothing else, and the loss is only visible against the journal the inspection app writes. Measured: 9,000 findings ever raised, 3,213 still present, so 5,787 destroyed by the cascade. ON DELETE RESTRICT forces the purge to confront the findings instead of silently taking them, and the deleted findings are recoverable from the journal. Every surviving finding is attached to a real visit, every visit names a real depot and inspector, and the journal is complete.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.finding_journal j WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ops.visit_findings f WHERE f.visit_id = j.visit_id AND f.finding_text = j.finding_text)

defects.title: 9,000 import costs took one of two duty rates and nothing recorded which
defects.why: The duty rate on every import was set by an UPDATE that joins the rate table on the country alone, every country has two rates because the rate changed at the start of this year, and an UPDATE that matches two source rows applies one of them and discards the other without saying which. This is the one place PostgreSQL will not protect you. A SELECT that joins two rows returns two rows and the fan out is visible; an UPDATE has to produce one value per target row, so it takes the first match the plan happens to reach and does not warn. The statement was written when each country had one rate, which was true for two years, and it was correct then in the way that matters least: it worked. Which rate each import got depends on the plan, the plan depends on the statistics, and the statistics change, so the same statement run again can produce different rates for the same imports and a rebuild of this database does not reproduce the same split. The duty is reclaimed from the revenue authority per consignment, so a wrong rate is a wrong claim, in both directions. Measured: 9,000 import costs, every one of them against a country carrying more than one duty rate, so every rate on the table was chosen arbitrarily rather than selected. On the build this was measured from, 5,250 took the superseded rate; that number is not stable across rebuilds, which is the defect rather than an artefact of it. A DISTINCT ON over the rates ordered by effective date, or a lateral picking the rate in force on the consignment date, makes the choice explicit. Every consignment, country and goods value is correct, and both duty rates are genuine.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.import_costs c WHERE (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.duty_rates d WHERE d.country_code = c.country_code) > 1

defects.title: 3,600 rebates in euros and dollars are added into a sterling total
defects.why: The supplier rebate lines carry the currency they were agreed in, the period totals are labelled sterling, and the total is a plain sum over every line regardless of currency, so three thousand six hundred amounts in euros and dollars are added to sterling as though a euro were a pound. The currency column is right and it is populated on every line. It is simply not in the GROUP BY and not in the sum, because the totals table was built when every supplier was domestic and the column was added later for the European and American suppliers without revisiting anything downstream. Nothing errors, because the amounts are all numeric and adding numerics is what addition does. The total is labelled GBP, which makes it look checked. It overstates by roughly the difference in the exchange rates on the non sterling lines, which is a few per cent, small enough to look like the rebate accrual being slightly optimistic and large enough to matter on a number that goes into the year end. Measured: 9,000 rebate lines summed into period totals labelled GBP, of which 3,600 are not in GBP. Converting at the rate on the line date before summing, or totalling per currency and never adding across them, both give a defensible number. Every line names a real supplier and period, every amount is correct in its own currency, and the currency code on every line is right.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.rebate_lines r JOIN analytics.rebate_totals t USING (period_start) WHERE r.currency_code <> t.currency_code

defects.title: 1,800 brand synonyms point at a brand they cannot be joined to
defects.why: One of the two loaders reads a fixed width supplier feed without stripping the padding, so eighteen hundred synonyms carry a brand name with two trailing spaces and no equality join to the brand list will ever match them. Trailing space is the hardest difference to see. It is invisible in every grid and every log, it survives copy and paste, and the two values look identical side by side in a screenshot, which is how this gets argued about rather than fixed. The type is text, which preserves the padding exactly as given; the same value in a char column would compare equal, which is a difference between two types nobody remembers until it bites. The synonyms exist so that a search for a colloquial name finds the brand, and these eighteen hundred find nothing, so the brand appears to have no alternative names and the search returns an empty page for the name customers actually use. Measured: 9,000 brand synonyms of which 1,800 name a brand that exists once the padding is removed and does not exist with it. Trimming on the way in fixes the loader, and the stored rows can be trimmed in one update because the untrimmed value is otherwise correct. Every synonym is unique, the brand list is complete, and the 7,200 synonyms from the other loader join correctly.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.brand_synonyms s WHERE btrim(s.brand_name) <> s.brand_name AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM catalog.brand_list b WHERE b.brand_name = s.brand_name) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM catalog.brand_list b WHERE b.brand_name = btrim(s.brand_name))

defects.title: 15,000 lane slots are indexed by date first and always searched by lane
defects.why: The only index on the lane slots leads with the booking date and the transport desk searches by lane, so the index cannot be used for the search that is actually run and every lookup reads the table. A multi column btree can be used for a filter on its leading column, or on a leading run of its columns, and for nothing else: a filter on the second column alone has no starting point in the index, so the planner ignores it. The index was created for a report that lists a week's bookings, which does lead with the date and which runs once a day. The desk screen asks for a lane and gets every booking on it, which runs a few hundred times a day and is the query people wait on. Both queries return the right rows, so the only symptom is that the screen is slower than the report, which sounds like the screen's fault. Reversing the column order serves both: a filter on the lane uses the leading column, and the date report can still use the index for its range once the lane is known, or keep its own. Measured: 15,000 lane slots behind 1 index whose leading column is the booking date, and 0 indexes leading with the lane. Every booking names a real lane and carrier, the pallet counts are right, and the index is valid and correctly maintained.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.lane_slots) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = i.indrelid AND a.attnum = i.indkey[0] WHERE i.indrelid = 'ops.lane_slots'::regclass AND a.attname = 'booked_on') = 1 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = i.indrelid AND a.attnum = i.indkey[0] WHERE i.indrelid = 'ops.lane_slots'::regclass AND a.attname = 'lane_code') = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 4,800 customers were never asked for consent and are counted as refusing
defects.why: The marketing consent flag has three states and only two of them are written down: true is yes, false is no, and null means the customer has never been asked, which is recorded nowhere except in the absence of a value. A nullable boolean is three valued and it is almost always used as though it were two valued. Here the third state is the one that matters most, because it is the only one that can still be changed: a customer who refused has decided, and a customer who was never asked has not. The asked date column is the evidence, and it is null on exactly the same rows, which is the only reason the two can be told apart at all. Every report that counts consent writes marketing_ok = false or NOT marketing_ok, and both of those exclude nulls, so the nulls fall out of the yes count and out of the no count and are then reported as no by subtraction from the customer total. So four thousand eight hundred customers appear in the refusal figure that goes to the regulator, and appear nowhere in the list of people it is still legitimate to ask. Measured: 12,000 consent rows of which 4,800 hold no value and carry no asked date. Splitting the column into a consent state with three named values, or a consent flag plus a NOT NULL asked date, removes the ambiguity. Every customer reference is real, the 7,200 answered rows carry the answer the customer gave and the date they gave it.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM support.opt_in_flags WHERE marketing_ok IS NULL AND asked_on IS NULL

defects.title: 24,000 stream rows have nothing that tells one row from another
defects.why: The event stream table has no primary key, no unique constraint and no index of any kind, and its replica identity is the default, which means the primary key it does not have. Three things follow and all of them are quiet. Logical replication of an update or a delete on this table fails outright, because the publisher has no way to name the row it changed, so the table can never be added to a publication without altering it first. Nothing can address a single row: correcting one event means matching on all four columns and hoping the match is unique, and it frequently is not, because the same session firing the same event twice in the same second produces two rows that are identical in every column. And any query that is not a full scan is impossible. The table was created by the analytics load, which only ever appends and only ever reads everything, so none of this was felt at the time and it is felt by everybody who has come to it since. Measured: 24,000 stream rows, 0 indexes, and a replica identity of d, which is the default setting and resolves to a primary key that does not exist. An identity column as the primary key costs almost nothing on an append only table and makes every one of the three problems go away. Every event name, session reference and timestamp is correct, and the table is complete.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.stream_rows) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'analytics.stream_rows'::regclass) = 0 AND (SELECT relreplident FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'analytics.stream_rows'::regclass) = 'd' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 2,700 zero rated items are sold as standard rated by the feed that omits the tax code
defects.why: The item feed is a view written as SELECT star, the tax code was added to the table afterwards, and a view does not mean star, it means the columns that existed when it was created. PostgreSQL expands the star once, at creation, and stores the resolved column list. That is the only sane thing it can do, because a view has a fixed row type that other objects depend on, and it is the opposite of what everybody assumes a star means. The feed therefore has three columns and the table has four, and nothing anywhere reports a discrepancy: the view is valid, it is not stale, and it returns correct values for every column it has. The tax code is the column that decides whether an item is charged at the standard rate or at zero, and the two thousand seven hundred zero rated items in the catalogue are food and children's clothing. The feed is what the storefront prices from, so those items are sold with tax added that should not be there, and the difference is refunded one complaint at a time. Measured: 9,000 items in the table with 4 columns, behind a view with 3, of which 2,700 carry a tax code other than the standard rate. CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW with the columns named explicitly fixes it and makes the next addition visible as a change to the view rather than a silent omission. Every item, name and price is correct, the tax code on the table is right, and the three columns the view does carry are accurate.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.item_master WHERE tax_code <> 'S') * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'catalog.item_feed'::regclass AND attnum > 0 AND NOT attisdropped) < (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'catalog.item_master'::regclass AND attnum > 0 AND NOT attisdropped) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 3,000 device pings are dated fifty six thousand years in the future
defects.why: The ping time is a bare epoch number, the old firmware sends seconds and the replacement sends milliseconds, and nothing in the column says which, so three thousand pings read as dates tens of thousands of years from now. An epoch is a count since the start of 1970 and the unit is a convention, not a property of the number. Both firmwares are internally consistent and both are behaving exactly as their own documentation says. The column is a bigint, which accepts either happily, and there is no constraint on it because any constraint would have to encode the convention that was never written down. A thousandfold error is not subtle, and it is invisible here because nothing converts the number back to a date: the monitoring compares pings to each other, so a device on the new firmware is compared with itself and looks fine, and a fleet wide gap analysis mixes the two and reports every old device as silent. The firmware version is on the row, which is the only reason the two groups can be told apart. Measured: 12,000 device pings of which 3,000 hold a value above one hundred billion, which cannot be a number of seconds for any date this system will see. Storing a timestamptz rather than a number removes the convention entirely, and the millisecond rows can be divided by a thousand safely because they are identifiable. Every ping names a real device, the firmware version is right on every row, and each firmware's numbers are correct in its own units.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.device_pings WHERE sent_epoch > 100000000000

defects.title: 1,200 pack lines lost the pack type they were counted under
defects.why: Retiring twelve pack types set the pack code to null on every line that used them, because the foreign key is declared ON DELETE SET NULL, so twelve hundred consignment lines now record a quantity against no pack type at all. ON DELETE SET NULL keeps the referential rule true by removing the reference, which is right when the link is genuinely optional and wrong when it is the thing that gives the row meaning. It was chosen over RESTRICT because RESTRICT once blocked a tidy up at five o'clock on a Friday, and SET NULL let the delete through. The column had to be made nullable to allow it, which removed the only protection the table had. A pack line without a pack type cannot be converted to a volume or a pallet count, so it falls out of every capacity calculation silently: the units are still there, the line is still there, and the group by on pack type simply does not include it. The retired pack types were not wrong, they were superseded, and the lines should have been repointed at the pack types that replaced them. Measured: 12,000 pack lines of which 1,200 hold no pack code, all of them lines whose pack type was retired. RESTRICT forces the repointing to happen first, and the twelve hundred are recoverable from the consignment paperwork. Every line names a real consignment, every quantity is right, and the 10,800 lines that kept their pack type reference one that exists.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.pack_lines WHERE pack_code IS NULL

defects.title: 12,000 components are indexed in a way the supplier part lookup cannot use
defects.why: The component attributes carry a GIN index built with the default jsonb operator class, and the lookup the buyers run asks for a single key by equality with the arrow operator, which that index cannot answer. The default class indexes containment and key existence, so it serves the containment operator and nothing else. A query written as attrs arrow arrow supplier part equals a value is an expression on a text result, and the planner has no index on that expression, so it reads the table. Rewriting the same query as containment, attrs contains a small object, uses the index and returns the same rows, and the two forms look interchangeable to anyone who is not thinking about index support. The buyers' screen was written by someone reading the jsonb documentation from the top, where the arrow operators appear first, and the index was created by someone reading the indexing page, and neither knew about the other. The index is real, maintained and used by other queries, which is why nobody has looked at it. Measured: 12,000 components behind 1 GIN index using the default jsonb operator class, with no index on the supplier part expression the lookup filters by. A btree index on the extracted supplier part, or jsonb_path_ops plus a containment query, both fix it. Every component reference is unique, every attribute document is well formed, and the lookup returns the right rows.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.component_codes) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_opclass o ON o.oid = i.indclass[0] WHERE i.indrelid = 'catalog.component_codes'::regclass AND o.opcname = 'jsonb_ops') = 1 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'catalog.component_codes'::regclass) = 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 4,007 settlements differ from the ledger by the width of a single precision float
defects.why: The settlement service holds the exchange rate as a single precision float and the ledger holds the same rate as a numeric, and single precision carries about seven significant digits, which is not enough for a rate with six decimal places multiplied by a six figure amount. So four thousand of nine thousand settlements are a penny or two away from the ledger. Single precision is half the storage of double precision and it is the right choice for a sensor reading. It is never the right choice for money or for a rate that money is multiplied by, and the two uses are easy to confuse because a rate looks like a measurement. The rate itself survives a round trip, because rounding it back to six decimal places hides the loss, which is exactly why this passed review: someone checked the rates and they matched.
