The loss appears in the product, after the multiplication, in the pence. Nothing reconciles automatically, so the difference is found by the month end break and written off as a rounding difference, which is what it is, and it is a rounding difference that never stops. Measured: 9,000 quotes of which 4,007 settle to a different amount under the float rate than under the numeric one. Declaring the rate numeric on both sides removes the difference entirely, and the affected settlements can be recomputed from the numeric rate, which is correct on every row. Every quote names a real currency pair and date, and both rates are the same rate to six decimal places.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.fx_quotes WHERE settled_exact <> settled_float

defects.title: 5,451 docket slices are piling up in the partition that was meant to be empty
defects.why: The docket slices are partitioned by month, the partitions run out at the end of June, and a default partition catches everything after that, so five and a half thousand slices are in one undivided heap instead of the months they belong to. A default partition is a safety net: it exists so an insert outside every declared range succeeds rather than failing. That is the whole point of it and it is also the whole problem, because the failure is the only signal that the partitions have run out. The job that creates next month's partition stopped running in June, and nothing noticed, because inserts kept working. Two costs follow. Every query that filters on a date after June has to read the default partition in full, since the planner knows only that it holds whatever did not fit elsewhere, so partition pruning does nothing for the most recent and most queried data. And a new partition cannot now be created for July without either moving those rows or detaching the default first, which turns a routine maintenance job into a planned outage. Measured: 18,000 docket slices of which 5,451 are in the default partition, behind 6 monthly partitions that end at the start of July. Creating the missing partitions and an alert on default partition row count is the fix; the default itself is worth keeping, empty. Every slice carries a real docket reference, date and unit count, and the six monthly partitions hold exactly the rows they should.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ONLY ops.docket_slices_default

defects.title: 15,000 session locks are on the one table autovacuum has been told to skip
defects.why: Autovacuum is switched off on the session lock table, which is the highest churn table in the database: every row is written, updated once when the lock is released, and deleted within the hour. Turning autovacuum off on a table does not stop the table needing vacuum, it stops anything doing it. Dead rows accumulate at the rate of the churn, the table bloats, and every scan of it reads the dead rows as well as the live ones, so a table that holds a few thousand live locks can occupy hundreds of megabytes and take a hundred times as long to scan as it should. It was switched off during an incident, because autovacuum was holding a lock the release job wanted and turning it off made the symptom stop that night. There is a second and worse consequence: autovacuum is also what advances the frozen transaction id, and a table excluded from it eventually forces the whole database into a protective shutdown to prevent wraparound, which is an outage for everything, not just this table. Measured: 15,000 session locks on a table whose storage options carry autovacuum_enabled switched off. Turning it back on, and tuning the thresholds rather than disabling it, is the fix; the lock contention it was hiding is a separate and smaller problem. Every lock names a real session and resource, and the held times are correct.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.session_locks) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'ops.session_locks'::regclass AND reloptions @> ARRAY['autovacuum_enabled=false'])

defects.title: 20,000 claims are planned from a single sampled value
defects.why: The claim status column has its statistics target set to one, so ANALYZE keeps a single most common value for it, and the status distribution is extremely skewed: almost everything is settled and the eighty claims that are not are the only ones anybody looks for. With a target of one, the planner learns that settled is common and learns nothing about anything else. Every other status falls into a single undifferentiated remainder and is estimated from it, so a query for the disputed claims is estimated at thousands of rows when it returns forty, and the planner takes a sequential scan over the index that exists precisely for that query. The setting was applied during a tuning exercise to make ANALYZE cheaper on a large table, where the column was believed to be almost constant and therefore not worth sampling. It is almost constant. The rare values are the entire reason the table is queried. Measured: 20,000 claims of which 80 are not settled, on a column whose statistics target is 1 and for which ANALYZE has recorded 1 most common value. Resetting the target to the default, or raising it, lets the planner see the rare statuses and use the index. Every claim names a real supplier, the values are right, and the index on the status is valid and correctly maintained.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.claim_rows) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT attstattarget FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'analytics.claim_rows'::regclass AND attname = 'claim_status') = 1 AND (SELECT array_length(most_common_vals, 1) FROM pg_stats WHERE schemaname = 'analytics' AND tablename = 'claim_rows' AND attname = 'claim_status') = 1 AND (SELECT count(DISTINCT claim_status) FROM analytics.claim_rows) > 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 9,000 payment batches are numbered from a sequence that skips a thousand at a time
defects.why: The batch number sequence caches a thousand values, so every session that takes a single number reserves a thousand and discards the rest when it disconnects. A sequence cache is per session and per backend. It exists to avoid touching the sequence on every call under heavy concurrency, and a cache of a thousand is appropriate for a sequence called a thousand times a second by a long lived connection. This one is called a handful of times by each nightly run, from a connection that exits afterwards, so nine hundred and ninety odd numbers are burned every time. Nothing breaks: the numbers are still unique and still ascending within a session, which is all a sequence promises. But the batch number is quoted to the bank on the settlement file, the finance team reads the gaps as missing batches, and reconciling a gap that does not correspond to anything is a morning's work each time it is queried. Worse, numbers handed out by two concurrent sessions interleave in blocks, so batch numbers are not in the order the batches ran, which is the one thing everybody assumes they are. Measured: 9,000 payment batches numbered from 1 sequence whose cache is set to 1000. Setting the cache to one costs nothing at this call rate and makes the numbers dense and ordered again. Every batch number is unique, every run label and start time is correct, and no batch is missing.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.batch_numbers) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT seqcache FROM pg_sequence WHERE seqrelid = 'payments.batch_no_seq'::regclass) = 1000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 2,400 batch records have no expiry under a rule that says they must
defects.why: The expiry date was made mandatory with a NOT NULL constraint added NOT VALID, which applies to every row written from that moment and to none of the rows already there, so two thousand four hundred batches still carry no expiry at all. Adding NOT VALID is the standard way to make a rule mandatory without taking the lock and the scan that checking the whole table requires, and it is exactly right as the first of two steps. The second step is VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, which does the scan without blocking writes, and it was never run, because the first step made the errors stop and the ticket was closed. The constraint reads as an ordinary NOT NULL everywhere except in the one catalogue column that records whether it has been validated. So the column is documented as mandatory, the application trusts it and no longer checks, and a stock rotation report that orders by expiry silently drops a fifth of the batches, which are then never pulled from the shelf. Measured: 12,000 batch records of which 2,400 hold no expiry, under 1 not-null constraint that is present and not validated. Backfilling the expiry from the goods receipt and then running VALIDATE CONSTRAINT completes the change that was started. Every batch reference is unique, every supplier is real, and the 9,600 batches with an expiry carry the right one.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.batch_records WHERE expires_on IS NULL) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'supply.batch_records'::regclass AND contype = 'n' AND NOT convalidated)

defects.title: 6,300 sizes sort before size 9 because they are text
defects.why: The size is stored as text and every size is a number, so the sizes sort as words: 10 comes before 9, 2 comes after 19, and the size list on every product page is in an order that is correct for text and nonsense for clothing. Text ordering compares character by character, so the first character decides, and 1 sorts before 9 regardless of what follows. The column is text because the sizing was going to include letters one day, which it still does not, and because the import file has them quoted. There is an index on it, which makes it worse rather than better: a range query for sizes between eight and twelve is a text range, it uses the index happily, and it returns the wrong set with no sign of trouble. The size list is also what the size chart is printed from, so the printed chart runs 1, 10, 11 and so on, and the buyers reorder it by hand every season. Measured: 9,000 sizes of which 6,300 are ten or more and therefore sort before size 9 in text order. Storing the size as a numeric, or as an integer with a separate label column for the day the letters arrive, fixes the ordering and the ranges together. Every size is against the right product, every value is a valid number, and the range labels are correct.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.size_codes WHERE size_text::numeric >= 10 AND size_text < '9'

defects.title: 500 shift logs are filed against the day before the one they happened on
defects.why: The logged day is stored as the date part of the timestamp read in UTC, the depots are in London, and London is an hour ahead in summer, so every log made in the first hour after midnight is filed against the previous day. A timestamptz holds an instant, not a date, and turning one into a date requires choosing a zone. The cast used here chooses UTC, which is the zone the server runs in and not the zone anybody works in. For eight months of the year the two agree and nothing is visibly wrong. Between the last Sunday in March and the last Sunday in October they are an hour apart, and the hour that falls off the end of the day falls onto the day before. The shift report is what the depot supervisors are paid against, so a log at half past midnight pays the wrong day, and the correction arrives from payroll a month later as a query about a shift nobody worked. Measured: 12,000 shift logs of which 500 carry a stored day that does not match the date of the same instant read in Europe/London. Storing the day as the London date, or dropping the column and deriving it with an explicit zone, removes the choice from the load. Every log names a real depot, the instants are all correct, and the minutes worked are right.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.shift_logs WHERE logged_day <> (logged_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London')::date

defects.title: 2,250 label codes fall outside a range that was meant to hold every one of them
defects.why: The label code column is declared COLLATE C while the database is en_US.utf8, so the codes sort by byte value, and the picker query that asks for everything between a and z quietly excludes every code that starts with a capital letter. A collation is what makes a text comparison mean something, and C means compare the bytes. Under the database collation the letters interleave, so an uppercase A sits next to a lowercase a and both are inside the range. Under C every uppercase letter is below every lowercase one, so all of them fall out of the bottom. The column was given the C collation for speed, which is real: byte comparison is markedly faster, and on a code column that was going to be all uppercase it costs nothing. Then the codes stopped being all uppercase. The query does not fail, the index is used, and the result is a quarter short. Measured: 9,000 label codes of which 2,250 fall outside the range under the column's own collation and inside it under the database default. Dropping the collation from the column, or writing the range query with an explicit collation, makes the two agree. Every code is unique, every label text is correct, and the 6,750 lowercase codes are returned properly.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.label_codes WHERE label_code NOT BETWEEN 'a' AND 'zzz' AND (label_code COLLATE "default") BETWEEN 'a' AND 'zzz'

defects.title: 1,333 ledger counters are within a sixth of the largest number the column can hold
defects.why: The ledger counters are stored in a four byte integer, which stops at 2,147,483,647, and more than a thousand of them are already above two billion. An integer overflow in PostgreSQL is not a wraparound to a negative number, which is what most people expect and would at least be visible. It is an error: the update fails, the transaction rolls back, and the ledger posting it was part of rolls back with it. So the failure mode is not a wrong number, it is a payment run that stops, at a moment nobody chose, on whichever counter crosses first. The column is an integer because it was a count of documents and four bytes was plenty for that. It is now a count of ledger movements, which is three orders of magnitude larger, and the type was never revisited because nothing about the change touched the schema. Measured: 8,000 ledger counters of which 1,333 hold a value above two billion, in a column whose maximum is 2,147,483,647. Widening the column to bigint is an ALTER that rewrites the table and is far cheaper now than during the incident. Every counter name is unique and every value is the correct count of what it counts.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.ledger_counters WHERE counter_value > 2000000000) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT atttypid FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'payments.ledger_counters'::regclass AND attname = 'counter_value') = 'int4'::regtype THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 16,000 page counters are indexed on the one column that changes on every request
defects.why: There is a btree index on the hit count, which is the column the recorder increments on every single request, so every increment writes an index entry as well as a row. PostgreSQL can usually update a row without touching any index, by writing the new version on the same page and chaining it to the old one. That optimisation is off the moment an indexed column changes. So an index on a counter converts a cheap in page update into a full row rewrite plus an index insert plus an index entry to clean up later, and it does so at exactly the rate of the traffic. The index exists because someone wanted the most visited pages, which is a reporting query that runs once a day and could sort sixteen thousand rows without an index in a few milliseconds. The cost is paid on every write to serve a read that happens once. Measured: 16,000 page counters behind 1 btree index on the counter column, which every request updates. Dropping the index removes the write cost entirely and the daily report will not notice. Every path is unique, every count is accurate, and the last hit time is right.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.page_hits) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_index i WHERE i.indrelid = 'analytics.page_hits'::regclass AND i.indkey::int2[] @> ARRAY[(SELECT attnum FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'analytics.page_hits'::regclass AND attname = 'hit_count')]::int2[])

defects.title: 2,000 vendor references name a vendor that does not exist
defects.why: The vendor reference is a plain text column with no foreign key behind it, and two thousand of the documents name a vendor code that is not in the vendor list. Without a foreign key the database has no opinion about what that column contains. It is text, the values look like vendor codes, every tool that reads the schema will guess that they are vendor codes, and nothing checks. The codes came in from a supplier portal that numbers its own vendors independently, and the overlap with the internal list is partial. The relationship is real and it is enforced nowhere, so it is enforced by whoever writes the next query, differently each time. A report that joins vendor to document silently loses those two thousand documents, and a report that counts documents finds them, and the two numbers are then reconciled by hand every month. Measured: 14,000 vendor references of which 2,000 name a code absent from the 600 vendors on file, under 0 foreign keys. Adding the foreign key after the two thousand are resolved makes the guess into a fact. Every document reference is unique, every date is right, and the 12,000 references that do match point at the correct vendor.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.vendor_refs r WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM supply.vendor_master m WHERE m.vendor_code = r.vendor_ref)) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'supply.vendor_refs'::regclass AND contype = 'f') = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 2,000 queue items are recorded as having been tried once when they have never been tried
defects.why: The attempt count was filled in by a query that groups a left join and counts star, and count star over a left join counts the row the join invented for an item with no attempts, so every untried item came back as one. A left join guarantees at least one output row per left side row. When there is no match the extra columns are null, and count star does not care about null, because it counts rows. Counting the joined column instead, count of the attempt id, would have returned zero, because that is what counting a column does: it ignores nulls. The two forms are one word apart and they differ only on exactly the rows this table cares about. The consequence is that the retry job, which looks for items with no attempts, finds none of the two thousand that have never been tried, and they sit in the queue permanently, counted as in progress, retried by nobody. Measured: 10,000 queue items of which 2,000 record 1 attempt and have no attempt rows at all. Counting the attempt id rather than star fixes the backfill and the two thousand can be recomputed. Every payload reference is unique, every attempt row is real, and the 8,000 items that were tried carry the right count.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.queue_items q WHERE q.attempt_count = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ops.queue_attempts a WHERE a.item_id = q.item_id)

defects.title: 11,000 card numbers are masked on the table and in the clear in the audit
defects.why: Two BEFORE INSERT triggers run on the card entries, one writing the row to the audit table and one masking the card number, and they fire in name order, so the audit is written from the unmasked value every time. PostgreSQL fires triggers of the same type in alphabetical order by trigger name. That is the whole rule, it is documented, and it is a property of the names rather than of the order the triggers were created in or written down in. The masking trigger was added second and given a name that happens to sort second, and the masking works perfectly on the table everybody looks at. The audit table is not looked at, because it is an audit table, so nothing has ever compared the two. The result is that the database holds every card number in the clear in a table nobody remembers exists, under a schema that is granted more widely than the card table is, and every compliance review that checks the card column passes. Measured: 11,000 card entries, all masked on the table, and 11,000 audit rows holding the unmasked number. Renaming the masking trigger so it sorts first, or better, doing the masking in the audit function itself so the order stops mattering, closes it. Every order reference is correct, the audit is complete and no entry is missing.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM payments.card_entry_audit WHERE card_digits NOT LIKE '****%'

defects.title: 7,500 product names were cut to twelve characters on the way in
defects.why: The short name column is a varchar of twelve and the load writes the long name into it with an explicit cast, and an explicit cast to a length limited type truncates rather than raising an error. This is the one place PostgreSQL will quietly lose characters. An ordinary assignment of an over long string to a varchar column fails with a clear message about the value being too long. Writing the same string with a cast to the same type does not: the cast is read as an instruction to make it fit, so it cuts. The load was written with the cast precisely because the unqualified version kept failing, and the failures stopped, which was taken as the fix. The short name is what the shelf label and the till display print, so three quarters of the products are labelled with a fragment that stops mid word, and two products whose names share an opening are labelled identically. Measured: 10,000 products of which 7,500 hold a short name that differs from the long name it was cut from. Generating the short name deliberately, with a rule about where to cut and what to do about collisions, is the fix; the cast only hides the question. Every product reference is correct and every long name is intact, which is why the short name can be regenerated.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.short_names WHERE name_short <> long_name

defects.title: 13,000 holdbacks are behind a policy the account that reads them ignores
defects.why: Row level security is enabled on the holdback table and there is a policy restricting each depot to its own rows, but it is not forced, and an unforced policy does not apply to the table's owner. Row security in PostgreSQL has two switches. ENABLE turns the policies on for everybody except the owner. FORCE turns them on for the owner as well. Only the first was set, which is the default and the one every example uses, so the policy is real and correct and simply does not run for the account that owns the table. That account is the one the application connects as, because the application also creates and alters these tables. So the protection works exactly when it is tested, by a depot login, and does not work at all in production traffic. Nothing warns: the policy exists, the table shows row security enabled, and a review that lists policies sees a correct one. Measured: 13,000 holdbacks on a table with row security enabled, 1 select policy, and force row security off. FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on the table, plus a separate owner for DDL, makes the policy mean what it says. Every holdback names a real depot, every reason code is valid, and every amount is right.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM ops.holdback_rows) * (CASE WHEN (SELECT relrowsecurity AND NOT relforcerowsecurity FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'ops.holdback_rows'::regclass) AND (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_policy WHERE polrelid = 'ops.holdback_rows'::regclass) > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

defects.title: 9,000 intake tokens sit behind an insert grant that cannot be used
defects.why: The goods in writer has INSERT on the intake tokens and no USAGE on the sequence the token id defaults from, so every insert it attempts fails on a permission error about the sequence, not about the table. A column defaulting to nextval evaluates that default as the inserting role, so the role needs USAGE on the sequence as well as INSERT on the table. An identity column would not need it, because an identity sequence is owned by the column and inherits its permissions, and that difference is the whole trap: the same table written two ways needs two different grants. This table was written the older way, with an explicit sequence and a default, and the grant script was written against a table that used identity. The error message names the sequence, which is an object the person reading it has usually never heard of, so the ticket is filed as a database fault rather than a missing grant and sits. Measured: 9,000 intake tokens on a table where goods_in_writer holds INSERT and does not hold USAGE on the sequence the default calls. Granting USAGE on the sequence, or converting the column to an identity column, fixes it. Every token is unique, every issue time is right, and nothing already loaded is affected.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.intake_tokens, (SELECT has_table_privilege('goods_in_writer','ops.intake_tokens','INSERT') AS a, has_sequence_privilege('goods_in_writer','ops.intake_token_seq','USAGE') AS b) p WHERE p.a AND NOT p.b

defects.title: 1,307,067 pence fall out of the monthly totals, one last day at a time
defects.why: The monthly total sums everything between the first of the month and the last day of it, and the last day of it as a timestamp means midnight at the start of that day, so all but the first instant of the last day of every month is left out. BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends, which is why it reads as safe, and the upper end here is a point in time rather than a day. Comparing a timestamp against a date promotes the date to midnight. So the range closes twenty four hours early, every month, and it is the last day that goes, which is the busiest day of the month in a business that settles monthly. The totals are close enough to look right and they are never reconciled against the lines, because reconciling them is what the totals table is for. Measured: 12 monthly totals of which 11 are short, by 1,307,067 pence in all. A half open range, greater than or equal to the first of the month and strictly less than the first of the next, is the form that has no end to get wrong. Every line is correct and carries the right instant and amount, so every total can be recomputed exactly.

detect.sql: SELECT coalesce(sum(c.correct - t.total_p), 0) FROM analytics.month_totals t JOIN LATERAL (SELECT coalesce(sum(l.amount_p), 0) AS correct FROM analytics.month_lines l WHERE l.line_at >= t.month_start AND l.line_at < (t.month_start + INTERVAL '1 month')) c ON true WHERE c.correct <> t.total_p

defects.title: 6,000 contact addresses are three thousand people counted twice
defects.why: The unique index on the contact address is on the text exactly as stored, the portal re registration sent every address back in upper case, and an upper case address is a different string, so three thousand buyers are now on file twice. The domain part of an email address is defined to be case insensitive and the local part is, in practice, treated that way by every mail server anybody uses. The database has no such opinion: it compares text, the strings differ, and the unique index is satisfied. So the constraint that was put there to stop exactly this did not fire, and it did not fire correctly, by its own rules. Every mailing now goes twice to the same person, which reads as carelessness and gets the sender marked as spam. Worse, the two rows carry different added dates and either can be picked as the current contact, so a change of address applied to one leaves the other in place. Measured: 11,000 contact addresses of which 6,000 have a counterpart differing only in case, under 1 unique index on the exact text. A unique index on lower of the address, or citext, enforces what was meant. Every address belongs to a real supplier, every address is well formed, and the 5,000 with no counterpart are correct as they stand.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM supply.contact_addresses a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM supply.contact_addresses b WHERE b.address_id <> a.address_id AND lower(b.email_text) = lower(a.email_text))

defects.title: 600 route nodes are on a loop the route walker cannot leave
defects.why: Each route is a chain of nodes where every node points at the next one, and one route in ten was joined up into a circuit, so the last node points back at the first and the chain has no end. A self referencing foreign key guarantees that whatever a node points at exists. It says nothing at all about whether following the pointers ever stops, and there is no constraint in PostgreSQL that can say so. The loops are not a mistake in the data: the depots genuinely asked for circuits rather than out and back runs, and a circuit is a loop. The mistake is that everything reading the table assumes a chain. The route walker follows next node until it finds a null, so on a circuit it runs until the recursion limit, and the driver app that calls it times out rather than failing, which reads as a network problem. The route printout for a circuit is the first ten stops repeated. Measured: 6,000 route nodes of which 600 lie on a cycle that returns to where it started within 12 steps. A recursive walk with a CYCLE clause, or an explicit circuit flag on the route so the reader knows to stop after one pass, both work. Every node names a real depot, every pointer names a node that exists, and the 5,400 nodes on ordinary chains walk correctly.

detect.sql: WITH RECURSIVE w(start_id, node_id, depth) AS (SELECT node_id, next_node_id, 1 FROM ops.route_nodes WHERE next_node_id IS NOT NULL UNION ALL SELECT w.start_id, r.next_node_id, w.depth + 1 FROM w JOIN ops.route_nodes r ON r.node_id = w.node_id WHERE w.depth < 12 AND r.next_node_id IS NOT NULL) SELECT count(DISTINCT start_id) FROM w WHERE node_id = start_id

defects.title: 9,000 rollups all claim to have been computed in the same second
defects.why: Two thirds of the rollups carry an identical timestamp, to the second, because the backfill that created them stamped every row with the clock at the moment it ran rather than the time the rollup covers. A default of now inside a single transaction returns the transaction's start time, the same value for every row, which is usually what you want and is exactly wrong for a column that is supposed to say when each thing happened. So nine thousand rollups spanning months of history all say they were computed at seventeen minutes past two on the fourth of May. The column is what the incremental job reads to decide where to resume, so it resumes from the backfill date and recomputes everything after it, every night. It is also what the staleness alert reads, so the alert has fired continuously since the backfill and has been muted. Measured: 14,000 rollups of which 9,000 share one single timestamp value. Deriving the stamp from the period each rollup covers, and keeping the run time in a separate column if it is wanted, separates the two facts that were collapsed into one. Every metric code is real and every value is the correct rollup of its period.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM analytics.rollup_rows WHERE rolled_at = (SELECT rolled_at FROM analytics.rollup_rows GROUP BY rolled_at ORDER BY count(*) DESC, 1 LIMIT 1)

defects.title: 3,000 delivery flags are in upper case because the normaliser is turned off
defects.why: The trigger that lowercases and trims every delivery flag is disabled, so three thousand flags are stored in upper case and every comparison against the lowercase form misses them. A disabled trigger is still there. It is listed, it has a function, its definition is correct, and it does nothing. DISABLE TRIGGER was run during a bulk load, because the per row trigger made the load take hours, and that is a reasonable thing to do; re-enabling it afterwards is the step that was missed, and nothing marks the difference except a single character in the system catalogue. The flag is what the hold report filters on, and it filters on the lowercase value, so a fifth of the held deliveries are not on the hold report and are released. The rows are not invalid by any constraint, because the rule was only ever expressed as a trigger. Measured: 15,000 delivery flags of which 3,000 differ from their own lowercase form, behind 1 trigger whose enabled state is D. Enabling the trigger and normalising the three thousand rows that came in while it was off restores both. Every delivery reference is unique and real, and the 12,000 flags written before the load are correct.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM supply.delivery_flags WHERE flag_text <> lower(flag_text)) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgrelid = 'supply.delivery_flags'::regclass AND NOT tgisinternal AND tgenabled = 'D')

defects.title: 7,000 refund lines are totalled by a function any caller can redirect
defects.why: The refund total function runs as its owner and has no search path fixed on it, and its body names the refund table without a schema, so the table it reads is whichever one the caller's search path finds first. SECURITY DEFINER means the function runs with the owner's privileges rather than the caller's, which is the entire point: a reporting role can get a refund total without being able to read the refund table. Resolving an unqualified name, though, happens at run time against the caller's search path. A caller who can create a table in any schema on that path can put their own refund table in front of the real one, and the function will read it, as the owner, with the owner's privileges. That turns a read only report into a way of running the owner's code against attacker chosen data. Nothing flags it: the function is correct, the grant is narrow, and the danger is in a setting that is absent rather than wrong. Measured: 7,000 refund lines behind 1 security definer function with no search path configuration set on it. SET search_path = pg_catalog, payments on the function, and schema qualifying the table in the body, closes it. Every refund names a real order, every amount is right, and the function returns the correct total when the path is honest.

detect.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM payments.refund_entries) * (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_proc WHERE oid = 'payments.fn_refund_total(text)'::regprocedure AND prosecdef AND proconfig IS NULL)

defects.title: 120 pick zones are being given their newest job instead of their oldest
defects.why: The next pick function orders the queue by the pick reference and takes the first one, and the pick reference counts downwards, so every zone is handed its most recent job and its oldest job is never handed out at all. The function is deterministic and it is wrong, which is the harder kind to find. An ORDER BY that returns the same answer every time reads as correct, and the ordering column looks like a sequence number because it is one, so the reference ordering was taken for the queue ordering without checking which way it runs. The references were generated downwards so that the newest job would sort first in the picker's own list, which was a deliberate choice made somewhere else and never written down. The effect is a queue that is serviced newest first, so the oldest job in each zone is never picked while any newer one exists, and the twelve thousand item backlog has a floor that never moves. Measured: 120 pick zones, in all 120 of which the assigned pick is not the oldest queued one. Ordering by the queued time, which is the column that means what the function needs, fixes it in one word. Every pick names a real zone, every queue time is right, and the backlog is complete.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM ops.pick_assignments a WHERE a.chosen_ref <> (SELECT q.pick_ref FROM ops.pick_queue q WHERE q.zone_code = a.zone_code ORDER BY q.queued_at LIMIT 1)

defects.title: 2,500 stock lines hold minus one and it is not a quantity
defects.why: A quarter of the stock lines hold minus one in the on hand column, which does not mean minus one unit, it means the line was not counted, and nothing in the schema says so. The column is a plain integer with no check constraint, no comment and no companion flag. The convention exists entirely in the heads of the people who wrote the stocktake import, where minus one was chosen because null was not allowed by a column that had been made mandatory years earlier for a different reason. Every arithmetic use of the column is therefore wrong by the count of uncounted lines: a sum of stock on hand is two and a half thousand units light, an average is dragged down, and a check for negative stock reports two and a half thousand impossible rows that are then ignored as known noise, which is how a genuine negative would also be ignored. The value is out of range for what the column claims to hold, and the database has no way to know that. Measured: 10,000 stock lines of which 2,500 hold minus one in a column that counts units. A nullable column, or a separate counted flag, states the fact the magic number is standing in for. Every product reference is real, every count date is right, and the 7,500 lines that were counted hold the correct quantity.

detect.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM catalog.stock_levels WHERE on_hand = -1
